title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Fathers: Theodoret and Cyril — the universal cause needs faith’s application
english: Third in place let Theodoret come forth, writing on those words of the Apostle (Romans 3:25): Whom God set forth to be a propitiatory through faith in his blood, and so on. The Lord Christ, he says, is the propitiatory, and by his blood procured our salvation, requiring from us faith alone.

From which words we gather that Christ, with his death and all his merits, has been so constituted the universal cause of our redemption, reconciliation, and salvation, that before the fruit of this redemption and salvation procured through Christ is participated by anyone, this universal cause must be applied specially to individuals. Now that this fruitful application may happen, as Theodoret well warned, God requires faith from us. Faith being absent, Christ’s death considered in itself confers on no one the state of actual reconciliation, grace, and salvation.

Cyril also stands in the same sentence. Explaining those words of our Savior (John 3:36) — He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life — he gathers thus (book 2, chapter 74): Therefore Christ vivifies believers in himself, because, since according to nature he is life, he dwells in all the faithful through faith.

However much, then, Christ is life itself, yet he does not vivify anyone except believers — which Cyril confirmed by an excellent and most valid reason, namely because he does not dwell in human beings except in believers. As if he had said: the fountain of life does not actually vivify except those joined to himself, and the joined are held to be the faithful alone. Badly, therefore, do they argue who from either the death or the very life of Christ gather that either all or any human beings are constituted in the state of life, grace, and salvation before they are united to Christ by this bond of faith.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Fathers: Bede — each is reconciled when he believes the slain
english: Last I will bring forward the most express testimony of the Venerable Bede, found in his Commentaries on 2 Corinthians 5: Through faith the world is reconciled to God, when it believes in Christ who was sent by God.

The Apostle had said that God in Christ reconciled the world to himself — that is, that Christ by God’s ordination paid that ransom to the Father, whereby it was effected that God does not exact from us satisfaction for our sins before he returns into grace with us, but, content with this alone, is ready to receive anyone into grace.

If you still ask whether, this price having been paid, by the very fact of the payment all human beings are at once reconciled, Bede answers: By no means that; but each one is then reconciled to God when he himself believes in Christ who was sent by God.

Those words of the same author on Luke 15 have the same mind: Then for each of us Christ is slain, when he believes him slain. He was slain from the origin of the world in the Divine acceptation; slain also, when the fullness of time came, on the cross itself; yet for you and for me — that is, for each singular human being — then slain when he believes in the slain. Which is just as if he had said: the benefit of the slain or dead Christ then pertains to us when we begin to believe in him.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Fathers close: Actual reconciliation needs the receiver’s consent
english: From orthodox antiquity, therefore, they have departed who state that by the very passion of Christ all human beings are placed in the state of grace; nor less those who teach that the predestinate themselves, in this death of Christ, obtained the remission of their sins, or justification and reconciliation with God, from eternity — since this justification or actual reconciliation (as Bernard truly and skillfully) cannot belong to the receiver without consent any more than without the grace of the giver.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Obj. 1: If the death is a sufficient ransom, all must already be restored
english: Either Christ's death was a sufficient ransom to wipe away the sins of the human race and put every human being back into grace and reconciliation, or it was insufficient. Call it insufficient, and we diminish divine grace and trample Christ's merit. Grant that it was sufficient, and then—once that sufficient cause has been put into act—nothing else is required to bring about the effect. From Christ's very act of offering himself to God, therefore, there would follow at once the universal liberation of all people from the guilt of their sins, and a universal reconciliation: that is, the reception of everyone into divine grace.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Solut. 1: A universal cause still needs each one’s application by faith
english: We acknowledge the fullest sufficiency of the ransom—indeed its infinite superabundance. Our answer, however, is this: Christ's merit, considered in itself alone, does operate sufficiently as a universal cause of human salvation; yet a universal cause does not produce effects in particular persons before it is applied to each one. By Christ's death itself, therefore, a most sufficient universal cause was instituted, from which (as Aquinas says) any sins of any persons could be expiated. But before that cause puts forth its expiatory power for the liberation and reconciliation of individuals, it must be applied to each by faith. The Apostle himself teaches this clearly in Romans 3:25: "Whom God set forth as a propitiatory through faith in his blood," and so on.

So although Christ's death is a sufficient satisfaction for the sins of the human race, it cleanses us by way of a remedy: it must first be applied to each person before it can produce the effect of reconciliation and healing. And that application is made only through faith.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Obj. 2: No injury when the gospel binds the fruit to faith
english: Suppose that after accepting a sufficient ransom God still does not receive everyone into grace. Then, the objection says, he would wrong Christ, because he would not grant to human beings what Christ merited for them by dying. He would also deal unjustly with human beings, because he would still hold them bound by sins as by debts, even though Christ wiped out all those debts with his blood.

Neither side is injured. Not Christ: he himself did not will that the satisfaction he offered for the sins of the human race should avail for the actual reconciliation of particular persons unless their faith intervened, as we proved above. It would therefore be an insult to Christ if anyone were admitted into the actual fellowship and share of this grace while still not believing in Jesus Christ, the Author of salvation and our Redeemer. Nor are human beings injured when they are not received at once into God's favor simply on account of Christ's dying act, for that was neither owed to them nor promised. We cannot claim from Christ's death any benefit against or beyond the order and covenant established by God and by Christ and opened to us in the Gospel.

That order stands fixed, and the Gospel expressly sets this condition: the grace of reconciliation and the gift of eternal life overflow to sinners from Christ's death if they believe; if they do not, they remain bound by sins and perish in their unbelief. "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, and the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36).

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Obj. 3 Solut close: Regeneration and election govern actual efficacy
english: This argument smuggles in a false assumption. Its major premise treats it as conceded that the efficacy or virtue of a cause is always to be rated greater or lesser according as it reaches more or fewer subjects. That is quite false. A cause's efficacy—or excellence—must be judged from the nature and excellence of its effects, not from how many subjects it touches. Restoring sight to one blind person shows greater virtue than gouging out the eyes of a thousand; healing one mutilated and sick person shows more than mutilating or poisoning a thousand who are healthy and whole; in a word, recalling one human being to life shows more than handing a thousand over to slaughter. By the same measure, Christ's power in saving even one human being by his death is greater and more efficacious than Adam's power in destroying the whole human race by his sin.

To the minor premise one may also reply that Adam's very act of sinning binds no one with the guilt of death, and makes no one liable to divine wrath, except insofar as that person is propagated from sinful Adam by natural generation. In exactly the same way, Christ's dying act snatches no one out of the state of death, and frees no one from divine wrath, except insofar as that person is derived from Christ by supernatural regeneration. On both sides, then, the condition is equal if the comparison is just. All who are generated from Adam by nature lost God's grace and life; all who are regenerated from Christ by grace recover God's grace and life. No one is subjected to death or divine wrath by Adam's fault unless he has drawn natural origin from Adam; no one is exempted from death or divine wrath by Christ's merit unless he has drawn heavenly birth from Christ.

Aquinas explains this prudently and learnedly in Against the Gentiles, book 4, chapter 55: the effect of the first parent's sin reaches each person through the origin of the flesh; so the effect of Christ's death reaches each through spiritual regeneration. Anyone who wants Christ's merit to work in himself must be regenerated by Christ's Spirit. If someone still presses the point—propagation from Adam, from which wrath and the guilt of death follow, is common to all; why then is regeneration through Christ, on which our reconciliation and salvation depend, not made common to all in the same way?—I have nothing else to answer than this: God himself did not will that what flows to human beings by way of grace should be common to all in the same way as what comes by way of nature. He willed his grace to distinguish one person from another, and therefore did not will to make it equally common to all. Augustine noted this in On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 5; read him at leisure. Let no one murmur against God, then, because by the working of special grace he regenerates some and grafts them into Christ through faith; let no one ask why he frees that one rather than this. To stop every mouth it is enough that God himself answers (Matthew 20:15), "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine?" and so on; and that the Apostle says (Romans 9:18), "He has mercy on whom he wills." See also Augustine, On the Good of Perseverance, chapter 8. So although, as to sufficiency, Christ's death stands equally related to all, as to efficacy it depends on divine election: the effects of Christ's merits are mercifully applied to some, while others, hindered by their own unbelief, do not receive that application.

So far we have answered those who contend for a universal and likewise actual reconciliation of all human beings, each and every one. Now let us hear what can be urged by those who hold that the elect themselves, by the efficacy of Christ's death, were justified from eternity and reconciled to God.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Elect Obj. 1: Immutability seems to force eternal actual reconciliation
english: Objection 1. Those who say that toward the elect themselves, before their faith and repentance, God is only placable and reconciliable—not actually reconciled and placated—seem to put acts and potencies in God, and to admit that God can be what he is not. But God is pure act and altogether immutable. It is therefore impossible that he should now be what he was not before. So if he is reconciled to Peter or Paul after they are known to repent and believe, he was already reconciled to them from eternity. Otherwise some variation would seem to be given in God, who is purest act and altogether immutable. Yet no sane person will deny that such variation is utterly alien to the divine nature, which is free of mutability on every side—especially since that conclusion agrees not only with the dictates of right reason and with the sounder philosophy (which teaches that the same, as the same, always does the same: that is, what remains the same way always produces the same effect), but can also be confirmed and settled by not a few, and those the clearest, places of sacred Scripture: by Malachi’s prophecy (Malachi 3:6), “For I the Lord do not change” (Junius: “I Jehovah do not change”); likewise by Numbers (Numbers 23:19), “God is not as a human that he should lie, nor as a son of man that he should change.” A plainly similar place gives support from the Epistle of James (James 1:17): “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.” So far is any change from belonging in God that in him there is not even the least shadow of turning. But if one may say of God that he is now placable, now placated, now only reconciliable, now reconciled, one may fairly and not without cause doubt whether God always remains like himself and always holds himself in exactly the same way. Placability seems to suggest only a prior disposition and an inclination toward a future placating; reconciliability likewise suggests a readiness and propensity in God toward reconciliation—which at last, when human beings believe, is drawn out from potency into act.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Elect Obj. 1 Solut: Relative names change with the creature, not God
english: That God is reconciliable to this or that elect person before that person’s faith and repentance, and is actually reconciled to the same person after faith and repentance, no more proves a change in God from act to potency than this does: that a human being is not justified at all until he believes, and is actually justified by God after he believes. Nor does it prove a temporal change of the divine essence or will from potency to act that someone’s sins are remissible and, after repentance, are actually remitted by God. No one will rightly say that because Paul is now justified as a believer in Christ—though he was not justified at all while he blasphemed against Christ—God himself undergoes some change. So neither does it follow from saying that a person is now reconciliable to God and now actually reconciled. To be justified and to be reconciled to God are either plainly the same, or at least inseparably joined.

To clear the scruple more openly, this must be known: although nothing absolute can newly arrive to God without a change in him, yet countless relative names can newly be predicated of God—at one time, and not at another—according to differences of time, while the divine essence and will remain without any shadow of change. What is affirmed of God in a mutable and temporal way is not affirmed because some change has come upon God, but because a change has come upon the creature. For example, one could truly say “Adam is creatable by God” when one could not yet truly say “Adam is created by God.” By the same measure, one could say before Adam’s actual repentance, “Adam is justificable by God,” or “Adam is reconciliable to God”; but one could not say, “Adam is actually justified and reconciled to God.” Even so we do not put acts and potencies in God, or any mutability at all. These things are said of God in different ways not by a change of God in himself, but by a change of the creature that comes from him.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Elect Obj. 2: Eternal love is not yet actual reconciliation
english: Objection 2. God is actually reconciled to whoever he actually loves. He loves every elect person from eternity. So, the objection runs, he has been actually reconciled to them from eternity—and they have been actually reconciled and justified from eternity.

Solution. Follow the distinction in Aquinas. God loves in two senses: by the purpose to communicate his goodness, and by the very act of communicating it (Sentences, book 3, distinction 19). The love that tracks the eternal purpose—theologians call it the love of eternal benevolence—does not already count the beloved as actually justified or actually reconciled. It only ranks that person among those who will infallibly be justified and reconciled. Words for acts that stay inside God, and words for acts that pass from God to us, therefore do different work. Dilection, Election, and Predestination name eternal, inward acts of God; people are called Beloved, Elect, and Predestined from the hidden good pleasure of the divine will conceived and kept in God himself. Calling, Justification, Reconciliation, and Glorification name outward acts that terminate on a creature who already exists and are as it were received into that creature. No one is properly Called, Justified, Reconciled, or Glorified from the hidden eternal purpose alone, but from the finished execution of that purpose and the effect it produces in human beings. We gladly grant that God has an eternal will to justify every elect person and reconcile each to himself. We still refuse to say they were justified or reconciled from eternity. In the same way we grant God an eternal will to create the world, yet deny that the world was created from eternity. What Zanchi said of the actual remission of sins fits the elect's actual reconciliation: it is most certain in the divine destination from eternity, yet it is not actually given on God's side, nor actually received on the human side, before the person repents and believes (Thomson, Diatribe, p. 96).

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Elect Obj. 3 Solut close: Eternal love yields certain means, not eternal justification
english: Objection 3. Why do the means work in some people and not in others? Not, they say, from any difference of free choice, but because God is already reconciled to all the elect in Christ before the world's foundations were laid, and is not reconciled to the rest. So we must not deny that every elect person is actually reconciled to God before conversion and faith—since the very dispensing of means powerful enough to produce faith and repentance in them sprang from that eternal, prior reconciliation.

Solution. We gladly admit that the infallible efficacy of means ordained to salvation does not hang on the human will. It hangs on a certain eternal and special love of God for his elect. But so far as that love regards people who are still unbelieving and unconverted, it is nothing but a free purpose to supply them with what will later convert them, justify them, reconcile them to God, and lead them without fail to eternal life. Inferring from that eternal love an eternal justification, an eternal reconciliation of the elect, and an eternal glorification of them is therefore just as bad a leap. What follows is only their certain and infallible justification, reconciliation, and glorification. That certainty—the infallible efficacy of means that tend toward salvation—is born from the love of God just named, not from free choice's power. If someone wants to label this eternal love (the ground of the certainty that conversion and reconciliation will be produced in time) "actual reconciliation," because God himself "calls the things that are not as though they were" (Romans 4:17), I will not stop him—provided he also admits he is using the name of a finished deed for the purpose of a deed still to be done. For God's predestination had already fixed what would come in its own time, as Augustine puts it (City of God, book 12, chapter 16).

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Scripture elect Resp: Election wills justification in time, not coeternal with election
english: Response. Electing someone to life before the world’s foundation is one thing; actually justifying and reconciling that same person to himself before the world’s foundation is another. Election names in God an eternal will to justify, reconcile, and save the elect person—but to justify, reconcile, and save him in his own time through faith. So the elect person’s actual justification, reconciliation, and sanctification flow from eternal election; they are not coeternal with it. That is easy to gather from Paul’s whole argument in Ephesians 1. He affirms that we were elect before the world’s foundations were laid (Ephesians 1:4), yet he does not say we were therefore sanctified before those foundations were laid. He says we were elect so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love. Nor does he teach, by the power of eternal election, that we were justified or reconciled from eternity. He teaches that this happened in the dispensation of the fullness of time, after we applied faith to the gospel that had been opened (Ephesians 1:9–10 and following).

If we trust Paul, then—however eternal human election and predestination are from God’s eternal love—their justification and reconciliation are not to be called a mere manifestation or unveiling when they believe in Christ. title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Scripture elect: 2 Tim 1 grace given before ages is destination, not collation
english: 2 Timothy 1:9–10. The Apostle says grace was given to the elect in Christ Jesus before the ages of the world, and that the same grace was made manifest through the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ. So God seems plainly reconciled already, before the ages, to those to whom he gave grace in Christ before the ages.

Response. Because the divine purpose is firm and unmovable, that grace is said to have been given to the elect before the ages which was destined for them before the ages. In this place, then, eternal giving is eternal preparation of the grace that will be given to the elect without fail in their own time. So Augustine: the Apostle said grace was given when those who would receive it did not yet exist, because in God’s disposition and predestination what was to come in its time was already fixed (On Christian Doctrine, book 3, chapter 34). So Junius on these very words: grace was given from eternity, the grace to which we were predestined from eternity. Calvin expounds it no other way. “This donation of grace of which the Apostle speaks,” he says, “is nothing but the predestination by which we are adopted as God’s children.” A little later: “He gave”—what, with no merit prompting him, he assigned to those not yet born and kept stored in his treasuries until the thing itself would show that he decrees nothing in vain. From this we may rightly gather that the grace of justification, reconciliation, and salvation was by an eternal act assigned to all the elect, and as it were stored and reserved for them in the treasury of divine love. That it was by an act conferred on them before their faith and conversion does not follow. The elect’s justification and reconciliation themselves are not said to be opened and manifested when they believe in Christ; they are then given and constituted. What is said to be revealed and manifested then is God’s eternal good pleasure—his purpose to save the elect—which becomes known to us after, gifted with the Spirit and with faith, we have obtained justification and reconciliation with God.

title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Scripture elect: Rom 5, Eph 2, Col 1 seem to reconcile enemies before faith

So is Ephesians 2:4–5: "because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ." God, they say, is already reconciled to his own even while they still stand unbelieving and hostile to him. title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Scripture elect close: Those loci confirm faith-timed reconciliation; Cap. 5 thesis ends
english: Response. If by reconciliation nothing is meant but an inclination and readiness of the divine will to grant remission and to make peace with all who will embrace the Redeemer by faith, then we confess that God stands reconciled to the whole human race by the force of Christ’s death, even while we remain his enemies. But that (as said above) is a step toward our actual and personal reconciliation, not yet the actual reconciliation of particular persons. Further, if by reconciliation we mean God’s eternal love—by which he decreed to call, justify, reconcile to himself, and save certain people in time—I do not deny that God in that sense can be called benevolent to all the elect, even while they are still sunk in impiety and unbelief. But that benevolence, which precedes faith breathed into the elect’s hearts, holds only the purpose of making peace with them. It does not give them the state of peace already obtained, or of actual reconciliation.

With that said, I answer that in all those places the talk is either about that step toward personal reconciliation, or about believing elect people already set in the state of actual reconciliation only with faith intervening. So the places confirm our view rather than the contrary. Romans 5:10 (“when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of the Son,” and so on) means nothing else than that people are moved from enmity into actual reconciliation with God through Christ’s death as soon as they have believed in Christ. That is plain because in verse 1 of the same chapter the Apostle restricts this peace—or reconciliation—with God to those alone who are justified through faith (Romans 5:1); and in verse 11 he speaks of the same actual reconciliation as newly constituted: “Now,” he says, “we have obtained reconciliation”—that is, now after we have believed in Christ (Romans 5:11).

As for Ephesians 2:4–5, it is most true that God made us, who were dead, alive with Christ. But just as he did not make us alive in act until faith was first inspired, so neither did he reconcile us. To be reconciled to God is to be freed from death’s guilt, placed in spiritual life, and gifted with a hereditary right to eternal life. Those goods do not belong to the elect merely because they are elect. They belong at last when they have been effectually called and turned to God. The Apostle himself teaches this in verse 8: “By grace you have been saved through faith—and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).

The last place, drawn from Colossians 1:21–22, expressly confirms our sentence: neither God’s eternal predestinating act itself, nor Christ’s merit itself in dying for his elect, makes people at once justified and reconciled to God. What else do the words “once alienated, he has now indeed reconciled” mean, except that we obtain remission of sins and actual reconciliation with God through Christ’s blood only when, inserted into Christ by faith, we are admitted into actual share and possession of his merits and righteousness? There is no need to pile up more for explaining this thesis. From what has been said it is plain enough that those stretch the universal force of Christ’s death beyond its just limits who, by the bare deed of Christ dying, judge every mortal indiscriminately restored into the state of grace—and no less those who defend that all the predestined, for Christ’s merit, were justified from eternity and actually reconciled to God even before faith was applied to the gospel.

title: Cap. 6 Thesis ultima open: Three theses reviewed; a fourth checks over-extension of universal efficacy
english: Chapter 6. The last thesis is set out and confirmed.

We have already laid before you the universal force and efficacy of Christ’s death in three theses. In the first we showed that God appointed this death of Christ and set it before the human race as a universal remedy applicable to every human being. In the second we explained in what sense Christ is said to have died for all—or in what sense his death is owned as a universal cause of salvation established for the good of the whole human race. Not, as some want, merely by bare sufficiency or intrinsic worth, in which respect Christ’s death, or the blood of the Son of God, is a price more than enough to redeem every human and every angel. Rather, by the gospel covenant established and confirmed in this death and blood of Christ. By the terms of that covenant every human being gained a right, under the condition of faith, to claim remission of sins and eternal life.

To those two theses we added a third. Even with this universal force of Christ’s death in place, and with this universal gospel covenant looking to any person whatsoever, this or that particular person does have, by the sole benefit of that death, God bound to make peace with him and to give him life if he believes. He does not yet have actual justification or reconciliation—or the actual state of grace and salvation—before he believes. There remains a fourth and final thesis. Its chief work is to clear a scruple from the minds of those who stretch this universal efficacy of Christ’s death, which we defend, farther than the truth of the matter will bear.

title: Cap. 6 Thesis IV: Nature-as-grace adversaries and the thesis that God may give or deny application-media
english: Some people argue at once from the claim that Christ’s death, in the sense already given, was spent for the human race—for every human being—that divine justice and goodness now require God to administer to all for whom he thus gave Christ to death the means needed to generate faith. Yet it is clearer than noon that ethnics and pagans, on whom the light of the gospel never shone, have not been given means that immediately suffice to produce faith in them. So the same people take refuge here: they say even such people are always given sufficient means by which, mediately and as if by degrees, they could have been led to faith in Christ if they had used those means well.

Ask what those means of grace are that could have stood ready for all and led all sufficiently to faith in Christ, and they thrust Nature upon us wrapped in the name of Grace. They say remnants of spiritual life remain in every human—some knowledge of God in the intellect, some desire for the known good in the affection—and that if a person uses those natural gifts rightly, God will heap greater grace on him and gift him with saving faith. Aquinas seems to lean that way in De veritate, question 14, article 11, reply to the first objection, where he writes: if someone reared in the woods followed the lead of natural reason in appetite for good and flight from evil, it must be held with full certainty that God would either reveal by inward inspiration what is necessary for belief, or send some preacher of the faith to him.

So their view comes to this: by the efficacy and merit of Christ’s death God is already bound as by statute to supply everyone with sufficient means to be led to Christ if they will, so that nothing is wanting on God’s side to keep anyone from faith and a fruitful share in Christ’s death. To untie that knot we have taken up this thesis to explain and confirm it.

Thesis IV. Once Christ’s death is posited as applicable to all humans under the condition of faith, it stands with divine goodness and justice to supply or deny the means of application—to nations or to particular persons—according to the good pleasure of his will, not according to the disparity of human wills.

title: Cap. 6 preliminaries: No fixed law that good use of nature buys supernatural light
english: A few preliminaries, then I turn to confirming the thesis. First, notice that those on the opposite side think God is bound by a fixed decree and statute to give the talent of grace to those who use the talent of nature well. Second, they presume that any pagan, even one sitting in the shadow of death, can by free choice use that natural talent well or badly. Third, from that difference between those who use natural gifts rightly and those who do not, they try to explain why God deigns to light some with the gospel and the knowledge of Christ and does not deign to light others. Use the gifts rightly, they say, and the person is gradually to be led into saving knowledge of Christ; abuse them wickedly, and he is justly stripped of that knowledge.

Augustine seems to stand on the opposite side in De Natura et Gratia, chapters 8 and 9. There he grants that for certain infants the means of salvation could not be applied; and he also owns that adults who died in a region where they could not hear Christ’s name could in no way become just by nature and free choice. We likewise affirm that no decree, law, or promise of God exists by which anyone could safely conclude: this person used natural light rightly, or less badly; therefore God will illuminate him with supernatural grace.

Arminius does say God pledged this by Christ’s word, “To the one who has, it will be given” (Matthew 13:12). But the Reverend of Salisbury speaks more truly and more learnedly: Arminius hints a fallacy here, and commits it—leaping from the one who has in the state of nature to a gift in the state of grace, and making the light of faith the wage of unbelievers’ diligence. For what is promised, and in what kind the use falls, is increase in that same kind. Alvarez, a Roman Catholic writer, votes with us here: no law was ever enacted that helps of grace must be given to those who do all that is in them from nature’s faculty; nor did the Lord Christ by his death merit, or will to merit, such a law. The Apostle Paul teaches that the dispensation of supernatural grace runs not according to the use and works of the human will, but according to the purpose and counsel of the divine will: “He works all things according to the purpose and counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11).

title: Cap. 6 Secundo: Corrupted nature cannot haul grace to itself
english: Second, though we grant that in ethnic people some sparks of natural light remain, and a certain imperfect desire for moral good, still—as the same Salisbury we praised earlier puts it best—those deformed ruins have no inhabitant but the Devil, and of those remnants in the midst of corruption there can be only a corrupted use. Let the adversaries show us even one person since the world began who by good use of nature drew the gift of grace to himself. Speaking morally, it is impossible that an ethnic person in corrupted nature should not set very many obstacles in grace’s way. Far from it that by using natural things well he can haul gratuitous and supernatural gifts to himself.

Aquinas says truly in Contra Gentiles, book 3, page 160: if through a prior disorder free choice has declined to evil, it will not be altogether in its power to present no impediment to grace. So those who think evangelical grace is given to everyone who uses nature’s light rightly and does not oppose an obstacle to grace are dreaming up people in corrupted nature such as it is not credible ever existed, exist now, or ever will. Whatever is objected, no one can remove that obstacle but God—as Bradwardine truly teaches in De causa Dei against Pelagius, book 2, chapter 32.

title: Cap. 6 Tertio close: Gospel given or denied by calling pleasure, not natural use
english: Third and last, we assert—with sacred Scripture and experience itself as witnesses—that the gospel and the other means of salvation were not granted or denied to people because some used natural light rightly, or at least less badly, while others abused the same light perversely and wickedly. Sacred Scripture shows that the light of the gospel shone on people who did not expect it, people who were abusing natural light or talent in the worst way. Such were the Romans, Corinthians, and Ephesians: through the apostles the torch of the gospel was lit for them while they were still wallowing in the filth of superstitions and lusts. No less plain is this: to very many who lived less wickedly the gospel was never revealed.

Who does not know that among the philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Xenocrates, and among the Romans Fabricius, Scipio, and Cato, used nature’s light well beyond other people? Yet none of them became a partaker of evangelical grace on that account. So the cause of the gospel and of supernatural light, given or denied, is not to be sought in better or worse use of natural light, but in the good pleasure of God who calls or does not call. With those points tasted first, we come to the thesis itself. We confirm it first by an argument drawn from the death of Christ—the very place from which the adversaries think they can infer the contrary.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 1 close: No covenant ties Gospel revelation to better use of nature
english: If by Christ’s death a covenant has been established under which remission of sins is promised to any believer, but no covenant has been established under which the gospel is promised to any ethnic person who uses natural gifts rightly, or less badly, then it is rash—Christ’s death being granted—to conclude that God is bound by faithfulness, goodness, justice, or any bond whatever, on account of better use of nature, to reveal to people the mystery of evangelical grace. Yet it is most certain that no such covenant exists anywhere. Therefore the revelation or denial of the gospel depends on God’s good pleasure, who hides it or reveals it as he pleases, not on the varied acts of human beings.

We confirm the major premise from this: God is bound to no one and owes nothing to anyone except by a free and voluntary promise—“For who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Romans 11:35). Into that sense Augustine speaks: the Lord makes himself a debtor not by receiving, but by promising (on Psalm 83). He promises nothing spiritual to the works of corrupted nature, however splendid. He has set himself no law that would bar him from giving spiritual goods to people, however wicked and covered with every kind of crime. So we must not explain from the disparity of persons or of human works why the gospel and the knowledge of Christ are given to some and not to others. We must rest in the good pleasure of the divine will, according to the Apostle: “He called us with his calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (2 Timothy 1:9).

Still someone may press: even if God is bound neither by debt nor by any promise sealed by Christ’s death to reveal Christ to those who use nature’s light well, still—since from unpromised grace he often gives many things to people—what keeps us from saying he keeps this common pattern in distributing evangelical grace: grant it to those who use natural light more rightly, and withhold it from those who, by abusing nature’s light worse than others, have made themselves more unworthy of the light of grace? Scripture’s steady witness against that blocks us. It refers the gift of saving grace not to the person who works better, but to God loving and pitying one more than another (Romans 9). Experience blocks it too. Often a person more modest and temperate from early childhood, and for the most part master of lusts, lives and dies where Christian grace cannot be preached to him at all; while another given to lust and covered with crimes is so governed by God that he hears, believes, and is saved.

So we say every mortal by bad use of nature makes himself unworthy of the gospel; and that God, in giving or denying the gospel, does not weigh degrees of human dignity and unworthiness and from them draw a common rule for indulging grace or withholding it. Sometimes he denies it to those who have used nature’s remnants less badly, and meanwhile grants it to those who abuse the same remnants far worse; sometimes the reverse. So the reason why God deigns to give grace to this one and not to that one must be referred to God’s own good pleasure, not to unequal human works.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 2: Divine goodness leaves application-media to free good pleasure
english: Second, we prove that it is not contrary to divine goodness—even once Christ’s death is granted—still to withhold the means of application from any people he pleases. Christ’s death itself is a benefit God freely spent on the human race. It is fair and fitting that free application of that benefit remain with the benefactor. From giving one gift he is never bound to give another unless a promise intervenes; and no one can rightly claim such a promise about the means by which Christ’s death is applied—neither the whole race in a lump, nor any single person for himself alone.

What jars with divine goodness is not that God does not lavish every benefit on every person, but that he would injure anyone, or unjustly deny or withdraw a good that is owed. Illumination by evangelical grace, even with Christ’s death supposed, is still not owed to nature already corrupted by sin. So Bannezius (on the First Part, question 23, article 3, page 279): natural and supernatural illumination do not stand on the same footing, for natural light is owed to nature itself, while the light of grace is not owed to nature—least of all to nature already spoiled by sin—but is conferred by grace. If it is conferred by grace, it is not owed to all. Among twelve sentences that belong to the Catholic faith, Augustine set this second one in Epistle 107: that the grace of God is not given to all people. If it is conferred by grace, it is not given or denied according to good or bad use of natural light. Prosper is right (Response 8 to the Chapters of the Gauls): it is impiety to say that the grace by which we are saved is either repaid to good merits or fenced off by evils. And in On the Calling of the Gentiles: there are no crimes so detestable that they can fence off the gift of grace.

Those who try to defend God’s justice and goodness by human guesswork, and contend that he supplies free means of salvation to everyone who uses natural gifts rightly or less badly, but denies them to those who have abused the same gifts, are—speaking with Augustine—ignorant of the height of grace, and have woven improbable fables. Like it or not, if we ask why those means by which people apply Christ to themselves for salvation are granted to these particular persons and not to others, we must set aside the disparity of persons or of human works and rise to God’s freest good pleasure: “When the same cause binds all at once, / nor are they discerned by merit who differ by gift,” as Prosper puts it elegantly in the Poem On the Ungrateful, chapter 25.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 3 open: From fact to right—immediate media given or denied by mercy
english: From fact to right we argue this way. God leaves undone nothing that it would be alien to divine goodness, justice, or prudence not to do. It is wrong to doubt that, for he who is Goodness, Justice, and Wisdom themselves cannot, in acting or not acting, ever leave the rule of goodness, justice, or wisdom. So I attach the minor and affirm: even with Christ’s death granted, God has denied in the past, and still denies, to many nations and many particular people those means without which Christ’s death is applied to no one.

That will be plain if we look either at the immediate means of salvation—repentance, faith, regeneration, sanctification—by which a person is set in spiritual life and salvation and in actual share of Christ’s death and merits, or at the external means God uses as instruments to produce those first ones: the sending of teachers and pastors, the preaching of the gospel, and every other help without which those inward, immediate means cannot ordinarily be wrought.

As for the first set, faith itself and saving knowledge of Christ is a special gift given to some and denied to others, according to the good pleasure of the divine will: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; to them it has not been given” (Matthew 13:11). “No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father” (John 6:65). “By grace you have been saved through faith—and this not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). “Faith is not of all” (2 Thessalonians 3:2). The same holds for repentance, regeneration, and sanctification: a special mercy that procures them gives them to some, and the same mercy, not unfolding its riches, denies them to others. “Turn us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be turned” (Lamentations 5:21). “He has mercy on whom he wills; whom he wills he hardens” (Romans 9:18). “Not of bloods, nor of the will of man, but of God they were born” (John 1:13). “Blessed be God who according to his mercy has regenerated us” (1 Peter 1:3). I pass over the rest. From these it is clear that God gives or denies those means in which union with Christ and salvation are immediately set according to the good pleasure of his will, not according to a difference in the human will.

All the orthodox Fathers press this hard against the Pelagians. Ambrose on Luke 7:9: God calls whom he deigns, and makes devout whom he wills. Augustine, Epistle 107: We know grace is not given to all people, nor according to the merits of the will of those who receive it. In the same letter he adds that those denied this grace often differ by no merit and no will, but share a like condition with those who receive it. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 19: As in fleshly birth the formation of the divine work precedes every will of the one being born, so in spiritual birth, by which we begin to put off the old self, no one can have a good will by his own motion. And chapter 21: If God has not given to a person through his grace, that person can never will to believe in God, because grace does not find this will already there—it works it in the person. So God does not hand out these inward means promiscuously to everyone who might apply Christ’s death to himself. Nor may our opponents claim that God’s giving or withholding of faith springs from human wills resisting or not resisting, since Scripture expressly refers this to God’s good pleasure to pity or not to pity, and the Fathers in plain words shut out any disparity of human wills before grace is received.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 3: External media withheld from nations under Old and New Testaments
english: So far we have argued about the immediate means. Now we come down to the means of those means. Christ’s death and merit have had their force in God’s acceptance from the world’s beginning. Yet under the Old Testament God did not grant the external means of application to every human being alike. As the Psalmist says, “He declares his word to Jacob; he has not done thus to every nation” (Psalm 147:19–20). Paul speaks the same way: “In past ages God allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14:16).

Prosper marked the same point: it is not far from ordinary observation, he says, through how many ages countless thousands of people, left to their errors and impieties, have perished without any knowledge of the true God (On Free Choice, page 225). Looking to New Testament times (On the Calling of the Gentiles 2.17), he adds: even now in the farthest parts of the world there are nations on whom the Savior’s grace has not yet shone. From this it follows that even with Christ’s death granted, God is still not bound by his goodness or justice to provide and offer to every person the means by which they can apply Christ to themselves. In God the move from fact to right works both ways: God does this, therefore he does it justly; God does not do this, therefore no right binds him to do it.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 3 Obj. 1–2: Preacher neglect and ancestral contempt do not bind God
english: Some meet this argument by saying the gospel is not preached everywhere less because God fails to send preachers than because those who are sent refuse to go. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 105. But if God, by his goodness and justice, as if by a kind of congruence, and with Christ’s death supposed, were bound to communicate sufficient means of application to everyone, he would not let anyone be cheated of an owed benefit by another’s carelessness—least of all a benefit without which no salvation can be hoped for. It is even a contradiction to say that by ordinary law God provides and administers to all these means that look to applying Christ, and yet withholds them from some because of the preachers’ neglect—when the very care of the preachers would have to be counted among those means, without which knowledge and application of the Christ who is preached cannot be had.

Further, if God’s goodness or justice required that these means of applying Christ be administered to all, he would without doubt have kindled in at least some preachers the will and care to preach and carry the gospel to every nation. He himself knows how to thrust laborers into the harvest according to his good pleasure. Finally, what preacher-neglect explains that two hundred years ago the gospel was preached by no one among the Americans, when no one had even dreamed those nations existed? We must therefore rise to a higher cause: God’s free good pleasure in granting or denying these means. By a special providence he sees to it that they are administered to peoples, or not administered, through his ministers—as Acts 16:6 and following shows: “They were forbidden to speak the word of God in Asia, and they were intending to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit did not permit them,” and so on.

Second, they answer that those long without evangelical grace had already repudiated it in their ancestors, and so the descendants are rightly stripped of the gospel proclamation their ancestors despised; therefore the fact that some are not lit by the gospel’s saving light should not be referred to God’s absolute will. But this does not hang with their own views. If God, with an eye to Christ’s death, is bound to administer sufficient means of salvation to all people, it is hardly fair that, because ancestors despised the preached word in Noah’s day, the gospel should be denied to their posterity after many thousands of years. If—Adam’s sin notwithstanding—Christ’s death has (on their showing) secured that sufficient means of salvation be administered to all, it is alien to reason and equity to break that quasi-ordinary law on the pretext of sins committed by any other ancestors of ours.

Just as God could justly deny any spiritual benefit to Adam’s posterity because of Adam’s own sin, so we grant that from other ancestors’ sins God may also take occasion to deny us any free benefit. But if by Christ’s death, with God’s goodness concurring, a law has been set about administering the means of grace, then just as God will not abrogate that quasi-statute because of Adam’s sin—who bore in himself the person of all his posterity—so it is far less fitting that posterity be robbed of this benefit because of the sins of others who do not sustain that common person of the human race. They flee in vain to ancestral sins to explain the denial of a thing which, by the virtue of Christ’s death and of divine goodness, they themselves claim was prepared for all and each by divine decree and as if owed by fixed law.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 3 close: Human unworthiness is circumstance, not the discriminating cause
english: Third, they answer that evangelical grace is denied to some because by continual law-breaking they have made themselves unworthy of those to whom divine grace should be offered. This reply will only make our position clearer. First I take what no sober mind will deny: every person in corrupted nature has made himself unworthy of evangelical grace, if you attend to his sins. Then I add that human dignity and unworthiness—or greater and lesser unworthiness—is not the rule by which God proceeds in dispensing or denying the gospel to particular persons or to nations. That being so, unworthiness is always found in those denied the gospel, and also in those who receive it. So this unworthiness has the nature of a circumstance that always accompanies both those who get the gospel and those who do not; it does not have the force of a discriminating cause why it is given to these and not to those. In this matter we must come down to the sole pleasure of the divine will, who, when it pleases him, confers helps both on those who do and on those who do not do what is in them—as Alvarez says in On Helps, disputation 58.

But because this reply, which teaches that human unworthiness fences off evangelical grace, seems quietly to hint that some could have procured the same by their dignity, hear what the orthodox Fathers taught the Pelagians on this very point. Augustine, Epistle 107, page 500, shows that Christ’s saving grace is not granted or denied by the rule of greater or lesser unworthiness. For brevity I omit the words. Prosper presses this again and again (On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, chapter 15): a part of humankind is set free while a part perishes; and if we ascribe that to the merits of wills, so that grace seems to have neglected the bad and chosen the good, the case of innumerable peoples will rise against us, to whom through so many ages no announcement of heavenly teaching has flashed. Nor can we say that those later ones on whom the light has risen were better, and so on. In the Poem On the Ungrateful, chapter 12, the same Prosper shows that the Pelagians’ own opinion was this: God by his goodness wills to call all to grace, but the will of some, oppressed by vices under the first light, has been made unworthy of the second. Against them, in chapter 14, he contends that examples can be brought of wicked hearts converted by God’s power, hearts in which nothing of the matter had ever settled, and which bore no sign or sense of justice.

The sum of the argument comes to this: evangelical grace is not given because people are judged worthy of it—no one worthy of so great a gift is found—nor is it denied because some have stood more unworthy than the rest, since this light has been granted to the worst and meanwhile denied to others less depraved. We must therefore rest in the secret good pleasure of the divine will, who, that his mercy may shine the more, does not regularly grant the gospel’s light to those who use nature’s light well or less badly, but on the contrary calls the faithless and negligent to himself, and unworthy, ungrateful sinners. From this it is plain that it always remains free for God, and in no way alien to his goodness, to give or not to give to any people whatever the gospel and the other means needed for applying Christ’s merits, according to the good pleasure of his will, with no account taken of dignity or unworthiness, or of greater and lesser human unworthiness.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 4 open: Contrary inconveniences—uneven grace pinned on the human obstacle
english: The same point can be proved from the plain inconveniences that press the contrary view. If by Christ's death it has been universally obtained that God is bound—by the decree itself, or by some law of congruity—to grant, as far as in him lies, to every human being the grace of gospel preaching and of inward sanctification, then the chief reason why one person in fact shares both graces and another does not will lie here: that one has thrust up an obstacle and pushed the grace away, or has blocked it from being offered at all, while the other has neither pushed it away nor blocked it. Our opponents do not shrink from that consequence. They do not reduce the difference between evangelical calling and saving grace denied or granted to God's bare will, but to different conditions or dispositions on the human side. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 489: though God does not preach the word of the cross everywhere, he is still ready to preach it to all who duly submit themselves to the ministry of the law—that is, who follow the light of the natural law alive even in Gentile hearts. Writing on natural gifts, page 118, he says God left those gifts to the nations so that if they used them according to God's intention, they would be led to glorify God in the measure of their knowledge, and on to Christ and the knowledge of him; but if they held down in injustice the truth they had, they would be left in their ignorance. Here he openly hangs the gospel call on the use or abuse of natural gifts.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 4: Internal grace reduced to human wills—first inconvenience against Paul
english: The same Corvinus so defends inward life-giving grace as laid open to all by an ordinary law that he reduces the very difference why one person in fact shares that grace and another does not to a difference of human wills, not to the divine good pleasure. Indeed he says it is certain that no one's conversion is precisely intended by God. But however much this flatters human reason, it still runs against divine Scripture and can be crushed by plain inconveniences. If we grant that either the outward gospel call, or the inward and effectual infusion of regenerating grace, is given and denied according to different human dispositions or operations, then first it would follow that free choice in the corrupted state, not yet lit by gospel light, can so well use its natural gifts that God is bound—by the ordinary law his own goodness dictates to him—to give spiritual grace to the natural man. That is against the Apostle: if it is from works, grace is no longer grace (Romans 11:6). We would receive it not by the pity of the giver, but by the equity of a repayor, as Fulgentius says in On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ, chapter 18.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 4: Second and third inconveniences—preterition and prevenient grace in Paul
english: Second—and every orthodox writer shrinks from this—it would also follow that the reason of predestination and of preterition must be assigned from people's different qualities or acts. For the reason of predestination, which is the preparation of grace, cannot differ from the reason of grace, which is the gift itself. So anyone who teaches that the reason grace is given or withheld must be sought in human dispositions or operations must of necessity seek the reason of predestination and preterition there too. Third, it would follow that God breaks the law he himself set when he as good as forces this grace on those who have put an obstacle in its way—which the Apostle himself most humbly confesses happened to Paul: caught in open sin and rushing against Christ, God mercifully called him to the knowledge and grace of Christ. Fulgentius puts it finely in On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 18: how God's mercy goes before us, and what sort it finds when it does, the Teacher of the nations shows not in someone else but in himself, saying, I who was formerly a blasphemer, and so on (1 Timothy 1:13). The Father hints that every mortal is refractory until preventing grace has brought him under.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 4: Fourth inconvenience—Diospolis, African synod, and Orange overturned
english: Fourth, grant that grace is given or denied according as human wills have or have not set an obstacle, and you overturn nearly everything the Councils defined against the Pelagians. First among them is what the Council of Diospolis sanctioned against Pelagius: let him confess that grace is not given from merit, so that it may be true grace—that is, freely given—through the mercy of him who said, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15). For to give or withhold grace according as someone has used natural gifts rightly or not, or (as others put it) according as someone has or has not done what lies in him, is for the Fathers the same as giving from merits and denying from demerits. Nor will that word of the African Fathers in their synodical letter stand: grace itself is not recognized at all unless it is given; and as long as it is not in a person, he must of necessity resist it in word or deed. How can it make sense that Gentiles in corrupted nature are to receive evangelical grace by that quasi-law if they have not set an obstacle to grace, when by the necessity of a depraved and habitual disposition they must resist grace the whole time they lack it? Finally those decrees of the Council of Orange fall—canon 4: if anyone contends that God waits for our will so that we may be purged from sin, but will not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the Holy Spirit's operation and infusion, he resists the Apostle; and canon 6: if anyone subjoins the help of grace to human humility and obedience, and so on, he resists the Apostle. I leave the rest.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 4 close: Application-grace given or denied by free good pleasure, not human operations
english: Let them explain how God is not said to wait for the human will, and to hang the help of supernatural grace on obedience to the natural law written in human hearts, if—Christ's death once granted—God on this way of acting gives grace to all who use natural gifts rightly, and withholds it from those who do not. Since all of that is utterly foreign to the truth, it remains to say that God, the merit of Christ's death notwithstanding, can give or deny the grace of applying that merit, and ordinarily does so to particular persons by the good pleasure and freedom of his will—not by merits, or by the different operations of human wills.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 5 open: Useful ends that confirm application-grace by good pleasure
english: Our view is confirmed by the most useful ends it serves to bring out—ends the contrary view plainly abolishes. Take this case: grant Christ's death, and still take God as distributing or withholding the grace by which that death is applied to human beings according to his good pleasure, and not according to some difference among human wills or actions.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 5: Absolute liberty of God in first-grace—Matt. 20 and Rom. 9
english: First, absolute liberty of God in giving first grace then shines out—an attribute everyone must acknowledge here. "I choose to give to this one as to you," even when human merits are unequal, is God asserting his own liberty (Matthew 20:14). And "I choose to give to this one, and not to you," where on the human side everything is equal, is a voice just as worthy of God, and likewise serves to display his supreme liberty, as Paul proves (Romans 9). For although by the power and efficacy of Christ's death God willed himself bound to give remission to believers, and glory to the regenerate grafted into Christ, yet he did not will himself bound—by any act of theirs, or any disposition of theirs considered in corrupt nature outside Christ—to give the Gospel to these nations or these particular persons, or to give faith and efficacious grace to these definite individuals. So those who teach that grace is given or denied according to the good or bad use of nature diminish the divine liberty God reserved for himself: which is as much as to say that nature anticipates grace.

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 5: Special mercy—Prosper against Faustus; Augustine on giving and withholding
english: Second, our view makes conspicuous what Scripture presses so hard: God's free and special mercy in giving certain people both the light of the Gospel and saving grace. Prosper puts it well: "There is a certain part of the human race that is brought on to eternal salvation by special benefits" (De vocatione gentium 2.31). Those who think Christ's death has this effect—that God offers the means of saving grace to all, yet leaves it to each person's own choice whether to obey or resist the grace offered, so that if they raise no obstacle they receive grace, and if they raise one they are stripped of it—plainly cancel that special mercy. On their view God showed Jacob or Peter no special mercy he did not show Esau and Judas; Jacob and Peter merely applied to themselves by some special act what Esau and Judas neglected to apply. Faustus of Riez taught that openly (De libero arbitrio 1.10), denying any special divine dispensation for the salvation of certain people—a lesson he learned from Pelagius, as Prosper shows (Carmen de ingratis 10). Augustine speaks otherwise: "The Lord gives to whom he wills, because he is merciful; and he does not give to whom he does not will, that he may make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy" (De bono perseverantiae 12).

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 5 close: Boasting cut off; glory of human salvation wholly God's
english: Third, our view leaves human beings no handle for boasting, and assigns the glory of human salvation wholly to God, who makes one person differ from another—as the Apostle says: "Who makes you differ? What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Corinthians 4:7). "From whom," Augustine asks, "except from him who distinguishes you from another, to whom he did not give what he gave you?" (De praedestinatione sanctorum 9). But if their view wins—that by Christ's death God has become equally kind to all people, and that from this equal bent toward all he administers grace so that whoever uses nature's light well, or does what lies in him, draws grace to himself, while whoever uses that light badly, or fails to do what lies in him, does not—then the person who ends up sharing in grace has from himself a fair ground of boasting: by his own choice he set himself apart from another whom no special gift of divine mercy had set apart.

Natural close of Arg. 5 before Arg. 6

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6 open: If grace turns on human disparity, Gospel and faith get an easy human account
english: Suppose Christ's death is granted, and yet by God's decree the gift or denial of grace to particular persons does not proceed from the absolute liberty of the divine will, but from the disparity of human wills and actions. Then anyone can give a ready reason why the Gospel was withheld from this nation and granted to that one, and why these particular people receive faith and vivifying, regenerating grace while others do not. Of those who have it, the story runs: they got the light of the Gospel because they used nature's light well, or at least less badly. Of those who lack it: they stay without Gospel light because they used nature's light less well. Ask among Christians why this person has faith and regenerating grace and that one does not, and you hear the same human ledger—those who have it willed to believe and would not raise an obstacle; those who lack it would not believe and would not clear the obstacle away. Of the special calling according to purpose, by which God powerfully turns the hearts of those he specially chooses to pity toward belief, there is meantime not a word.

Silence about special vocation according to purpose

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6: That easy human account of obtained grace is Pelagian—Rom. 9 and Phil. 2
english: I add this: to give so ready a reason, from the human side, why grace is obtained or missed is the Pelagian trademark—and every orthodox writer has condemned it. The orthodox have always traced the gift or denial of efficacious grace back to the secret purpose of God's good pleasure. They never held that, once Christ's death is granted, God is so bound to administer his grace indiscriminately that having it or lacking it turns on the disparity of human wills. We do not deny that those who stay without grace have earned their unworthiness and choose their wickedness. We do say that everyone labors under that disease until special grace cures it; and that no unregenerate person pulls grace to himself by a better will. Rather, by a more efficacious grace given from God's mere good pleasure, he receives a better will—as the Apostle says: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16). "It is God who gives us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:13).

Rom 9:16; Phil 2:13; efficacious grace from mere good pleasure

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6: Prosper—many hear; wills prepared or not; mercy and judgment in the wills
english: Prosper brings the difference between believers and unbelievers back to the same point (Ad excerpta Genuensium, reply to Doubt 4): "Many hear the word of truth, but some believe and others contradict—so these will to believe, and those will not. Who does not know that? Who denies it? Yet when the Lord prepares the will for some and does not prepare it for others, we must ask what comes of mercy and what of judgment." And a little later: "Mercy and judgment have been done in the wills themselves."

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6: Augustine—actual share in grace rests on secret good pleasure, not free application
english: Augustine too, everywhere, traces actual share in grace to this secret good pleasure of God—not to the difference among human wills that, by their native freedom, do or do not apply themselves to grace offered. De bono perseverantiae 8: of two already adult ungodly persons, why one is called so that he follows the Caller, while the other is either not called, or not called so as to follow—God's judgments are inscrutable. And De praedestinatione sanctorum 8: "Why," he asks, "does God not teach everyone? If we say it is because those he does not teach refuse to learn, the reply comes: Where then is the word, LORD, YOU TURN US AND GIVE US LIFE?"

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6: Aquinas—saving gifts rest on simple divine will; prevenience for some who block grace
english: Aquinas too will give no other reason why these particular persons receive the gifts of saving grace, and others do not, than the simple will of God (Contra Gentiles 3.161). "Though the sinner," he says, "puts an obstacle in grace's way, and so far as the order of things requires ought not to receive grace, yet sometimes, from the abundance of his goodness, God also goes before with his help even those who put that obstacle there, turning them from evil and converting them to good," and the rest. He adds at once: "He does not go before with his help all who block grace, but some in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in others the order of justice may be shown."

Simple divine will; prevenient help for some obstructers

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6 close: Obstacle and non-obstacle resolve into bare good pleasure—no promiscuous-grace decree
english: Finally—lest we pin on the disparity of human wills the fact that these obtained efficacious grace and were converted, while those did not and stay unconverted—he adds in the same place these weighty words: "When God, among people held in the same sins, converts some by going before them, but sustains or permits others to go on according to the order of things, we are not to ask why he converts these and not those. That hangs on his simple will—just as it was by his simple will that, when all things were made from nothing, some were made more worthy than others." So far Thomas. Christ's death, then, established no divine decree that grace should be administered promiscuously to all, with a kind of annexed law that particular persons share or do not share in that grace according as they will or will not raise an impediment. The very distinction between those who raise an obstacle and those who do not must be resolved into God's bare good pleasure as its first and radical cause.

Arg. 6 close: no promiscuous-grace decree; obstacle discrimination into bare good pleasure

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 7 open: If grace is fixed for all who apply Christ, the last reason falls to human choice
english: Suppose God's will, by Christ's death, is taken as somehow fixed to administer grace to every person who applies Christ to himself and is saved—yet so that only those receive and keep it who either used nature's light well, or raised almost no obstacle against the grace offered them, while everyone else does not receive it. Then the last account of grace obtained or missed, and of salvation gained or lost, would be charged not to the divine good pleasure but to human free choice. The consequence is plain and solid. On that view God is presumed, because of Christ's death, to administer grace and to offer everyone a grace sufficient for applying Christ and obtaining salvation; and he is also presumed, by absolute will or bare will, to give saving grace to no one specially.

Last reason of obtained grace assigned to human arbitrium

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 7: Remonstrants—saving efficacy hangs on not opposing, not on omnipotent force
english: So the Remonstrants put it in the Declaration of their view on the third article (Acts of the Synod of Dordrecht, p. 15). Saving efficacy of grace, they say, hangs neither on the fitness of the calling (as some Roman writers hold) nor on omnipotent divine force (as Prosper in the Carmen De Ingratis 14-15, and Augustine Against Julian 5.3, On the Predestination of the Saints 2, On Grace and Free Choice 20, and On Rebuke and Grace 14), but on an operation that most surely gets its effect when a person does not set rebellion against it—rebellion he could of himself have set.

Efficacy neither congruity nor omnipotent force but non-opposition

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 7: They reverse the order—obstacle cleared because efficacious grace was given
english: As if they said grace is efficacious in this or that particular person because he himself raised no obstacle—when they ought to have said he raised none because God, of his good pleasure, gave him efficacious grace. I now add the Minor, and I affirm it is wholly alien to theology and to truth for anyone to hold that Christ's death established a decree by which the sure attainment of grace and salvation is shifted from God's absolute will onto the free choice of the human will.
notes_covered: Causal order: non-opposition because efficacious grace given
Minor: alien to revoke certain attainment to human arbitrium

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 7: First Adam's liberty-resolved grace vs Christ's stronger grace that makes willing conquer
english: For that account of gaining or missing salvation which resolves into the liberty of human choice belonged to the first grace given to the first Adam—as Augustine well noted. But the grace given in Christ to all who are to be saved is far stronger: by it they will, and will so strongly, that in fact they always overcome the flesh's unwilling will. (See Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 11-12.)
notes_covered: Adam first-grace vs Christ stronger grace
Augustine De corrept. et grat. 11-12 margin

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 7 close: After Christ, who has applying grace turns on divine good pleasure, not human disparity
english: So after Christ has been given us, the distinction that some have the grace by which they apply Christ to themselves for salvation, and others do not, is brought back not to the unevenness of human wills, but to the good pleasure of the divine will.
notes_covered: Arg. 7 close: discrimination to divine good pleasure
Natural stop before Arg. 8 Patrum testimonia

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 open: Fathers testify that God withholds media and gifts by good pleasure
english: Our last argument comes from the Fathers themselves. They freely grant that some people are not given the means and gifts by which they can believe in Christ and obtain salvation—and that this denial rests on the good pleasure of the divine will. God would never leave that undone if, once Christ's death is granted, divine goodness, prudence, or justice already required those means to be supplied to every person. We will not parade every Father in turn. We will take a few passages from those who fought the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians.
notes_covered: Arg. 8 open: Patrum testimonia
media/dona denied by divine good pleasure

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Do not stretch the word grace beyond just limits—Pelagian abuse
english: One caution first. When we say the orthodox Fathers who fought Pelagius refuse to grant that grace is given to all merely because of Christ's death, we are not letting the word grace run loose past its proper bounds—the very move the Pelagians once made. Anything God freely grants to people can, in a loose sense, be called grace.
notes_covered: Grace vocabulary caveat before Patrum cites
Pelagian stretching of gratia

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Broad-sense grace—natural light, creatures, outward benefits, inward motions
english: Natural light by which God lights every person who comes into the world; the witness of the creatures that steers the nations toward some knowledge of the Creator; outward benefits by which God shows his love of humankind to the whole world; inward stirrings that sometimes check a Gentile from evil or move him toward good—all these can, in that wide sense, wear the name grace. Under that blanket the Pelagians hid the poison of their teaching. Scripture does not mean the grace given through Christ that way, and neither do the holy Fathers once Pelagius forced them to speak more carefully.
notes_covered: largo sensu gratiae examples
Pelagian concealment under broad grace
Scripture/Fathers refuse that sense for grace through Christ

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Saving grace of Christ—supernatural gifts; non-infallible media called grace
english: So by "grace of Christ" or saving grace, in Scripture's sense, we mean only those supernatural benefits and gifts aimed straight at salvation in Christ and eternal life. They fall into two ranks. Some are ordered to salvation through Christ, but not infallibly: Gospel preaching, illumination of minds in the mysteries of the faith—in short, whatever supernatural help tends to join people to Christ and set them in a state of salvation, yet has not actually joined them or moved them from death into life. The Apostle himself calls that preaching and knowledge of the Gospel "grace" (1 Cor. 1:4; 2:11). That is why 1 Peter 4:10 names preachers stewards of God's manifold grace. Augustine calls the Gospel itself Christian grace; Prosper calls it the Savior's grace—and in that sense says some nations live outside God's grace when no one there preaches Christ to them.
notes_covered: gratia Christi / salutifera defined
non-infallible supernatural media
1 Cor 1:4; 2:11; 1 Pet 4:10; Augustine; Prosper

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Proper vivifying grace—faith, conversion, regeneration; Augustine's colors
english: Other supernatural gifts actually bring the state of salvation: a good will, faith, conversion, regeneration—in short, what belongs only to people grafted into Christ and reconciled to God. Those, Augustine says, deserve the name "grace of Christ" in the proper sense. Preaching and knowledge of Christian doctrine he refers to that proper grace only so far as they help produce and advance it. In On the Grace of Christ he makes the point expressly: the name does not mean mere lighting of the mind or stirring of the will, but the gift of faith itself and of a good will. He paints that grace in bright colors—the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness; a grace we barely share with the ungodly, but the grace by which we are children of God. Now for the Fathers' own words.
notes_covered: proper gratia Christi = vivifying gifts
Augustine De gratia Christi; depiction
transition to Patrum testimonia

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Primo: Augustine—some not called; media withheld by the abyss of predestination
english: First, the Fathers who deny that—Christ's death granted—the grace of Gospel preaching is owed or given to all, and even say it is withheld from some by the purpose of God's will. That could not happen if grace were owed to everyone on the strength of Christ's death. Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 8: take two ungodly adults—why is one called so that he follows the Caller, while the other is not called, or not called that way? God's judgments are inscrutable. He plainly owns that some are not called at all.
