Chapter 14 adds that for some not cut out of the mass of perdition by God's higher judgment, the means by which they could believe are simply not applied. In both places he affirms that the means are denied, and he traces it to the unsearchable depth of divine predestination—not to uneven human wills or works, the Pelagian and Semi-Pelagian habit. Chapter 11 says the same: God chooses not to help some, and that rests on his will and hidden predestination.
notes_covered: Primo locus: evangelical preaching grace not owed to all
Augustine De bono persever. 8, 11, 14
Natural stop before Prosper Resp. 4

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Primo: Prosper—no Gospel calling where Mother Church has not regenerated
english: Prosper grants the objection that not all are called to grace, at least of everyone to whom Christ's cross and the redemption of his blood have never been made known. Sentence 4 on the Chapters of the Gauls: we cannot say there is a calling of grace where Mother Church has not yet regenerated anyone. That strikes those who, to keep grace prepared and offered to all because of Christ, invent some calling and enough-grace in the thick of pagan darkness. What Prosper said of little children we may say of adults: prove them called somehow, when neither planter could preach to them nor irrigator help them (Response to Objection 4).
notes_covered: Prosper Sent. 4 Capit. Gallor. no calling without Church regeneration
Resp. ad Obj. 4 planter/irrigator against pagan-darkness vocation

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Primo close: Fulgentius and Aquinas—original demerit justly withholds Gospel grace
english: Fulgentius, On the Truth of Predestination book 1: to people who use reason God either supplies or withholds the persons fitted for their salvation—holding justice toward some, showing mercy to others. Meaning: he sends Gospel preachers, or does not, by his good pleasure—sends when he means to display mercy, withholds when he means to exercise justice. From the same Fulgentius I add: the common guilt all contracted in Adam is enough for Gospel grace to be justly denied to anyone. So he says there: the grace by which we are saved is never given for a prior good desert, yet it is denied only for a prior evil desert; for the first man passed the deserts of his sin to all. So for Fulgentius original demerit is already a just reason to withhold Christ's grace from anyone. Aquinas owns the same (2a 2ae q. 2 a. 5 ad 1): helps of grace are given to some in mercy, and in justice not given to others, as punishment for prior sin—at least original sin. All this confirms what we set out first: there is no decreed law, tied to Christ's death, that the means of Gospel grace must be administered to the whole human race. God, even with Christ's death in view, can by right deny—and has in fact denied to some—the very calling of grace.
notes_covered: Fulgentius De verit. Praedest. 1: send/withhold preachers
Original demerit justly denies Gospel grace; Aquinas 2a2ae 2.5
Primo close: no statute of universal Gospel media

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Secundo open: Vivifying grace κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν—Augustine, calling according to purpose
english: Second, from the same Fathers we show that the grace we call Christ's grace by preeminence—the grace that makes a person a living member of Christ and a sharer in salvation and eternal life—is not, because of Christ's death, prepared or offered to all, still less given to all. It is prepared, offered, and given to some; to others neither prepared nor given—and that by God's absolute good pleasure. Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7: according to God's purpose one is called, another is not. To the called a free gift is given, and the calling itself is that gift's beginning; to the uncalled evil is paid back, because all are guilty since [[through one man sin entered the world >> Bible:Romans 5:12]]. So the calling according to purpose—which pours in faith and charity and sets a person in the state of salvation—is given to some and denied to others. Clear too: those who receive it receive it not because their will specially obeyed first, but because God who calls specially showed mercy and softened the will to obey. And the common guilt all contracted in Adam is already enough to uphold God's justice toward anyone he passes by in the gift of saving grace—Bellarmine himself does not dare deny it (On Grace and Free Choice 2.4).
notes_covered: Secundo: vivifying grace not prepared/offered/given to all
Augustine Contr. duas Epist. Pelag. 2.7 secundum propositum
Bellarmines concession on Adamic justice

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Secundo: Augustine—who are made sheep; no decree to give all the grace that makes believers
english: Augustine's second witness is Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 4.6: the One who makes people sheep is the One who frees human wills for the obedience of piety. Why he makes these sheep and not those—that is the question that belongs to the depth the Apostle feared to look into and cried, [[O the depth >> Bible:Romans 11:33]]. Making sheep or not making them means nothing but making people faithful and obedient—or not. Both acts are God's, and both run by the purpose of his hidden will. So Christ's death did not fix the decree some invent: that the grace which makes believers and the obedient is prepared, offered, and given to everyone, on condition that free choice embrace it.
notes_covered: Augustine Contr. duas Epist. Pelag. 4.6 make sheep / O altitudo
No universal decree of vivifying grace under free-choice condition

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Secundo: Augustine—faith is God's gift; birth-guilt already justifies withholding it
english: Third witness: On the Predestination of the Saints 8. Faith begun and faith perfected is God's gift. No one who will not fight the plainest Scripture should doubt that this gift is given to some and not to others. Why not to all should not unsettle the believer who holds that from one man all went into condemnation. Augustine teaches outright that the grace of faith is not given to all; we need no further reason for the gift withheld, because the damnable state in which we are all born already upholds God's justice—even if he gave saving grace to no mortal at all.
notes_covered: Augustine De praed. Sanct. 8: faith gift not to all
Birth-guilt suffices; no further reason required

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Secundo: Augustine—rebuke, original pravity, and grace infused not merely offered
english: Fourth, On Rebuke and Grace 5. Unbelievers and rebels argue: I would deserve rebuke if by my fault I lacked faith and obedience—if I could give or take it myself and would not, or if when God gave it I refused. But if the Lord himself prepares the will, why rebuke me? Chapter 6 Augustine answers: the first crookedness that disobeys God is from the human, who by his own evil will fell from the uprightness God first made in him. So rebuke the damnable root, that pain may birth a will to be regenerated—yet only if the one rebuked is a child of promise, so God works inwardly in him by hidden inspiration even to will. Epistle 105 is the same case. Pelagius asks: what have we done who live badly, if we never received the grace to live well? Augustine answers only that people who live badly of themselves cannot truly claim they have done no evil. A little later: let them blame themselves; they were made from the mass God justly condemned for one man's sin. In both places Augustine grants that God has denied his grace to some; that those not given it could not take it for themselves; and that original guilt and pravity are reason enough for God, of his will, to withhold Christ's grace from anyone. Note too: he does not picture saving grace as something merely offered to the human will, knocking to be let in, but as something poured in—healing and vivifying the will that receives it.
notes_covered: De corrept. et grat. 5-6 rebuke and child of promise
Ep. 105 Pelagian objection; infused vs knocking grace

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Secundo close: Ep. 107, Prosper, Fulgentius—vivifying grace not seized by native liberty
english: Our last Augustine witness is Epistle 107. Against the Pelagians he lists twelve catholic sentences; the fourth is, We know God's grace is not given to all. And lest anyone claim Christ's death made this grace prepared and offered to everyone, had or missed only as people choose to take or refuse it, sentences five and six shut that door too—more on that shortly. From Augustine we come to Prosper. In the Genoese Excerpts, answer to doubt 7: when the word of truth is preached, some believe willingly and some do not—but only because God has opened some hearts and not others. That is to say, the grace of faith is given to some and denied to others. Answer to the eighth doubt: of Tyre and Sidon what can we say but that it was not given them to believe? Why denied—let them tell if they can. Prosper asserts two things: the gift of faith is denied to some, and the reason is unsearchable. In On the Ungrateful 6 he sets out the Pelagian error: that without choosing persons, law or Christ's grace wills to save every human, and the Caller's gift is so laid open that anyone can reach it by his own liberty and strength. Chapter 10 paints the Semi-Pelagian colors; chapter 11 rejects them: Tell us how you prove Christ's grace passes by none of all who are born. For Prosper, to defend grace given to all is a strand of Pelagian poison. Hear Fulgentius. On the Truth of Predestination: the holy Fathers, holding apostolic truth, knew for certain—and left it in books—that God's grace is not given generally to all. A little later: no one can desire, ask, or even know that grace unless he first receives it from God. Again: do not think God's grace is given to all. Not all have faith; some do not receive God's charity so as to be saved. That they neither believe nor love the Lord is the fault of the human will, which, until divine gift-grace changes it, either fails to understand God's commands or despises them once understood. What could be plainer? Vivifying grace is not given to all, and no one has it unless it is given from above. Clearer still, On the Incarnation and Grace of Jesus Christ, p. 89: God who prepares the will is the One who gives it. If he has not given that will by his grace, a person can never will to believe in God—because grace does not find the will ready; it works the will in the person. So the Fathers who warred on Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians speak with one voice: vivifying, saving grace is not given to all; the spoiled will that lacks it can by its own fault scorn grace and push away what is offered in outward means; but it cannot, by right of native liberty, snatch this life-giving grace and drag it to itself.
notes_covered: Augustine Ep. 107 sentences 4-6
Prosper Genuensia + De Ingratis 6/10/11
Fulgentius De verit. praedest. + De incarnat.; Secundo concord close

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 after Secundo: Pelagian-mode digression—vivifying grace offered to all, given by human will
english: But the marrow of Pelagianism sits in the mode they invent for how God administers vivifying grace and how people take it. So we will set out what the Pelagian party claims and what the orthodox Fathers settle, with witnesses from both. The Pelagians hold that from Christ’s death and merit vivifying, regenerating grace flows to everyone from God’s mercy in such a way that being vivified and regenerated—or not—depends first on the human will that embraces or spurns the grace. Their view comes to this: saving grace is offered to all from sheer mercy in Christ, yet given to no one by absolute good pleasure. Ask why this person received Christ’s saving grace and that one did not, and they answer: the one willed to take what was offered; the other would not. Let them speak for themselves. Vitalis of Carthage, in Augustine Epistle 107, holds that grace follows the human will and is therefore given because people willed it. The Massilian leftovers of Pelagian heresy, in Prosper to Augustine, say that as far as God goes eternal life is prepared for all, but as far as free choice goes it is seized by those who freely believed God and received helps of grace by the merit of that belief. Pelagius himself, in Augustine, says people who use free choice well merit the Lord’s grace; others who have free choice by which they could come to faith and deserve God’s grace, by misusing their liberty, lack grace and run into damnation. Faustus of Riez: from God’s goodness that a person is called; from his own will that he promptly obeys.
notes_covered: Pelagian-mode digression open after Secundo
Vitalis Ep. 107; Massilians; Pelagius; Faustus Rhegiensis

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Pontificii, Arminius, Remonstrants, Corvinus—efficacious grace hung on human consent
english: From the old Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians we come down to people who hate the Pelagian name yet will not drop the error. In that class I put those Papists who teach that grace is efficacious by the consent of the human will: if the will happens to assent, God pours in vivifying grace; if it resists, God’s operation that would vivify and regenerate the soul is made void. With them I also count Arminius and his disciples, who hang the gift or denial of saving grace so far on human wills that they say God by absolute good pleasure wills to convert and regenerate no one, yet wills to convert and regenerate all on condition they have not resisted his exciting grace—and leaves them unconverted if they have resisted. So the Remonstrants: ask why this person is converted and that one is not, and the answer is that God converts the one who does not oppose with fresh obstinacy, and the other is not converted because he does oppose with fresh obstinacy. They take the reason for given or denied saving grace from different acts of human choice. About God removing the stony, stubborn heart by special mercy—or not removing it by the freedom of his own will—they keep a deep silence. Corvinus likewise refers whether we have or lack the grace by which we are converted and saved not to a discrimination of God’s will but of ours. Against Bogerman, p. 263: It is certain that nobody’s conversion is precisely intended by God. A little later: once all the operations God uses to work conversion in us are in place, conversion still remains so much in our power that we can refuse to be converted. That is their position.
notes_covered: Pontificii consensus-efficacy
Arminius/Remonstrants/Corvinus vs Bogerman

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Fathers reply: Augustine—conversion hangs on God preparing the will, not excited assent
english: The holy orthodox Fathers speak far otherwise. They taught that vivifying, regenerating, converting grace for the soul itself is not given or withheld by the contingent yes or no of free choice, but by God’s free and absolute will, which does or does not choose to take away the mad hardness of the human heart. Augustine comes first. He always held that, once the work of human redemption was finished on the cross, some people have grace because God by special mercy worked in them so that they received it; others lack it because God would not, by pitying them, soften their rebellious hardness. Fine is Retractations 1.10: When I said all people can turn themselves to keep God’s commands if they will, let the Pelagians not take that as spoken on their side. It is wholly true that all can do this if they will; but the will is prepared by the Lord, and is so enlarged by the gift of charity that they can. From those words it is plain that conversion of the human will to God does not hang on this condition—If the will, once excited, chooses to obey—but that its very willing and its very ability hang on a preparation of God and an infusion of charity. The same Augustine, Epistle 107: How can one say everyone would have received grace if those to whom it is not given had not refused it by their own will, when it is not given to many infants who have no contrary will? A little later: How are merits of human will weighed here, when those to whom that grace is not given have a like case with those to whom it is given, and yet by God’s just judgment it is not given?
notes_covered: Fathers reply open
Augustine Retract. 1.10; Ep. 107 infants

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Fathers reply: Prosper—grace given makes obedience; De vocat. Gent. on hidden election
english: Hear others too. Prosper: Who doubts that free choice obeys so great a call from the Caller, when in that choice God’s grace has already generated the affection of believing and obeying? So God’s grace is not given to the will on condition that it obey; once given, it makes the will obey. The same writer, On the Calling of the Gentiles 1.18: for people of every condition and age, the cause of receiving grace is God’s will, with whom the reason of election is hidden—merits begin from that grace which they receive without merits. Note the witness. Even if this author (whoever he was) holds that helps of grace have not been wholly withdrawn from anyone, he still does not think grace stands ready and offered to all in such a way that the difference—why this person received it and that one did not—is traced to one willing to take and the other willing to resist. He reduces the cause of grace received to God’s hidden election; and, as far as non-reception is a mere negation, he reduces that too to hidden non-election. If you treat it as a moral omission by people who resist grace, then refer it to human viciousness. But that is by the way.
notes_covered: Prosper on grace making obedience
De vocat. Gent. 1.18 hidden election

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Fathers reply: Fulgentius—saving grace not by a law of willing to take or refuse
english: Fulgentius everywhere beats back the Pelagian error that imagines saving grace prepared and offered to everyone in Christ the Redeemer under a kind of law: some have it because they willed to take it; others lack it because they willed to push it away. He teaches instead that the good will itself is given to some, and that everyone to whom it is not given cannot help but refuse it. We have already cited witnesses of that kind; now we add more. On the Truth of Predestination 1, p. 158: Not because we will have we received grace—nor was grace given even while we were willing. A little later, p. 159: Grace alone makes a good will in us; grace alone gives faith to the will. A will that does not have faith can have no merit toward receiving faith, because not to have faith is to displease God.
notes_covered: Fulgentius against law-of-offer
De ver. praedest. 1 pp. 158-159

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Fathers close: Fulgentius—grace by election cuts the throat of Pelagian and Arminian contingency
english: The same writer, book 2 near the start, p. 169: It is God’s to decide which people receive his grace, and how much. He does not pay it as wages owed to human wills or works; as merciful and kind he pours it freely into hearts he means to light. So he gives it to whom he wills and as much as he wills, because no rising of a good will and no fruit of any good work invites him before he bestows grace. That cuts the throat of the Pelagian view—and of the Arminian too—which will not have vivifying, saving grace (Fulgentius’s subject) prepared or given to anyone by the purpose of divine election, but given or denied to people by chance, under the shifting condition of a human will that yields or fights. Sounder Papists disliked that theology. A few of their witnesses we will add to the places already set down.
notes_covered: Fulgentius De ver. praedest. 2 p. 169
jugulum Pelagian/Arminian; bridge to papist schoolmen

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Schoolmen: Bannes—supernatural helps not given to all; difference not from free choice
english: Dominicus Bannes, on Aquinas I q.22, last conclusion, p. 278: God, he says, decided from eternity—by a will either absolute or consequent—not to give supernatural helps to everyone. If anyone asks why he confers these gifts on certain people in particular and denies them to others, that hangs on God’s bare will; as Augustine and St Thomas teach, you should not hunt a further reason. A little later: So the Christian theologian who is humble should learn with St Thomas and Augustine to leave some things unknown rather than, with the curious, to know more than he ought, lest he slide into the Pelagian heresy by tracing this difference to free choice as its first cause and root—“because this one wanted to convert, and that one did not.” He also adds a line that cuts the sinews of Pelagian and Arminian theology: the will’s own concurrence is itself an effect that necessarily follows, by necessity of consequence, from efficacious divine help.
notes_covered: Bannes in 1 Sent./Aquin. q.22 conclus. ult. p. 278
difference of helps not from liberum arbitrium; concurrence as effect of efficacious help

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Schoolmen: Bannes rejects universal prepared grace and will-based discrimination
english: With those rulings the learned Bannes rejects and condemns the view that regenerating, life-saving grace is prepared and laid open to every human being because of Christ’s merit. He also refutes those who locate the reason why some are regenerated and others are not—or why some convert and others do not—in human willing and refusing. And he teaches that our concurrence, or our non-resistance—our willing—is a necessary effect of efficacious grace once given, and so is not the reason or condition for its being given and received.
notes_covered: Bannesius application against universal prepared regenerating grace
velle/nolle not root of discrimination; concurrentia as effect not condition

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Schoolmen: Alvarez—efficacious grace’s start not from nature’s use of sufficient help
english: Alvarez, On the Helps of Divine Grace, Disp. 58, p. 263: Suppose we assert a law God has set, that he will infallibly give efficacious help to those who use well—or who choose to use—sufficient help from their innate liberty alone. Then the start of efficacious grace would already come from nature and from the creature’s innate liberty of willing to use sufficient help well. That is the very law, the very decree of God, that Arminius, Corvinus, and the rest of that school defend with such zeal. They say sufficient grace is given to all because of Christ the Mediator’s merit; but efficacious grace—grace that in the act itself converts and regenerates—is to be given only if people use that exciting or sufficient grace well, that is, if the will, once stirred by grace and made able, puts forth the power of willing planted in it. That makes the beginning of efficacious grace belong to Nature. The same Alvarez, same place: this causal is false—“because the person stirred by God wills to consent, therefore he is helped.” This causal is true—“because the person stirred by sufficient grace is helped by efficacious help, therefore he cooperates.” He proves it at length in Disp. 59, and there also holds this proposition most true: because God wills that the person will, therefore the person wills.
notes_covered: Alvarez De auxiliis Disp. 58 p. 263 vs Arminian lex of sufficient→efficacious
false vs true causalis; Disp. 59 Quia Deus vult ut homo velit

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Schoolmen: Alvarez against Arminians who root salvation’s difference in human will
english: That stands diametrically against Arminian teaching. They deny that any antecedent will of God is why some rather than others believe, convert, and are saved with effect. They put the whole difference down to the prior human will of people who, stirred by the same common grace as others, chose ahead of the rest to believe, to turn, and to take hold of salvation.
notes_covered: Alvarez anti-Arminian: antecedent divine will vs antecedent human will

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Schoolmen: Estius—no frustrated divine striving blocked by human bad will
english: William Estius, once professor at Douai, on I Sentences disp. 46 §2, p. 222: We must not picture in God a will, a zeal, some straining by which he wills, labors, presses, and does all that is in him so that every human being may be saved—only to fail because human bad will blocks his good will and, by prevailing and getting in the way, frustrates God’s will. Yet that is nearly the whole of what some claim Christ’s death procured: that God, by offering saving grace to all alike, wills to save those who freely apply themselves to grace and to damn those who resist it.
notes_covered: Estius 1 Sent. disp. 46 §2 p. 222 against frustrated divine conatus
Arminian reading of Christ’s death as promiscuous offer + free application

title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Schoolmen: Bellarmine—efficacious grace not conditioned on not rejecting it
english: Last, let Bellarmine step forward. He does not grant that Christ’s death is tied to any divine decree by which God would give efficacious grace—grace that regenerates in very fact—to every human being on the condition that they do not refuse it by their will. In On Grace and Free Choice book 1, chapter 12, he rejects those who teach that people have it in their power to make grace efficacious when otherwise, of itself, it would be only sufficient. He shows they stand against Augustine and Holy Scripture when they say everyone would have received God’s grace if those who do not receive it had not refused it by their will (p. 423). He presses the view with this trouble: if efficacious calling hung not on God’s purpose but on the human will, no room would be left for predestination. Add book 2, chapter 8, p. 455: We believe God by absolute will wills to save many, both infants and adults, and by absolute will does not will to save others, both infants and adults. See Augustine’s Enchiridion, chapters 102–103.
notes_covered: Bellarmine De grat. et lib. arbit. 1.12; 2.8 p. 455; Aug. Enchir. 102–103
no decree of efficacious grace to all Si non respuerint

title: Cap. 6 close: why grace and free choice—universal covenant of faith, not of efficacious means to all
english: But why so much on grace and free choice, when our question is the Death of Christ as the universal cause of human salvation? Because the Pelagians once taught—and many today still slide into—the view that by the Redeemer’s death and merit, saving or efficacious grace stands open equally to every human being, to be given if they do not refuse it by their will, and denied if they do. As if Christ’s death itself had been granted from pure mercy, while efficacious or saving grace reaches people only as they use free choice well or badly in embracing or rejecting exciting grace. Then salvation would belong to those “worthy to be saved” as willing from themselves—as Prosper sang in On the Ungrateful 1.6. So in this Dissertation on the universal efficacy of Christ’s death, just as we had to show against those who try to narrow it that a universal covenant stands with the whole human race to give remission and eternal life to each person under the condition of faith, so we also had to show against those who stretch that universal efficacy past its bounds that no law and no decree stands, in connection with Christ’s death, to give the means of supernatural grace—or saving efficacious grace itself—to everyone on the condition that they use nature’s light well or less badly, or that they do not refuse that grace by their will. Christ’s death being granted, God is bound by faithfulness, under the gospel covenant, to give remission of sins and eternal life to anyone who repents and believes. By no covenant is he bound to give faith itself, charity, or saving grace to someone who only performs some other act by free choice’s own powers. Indeed, once Christ’s death is granted, the gift or denial of efficacious saving grace remains as free to God as the gift of Christ himself, which is owed to no human acts of choice. So the coming of efficacious saving grace must be traced to God’s purpose of mercy or non-mercy as its first root—not to the human choice of willing or not willing. Thus far we have had to treat Christ’s death as its force and efficacy reach all. Next we must explain how it is restricted to God’s elect children.
notes_covered: Cap. 6 close: why grace/free-choice digression; Prosper De Ingratis 1.6
universal pact under faith vs no decree of efficacious means to all
bridge to Cap. 7 elect sons

title: Cap. 7 open: universal death under faith and electing grace—two decrees do not collide
english: We have treated Christ’s death as it regards the whole human race—with the universal scope of his life-giving power, under the condition of Faith, as that power is to be brought into act for any person. For although, when that condition fails, Christ’s death does not put forth its saving force in the greater part of humankind, still it must neither be denied—what the Scriptures everywhere and clearly witness—nor doubted that God has within himself most just and wise reasons for his counsel when he ordained his Son’s death applicable to all under the condition of faith, and yet did not decree to effect or procure that the same death be applied to all by a faith given to each. So we must not set these divine decrees against each other as if they collided: “I will that my Son so offer himself on the cross for the sins of the human race that all and each who believe in him can be saved”; and “I will so dispense my efficacious grace that not all, but the elect alone, receive this saving faith by which they are saved.” If anyone thinks those two decrees fight, he ought rather to own the weakness of his understanding than to deny anything so plainly set down in Holy Scripture. Let this then stand fixed: by God’s own decree Christ was so offered on the altar of the cross for all human beings that his death is already established as it were a universal remedy for all and each, applicable by faith for obtaining remission of sins and eternal life.
notes_covered: Cap. 7 title locus; Egimus...; Volo...Volo decrees; universal remedy under faith

title: Cap. 7 open: special elect prerogative—not Pelagian parity or Grevinchovius bare impetration
english: But now, lest under this universal virtue of Christ’s death—which extends to all by power—we crush that special efficacy of the same which belongs and reaches to the predestined alone, we must take up the other part of the dispute we have undertaken. It will explain and defend the elect’s special prerogative in Christ’s death, both from the will of God the Father who gave his Son to death and from the Son who offered himself. For we must not so defend that Christ died for all that, with the Pelagians, we believe the life-giving efficacy of that death stands open in equal measure to all in common from the intention of the divine will, and yet in the event becomes saving for some and not for others from nowhere but the contingent use of human liberty. Nor must we rave with the Arminians as if God gave his Son to death intending absolutely nothing else than that he himself should thence have a bare power of saving any sinners he pleased, his justice notwithstanding, and that any sinners should have a way or means by which they could be saved, their sin notwithstanding. Hence that famous corollary of Grevinchovius in his dissertation On the Death of Christ, p. 9: that the dignity, necessity, and usefulness of the obtaining could have stood abundantly even if the redemption obtained had never been applied by him to any individual. Likewise also that at p. 14: that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none, because of the intervening unbelief of all. But we by no means judge that Christ’s death was cast like a die; rather it was decreed from eternity by God the Father and by Christ that by the merit of this death certain persons, whom Scripture marks by the name of the elect, should be saved infallibly; and so by God’s will Christ’s death was offered and accepted for redeeming those same persons in a special mode and counsel.
notes_covered: special efficacy for praedestinati; anti-Pelagian; anti-Arminian; Grevinchovius pp.9,14; death not dice

title: Cap. 7: decree-order digression set aside; thesis aimed at the predestined alone
english: Nor is it necessary here, for defending this special counsel, to settle that thorny little question—vexed by many, and vexing all who take it up—whether the decree by which certain persons are predestined to the infallible sharing of eternal life is prior, or that other by which Christ was ordained to the Mediator’s office. For although, to shore up the weakness of human understanding, we are forced in God’s eternal decrees to conceive some as prior and some as posterior, still to contend about these imaginary signs of our reason, or to take from them questions of faith to establish or refute, seems to me slippery and very dangerous. This at least must be set beyond every cast of doubt: those decrees of God which we think according to an order of prior and posterior stand, in God himself, in the equal eternity of infinity; nor can or should any separate instant be given in which, one decree being fixed, the other is rightly thought not yet reviewed and fixed. Conceive then as prior in order the decree of constituting and sending the Mediator (which seems to me fitter to our way of understanding), and as posterior the decree of electing certain persons to the unfrustrated obtaining of eternal life in the Mediator so constituted; yet never so pull these apart that the Mediator’s passion was not from eternity foreseen as to be offered in a special mode and regard for those to be elected, and as specially offered for them was from eternity accepted by God. Or on the contrary, conceive as prior the decree of electing certain persons to salvation, and as posterior the decree of destining Christ to the Mediator’s office; yet never so separate them that Christ’s passion, specially offered and accepted for those same persons, was not the cause of preparing and giving those elect both efficacious grace and salvation. Since therefore either opinion serves our purpose alike, leaving aside a question of little necessity, we will propose and confirm a single thesis on Christ’s death, under a special consideration restricted to the predestined alone. It runs thus:
notes_covered: utraque opinio; missa disquisitione; unicam thesin ad solos praedestinatos

title: Cap. 7 Thesis: death destined to the elect alone—vs Grevinchovius foresight application
english: Thesis. Christ’s death, from the special Intention of God the Father who from eternity ordained and accepted that sacrifice, and of Christ who offered the same to God the Father in the fullness of time, was destined for certain human beings (whom Scripture calls the Elect) and for them alone, to be applied efficaciously and infallibly for the obtaining of eternal life. We oppose this thesis to the Arminians’ error, which Grevinchovius tries to establish in his Dissertation On the Death of Christ, p. 7 ff., where he teaches that God, in delivering his Son, intended the obtaining of reconciliation to be common to all and each, but absolutely willed the application of that obtained reconciliation for no mortal. “I acknowledge,” he says, “in God indeed a constant and perpetual affection of applying the obtained good to all and each: I deny that the application itself is destined by God’s sure counsel and will to any human being except as a believer, and as a believer.” So this new little master thinks God wills eternal life in Christ equally for all, and does not by an absolute and antecedent will destine and prepare for some efficacious grace by which Christ is infallibly applied to them; but by his eternal foreknowledge looks ahead who will believe and who will remain in their unbelief, and only then destines to believers as believers the efficacious application of Jesus Christ’s death and merits. But we hold that in predestination to faith itself the application of Christ’s death is infallibly destined to certain persons; and we say this faith is prepared not for believers as believers, but for unbelievers, that by it they may become believers. So application not destined but done is understood in those considered as believers; but destined application is understood in those for whom the gift of faith is destined, through which that application will be made. And these are the elect, and the elect alone, whose special prerogative is that by the absolute will of God the Father and of Christ the Mediator they are decreed and procured to be saved infallibly through Christ’s death. With these preliminaries we come to the arguments, and first take up the plain testimonies of the Scriptures.
notes_covered: Thes. Mors Christi...; Grevinchovius Diss. p.7; praedestinatio ad fidem; soli electi

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 1: persons given to the Mediator—John 6 / 17 / Ephesians 1; Augustine
english: 1. First here belong those places that mark the Father’s absolute will to give certain persons to the Mediator and as it were commend them, to this end: that from him and through him they may receive all things needful for salvation, and finally salvation itself. John 6:37, 39: “All that the Father gives me will come to me; and him who comes to me I will not cast out. This is the will of the Father who sent me, that of all he has given me I should lose nothing,” and so on. It is clear from this context that not all promiscuously, but certain persons, were given to the Mediator by the Father’s singular mercy, from a sure and gracious purpose of bringing those same persons infallibly and efficaciously to eternal life. Like texts are found in John 17:2: “You have given him authority over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to all you have given him.” This special donation can be understood as done in no other way than in eternal election. And that those so given to the Redeemer have a special prerogative in the very work of redemption no sane person will doubt. Certainly the Apostle marked it openly in Ephesians 1:4, 5, 6, and following: “He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world was laid. He predestined us to adoption as sons through Christ according to the purpose of his will.” Here you have that special donation of certain persons known to God alone. Then verse 7 shows that according to God’s purpose those same persons always obtain efficacious and applied redemption in the Mediator—“in whom we have redemption through his blood,” and so on. Therefore those specially given to Christ in election always draw faith, remission of sins, sanctification, and salvation from Christ’s death, the fruitful application of that same death being given them together with it. Saint Augustine understood by this donation nothing other than eternal election (On John, tract. 107): “The Father,” he says, “would not have given them to the Son unless he had chosen them.” The same Father, in On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 16, shows that those so given to the Son are also called in that peculiar way, so that Christ crucified does not become to them a scandal or foolishness, but the power and wisdom of God for working faith and salvation efficaciously in them. See the author’s words, which for brevity I omit. Either, then, it must be denied that certain persons were specially given by God the Father to Christ the Mediator, or it must at once be granted that the Mediator in his offering had a special regard to those same persons.
notes_covered: John 6:37,39; John 17:2; Eph 1:4-7; Aug. In Joh. 107; De praed. sanct. 16

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 2: Christ keeps and sanctifies the given—John 17; Hebrews 2:13
english: 2. The same is proved from those places that teach Christ, conscious of the Father’s will, directs and infallibly leads to salvation the aforesaid persons specially given to him, with special care. That would doubtless not happen unless Christ’s death—which is the meritorious cause of every saving grace granted us—had been destined to those same persons as saving and life-giving by a special intention. But let us hear the words of Scripture. John 17:9: “I ask for them; I do not ask for the world, but for those you have given me, because they are yours.” And verse 12: “I have kept them; those you gave me I have guarded.” And verse 19: “For them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.” Nothing is clearer than that two things are affirmed in these places: first, that not all promiscuously, but certain ones, were specially given by God the Father to Christ the mediator—which has been shown to be understood of the Elect; second, that Christ, in discharging the very office of Mediator and Savior, embraces and pursues those same persons with special love, intention, and care—that is, with such love, intention, and care as produce in them the infallible effect of eternal life. That is plain from Hebrews 2:13, where Christ presents these children given him by the Father to his Father safe and sound: “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
notes_covered: John 17:9,12,19; Heb 2:13 Ecce ego et pueri

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 2 close: absolute intercession (Bannes/Suarez)—oblation intends the same elect
english: But now, to gather all this as into one bundle: those whom Christ by special intercession commended to the Father—that is, by absolute prayer (as Bannes has it on I q.23 art.5 p.297), or (as Suárez in tom. 3.1 q.19 disp.31 p.634) those for whom he prayed with an efficacious and absolute will that the merit of his death be applied to them efficaciously; those for whose keeping and guarding he mounts as it were extraordinary watch; those for whom he so sanctified himself that from him they efficaciously receive that sanctification which is worked in the hearts of the saved by the teaching of the Gospel; finally, those whom he will at last present to the Father, every one, safe and glorious—those, beyond all controversy, he also embraced with special intention in the very act of offering, and so in the whole work of redemption. For it is absurd that salvation was procured for them by the Mediator with special intention, if Christ’s death, which is the cause of human salvation, was not destined to them with special intention.
notes_covered: Bannes 1 q.23 a.5 p.297; Suarez; absurd without special destination of death

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 3: death bound to absolute purpose for certain persons—sheep, sons, Church texts
english: 3. The third argument is drawn from those Scripture testimonies in which Christ’s death, joined and as it were folded together with a sure and absolute purpose of giving eternal life, is not spread out to all human beings but is restricted to certain persons—and that by Christ’s own special intention. Such are John 10:15: “I lay down my life for my sheep.” John 11:51–52: Jesus was about to die that he might gather into one the scattered children of God. Ephesians 5:25–26: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her and present her to himself in glory.” Titus 2:14: Christ gave himself for us that he might cleanse for himself a people of his own, and so on. He purchased the church with his blood (Acts 20:28). Ephesians 1:22–23: he gave him as Head over all things to the church, which is his body. Add also Ephesians 5:23: “He himself is the Savior of his body.”

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 3: three observations—elect titles, not the promiscuous race, efficacious will
english: In all these places three things must be noticed. First, by the names sheep, Church, children of God, and body of Christ are meant sheep, children of God, or members of Christ—not so much already united in act by a faith received as still to be united by God’s counsel and intention through a faith yet to be received. Second, under those titles the human race cannot be meant promiscuously. Third, when it is said that Christ died that he might gather these children, sanctify this Church, acquire this Church, and the like, what is marked in Christ as he offers himself is not an inefficacious will, or some conditioned intention that might miss its intended effect, but an efficacious will and an intention joined to an infallible outcome.
notes_covered: tria observanda: elect titles; not promiscuous genus; efficacious not conditioned will

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 3 Probatur 1: sheep/members by eternal election—Augustine Tract. 46 / 49
english: First, then: in those places the speech is of sheep, members, and children taken according to God's eternal and hidden purpose of election, not according to what they are in the present act. Nobody becomes Christ's sheep in fact, or a child of God, or a member of his mystical body, unless the merit and benefit of Christ's death are actually and efficaciously brought down and applied to him. So Christ died for the sheep, for the children of God, for the Church, for the members destined to him from eternity under the purpose of election—so that by the merit of his death God's predestination might be fulfilled in them. Augustine puts it so on John, tract. 46: "The Lord knows who are his; they are sheep according to that predestination, that foreknowledge, that election of sheep, before the world was founded." And in tract. 49, p. 366, on the scattered children of God: "These things were spoken according to predestination; for neither his sheep nor the children of God yet existed, because they had not yet believed."
notes_covered: Probatur primum; election vs present act; Aug. In Joh. tract. 46 and 49 p.366

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 3 Probatur 2: Scripture’s elect titles mark restricted intention—vs John 3:16
english: The second point is proved: in the places alleged Christ’s death is marked as restricted under a special reason to certain persons. For otherwise why would Scripture have named sheep, children, and church, if it had meant to designate that death as it extends to all? It would have used in vain words that mark out a small part of the human race, unless it also meant to show that Christ’s intention in that matter looks not to the whole human race but is referred to those few. Christ’s death and God’s intention embracing all promiscuously is best expressed in John 3:16: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” And so he loved the sheep, the children, his Church, that by his death he decreed to merit for them faith and eternal life efficaciously.
notes_covered: Probatur secundum; oves/filii/ecclesia vs omnes; John 3:16 contrast

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 3: special love in the offering—Aquinas; Probatur 3 open (John 10:28 / 17:24)
english: Holy Scripture meant to open to us this special intention of Christ in offering himself, sprung from special love, whenever it mentions Christ’s death as related to the Church alone, to the sheep alone, to the members alone of the mystical body—according to that word of Aquinas (Part 3, q.24 art.4): “God preordained the salvation of the elect, by predestining from eternity that it be completed through Jesus Christ.” The last point is proved: the testimonies brought forward contain the will of God the Father and of Christ—not inefficacious or conditioned, but absolute and efficacious—concerning the saving of those sheep through Christ’s death. For speaking of the same sheep Christ says in John 10:28: “I give them eternal life, and they will not perish forever.” And in John 17:24: “Father, I will that where I am, they also whom you have given me may be with me.”
notes_covered: special love in offering; Aquinas ST III q.24 a.4; Probatur ultimum John 10:28; 17:24

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 3 close: absolute will—Savior of the world vs Savior of his sheep (Eph 1:18)
english: And of this Church for which Christ gave himself up, the Apostle says in Ephesians 5:23: "Christ is head of the church, and Savior of his body." All of that marks an absolute will joined to its effect. So Christ is truly named Savior and Redeemer of the world insofar as he brought a remedy that is salutary for the whole world and applicable by faith; yet he is Savior and Redeemer of his sheep, of his Church, of his body—in one word, of the predestined children of God—insofar as by special intention he destined and procured that this same remedy be applied to them, giving them enlightened eyes of the heart (Ephesians 1:18) so that by faith they may possess Christ as efficaciously united and applied to them.
notes_covered: Eph 5:23; Servator mundi vs Servator ovium; Eph 1:18; Arg. 3 close before Arg. 4

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 4 Ultimo: Gen. 3:15 seed promise—Satan crushed under the elect (Rupert / Marlorat)
english: 4. Lastly, we can confirm our view from those places in which God absolutely promised Christ, as he died, that by the merit of this death the Church would infallibly be set free from death and given eternal life. Genesis 3:15: “The seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent’s head.” What else is that than that by the power and merit of Christ’s death Satan will be trampled down, and that all those of whom God in Christ specially willed to have mercy will be freed from his power? Who then can doubt that Christ referred his death—Satan’s vanquisher—with special regard to those who were to be freed through him by a special benefit? And that those to be infallibly freed were the elect is confessed by all sound theologians. Rupert (On the Victory of the Word of God, book 2, chapter 18) expressly calls the elect the serpent’s conquerors, because the efficacy of Christ’s death and resurrection crushing the Devil is destined and procured to be applied efficaciously to them alone from special mercy. So Marlorat on this place: the Devil and the wicked generation fight against God’s elect, but the elect at last prove stronger because of their Head, Christ, who by his death abolished him who had the empire of death. Christ’s death was therefore specially intended and destined to crush Satan under the elect’s feet and to save them efficaciously—and that from God’s own most firm promise.
notes_covered: Arg. 4 Ultimo open; Gen 3:15; Rupert De victoria verbi Dei 2.18; Marlorat; Satan under elect feet

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 4: Isa 53:10–11 long-lived seed—Luther, Calvin, Musculus on elect Church
english: Isaiah 53:10–11 gives a like promise of God the Father about the efficacy of Christ’s death for the elect. The words run: “If he shall put his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed; and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. For the travail of his soul he shall see and be satisfied,” and so on. By these words the Father promises the Son that his passion and death will not be useless or barren, but will surely yield him seed. I ask, then: does this promise look to vague, indefinite individuals, or to certain persons singularly known to the Father and to Christ the Mediator? To invent a confused promise of some who will be saved, yet not yet singularly designated by God himself, is most unworthy of divine perfection and wisdom. But if God and Christ have settled that this seed will be efficaciously saved through Christ’s death, it follows that in the dying Christ there was, with respect to their salvation, an efficacious and singular intention. All interpreters of the place have taken it so: that through Christ’s death a most efficacious and certain liberation and salvation was promised to his mystical body—that is, to the Church, or the elect. So Luther: the posterity or seed spoken of is the Church; “he shall see seed” means he will have a kingdom and royal children. So Calvin: “he shall see seed” means Christ’s death will be the cause of begetting offspring, because the One who died, making alive, will acquire a people of his own. Musculus agrees, explaining “from the travail of his soul he shall see and be satisfied”: Christ already saw this bond of the elect and those to be saved, still sees it, and will see it to the world’s end, and is satisfied in seeing, because the Father’s good pleasure is directed in his hand. All agree that from the Father’s special good pleasure an efficacious salvation of the Church—certain persons known to God alone—was promised to Christ as the price of his passion, and that Christ intended and labored with a singular, efficacious will to save these elect, this peculiar people singularly given and committed to him by the Father.
notes_covered: Isa 53:10-11; long-lived seed; Luther/Calvin/Musculus; elect Church as promised seed

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 4 objection (Grevinchovius) and reply: tacit promise of faith to the elect
english: If someone objects with Grevinchovius that there was no absolute promise or will of God to redeem any particular persons efficaciously, but that God willed and refused the application of Christ’s death to each and all only conditionally—willing it for all if faith intervened, refusing it if unbelief mediated—and that therefore, even when Christ laid down his life, his death might be applied to no one, and he might be cheated of the promised seed by everyone’s intervening unbelief: the reply is that in this promise by which the Father as it were bound himself to the Mediator to give him seed if he put his soul for sin, there is contained a tacit promise of faith to be given to the elect themselves; without that faith they would not be Christ’s seed. So it was as much decreed that God, because of the Son’s death, give faith itself to some, as that he give the Son an everlasting offspring. Christ, foreknowing this promise and counsel, could not but offer the sacrifice of his death to the Father with special intention for this seed, for these future believers. So far we have argued from express Scripture testimonies; next we will add some reasons also grounded in holy Scripture.
notes_covered: Grevinchovius conditional application objection; tacita promissio de fide; bridge to rationes

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 4 Ratio 1: secret covenant (Jer 31:33 / Heb 8)—Mediator for elect Israel alone
english: He who by his death not only established that evangelical covenant looking promiscuously to all—“Whoever believes will be saved”—but also that secret covenant which takes in certain singular persons known to God alone, described by the prophet in Jeremiah 31:33: “This is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after these days: I will put my law in their mind and write it on their heart, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people”—he who procured such a covenant by his death offered his death and merit to the Father to be applied efficaciously to certain elect persons. That is clear, because putting his laws into people’s minds, writing them on their hearts, and making them God’s peculiar people marks the efficacious application of Christ’s merits and names the privileges of the elect, or spiritual Israel. I add the minor and affirm that by his death Christ was Mediator of this secret covenant, which includes application and embraces God’s Israel—or the elect children of God—and them alone. Besides the prophet’s words just cited, we have the Apostle citing the same prophet (Hebrews 8:6): “Our High Priest is Mediator of a better testament, established on better promises.” What are those better promises Christ the Mediator established? Verse 10 rehearses them in Jeremiah’s own words; they reduce to two heads—the promise of an inward reforming of hearts, and of free remission of sins—as Calvin notes on the place. So by his death Christ merited remission of sins for all if they believe and turn; and for some he also merited and procured this free, secret covenant to be fulfilled by the promising God—namely that they believe and turn to God, through and because of the Mediator reforming their hearts efficaciously and putting his laws into them. Those for whom he merited this (as Augustine makes plain) are all who belong spiritually to the house of Israel and Abraham’s seed: what else is that than all the elect? So from God’s and Christ’s intention the elect have had destined and given to them the special benefit of a fruitful application from Christ’s death.
notes_covered: Ratio 1; Jer 31:33; Heb 8:6-10; Calvin; Augustine spiritual Israel; elect application

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 4 Ratio 2: precious blood not left to chance—Malderus on elect fruit
english: A second reason is the price paid on the cross for redeeming the human race. That price was the blood of God’s Son, the only-begotten and beloved. It is not credible that so great a price was spent on an outcome dangling from the uncertain dice of human choice. So the Father and Christ the Mediator meant by this precious death to redeem and save certain people infallibly and efficaciously; and those can be none other than those who are in fact saved—the elect. Therefore Christ’s intention in offering himself regarded the elect in a special way. I know Grevinchovius and others of that school boldly claim the proper end of impetration God intended was only that he might save the sinner with his justice intact, and that this redemption obtained for all might still be applied to none because of everyone’s intervening unbelief. That is as much as to say God gave the Son to death with no certain purpose of saving anyone by that death’s merit, but only a bare possibility of salvation procured for all in general, leaving efficacious share in salvation to each person’s choice—so that Christ’s death, taken in the whole breadth of its merit, might have redeemed no one from death. But whoever weighs how precious the Son’s death was in the Father’s eyes cannot even think he meant to expose the Son to death without a certain purpose of applying that death efficaciously to some. Isaiah 53:10: “The will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.” Hear Malder, a papal writer far sounder than the Arminians here (Anti-Synod, p. 138): if you look only at the offering itself, it is equal for all; otherwise, if you look at that for whose actual obtaining he offered. For the elect obtain the perfect fruit of his passion that actually follows and is applied, as given them by the Father for this. So Christ’s blood could not run to waste; by the price of his blood, from God’s decree, he merited for the elect the fruitful application of that same price.
notes_covered: Ratio 2; precious blood vs alea arbitrii; Grevinch impetration; Malderus Anti-Synod 138; Isa 53:10

title: Cap. 7 Arg. 4 Ratio 3: Spirit’s gifts prove special intent—Heb 7:25 Savior of certain ones
english: Whatever spiritual, saving good Christ’s Spirit works in any people, Christ’s poured-out blood merited for those same people. But Christ’s Spirit produces in certain persons repentance and faith, and through faith and repentance an infallible application of his death. Therefore he merited these special goods for those same people; therefore, sacrificing himself on the cross’s altar, he meant to merit them. It is not right to suppose by chance that Christ procured greater spiritual benefits for these than for those. What will the adversaries say? That Christ’s Spirit gives people benefits Christ never merited for them? They will not dare so to trample Christ’s merit. That faith itself, the will, and the act of fruitful application are not special gifts of the Holy Spirit? They will blush at so crass a Pelagianism. Let them confess with us: just as through Christ’s death special goods were procured for the elect, so in the will of the dying Christ, and of the Father accepting that death, there was an efficacious intention to procure and confer those goods. And that is the singular privilege in Christ’s death we claim for the elect alone, because the fact shows God destined them alone to be saved efficaciously by his Son’s death. Hence Hebrews 7:25 establishes the office of Savior of certain ones—that is, of the elect—both by merit and by efficacy.
notes_covered: Ratio 3; Spirit faith/repentance; anti-Pelagian; Heb 7:25 Servator quorundam; before Quartum

title: Cap. 7 Quartum: sufficienter / efficaciter—death for elect by absolute saving will
english: A fourth argument is the distinction most received among all theologians: that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously. Just as from the first half we refuted those who deny that Christ’s death, by God’s decree, is an applicable remedy for all people, so from the second half those must be refuted who deny that Christ’s death, and that by God’s decree, is a remedy to be applied to the elect efficaciously and infallibly. What else can “He died for the elect efficaciously” mean than that he died with an absolute intention and efficacious will to save the elect?
notes_covered: Quartum open; sufficienter/efficaciter distinction; absolute intention for elect

title: Cap. 7 Quartum: not contingent human will—Suarez on intended efficacy
english: If someone twists the distinction as if Christ’s death, sufficient for all, became efficacious for some only by a contingent act of human free choice, the words themselves refute him: “Christ died efficaciously for these or those” marks a singular efficacy flowing from the dying one’s special will, not from the believer’s contingent act. Second, even the Jesuits do not take “efficacy” in this distinction as mere eventual efficacy, but as efficacy specially intended and merited by the dying one himself. So Suarez (On 3, disp. 41, p. 629): Christ did not merit remission of sins for all as to efficacy, because he did not apply his merit so that all would infallibly gain that effect. To merit efficaciously is to apply his merit to certain persons with the intention that they infallibly obtain eternal life from it. More plainly (p. 635): Christ’s merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy—understood not only in the effects (in one, not another) but also in the will by which Christ offered his merits differently for different persons. Scripture’s witnesses that join Christ’s death to a sure purpose of redeeming his sheep, gathering God’s sons, acquiring the Church, and cleansing a peculiar people show that the efficacy theologians speak of is drawn from the dying Christ’s will, not from contingent free choice. By a special intention in his offering Christ obtained that it be made efficacious for the elect; the elect did not make it efficacious for themselves by some free-choice apprehension.
notes_covered: Anti-contingent-arbitrium twist; Suarez disp. 41; sufficiency vs efficacy; sheep/Church purpose

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 5: predestination requires special saving regard—Scotus / Malderus
english: Ratio 5. From divine predestination we take a fifth reason. Given the predestination of certain persons before the world’s foundations, Christ’s will in offering himself must include a special regard for producing their salvation efficaciously by the merit of his passion. Whether we place election before or after the decree of the passion (as we understand the order), this stands: in Christ’s will—whether about to suffer or already suffering—there was an efficacious, singular intention to save these elect (or to-be-elect) efficaciously. His will never fails to conform to the Father’s. So it is incredible (as Suarez notes, On 3, disp. 41, §2, p. 615) that he offered his merits one way for those he knew the Father had chosen and another way for the rest, when he saw the Father’s will that they—and not others—be saved infallibly, and conformed himself to that will in all things. Isaiah 53:10 points here: “The will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand.” Election to eternal life from God’s free will is executed through Christ’s merits; therefore the Redeemer specially and efficaciously destined his meritorious death for these elect to be redeemed and saved infallibly, and offered it to the Father. Scotus puts it well (Book 3, dist. 19, p. 74): Christ foresaw his passion offered to the Father for the predestinate and elect, and so offered it efficaciously in effect; the whole Trinity accepted it efficaciously for them, and for no others was it efficaciously offered or accepted from eternity. By efficacious offering and acceptance he means offering joined to an absolute purpose to save those for whom it was so offered and accepted. Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, on this argument rejects those who think Christ died equally for all as to efficacy, and concludes (p. 137) that, given predestination, Christ by his death conferred far more on these predestinate than on others.
notes_covered: Rat. 5 praedestinatio; Suarez; Isa 53:10; Scotus dist. 19; Malderus Antwerp

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 6: offering matches intercession—John 17 / Suarez / Vázquez
english: Ratio 6. Sixth, keep the proportion between Christ’s offering for people and his prayer or intercession for them. From John 17, and from his named prayer for Peter that Peter’s faith not fail, it is plain that Christ interceded with the Father for the elect to keep a firm, unconquered faith to the end and obtain salvation efficaciously. Anyone who denies that the gift of perseverance was won for special persons by Christ’s special prayer would credit free choice with the greatest of all spiritual benefits. That granted, I add: just as Christ specially prayed for special benefits for the elect, so he specially offered himself to merit those same benefits. On this special prayer and offering Suarez says (On 3, disp. 41, p. 635): as Christ prayed in different ways for people, so he merited in different ways; though he is universal Redeemer of all and a sufficient cause of salvation, in a special mode he is the efficacious cause of salvation for those he makes obedient. So the prayer by which he specially and efficaciously prayed for the elect rests on the offering by which he specially and efficaciously offered himself for them. See the force: whatever Christ obtains for particular persons by special intercession, he merited for them with the Father by an offering specially pertaining to them. By intercession he obtains for the elect faith, perseverance, and salvation itself; therefore, to procure those goods for them infallibly, he specially offered himself for them. Vázquez does not doubt (On 1, q. 23, art. 5, disp. 94, ch. 3) that by peculiar prayer and will Christ applied his merits to those who were predestinate and elect.
notes_covered: Rat. 6 oblatio/oratio proportion; John 17; Peter; Suarez; Vasquez ST I q.23

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 7: death as medium tracks God’s diverse saving will
english: Ratio 7. Christ’s death and merit is the means God ordained to carry out his eternal counsel for human salvation. If God’s will stands differently toward effecting people’s salvation, then Christ’s death is likewise intended and applied differently toward that end. Means always serve the end, and the mode of application follows the agent’s intention. All sound theologians confess that God does not will everyone’s salvation in the same mode in which he wills some people’s. Therefore he did not will the means—Christ’s death—applied to all as it is applied to some. So for those for whom God by efficacious will decreed salvation, Christ’s death was destined so that by its merit everything needed to produce salvation infallibly would flow to them; for those for whom he did not so decree salvation, Christ’s death was not destined in that same mode. From the Father’s special intention in ordaining that sacrifice, and from Christ’s self-offering conformed to the Father’s will, the death is understood as destined and applied one way to the elect, whom God decreed to save infallibly through it, and another way to the rest, whom he allows to perish by their own fault even with this death. Whoever denies that discrimination in the offering and application can as easily deny that the wisest and most powerful God knows how—or is able—to intend and fit the means he instituted to different people as his will’s different reason requires.
notes_covered: Rat. 7 medium for eternal counsel; diverse will → diverse intention/application

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 8: fruitful application proves antecedent intention—Phil 2:13 / John 15:5
english: Ratio 8. The event shows that some people really and efficaciously apply Christ’s death, with its infinite merit, to themselves for salvation. Was that application made according to Christ’s antecedent, efficacious intention in offering himself on the cross—or against it, or without it preceding? If they grant in the dying Christ an antecedent special will for this efficacious application that falls to all the elect and to them alone, we have what we aim to prove: that by God’s and Christ’s special intention this death is destined for the elect as to be applied efficaciously. No one will say a person can apply Christ’s death to himself efficaciously against Christ’s intention. The only remaining claim is that people make the application efficacious by free will without any preceding special, efficacious intention of the divine will. Piety forbids that. First, in good and saving acts God’s efficacious will stands before the human: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2:13), and he works nothing in us antecedently that he did not antecedently decree to work. Second, in works that belong to salvation we can do nothing without Christ: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). What we can do through Christ we receive power to do because of Christ’s merit—which, without the dying and meriting Christ’s antecedent special intention, is assigned to no one. So whoever has obtained this excellent grace and already applied Christ’s merit to himself efficaciously must confess he received that applying faculty above others from the special kindness of God and of Christ, who specially intended, destined, and applied his merit to him. The fruitful application in the predestinate itself shows that in Christ offering himself, and in God accepting the sacrifice, there was a special efficacious intention of that application for the predestinate. And that is the singular privilege of the elect in Christ’s death this thesis aims to establish.
notes_covered: Rat. 8 event application; Phil 2:13; John 15:5; antecedent intention; elect privilege

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 9: without merited application elect have no privilege—Bannes / Rom 8:32
english: Ratio 9. Suppose Christ’s death, by God’s ordination and Christ’s intention, did not merit for the predestinate an efficacious application and the infallible obtaining of salvation that flows from it. Then this follows: the Mediator’s merit, under the Father’s accepting will and the Son’s exhibiting will, regards the elect no more than the passed-by, but reaches both alike. The consequence is clear, since it is granted that by God’s will the dying Christ’s merit extends to all under the condition: if by faith they apply it to themselves. Unless Christ by his death also meant to merit for the elect that, through faith given, this fruitful application be made in them, no singular privilege in his merit is assigned to them. By God’s ordination Christ’s death merited for Judas that he could, under the condition of faith, reach eternal life; for Peter it obtained besides that, because of Christ’s merit, he receive persevering faith and all other spiritual benefits required to obtain eternal life infallibly. Paul’s reasoning in Romans 8:32 looks here, treating the predestinate’s privileges: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things?” Just as he had hinted a special calling of the predestinate—“according to purpose”—so he marks a special offering of Christ for those same predestinate, an offering according to purpose: with a sure purpose to confer efficacious grace on the elect and lead them infallibly to life by this death’s merit. Those who erase that discrimination of divine intention in Christ’s death toward elect and passed-by, as Báñez truly says (On 1, q. 23, art. 5, pp. 296–297), make Christ’s merit no more perfect a cause of the predestinate’s salvation than of the reprobate’s. As to sufficiency the merit regards all equally; the difference is that it is applied to some and not to others. So if application itself for the elect does not fall under Christ’s merit, that merit regards predestinate and reprobate alike. So Báñez.
notes_covered: Rat. 9; Judas vs Peter; Rom 8:32 offering according to purpose; Bannes ST I q.23; before Rat. 10

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: without absolute elect-saving will grace no better prepared than in Adam
english: Ratio 10. If Christ did not offer himself to the Father with a peculiar absolute will to redeem and save the elect efficaciously by his death's merit, then efficacious grace and eternal life would be prepared or given to no one in Christ on any better footing than they were in Adam. The first Adam already gave the race the chance of grace and eternal life under a condition that hangs on our free choice.
notes_covered: Rat. 10 open; absolute elect-saving will; Adam parity premise

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: conditional-only merit leaves us no better off in Christ than in Adam
english: So if by his death Christ did not merit grace and life for anyone absolutely, but only for all alike under the uncertain condition that they choose to receive the offered grace, believe in him, and persevere in faith, leaving to each person's free choice whether to believe and persevere, then we would be no better off in Christ than we were in Adam. That is so as to how and how surely we obtain efficacious grace and eternal life.
notes_covered: conditional merit; free choice left decisive; no better condition in Christ

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: Adam parity contradicts Scripture’s sure purpose of good pleasure
english: But that clashes with Scripture. Scripture hangs the grace and eternal life prepared and to be given in Christ to all who will be saved on God's sure purpose of good pleasure, not on a contingent turn of human choice. The treatise on Election and Passing-by will show this.
notes_covered: Scripture; purpose of good pleasure; Election & Praeteritione forward ref

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: Augustine De corrept. & grat. 11—grace in Christ makes us will
english: It also clashes with the orthodox Fathers who opposed the Pelagians—above all Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace chapter 11. After showing what grace was given to the first Adam, he says of the grace prepared and given to the predestinate in Christ: “So much more largely is the help of grace given through Jesus Christ to those to whom God was pleased to give it, that it not only is present—without which we cannot remain even if we will—but also is so great and of such a kind that we will. For through this grace of God, in receiving the good and holding it perseveringly, there is in us not only the ability to do what we will, but also the will to do what we can.”
notes_covered: Fathers vs Pelagians; Augustine De corrept. & grat. 11; Adam vs Christ grace

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10 close: elect-only fruitful application by special decree via Christ’s merit
english: This grace, given for Christ's sake to the elect alone, and producing in them alone the fruitful application that saves, flows to them not from some special act of human choice but from a special decree of God's will, and that through Christ's merit. So Christ's merit was destined for those same persons in a special way by God, and applied by Christ himself.
notes_covered: elect-only grace; special decree; merit destined/applied; Rat. 10 close

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 11: equal divine efficacy left to human will is near-Pelagian
english: Ratio 11. We must reject any view that is the same as—or at least close kin to—the condemned Pelagian dogma. Those who hold that on God’s will and intention Christ’s death stands equally efficacious toward all, while on the human will’s side it happens that in the event it becomes fruitful for some, come as near Pelagius as can be. The orthodox, roused by Pelagius to weigh this carefully, have always taught against him that fruitful application of Christ’s merits hangs on the grace of predestination, by which faith and even the good will itself are mercifully given to some and, by God’s just judgment, denied to others.
notes_covered: Rat. 11 open; near-Pelagian equal efficacy; predestination grace

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 11 close: Prosper/Hilary/Augustine/Fulgentius on special saving purpose
english: That it is Pelagian to shift the fruit of Christ’s death—eternal life—from God’s special intention to a special act of free choice is plain from Prosper’s Letter to Augustine. Hilary’s Letter to Augustine shows the same: the Pelagian remnants treat eternal life in Christ’s death as so set before all that they flatly deny any singular purpose of God to save the elect by that death, and put the whole divide between the saved and the unsaved down to human wills. Against them, the orthodox saw a special hidden purpose in God accepting Christ’s death-sacrifice and in Christ offering it—toward efficacious fruitful application to certain persons. That is clear from Augustine’s On the Predestination of the Saints, On the Good of Perseverance, and his other anti-Pelagian and anti-Semipelagian books, where the special will to save the elect through Christ is if not the only then the chief conclusion. Prosper and Fulgentius say the same throughout: efficacious obtaining of salvation in Christ comes from God’s efficacious special will destinating Christ to the elect in a special way, not from human free choice applying Christ’s death and merits to itself as chance may have it.
notes_covered: Prosper; Hilary Reliquiae; Augustine Pred./Persev.; Fulgentius; before ultimum Patrum

title: Cap. 7 ultimum Patrum: open — Augustine In Joh. tract. 48 on sheep/price
english: Lest we seem to argue by empty labels, our last proof comes from the express witnesses of the Fathers and of later writers who give the predestined, in this death of Christ, a special privilege — nothing other than the sure attainment of grace and glory by God's special ordination, drawn from the dying Christ's merit and from his offering himself for them with a particular regard. Let Augustine speak first. 1. Outstanding is the word in In John, tractate 48 (vol. 9, p. 352): How did he say of those, YOU ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP? Because he saw them appointed to everlasting ruin, not bought for eternal life by his blood's price. Soon after: Of those sheep neither wolf snatches, nor thief carries off, nor robber kills. He who knows what he gave for them is sure of their number. Two points follow: first, our Savior offered his blood's price for redeeming the predestined in a special way — the way from which their sure salvation follows; second, for the passed-over or non-predestined he did not offer it that way, so they are denied to have been bought for eternal life by that price — meaning an absolute, efficacious ordering to eternal life that Christ's death is to carry out and bring into act.
notes_covered: ultimum Patrum & modernorum open; Augustine In Joh. tract. 48; sheep/price; absolute efficacious ordination

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Augustine Serm. 56 — came to redeem the predestined
english: 2. Closely related is Sermon 56 On the Lord's words (vol. 10, p. 194): The predestined were not yet gathered. Still, he who had predestined them knew them, and he who had come to redeem them with his blood knew them. He saw them while they did not yet see him; he knew them while they did not yet believe in him. Nothing is clearer: Christ came into the world to redeem the predestined by his blood — and to redeem them efficaciously and infallibly as people to be brought through to share eternal life. He never resolved with himself to redeem the non-elect in that way.
