notes_covered: Augustine Serm. 56 De verbis Domini; redeem predestined; never non-elect that way

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Augustine De natura & grat. 5 — vessels of mercy only
english: 3. A third witness from the same Augustine is On nature and grace, chapter 5: Those who are delivered are called not vessels of their own merits, but vessels of mercy. Whose mercy, if not his who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners? Whom he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified. As if to say: by a decree of special mercy God sent Christ to deliver and save the predestined efficaciously and infallibly — and in that sense they alone are vessels of mercy. Piling up more Augustine would be wasted work. Anyone at home in him knows his teaching on the absolute predestination of some to eternal life, and on the eternal gift of those same persons to Christ the Mediator so that he may lead them to that life without fail. That predestination, gift, and leading cannot be understood — or even thought — without this special intention of applying his death and merits to them. See On the Predestination of the Saints 18; On the gift of perseverance 7; On rebuke and grace 9.
notes_covered: Augustine De natura & grat. 5; vessels of mercy; Pred. Sanct. 18 / Persev. 7 / Cor. & grat. 9

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Ambrose — suffered for all, specially for the Church
english: 4. Ambrose supplies a fourth witness: And Christ suffered for all, yet for us he suffered specially, because he suffered for the Church. So she who received more doubtless owes more (On Luke, book 6, chapter 7). On Ambrose's reading, the suffering Christ had a special regard for his Church, and from that she drew a special fruit of the passion. He can say Christ suffered for all, and still hold that the will and intention of the suffering Christ does not regard everyone alike, but turns in a singular way upon his mystical body — the Church of the firstborn — which he meant by his blood to make his own and by the Spirit to join to a share in eternal life that cannot fail. He did not suffer for all under that special intention.
notes_covered: Ambrose On Luke 6.7; suffered for all / specially for Church; mystical body

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Remigius — Son delivered for predestined elect alone
english: 5. After Ambrose comes Remigius of Rheims on Romans 8: Those he predestined — or marked out beforehand — to reign with him in eternal blessedness he also called and justified through his passion, through baptism and faith adorned with good works, and he justified them to the world's end. Soon after, on Who did not spare his own Son, Remigius says: he did not keep him from death, but delivered him for all of us predestined to eternal life. That shows Christ suffered for the elect, and for them alone, with a fixed purpose to save them — the very special intention we are establishing, and which we insist must be limited to the elect alone in this offering of Christ.
notes_covered: Remigius Rhemensis on Rom 8; Son delivered for predestined; elect-only special intent

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Fulgentius — special will and predestination in Christ
english: 6. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and grace of Jesus Christ 29 (Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 6, p. 92): Those who treat God's will that all be saved as the same toward the redeemed and the damned — when asked why God wills all to be saved and yet not all are — what answer have they? Fulgentius implies that God by a special will decreed to procure, through Christ, the salvation of those who are in fact saved; and that their opponents have nothing solid left when pressed to explain why some are actually saved by Christ's death and others are not. He shows this difference cannot be reduced to a difference of human wills (chs. 30-31). 7. Another from the same Fulgentius, On the truth of Predestination, book 3: No Christian should doubt that those God predestined to the adoption of sons were predestined in Christ before the world's foundation not only to the reward of glory but to the grace of justification, and by that predestination's benefit called and justified according to purpose. Anyone who grants that God's elect sons were so predestined in Christ to grace and glory will freely admit that Christ's death and merit were ordained and accepted in a special way for those same elect, so that from them they might obtain without fail the grace and glory marked out for them.
notes_covered: Fulgentius Incarn. & grat. 29-31; De verit. Praed. 3; special will; elect predestined in Christ

title: Cap. 7 Patrum close: Paschasius, Gregory, Bernard before Scholastics
english: 8. Paschasius (Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 9, p. 930) on Matthew 1:21, He shall save his people from their sins: Hence Zechariah says, And he made REDEMPTION OF HIS PEOPLE IN THE HOUSE OF DAVID HIS SERVANT. So the people he foreknew as his he surely came to save; all the rest he left, by his hidden judgment, in the mass of damnation. That teaches Christ came and died with a special intention to save the predestined — an intention he did not have for making others' salvation actual, even while he willed to make salvation obtainable for all under the condition of faith. 9. Gregory the Great, Morals 22.18 (p. 132): For the Only-begotten to intercede for man is to present himself as man before the coeternal Father; to ask for human nature is to have taken that nature up into his Divinity's height. So he intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because what he would not have damned in the elect he set free by taking it up. Those last words show plainly that in his whole Mediator's work Christ kept a special eye on freeing the elect without fail. 10. Bernard on Psalm He who dwells in the help of the Most High, verse 9: Christ died for friends — that is, for friends to be won, to make friends out of enemies. A little later: So according to time Christ died for the ungodly, but according to predestination for brothers and friends — as much as to say that Christ dying on the cross had a singular regard for his predestined brothers and future friends.
notes_covered: Paschasius Matth 1:21; Gregory Morals 22.18; Bernard Qui habitat; before Sed missis Scholastics

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici open: Sed missis — Lombard sufficienter/efficaciter
english: Setting the older writers aside, we come down to the Scholastics and modern Romanists. They defend Christ as having died for all, yet they also grant he died for the elect alone with a special intention to apply that death to them so that eternal life follows without fail. 1. Start with Peter Lombard, master of the Scholastics: Christ offered himself on the cross's altar for all as to the price's sufficiency, but for the elect only as to efficacy, because he effects salvation only for the predestined (Sentences 3, dist. 20, litt. c). The reason he gives for calling Christ's death efficacious for the elect alone is worth marking. He does not say what Pelagians and Arminians would say — that only those were foreseen who, stirred by grace in free choice, would apply Christ to themselves — but that in them alone, by the kindness of special mercy, he wrought salvation. What his death wrought in the elect he surely decreed to work. That is the special intention under which we say Christ's death is related and ordained to the elect alone.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-lombard

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Aquinas — eternal ordination completed through Christ
english: 2. Aquinas (ST III q.24 a.4): God preordained our salvation by eternally predestining that it be completed through Jesus Christ. He is speaking of the elect, and he holds that from eternity God ordained their salvation to be finished through Christ without fail. How then could Christ have matched that eternal ordination of his Father if, in his saving passion, he did not apply his merits in a peculiar way to effect and complete the elect's salvation without fail? So we must grant a special intention — God accepting this victim, Christ offering himself — restricted to the elect alone, so far as Christ's passion is joined to an infallible saving effect in particular persons.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-aquinas-st

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Aquinas on merit — sufficiency vs efficacy; John 10:15
english: 3. The same Aquinas, On the Grace of Christ (disp. q.), art. 7 ad 4: Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy. That inequality comes partly from free choice, partly from divine election, by which the effect of Christ's merits is mercifully given to some and justly withheld from others. When he says free choice partly explains unequal efficacy, read that of the lost, who turn themselves from the fountain of salvation. When he says divine election partly explains it, read that of the saved, who, under God's special mercy according to election's good pleasure, receive from that fountain whatever is needed to effect their salvation. His reply to the last objection shows the mind: God freely confers on people that they obtain the effect of Christ's merit. If election mercifully gives that effect to some and denies it to others, who can doubt that Christ — knowing election and his own calling — specially offered himself and his merits for those persons, and added to a price already sufficient in itself a most effectual, singular will to work their salvation? John 10:15 points the same way: I lay down my life for my sheep — with a singular intention to redeem, free, and bring them to life, as the whole discourse there shows.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-aquinas-gratia

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Scotus and Hugh of St Victor on elect-directed passion
english: 4. Scotus (Sentences III, dist. 19, single q.) has much that illustrates our view. First: just as the Word foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the elect, so he offered it effectually unto its effect, and the whole Trinity effectually accepted that passion for them; for no others was it effectually offered or eternally accepted. So Scotus grants that by the Trinity's eternal decree Christ's passion was offered and accepted for the elect in a singular way, with special intention. 5. Hugh of St Victor (On the Sacraments I.8.7), treating Christ's passion: Human nature was corrupted by sin and wholly owed to damnation; if all had been damned, that would not have been injustice. But grace came and chose some from the mass of the whole by mercy unto salvation, and left some by justice unto damnation. Hugh teaches plainly that Christ, coming and offering himself for the race's sins, kept a singular eye on the elect he chose from that mass, whom he decreed — and in fact always does — to bring to salvation by his death's merits according to God's eternal good pleasure.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-scotus-hugo

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Cajetan on Romans 8 — special donation to the elect
english: 6. Cajetan on Romans 8: He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things? Paul saw that the earlier chain of gifts did not yet prove effectually that God works all things for the elect's good — only that he works with them unto good. So, to conclude ALL THINGS effectually, he added that God freely gave even the Son for the elect, and from that inferred that with the Son all things are given to them. Cajetan's words cannot be bent to a universal gift of Christ given equally to the whole world: if that were so, God would give all things equally to every human being — which is plainly false. A special donation must be granted, under which Christ is given to the elect alone, and which alone carries after it an infallible, most certain gift of everything needed for salvation.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-cajetan

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Stapleton and Estius — efficacy for future friends / elect
english: 7. Stapleton (Moral Promptuary, Second Sunday after Easter, p. 254): Dying, Christ died effectually for friends alone — for friends-to-be after each one's conversion, not for those who were already friends. This Romanist does not shrink from granting Christ's dying a singular intention toward the elect. They are the future friends after conversion for whose effectual redemption he laid down his life while, with the rest, they were still ungodly, enemies, sinners, dead in sins. He is said to have died for all humans as to sufficiency; for his sheep — his elect — as to this efficacy, that is, with a singular intention, from his death's merit, to give them the effectual grace by which they believe and are saved. 8. Estius on Titus 2:14, Who gave himself for us: that is, who in assumed flesh delivered himself up, whether for all humans or specially for the elect, in whose person Paul often speaks. Christ's death-price suffices to redeem and save all, yet is applied unto salvation to the elect alone. Estius thus hints two things: Christ's offering had a general respect to all and a special to the elect; and that special respect must be defined as joined to an intention of applying it with certainty. He did not say the elect alone apply Christ's death to themselves by free choice's powers, but that it is applied unto salvation to them alone — by electing God, intending this good for his elect from Christ's death by special favor.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-stapleton-estius

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici close: Suarez and Vasquez before Reformed Theologi nostri
english: 9. Next the Jesuits. However they defend universal grace and universal redemption, they dare not deny this special, effectual ordination and intention of the saving passion toward the elect alone. Let two chiefs speak: Suarez and Vasquez. Suarez on Aquinas III q.19 (Disp. p. 635 §41): as Christ prayed diversely for humans, so he merited diversely — for some sufficiently, for others effectually. So though he is everyone's universal Redeemer and a sufficient cause of salvation, in a special way he is the effectual cause of salvation for those he makes obedient. It is incredible he offered his merits no differently for those he knew the Father had elect than for others, when he saw the Father's will was that they be saved without fail, and not others. Suarez thus grants that Christ's death and merits save the elect from the special mode of offering and the offerer's will — not from a chance act of human will laying hold of them. 10. Vasquez clearly owns this special intention toward the elect in applying his merits (on Aquinas I q.23, disp. 49, c.3, p. 687): I do not doubt Christ by peculiar prayer and will applied his merits to those predestined and elect. The same on Aquinas III q.19, disp. 77, c.5, p. 384, cites Andreas Vega: Christ's merits do not profit all effectually, because for those they do not profit he did not pray effectually or offer his passion. So not only the old Fathers but even newer Romanists confess what we aim to prove: God constituted Christ's death a universal saving cause applicable to all, yet by a special intention of offerer and accepter it is also a particular saving cause to be applied without fail, and singularly, to all and only the elect. See also Malderus, Antisynod, p. 138.
notes_covered: cap7-scholastici-suarez-vasquez

title: Cap. 7 Theologi nostri open: Postremo — Bucerus on Matt. 1:21 elect
english: 11. Last, our own theologians. They do not deny that Christ suffered for all, yet they also confess that in his death he redeemed the elect under a peculiar regard. Bucer states it on Matthew 1 at He shall save his people — that is, the elect whom the Father himself brings to him. By his death he expiated all the elect's sins and merited that the propitious Father give them his Spirit. So Christ's death merited something for the elect that he did not merit for others. Whatever he merited for anyone, he merited under the Father's ordination and acceptance. From that Fatherly will and ordination, then, Christ's death belongs to the elect in a special way that does not reach the rest.
notes_covered: Cap.7 Theologi nostri Bucerus Matt.1

title: Cap. 7 Theologi nostri: Musculus — electorum gratia Christ came
english: Musculus, who in the Common Places presses hard that Christ must be held universal Redeemer, still grants Christ's special intention to redeem the elect. On Romans 8 he says Christ came into this world for the elect's sake — which can only mean he came with a peculiar intention to save the elect without fail. That special aim, securing for the elect the applied fruit of his passion, belongs to them so properly that it does not stretch to others.
notes_covered: Cap.7 Theologi nostri Musculus Rom.8

title: Cap. 7 Theologi nostri: Calvin — Heb. 2 children given; three notes
english: Calvin on Hebrews 2 at Behold I and the children God has given me: Christ brings none to the Father, he says, except those the Father himself has given him. That gift hangs on eternal election: those the Father destined for life he places in the Son's keeping to guard them. Mark three points. First, the Father from the election decree has singularly destined some for life. Second, Christ the Mediator received those elect as peculiarly entrusted to him by the Father. Third, Christ keeps a singular care of them, guarding and ruling them in this life until he brings them to eternal life. With that set down, it would offend all reason and piety to deny that, in the very work of his offering and of mankind's redemption, Christ intended these elect's salvation by a peculiar intention — absolute and effectual.
notes_covered: Cap.7 Theologi nostri Calvinus Heb.2

title: Cap. 7 Theologi nostri: Zanchius — sufficiently for all, efficaciously for elect
english: Zanchi (Miscellanies, On the Predestination of the Saints, p. 14): it is not false that Christ died for all men — his passion is offered to all in the Gospel. Yet he died efficaciously only for the elect, because they alone share the passion's efficacy. That they alone so share it must be referred to the special, effectual will of Christ suffering and of the Father accepting this victim — for the elect in a more peculiar way than for others. In sharing saving good, the divine will goes before the human.
notes_covered: Cap.7 Theologi nostri Zanchius Miscellanea

title: Cap. 7 Theologi nostri: Vorstius — Amica duplic peculiar redemption sense
english: Finally — not to weary by stacking more writers — even Vorstius could not deny that the redemption finished on the cross belongs to the elect in a peculiar sense. In the Friendly Duplicate (p. 230) he grants that redemption can be taken in different senses for several species of the same kind, so that some only, not all, may fitly be called redeemed in a special reason or peculiar sense, as Scripture often names them. On p. 235, answering Hebrews 13:20 (Christ the great Shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant), he concedes Christ is Shepherd of these sheep, and of these alone, in a peculiar way: as to the saving, spiritual act of feeding them (which includes the actual gift of the Holy Spirit), and as to a special acquisition of those sheep. So far Vorstius.
notes_covered: Cap.7 Theologi nostri Vorstius Amica duplic

title: Cap. 7 Theologi nostri close: Vorstius critique — Bridegroom/Head/Shepherd intent
english: What exactly does Vorstius grant us when he allows that not all but some were redeemed by Christ's death in a special reason and peculiar sense, and that Christ is Shepherd of his sheep in a peculiar way as to a special acquisition? If he means only that, in the outcome, by diverse acts of human wills, redemption's fruit reaches some — that is, believers — in a special way, he trifles and never answers the texts brought against him. For He purchased the Church with his blood; He gives salvation to his body; He lays down his life for his sheep; He died to gather God's children — these and like sayings do not mark some special act of the Church, body, or sheep. They mark the Bridegroom's, Head's, and Shepherd's special intention and work toward this Church, this body, these sheep, decreeing and securing their salvation by his death's virtue and merit under a special will.
notes_covered: Cap.7 Theologi nostri Vorstius critique close

title: Cap. 7 Contra open: Obj. 1 — mercy vs justice in elect application
english:
Against all we have argued about Christ's special dying intention toward the elect, and about the saving application of his death that hangs on and flows from that intention, objections can be raised.

1. If Christ's offering carries an intention limited to the elect, and from it they receive efficacious application and sure salvation, then we seem to ground their justification and salvation less in God's eudokia and special mercy than in a kind of justice. Ask why Peter rather than Judas received efficacious grace and salvation from Christ's death, and on our view the answer must be: because by special intention and application of his merits Christ merited for Peter what he refused to merit for Judas. Yet what comes from Christ's merits peculiarly applied to one person seems to come not from bare mercy of Divine good pleasure, but from justice — for it is just that what Christ merited for these or those persons be specially assigned to them. That seems to clash with the Apostle, who traces the grace and sure salvation of the predestined to God's pure grace alone.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 1: mercy fulfilled through Christ's merits
english: These two claims do not clash: God justifies and saves Peter by pure grace — his mere eudokia — and God justifies and saves Peter with an eye to Christ's merits specially ordained and accepted for Peter's salvation. The reason is plain. The same God who, from bare good pleasure and pure mercy, decreed faith and salvation for Peter also decreed to give them only through and because of Christ's merits, destined and granted to Peter in a singular way — and that from the same eudokia and pure mercy. God's eudokia stands against our merits; yet through Christ's merits applied to us it is filled out, not voided. So the Apostle says (Hebrews 13:21) that God himself works his good pleasure in us through Jesus Christ. It is therefore mere Divine eudokia that God wills to give Peter efficacious grace and save him; still that good pleasure is carried out only through Christ's merits. Our whole answer comes to this: every work of special grace in the elect is for Christ's merits specially applied to them, yet their justification and salvation show true mercy, not justice — because Christ, with his merits and with this very way of meriting and offering them under a special regard for the elect, drew the whole plan from God's free will toward them.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 2: merits applied before faith?
english: Suppose the elect gain efficacious grace — saving faith — because Christ's death and merit on the cross were applied to them by a special intention. Then we seem to allow the merits of his passion to be imputed or applied to some people before they believe. That clashes with the received theological rule that faith is the instrument or means without which Christ's passion-merits are not applied to particular persons. So whoever has Christ's merits singularly applied or imputed must already stand as a believer. How then can we defend this special application of Christ's merits to the elect before they are made faithful and believing?

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 2: God-side application; Scotus on joining the unjoined
english: To meet the objection, take Ephesians 1:3 as foundation: God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ — that is, every saving good that comes down from God is given through Christ and for his merits. Saving faith, proper to the elect, ranks among the chief spiritual blessings; so it is granted, for Christ's merits, to all who in fact receive it. When theologians say faith is the instrument by which Christ's merits are applied to us, they mean application on the human side: the elect cannot apply those merits to themselves for any spiritual benefit unless faith is already presupposed in them. But if we view application or imputation from God's side alone, God can and does apply — impute and communicate — Christ's merits to people so that, with regard to those merits, he gives spiritual goods even while they still count as ungodly and unbelieving. Faith, when first given, is not given to a believer but to an unbeliever; yet it is given to the elect for the Mediator's merits. So we must confess: no elect person could, by believing, apply Christ's merits to himself for eternal life's fruit unless God, from special mercy and for that merit of Christ, had first infused the faith by which they would believe. That is the special application of Christ's merits which, from Christ's special will in offering himself and the Father's in accepting the sacrifice, we say belongs to the elect by a peculiar privilege. Scotus saw this in a saying worth marking: the chief thing in Christ's merit was that he merited the joining of the unjoined (lib. 3, dist. 19, unique q., p. 75) — as if to say the main force of those merits is that some from among unbelievers should become believers and, joined to Christ by faith, obtain eternal life. That special ordination and application of Christ's merits hangs wholly on God's good pleasure, not on human choice.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 3 + Sol.: OT elects and meritorious cause
english:
Obj. 3. If Christ in offering himself, and God in accepting that sacrifice, had a special intention to vivify and surely save all the elect by that sacrifice's virtue and merit, we seem to shut Old Testament elect out of the privilege — those born and dead before Christ's sacrifice was shown on the cross.

Sol. On general sufficiency or special efficacy I answer: Christ's sacrifice had the same virtue under the Old Testament, before the outward act of exhibition, that it has under the New after Christ was really shown and offered on the cross. Just as special grace reaches New Testament elect from God's special intention by the merit of this sacrifice already actually exhibited, so special grace flowed to Old Testament elect from the same God's special will by the merit of that same sacrifice still to be exhibited. For Christ was the Lamb slain from the world's beginning, both in the readiness of his will and in the Father's acceptance. Note the difference: a cause that works physically or naturally must already be in act before its power yields an effect; a cause that works meritoriously or morally — such as Christ's passion — can yield an effect before it actually exists, if it at least stands beforehand in the knowledge and acceptance of him who, with regard to it, dispenses the benefits of his grace. Here a meritorious cause is kin to a final cause: not yet existing in act, but only foreseen and weighed, it still moves the agent to act. So we say Christ's passion and its dependent merits, foreseen as to be offered to God and applied specially to Jacob, not Esau, moved God to give Jacob the special grace he denied Esau. Suarez puts it well (In 3, q. 49, art. 4, comm.): that special love by which, for Christ's merits — exhibited or foreseen — God sanctifies and reconciles people can fall under Christ's merits, whether by meriting for us the effect of that love, or God's love (or election) freely fixed on us.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 4: incongruity of faith given only to elect
english: Obj. 4. Last comes this charge: it is hardly fitting — indeed plainly incongruous — that God, who willed Christ's death, with its rich treasury of merits, to be equally applicable to all under the condition of faith for obtaining eternal life, should meanwhile refuse to prepare and give that same faith, for those same merits, equally to all, and should give persevering saving faith to the elect alone — and that for Christ's merits by a special Divine intention, a special regard restricted and ordained toward them.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 4: three reasons; Rupertus and Ambrose
english: I answer: once a Divine fact stands, it is rash — not to say impious — to quarrel with its equity or fittingness. We have long shown that by Christ's death that covenant with the human race was fixed, by whose terms eternal life is promised to anyone under the condition of faith. On that covenant Rupert of Deutz (on Genesis 4.34) says: we call it a covenant many times promised but once struck, by which alone the enmities between God and humankind are dissolved — namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. There peace is settled without contradiction when God, receiving human faith, gives people the same Christ his Son that they may be saved through him. So there is no doubt about this Divine ordination, founded in Christ's death and merits and looking to every person. What is still doubted is whether, given this universal covenant of eternal life for all who believe, God may freely show special mercy in giving the elect the saving faith by which they believe — and that through Christ, for his merits applied to them by a peculiar privilege. The fact itself speaks. We see the elect alone, in the outcome, receive from God persevering saving faith. To imagine so great a gift given them in any other way or regard than for Christ's merits, ordained and applied by a special Divine intention, is plainly unlawful. As Ambrose says devoutly, every gift of grace is in Christ — pointing to Ephesians 1:3, He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. That settled, though it is needless to debate the fittingness of Divine deeds when the deeds themselves are clear, still, to leave no scruple: first, this special intention by which God decreed, for Christ's merits, to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation does not fight the conditioned covenant Whoever believes will be saved; it is rather a special counsel subordinated to that universal covenant's sure fulfillment. Those left to their own choice under any helps of grace either push faith away or shake it off. Lest that universal covenant bring salvation's effect to no one, God by this special and secret intention saw to it that Christ's death-merit would be applied to some for the sure obtaining of faith and eternal life. Second, nothing unjust or incongruous follows if this special intention of efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all: Christ's death is God's free gift to the human race, so free distribution and application of the overflowing merits ought by every right to hang on God's mere will. Third, God, who in the Gospel promised every person eternal life for Christ's merits if they believe, never promised any unbeliever that for those merits he would make him believe surely and perseveringly. So where is the incongruity? Not on the side of believers and the saved: to give singular persons, for Christ's merits, what was never singularly promised them is not blameworthy injustice but goodness to praise. Not on the side of the unbelieving and lost: to deny someone a benefit you owe him by no title is neither unjust in itself nor unfit for God's highest goodness.

title: Cap. 7 close: sufficient for all, efficacious for elect — Amen
english: Let this be the sum and close of the whole controversy On the Death of Christ. The Mediator between God and humankind, Jesus Christ, in sealing that evangelical covenant by which eternal life is due to every believer, made no partition or sorting of people by which we could say anyone was shut out from the benefit of his death if he believed. In that sense — with Scripture, the Fathers, and solid reasons agreeing — we hold that Christ suffered and died on the cross for all human beings, for the whole human race. We add this too: the same Mediator, when he decreed to lay down his life for sin, also had this singular intention — that by the virtue of his merits he would efficaciously and surely vivify and bring to life certain ones singularly given him by the Father. In that sense we defend that Christ laid down his life for the elect alone, or to acquire his Church — that is, he died for them alone with this singular, fixed purpose of efficaciously regenerating and saving them through the merit of his death. So Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, yet not as to efficacy — and that not only from the effect, which lands in one and not another, but from the will by which Christ himself merited and offered his merits in different ways for different people. The first root of that diversity was Divine election and will, to which Christ's human will conformed. From this Suarez rightly draws that this merit of Christ is the cause of spiritual regeneration itself, gives it efficacy, influences its effect, and is at once the cause that this person is regenerated for whom he specially offered his merit (In 3, q. 19, disp. 41, §2, p. 635). Let Robert of Salisbury, of rare learning and pious memory, speak for our side (in Thomson's Diatribe, p. 94): though we do not deny that Christ died for all, yet we specially and properly believe he died for the Church, and that redemption's benefit does not belong to all by equal right. On that benefit's peculiarity — not on human will — hangs the efficacy of every means, so that they are and are useful only for those whom Christ redeemed in himself as elect under a peculiar regard; nor do they take effect because we will, but because in the elect and redeemed, according to the purpose of his grace, God works the willing for which he chose them. He who by his death most sufficiently merited eternal life for all — to be given to all under the evangelical covenant if they believed — also, by a peculiar application of his merits, most efficaciously merited for some that they should believe and receive eternal life as God's free gift through and for our Lord Jesus Christ. That is the elect's peculiar lot. May the Father of mercies make us all partakers of it; to him, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, be honor, praise, and glory now and forever. Amen.

title: De praedestinatione: title — Rom 9:18 and Calvin
english: A DISSERTATION ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. By the Most Reverend John Davenant, lately Bishop of Salisbury, formerly Professor of Theology in the University of Cambridge, delivered in the Theological Schools to his hearers. [[Romans 9:18 >> Bible:Romans 9:18]]. Of whom he wills, he has mercy; and whom he wills, he hardens. Calvin on Romans 9:18: There is scarcely any doubt that Paul speaks here in his own sense — that God, by his own free decision, shows mercy to whom he chooses, and draws the severity of judgment against whomever he pleases. Printed at Cambridge by Roger Daniel, University Printer, 1650.

title: Prefatio: return to theological labor; scope of the inquiry
english: Preface delivered to the University. What the poet said of farmers — "The finished labor returns for farmers in a circle" (Georgics 2) — fits theologians still more truly, especially those whose chair itself demands labor and sweat, not leisure or quiet. So I will enter these rounds of theological work that my office requires, eager and willing; and I will ask God first to steer me through the whole course of this undertaking so that I do not swerve even a little from the fixed center of sacred truth. The work I take up is steep in itself and blocked with many difficulties. For what is higher, or farther from human sense, than that eternal decree of Divine predestination by which, before the world's foundations were laid, we confess that certain ones were chosen before others — indeed with others plainly passed by — to share eternal life in Christ? We have given our labor to explaining that business, yet under this rule: let no one of you expect that I will touch every question theologians treat in this matter (that would be immense labor, and superfluous too), or any of those curious little puzzles by which unhealthy little men torture themselves, vex others, and finally obscure and twist the Christian faith. Steady faith rejects captious and useless questions; and whoever truly hears as a believer shows himself devout toward Divine wisdom, not craving his own (Hilary, On the Trinity 1; so also Tertullian, On the Resurrection). In this inquiry, then, we will set ourselves only a few of the most necessary points, and we will not dig deeper than Scripture's light lets us go. If we keep to that rule, Augustine rightly judged that this doctrine of predestination should be taught not only among the learned but also to the people (On the Perseverance of the Saints 2.16), and that it can be said so as to be milk for little ones and solid food for the grown.
notes_covered: Georgics 2
Hilary De Trinitate 1
Tertullian De Resurrectione
Augustine De perseverantia sanctorum 2.16

title: Prefatio: preach free election; Pontifical reduction of the mystery
english: If we follow Paul's steps, imitate holy Augustine, and hold the doctrine received in this our Church, there is no danger of scandal. But if we let the doctrine of free election be overwhelmed and buried — or, worse, if we calmly endure it when certain Papal writers and others have badly corrupted it and twisted it the other way — that lazy silence will not escape suspicion. A ready defense of the truth would meet us if published falsehood displeased us. None of you, I think, fails to see that many Papal writers have reduced this whole mystery of election and reprobation — at which Paul stood astonished — to an all-too-clear and easy account of the difference, teaching that some are chosen from foreknowledge of merits, others rejected from foreknowledge of demerits.
notes_covered: Paul
Augustine
Pontificii on merits-foreknowledge

title: Prefatio close: Arminian fabric; elect unto faith; Anglican defense
english: And what hurts more: from the Arminian school new teachers have come out who try to shake the catholic Church's most settled doctrine, and to raise I know not what new fabric of election and reprobation, wholly unknown to orthodox churches. What Papists assign to foreseen works, these assign to foreseen faith and unbelief. So they think they have secured Divine justice if, before the world's foundations were laid, God is said to have chosen only those he foresaw would believe the offered call and persevere in faith to the end; and, on the other side, to have reprobated only those he foreknew would refuse grace, remain unbelieving, and die in unbelief. Fine theologians indeed — who bring in a man already justified by faith, already set in adoption and salvation, before God has predestined him or chosen him to salvation in Christ! Splendid heralds of Divine grace — who will not trace the difference of good and bad wills in believing or not believing to the electing God's special mercy toward believers, but strain to refer whatever difference there is to a contingent act of free choice in admitting, keeping, and exercising grace. How much better — and closer to the Apostle's mind — is Augustine, scourge of the Pelagians (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By choosing he makes them rich in faith, as heirs of the kingdom." So after Pelagius arose, Augustine and Catholics generally held and ratified this: people were chosen not from works but unto good works, not from faith but unto faith. That is: the elect became faithful and eager for good works; they were not chosen because God foresaw they would be such. This doctrine must be defended in the schools and preached in the churches. When Papal writers pour out their error's poisons everywhere, let us with no less care prepare antidotes for our own. Aristotle's saying is known. Let us also count it shameful to fall silent in God's cause while enemies of the truth shout against us on every side with writings and noise. Lest neighboring error's contagion seize ours too, I will, according to my slender measure, undertake to explain that most true doctrine which this Church of England has commended to all her people to embrace in the matter of predestination. And as far as I can I will refute those sophisms by which adversaries try to overturn the Church's sound teaching and to settle their new inventions.
notes_covered: Arminian school
Augustine De praedestinatione sanctorum 1.17

title: Cap. 1 Prolegomena: four points before the controversy
english: Chapter I. Prolegomena. But so that this whole matter may come into the light more easily, it will not be out of place to set a few things before the dispute itself — things whose explanation will open the way into this controversy. First: in questions of predestination or reprobation the very order of our thought breeds the sharpest fights, while one claims that in God's intellect and decrees this is prior which another holds is posterior. So we must speak briefly of this whole account of priority and posteriority under the diverse signs of reason. Second: because the words Election, Predestination, and Reprobation are used differently by different writers, we must explain the force of the words themselves, and show in what sense others take them, and in what sense we do. Third: because writers argue differently about the qualities or conditions of the subject, it will be worth setting out what is absolutely required and presupposed in the subject of predestination or reprobation when that subject is considered in common. Last: besides the common conditions required equally and without distinction whether someone is made the subject of predestination or of reprobation, some place further distinguishing qualities or conditions, by whose difference the act of Divine predestination falls on one and the act of reprobation on another. Those too must be weighed for what force they have. For some who refer the difference of election and reprobation to such things — whether our qualities or our acts — still will not let them be called causes, much less merits, and only grudgingly allow them even to be named conditions of our predestination. But let us gird for the work, and begin from those signs or distinct instants that theologians usually assign and separate according to prior and posterior order in the acts of both the Divine intellect and the Divine will.
notes_covered: four prolegomena heads
signs of priority

title: Prolegomena I: one eternal act in God; James 1:17; Ambrose and Hilary
english: First, then, this must be known and held: if we consider God's nature and perfection in itself, he does not first see one thing and then another, nor first decree or will this and then that. By one most simple act from eternity he has seen all things at once and decreed all things at once in himself. The firmest ground is Divine immutability — [[James 1:17 >> Bible:James 1:17]]: with God there is no change, or shadow of turning. Those words shut every change — in being or in working — out of the Divine nature. If we imagine God acting by turns in those operations understood as immanent in him, so that he first understands this then that, first wills this then another, we place in God a move from potency into act — which contradicts his most absolute simplicity. So Ambrose is right (or whoever wrote book 2 of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 10): In God there is no accident, motion, new will, or temporal counsel; his thought is not varied by the inequality of changeable things; he comprehends all times and temporal things together with an everlasting, steady gaze. Hilary agrees: he denies piecemeal thoughts of things in God, and holds that all things stand with God in the even infinity of eternity (On the Trinity 12, p. 193). Every Scholastic and theologian I have seen assents — except one Vorstius, whose ravings are not even worth refuting in a theological school.
notes_covered: James 1:17
Ambrose De vocatione Gentium 2.10
Hilary De Trinitate 12
Vorstius

title: Prolegomena II: signs of priority among decrees; Scotus, Occam, Biel, Bannes
english: Second: although every act in God's mind and will is eternal, and so not parted even by the lightest instant of before and after, still, from the side of the things God understands and has decreed, certain signs of priority and posteriority can be marked — according to our way of understanding. In that sense theologians ask whether God first decreed to give the elect eternal life, or faith and obedience that lead to eternal life; and whether he first reprobated some and cast them from eternal life before he foresaw them fallen and stained by sin. Hence nearly everyone who has written on predestination and reprobation draws a kind of series, almost a little table, trying to sketch the order of the Divine decrees — not because they judge that in God himself one decree is really before or after another, but because, given the ordered dependence of the things in themselves, our intellect ought to conceive one before another. Yet among the Scholastics themselves this teaching about those signs or instants of before and after — props by which our weak reason steadies itself when it thinks of God's decrees — is not very fixed or constant. Scotus, the chief craftsman of these signs, seems to some not only to have set them as prior and posterior in our mode of understanding, but also to have held that one is prior by nature to another in God himself — as if that before-and-after order could be assigned from the nature of the thing in the Divine acts themselves. But when I read carefully what Scotus teaches on these signs (1 Sent. dist. 41 q. unica; 3 Sent. dist. 7 q. 4 and dist. 19 q. unica), he seems to me to teach only this: that in the things themselves there is some foundation from which we conceive that one decree of God is to be set before another by a certain order of our reason. From the other side our Occam denied these signs however considered (1 Sent. dist. 9 q. 3); and Biel, taking that view, attacked them (3 Sent. dist. 2 q. 1 dub. 3): "Priorities are not to be placed in Divine things, any more than pluralities of ordered acts. For there is one act in Divine things, indistinct in reality and in reason, which is the Divine essence itself; by that one cognition God foresaw Christ's incarnation, the future beatitude of all the elect, the fall and the repair — not one before, another after." And he adds at once that not even according to our consideration can such an order of before and after be conceived in the Divine decrees without that consideration becoming a false speculation. Dominic Báñez, though he does not wholly explode these signs with Biel, still weighs the theologians' discord in assigning them and says: notice how freely, in the business of predestination and reprobation, theologians multiply instants, and how little those help assign the account of the difference between the predestined and the reprobate. So let this brief warning stand: do not trust too much, or cling as to fixed dogma, to any certain order of the Divine decrees, whether drawn by Protestants or by Papal writers. It is hard to find two — among ours or among adversaries — who agree to the line in every point when they describe this series of Divine decrees. Let each take care not to bring in a view of predestination and reprobation that runs against Divine justice or free grace; and since these decrees are in reality altogether simultaneous in God, it matters little in what order of before and after we distribute and arrange them according to our mode of understanding.

title: Prolegomena III: order founded in things' dependence; final vs efficient cause
english: Third: because our intellect is weak, we are often forced, when explaining predestination, to conceive something as before and something as after — as when we think God first considered the human being as fallen, before as elect in Christ; or when we say God first destines a person to eternal life, before to efficacious grace. So let us see where this order of before and after, which we mark in the Divine acts, is founded. Not in God's knowledge or will considered in itself: in Divine things all are simultaneous in duration. It is founded in the relation of the things themselves, insofar as one depends on another. Therefore, in our mode of consideration, that is prior in the Divine mind and will from which another hangs in the order of causality; that is posterior which hangs from another. If one stands wholly independent of another, neither is prior or posterior to the other. Next, mark carefully: the same thing can be prior and posterior to another in different kinds of cause. Compare an efficient or dispositive cause with a final one. In the kind of final cause, health is prior to the drug: it moves the physician to give it and the sick person to take it. But in the kind of efficient cause the drug is prior to health: by its virtue and efficacy the sick person is brought back to health. So in predestination: the will to give eternal life is conceived prior to the will to give efficacious grace in the order of final cause — for from the intention of giving life arises the decree to give such grace. But in the order of efficient cause the will to give grace is prior, and grace is given so that by its virtue and efficacy going before, the person may be led through to glory. That is what the Philosopher hints (Ethics 3.8): what is last in intention is first in execution, and the reverse. The reason is plain. In the act of willing and intending, that has the account of a cause which by desire and love of itself moves the agent to seek and apply such means; but in the act of executing, that has the account of a cause which advances the end itself and works toward obtaining it. So Báñez: the end which in the agent's intention has the account of a cause with respect to the means, when set in execution has the account of an effect, and the means themselves have the account of an efficient cause toward it. Mark this well: although in reality there is one and the same act of will in God by which he wills both means and end, the end through the means, and the means for the end, still in our mode of understanding all these are distinguished — and hence the tangled questions which of them is prior or posterior in the Divine will. To meet those questions, always weigh what order of causality the things themselves have among themselves: they are understood to carry the same order of priority. Add this too: although in the acts of the Divine will as to the thing there is no before or after, God does not will created things in a confused, unordered heap. It is true that in God there are not many volitions, nor one prior to another; yet by one most simple act of his will he willed one thing to be for another, and one to depend on another. Hence that consideration of before and after which properly belongs to the things themselves is attributed by us to the Divine decrees. So whenever the dispute is about God's knowledge — asking of two which he knew first — or about his will — asking of two which he decreed first — always remember: this priority or posteriority does not inhere really, truly, and formally in the acts of the Divine mind and will themselves, but is considered from the side of the things God has known and decreed, among which he willed a true and real before and after. And for our purpose, that is enough on this point.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Electio — Scripture senses (nation / office)
english: 2. Let us now explain the three words that will keep returning through the whole dispute ahead. First is Election. Scripture uses that word in more than one way. Sometimes it means setting a people apart to share the word and the ordinary means by which people are led to salvation. So God is said to have chosen the Jewish nation and passed by the other nations. "The Lord your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, out of all the peoples," and so on ([[Deuteronomy 7:6 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 7:6]]). Sometimes the same word means setting a particular person apart for an office in the state or in the church. So God is said to have chosen Saul as king of the Jews: "See whom the Lord has chosen" ([[1 Samuel 10:24 >> Bible:1 Samuel 10:24]]); and Christ chose the Twelve as apostles: "Did I not choose you, the twelve?" ([[John 6:70 >> Bible:John 6:70]]). Those elections are not our question now. Still, in them and in every case of the same kind, election always means taking someone — or some — out of a larger number for a special end the agent intends.

John 6:70

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Electio proper — glory; Thomas; vs praedestinatio
english: The election we must treat, then, is the singular act of the Divine will that from eternity sets certain ones apart for the end of glory — eternal life — and passes others by. Thomas rightly notes that this election, like love, is presupposed to predestination. All the predestined are understood as elect and beloved: beloved insofar as God wills them the good of eternal life; elect insofar as he wills them that good and does not will it to others. Taken properly, election looks only to the end: it is God's will to confer glory on particular persons while passing others by. Theologians do sometimes blur election with predestination. When the words are kept apart, election belongs chiefly to the end itself; predestination belongs to the means — as we will now show.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Praedestinatio — dual use; school sense
english: I turn next to Predestination. Theologians sometimes — though rarely — use that word for a bad end too: destination to death. So Augustine on John, Tractate 48: How did he say to them, "You are not of my sheep"? Because he saw them predestined to everlasting ruin, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood. And in City of God 15.1 he says there are two cities or societies of human beings: one predestined to reign forever with God, the other to suffer eternal punishment with the devil. Augustine's disciples Prosper and Fulgentius sometimes speak the same way. The Fathers at the Council of Valence even confess a predestination of the elect to life and a predestination of the ungodly to death. We, following what has nearly become school usage, narrow "predestination" and "the predestined" to that special providence of God by which from eternity he proposed to secure, by efficacious means, the salvation of those he chose in Christ — and, matching that eternal purpose, he works their salvation in time efficaciously and without fail.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Praedestinatio — two acts; Augustine; Aquinas arrow
english: In predestination, then, we can mark two acts: one of the Divine will, one of the intellect. The will's act is to will salvation for this particular person, to choose him before others, to show him mercy and not show mercy to others — an act Aquinas (as we noted earlier) treats as prior to predestination and calls election. The intellect's act is to foreknow, and to direct these particular persons by infallible means to the end destined for them. That second act is where predestination proper chiefly lives. Augustine's description fits here: Predestination is nothing other than God's foreknowledge and preparation of the benefits by which whoever are set free are set free with certainty. So by predestination we always mean that part of Divine providence which directs its elect by infallible means and leads them through to eternal blessedness. How necessary this is becomes clear once you see that the life of glory surpasses what human nature can reach: free election to that end is not enough unless Divine wisdom and power also supply fit, infallible means that guide us there. Aquinas's likeness is not strained. An arrow is first aimed at a mark by the archer's purpose; then by his power, through the bow, it is sent toward that same mark. So every person destined from eternity by God's purpose for the mark of eternal life is, in time, by that same power, through efficacious grace, directed to glory's goal and at last brought there. That whole account of transmitting the elect into eternal life — as it is understood to stand from all eternity in the Divine mind — is what we call predestination.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Reprobatio — Scripture voice vs school sense
english: On the opposite word, Reprobation, a few points. As for the bare term, Scripture's "reprobate" and "to reprobate" point more to the present state of the ungodly than to God's eternal decree about them. ἀδόκιμος — a reprobate — is one who lives ungodly, does not carry himself as a son of God, and by his deeds shows himself counterfeit, spurious, adulterate. God is said to reject or reprobate such people because of that impurity, as goldsmiths throw out counterfeit coins. Even in Augustine — who treated this matter more richly and clearly than the other Fathers — "reprobate" and "reprobating" in the school sense barely appear, or do not appear at all. Still, the thing itself is plainly in Scripture. First, when Scripture affirms what forces the reprobation of some by clear necessary consequence: as when certain named persons are said elect and predestined by God before the world's foundations were laid. Election of some imports passing by — rejecting — others. Second, when equivalent phrases express the decree: God is said never to have known some, not to have given them to Christ, to refuse mercy to some, not to have written some names in the book of life — and the like, which plainly prove that from eternity the Divine mind and will marked a difference between elect and non-elect. Finally, though Augustine and the other Fathers seldom use the school word "reprobation," they use other words that mean the same. Those the School calls reprobates, they call foreknown and predestined to destruction.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Reprobatio — opposite act; Bannes; negative vs positive
english: Drop the bare word; come to the thing. As to elect and to predestinate name that eternal act of the Divine will by which God decreed to direct certain persons to blessedness they will infallibly reach, so to reprobate names the opposite act: the decree to permit certain persons to fail and fall short of that end. That fits providence itself — which allows some defect in the things under its care. See Aquinas, ST I q.23 a.6. In reprobation we mark two quasi-acts of the Divine will. The first is unwillingness to elect someone to blessedness obtained without fail. Why that act lands on Judas rather than Peter has no reason on the reprobate's side; it is referred to the liberty of the Divine will. So Báñez: in the particular case, why God chose these and reprobated those has no adequate cause but the Divine will. In the same article he says this predestination of some and reprobation of others manifests the greatest liberty the Divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods — and that liberty is a great Divine perfection. The act we call passing-by or non-election, Bellarmine calls the negative act of reprobation. Guard this point: do not follow Scotus in treating God's will toward the reprobate — whom he does not choose but passes by — as merely negative. In the act we name by a negation there is an expressed, affirmative will of God; it does not mean God simply suspends willing about their falling short of blessedness. Read that act affirmatively, not only negatively. Passing-by / non-election involves affirmative decrees: I will to permit Judas to fall short of eternal life; I will and decree not to give Judas that special grace which, if he received it, would bring him to eternal life. So much for the first act. The second is to destine to punishment. That act terminates on the reprobate as foreknown and foreseen stained by sin — and that from the fault of his own will. Scotus calls this privative reprobation; Bellarmine, the positive act of reprobation. It designates the will to damn the reprobate person. Note also: God shows the reprobate certain effects that do not flow from their reprobation — that they are created, called to know the Gospel, illuminated with supernatural knowledge. Those are effects of common love and common providence, not of reprobation.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Reprobatio effects; against Pelagian calumny (Prosper)
english: The proper effects of negative reprobation are these: unwillingness to decree the efficacious liberation of a person lying under damnation; and the will to deny that person the efficacious helps by which he would in fact be converted. The last effect is the eternal punishment of the obstinate sinner. That does not properly rise from mere passing-by or non-election, but from the other reprobation-act one may call pre-damnation — which presupposes foresight of sin and leaving the person in it. Weigh this too: reprobation's effects are not chained to one another the way predestination's are. In predestination the earlier effect usually causes the later — efficacious calling begets faith, faith justification, and so on. In reprobation the effects are not ordered that way, though taken together they serve one end: the shining of Divine justice. Finally, against certain malevolent slanders, mark this: In the fallen human being, sins such as unbelief, wickedness, and hardening — and the penalty due them, eternal damnation — follow reprobation as infallibly as faith, holiness, and perseverance follow predestination; yet they do not follow in the same way. Acting from the decree of predestination, God works those earlier goods by the influx of efficacious grace. From the decree of reprobation he does nothing that makes the reprobate worse, nothing that blocks believing and holy living, nothing that drives him into unbelief or wickedness. Watch that carefully. Old Pelagians and new alike see that, given reprobation as we have described it, none of the reprobate perseveres in faith or holy life — and they cry at once that we make God the author of sin and the cause why people do not believe or spring back from faith and holiness. With the Prophet we answer every reprobate: your destruction is from you, though help is from God alone. Reprobation takes nothing from the reprobate's own power; God simply does not put forth toward him the efficacious power he could put forth if he willed. So Prosper long ago: God despoils no one of the possibility of the good. It does not follow — as the objectors think — that those to whom God has not given penitence he has robbed of repentance, or that those he has not lifted he has struck down, and so on. Reprobation causes in a far different way from predestination. God predestinating works every good in the predestined by grace's influx, and is properly called an efficient cause. God reprobating works no evils in the reprobate by subtracting grace; the evils break out from nature's corruption — and God is no more their cause than the sun is cause of darkness when it does not light the air. So much I thought should be set down first on election, Predestination, and reprobation.

title: Cap. 1 subject: Tertio — rationality as common condition
english: III. Third: the qualities or conditions of the subject taken commonly and without distinction — what must clothe that subject on which the Divine act of predestination or reprobation, taken without discrimination, terminates. First, beyond dispute: for either act to fall on any subject at all, that subject must be endowed with a rational nature. Rationality is therefore a necessary condition always to be supposed in the predestined or the reprobate. The reason is plain to anyone. Both predestination and reprobation are God's decree about the supernatural end of eternal blessedness, and brute nature cannot be capable of that end. So when we say someone is ordered to blessedness by predestination, or shut out of it by reprobation, both must be understood of a rational creature. What is clear need not be long.

title: Cap. 1 subject: sin-infection debated — Scotus / Suarez before foresight
english: Another quality most writers treat as necessarily presupposed in predestinating and reprobating — though not all agree: the infection of sin, which they think God foresaw in the subject before it could be predestined or reprobated. On their view rationality is not enough; the creature must also be presupposed a sinner, stained with sin. I do not gladly make this quarrel my own; still I will open briefly what others hold and what I hold. We must admit that the opinion which puts predestination before foresight of sin is neither new nor the property of obscure theologians. Nearly everyone who took predestination as bare designation to the end itself, rather than preparation of means, reasoned this way. Scotus, ordering instants in the Divine mind and will, always set the will to give beatitude before foresight of the fall (I dist. 41; III dist. 19 q.1): God first wills glory for a fixed number of elect, next orders grace for them, then foresees their fall in Adam. With Scotus stand many who claim the Scotist name. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonso Mendoza, and countless others teach the decree of predestination prior even to permitting the fall — and prior to creating man. So they do not treat foresight of sin as a condition of the subject on which predestination falls. Among recent Jesuits Suarez follows the same line and calls it the common opinion: I judge more probable the theologians' common view that the election of the predestined preceded permission of original sin.

title: Cap. 1 subject: angels prove election before stand/fall; Thomas terminus
english: That God can elect and reprobate before any foresight of sin is plain in the angels. Those who stood were elect; those who fell were passed by or reprobated — and that before any foresight of standing versus falling. Before the decree to create or save them, God knew which angels, given such grace, would in fact persevere and reach eternal blessedness, and knew which would infallibly fall if given only the grace he later in fact gave. Why give the good angels grace he knew would bring them to glory? Only because a will to save them — election or predestination — came first. Why give the wicked angels grace he knew, taken alone, would leave them to perish? Because a will to permit their falling short of blessedness came first: otherwise he knew and could have given them, no less than the others, grace that would have carried them infallibly to glory. So toward the angels God's will to elect some and not others did not arise after foresight of who would stand or fall; it is rather the cause of that different outcome, and prior in order. Election and passing-by therefore do not, from the nature of the acts themselves, necessarily presuppose foresight of sin in the subject — not in angels. Nor does it seem necessary in humans to place foresight of sin as a condition in the subject prior to the decree of predestination and reprobation. Thomas notes rightly: motion takes its species from the terminus to which, not from the terminus from which. As whitening does not care whether the thing whitened was black, pale, or red, so predestination does not care whether someone is destined to eternal life from a state of misery or not. On Thomas's showing the act of predestination can fall on a subject not yet tangled in sin's misery.

title: Cap. 1 subject: Aquinas on reprobation/permission; Calvin not inventor
english: Aquinas even seems to lean toward saying reprobation in fact preceded foresight of original sin. When he calls reprobation that part of Divine providence which permits some to fall short of beatitude, he implies that permission to fail from the means that lead to beatitude flows from reprobation — and so, in our way of understanding, is posterior to it. If permission to fail follows reprobation, then foresight of the actual fall follows all the more: it is foreseen only on the hypothesis of permission. I bring this in not because I cling to that opinion, but to touch in passing the ignorance — or malice? — of those who curse Calvin or Beza as if they invented a view no less current among Scholastics and even Pontificians than the contrary view that puts the sin-infected human as predestination's subject. As for Calvin (so far as I can judge): he rightly denies that foresight of sin is the cause of predestination or reprobation; yet with Augustine he always holds that consideration of foreseen sin stands before God as he predestinates or reprobates — as a common condition of the subject. Clear words: If all whom the Lord predestines to death are by natural condition liable to death's judgment, if all are taken from a corrupted mass, no wonder they lie under damnation. Hear clearer still. After Paul taught that God from a lost mass elects and reprobates whom he wills, why and how so little helps that, terrified, he breaks into O the depth! (Tractate on God's eternal predestination, p. 711). Beza, Zanchi, and other learned men speak more harshly and set consideration of the corrupted mass wholly after the decree of predestination — yet they never think anyone's damnation decreed except on presupposed sin.

title: Cap. 1 subject: bare election vs means — Davenant's judgment
english: My judgment in brief. First: if by Predestination you mean bare designation to the end of glory (as many older Scholastics do), and by Reprobation only the negation of that act — the decree to pass by and not elect — I do not think foresight of sin must be supposed as something prior in the subject so predestined or reprobated. Why? In God's mind and will no act is really prior to another; all before-and-after is taken from the mutual dependence of the things themselves. Where the things have no causal dependence, Divine decrees about them admit no before or after. Sin is altogether beside the point for the act of Divine election or non-election. It is not the reason of either act (all confess that), nor a qualification of the subject without which those acts cannot fall — as rationality is; the angels already showed that. Since sin is neither cause why someone is elect to glory or permitted to fall short of it, nor a disposition required for either act, it is improper to say the decree to elect or not elect is prior in God's mind to foresight of sin — and improper to say foresight of sin was prior to that decree — for among independent things there is no before or after in God's mind or will. Those who try to blacken, with I know not what horrid consequences, the view that considers election and passing-by without foresight of sin are twisting ropes out of sand.

title: Cap. 1 subject: Scripture sense — means & praedamnatio presuppose sin
english: Yet Scripture and Augustine, glory of the Fathers, do not take predestination and reprobation as bare election to the end, or bare passing-by. With the decree to give the end they join the decree to prepare and give certain, designated, infallible means; with the decree to permit falling short of the end they couple another — to punish and damn forever the one who fell short. For that reason I judge it better, fitter, and in this sense truer that foresight of sin be presupposed as a condition of the subject on which such a decree of predestination and reprobation falls. In Scripture predestination usually means not bare designation to glory's end, but destination to glory through means — and not any means, but means of efficacious grace derived from Christ our Head and Mediator. So Ephesians 1:4: he chose us in him that we should be holy; 2 Timothy 1:9: he saved us according to his purpose and the grace given us in Christ before the ages. From these and many like them it is plain the Apostle means destination and direction to glory's end by infallible means of efficacious grace from Christ. Augustine, as everyone knows, takes predestination as preparation of the grace that leads infallibly to glory: Predestination is the preparation of God's benefits by which whoever are set free are set free with certainty. So Aquinas describes it as special providence ordering and directing the elect to salvation's end not by any means, but by means that produce the event infallibly. Take it thus: Predestination in Scripture is not an abstract decree about the end alone, but a compounded decree — to give eternal life through means of grace in Christ. Reprobation in Scripture's use is not bare passing-by or non-election, but pre-damnation — appointment to destruction — bound inseparably to non-election, at least as to the event. Scripture calls the reprobate vessels of wrath fitted for destruction ([[Romans 9:22 >> Bible:Romans 9:22]]); formerly marked out for condemnation ([[Jude 4 >> Bible:Jude 4]]). Augustine calls reprobation predestination to destruction. Under "reprobation" we must include not only the bare decree to pass by, but also the will to pre-damn. That kind of predestination and reprobation cannot be conceived or explained rightly unless sin is preconceived as a common condition in the subject.

2 Tim 1:9

title: Cap. 1 subject: reasons — Christ medicus; media; justice — common close
english: That can be shown by these reasons. First: predestination of humans to eternal life includes giving certain ones to Christ as Physician and Life-giver, and freeing them from the stock and head of old Adam, corrupter and killer of his posterity. So Scripture: "Those you gave me I have kept" ([[John 17:12 >> Bible:John 17:12]]); "Behold, I and the children God has given me" ([[Hebrews 2:13 >> Bible:Hebrews 2:13]]); "He chose us in Christ" ([[Ephesians 1:4 >> Bible:Ephesians 1:4]]); "Those who are well have no need of a physician" ([[Luke 5:31 >> Bible:Luke 5:31]]); "While we were still weak, Christ died for the ungodly" ([[Romans 5:6 >> Bible:Romans 5:6]]); "If many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many" ([[Romans 5:15 >> Bible:Romans 5:15]]). From these we gather: in the decree of predestination all the elect were given to Christ as Redeemer, Life-giver, and their future Physician. But a redeemer presupposes a captive, a life-giver a dead person, a physician a sick one — so those predestined in Christ the Redeemer are considered by God as such. As any act presupposes an object, such an act presupposes such an object: the acts of redemption, vivification, and healing, all included as future in our predestination or election in Christ, presuppose an object to be redeemed, made alive, healed — which is nothing other than one corrupted by sin. So Augustine (Serm. 9 on the Apostle's words): There was no cause for the Lord Christ's coming except to save sinners. Take away diseases and wounds, and medicine has no cause. If Christ was incarnate in time to save sinners, then from eternity too those given by predestination to the incarnate Christ to be saved were considered as sinners. Second: predestination means not only giving some to Christ as Redeemer and Liberator, but also the eternal preparation in God's mind of the means by which they are most certainly set free. All those means prepared for the elect can exercise their proper force only on a subject stained with sin — so predestination presupposes such a subject. Begin with efficacious calling to repentance and faith: what use is repentance except in a sinner? what force has faith except to justify a sinner? what does the Spirit of regeneration do but reshape the sinner to the image of Divine holiness lost in Adam? Since predestination prepares these and like means for the elect, God clearly considers them corrupted by sin and to be drawn out of that corruption by those efficacious means. As for reprobation, one argument seems enough: it falls only on a human considered as a sinner. Its aim is to display Divine glory by way of vindicating justice, as predestination's aim is to display that glory by way of sparing mercy. It does not serve God's glory to conceive him as destining to eternal punishment a creature not yet worthy of punishment. By absolute liberty God may decree not to communicate to an innocent creature some good he will give others; yet standing in his justice he cannot decree to inflict punishment on an innocent creature. Since reprobation includes the will to inflict punishment on the reprobate, on that side the person must be set before God as bound and stained by sin. Scripture always teaches wrath and vengeance provoked by sin: tribulation and anguish on every soul that does evil ([[Romans 2:9 >> Bible:Romans 2:9]]); the wages of sin is death ([[Romans 6:23 >> Bible:Romans 6:23]]); because of these (their sins) the wrath of God comes on the sons of disobedience ([[Colossians 3:6 >> Bible:Colossians 3:6]]). The Fathers carefully refuse to attribute to God a will to punish or damn anyone except as arising from preceding sin. Tertullian (On the resurrection): God is good from his own, just from ours — meaning vindicative justice. Augustine (Against Julian 3.18): God can free without good merits, because he is good; he cannot damn anyone without evil merits, because he is just. Prosper (Reply to Vincent's objections 2): That many perish is the merit of those perishing; that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. And in the Reply to the eleven: Nothing can be referred to God's predestination except what belongs either to due retribution of justice or to undue largess of grace. From all this I judge it clear enough: not only a rational nature but a sinful one underlies the Divine act of predestination or reprobation — as common conditions of the subject without which neither act can fall on humans in the way Scripture describes those acts.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: distinguishing conditions defined — free-will use
english: A few words now on distinguishing conditions. IV. By distinguishing conditions I mean contrary acts or qualities which, when foresight and weighed beforehand in the subject, bring about contrary acts in God toward that same subject. Take free choice: its good use and its bad use are contrary acts. If someone holds that, by God's ordination, foresight of the good use always means predestination, and foresight of the bad use means reprobation, then that person makes the good and bad use of free choice into distinguishing conditions required in the subject of predestination or reprobation.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: works foresight and faith foresight as distinguishers
english: So too if someone maintains that only those are elected to glory whom God foresees clothed with merits or good works to the end of life, and that only those are reprobated or not elected whom he foresees clinging perseveringly to demerits or evil works — then that person makes foresight works, good or evil, into distinguishing conditions, and by their difference different Divine acts of predestination and reprobation are assigned to different people. Likewise if someone teaches that God elects only those he foresees will persevere in faith, and passes by and rejects only those he foresees will persevere in unbelief — then faith and unbelief become the distinguishing conditions by whose discrimination the distinct acts of predestination and reprobation fall on distinct persons.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: common vs distinguishing — Davenant denies foresight discriminators
english: You already see the great difference between those earlier subject-conditions we called common, and these later ones we call distinguishing.
