Rational nature, and nature under sin, is presupposed in the predestined and the reprobate so that nothing in them is set as cause, reason, or occasion of the divide. Good and evil works, faith and unbelief, are instead set as foresight conditions in people so that the very divide between the predestined and the reprobate proceeds according to them. We grant the earlier conditions as prerequisites — so that a subject can, commonly and without distinction, lie under God as he predestines and reprobates. But these later ones, which many try to fix in place, we flatly deny: they are not presupposed or foreseen by God in the person to be predestined or reprobated, nor do different foresight varieties of them always drive different acts of predestination and reprobation onto different persons.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: Pontificii admit causes; Arminians mode-without-cause tergiversation
english: One more prelude. Pontifical writers who hold that foresight works or sins are conditions God looks to in predestination to glory and in reprobation also frankly grant that those conditions are causes why some are elected to glory and others are not — just as, once the decree is executed, they are causes why some are admitted to the kingdom of glory and others shut out. Recent doctors of the Arminian school press hard that there is no election or reprobation of humans except by the foresight divide of faith or unbelief in them, yet they stubbornly deny that faith is the cause of election. They call it a Mode by which God regards the person to be elected, an antecedent of election; but they deny it is election's cause, and at the same time deny it is an effect flowing from election. That dodge shows how weak their case is. If they set faith only as an antecedent condition without which this or that person's election would not occur, they could fairly say they do not make faith the cause of that election. But when they further teach that faith posited means election posited, and foresight faith denied means election denied, they openly give faith not bare precedence but causality as well.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: Fathers treat such conditions as meritorious causes — Aug. Ep. 105
english: I dare say Augustine and the other Fathers treat it this way: whenever some human quality or act is so required beforehand that when it is present some following gift of God is present with it, and when it is absent that gift is denied, they set that quality or act in the place of a cause — a cause, as they put it, meritorious in its own way. A condition demanded by God's ordination and performed by the person through God's grace has, for the Fathers, the force and nature of a meritorious motive cause with respect to the benefit conferred under that condition. So Augustine in Epistle 105: the very remission of sins is not without some merit, if faith obtains it. By the same reason, election to glory will not be without some merit on the elect person's side, if faith obtains it. For among the Fathers merit is nothing but a work which, by God's ordination, obtains some benefit. So if the benefit of election is conferred on us from our foresight act of believing, that is not a mere condition sine qua non — it is a cause, indeed the merit of the following benefit, in the sense in which the Fathers use the word merit.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: against Pelagian merits and scholastic merita congrua
english: When the Fathers argue against the Pelagians that grace is not given or withheld according to free choice's merits, they mean simply this: it is not given according to a foresight condition of free choice's good or bad use. Had the Pelagians proved that, the Fathers would never have denied it was a true cause of the grace conferred. So too when our theologians contend against some Scholastics that God does not predestine people from foresight congruent merits, they mean that these so-called congruent merits are not antecedent distinguishing conditions by which everyone in whom they were foresight is elected and everyone in whom they were not is rejected. If the Scholastics ever prove such conditions, their case is finished — and we will freely admit that those conditions are causes of the divide between elect and reprobate, in the sense in which cause and merit are spoken of.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV close: word-tricks on faith; preface ends — theses next
english: So it is mere word-trickery when they say foresight faith and unbelief are conditions — not only ones that precede predestination and reprobation taken commonly and without distinction, but ones from which the very distinction of elect and reprobate arises — and yet deny those conditions any causality. Every theologian who has ever argued the reason or cause of election assumes this: whatever, when posited and foresight by God, brings election with it, and when denied or not foresight leaves election absent, has the force of a cause. These are the points I thought should stand as a preface. From here our whole coming dispute will be drawn into certain fixed theses.

title: Cap. II open: Variæ sententiæ — election from foresight merits; agenda
english: CAP. II. Here I set out the various opinions of those who teach that election rests on our foresight merits. We come at last to the business this labor was meant for. First we will argue election — or predestination — to salvation and eternal blessedness; then the other half of the controversy: non-election, passing-by, or reprobation.

title: Cap. II: principal question — foresight act as merit/cause of election?
english: The chief question for the first half of the coming dispute is this: in those elected and predestined to glory, is there some act or quality God foresaw and weighed beforehand — or anything at all — that stands as merit, cause, reason, condition, or antecedent so bound to the decree of election that when that prior thing is set in the Divine foresight election follows, and when it is denied election is denied? Let us see what Pelagians, Scholastics, and certain recent doctors hold on this.

title: Cap. II: Pelagian opening — free will alone; election from foresight holiness
english: Blinded self-love in human reason claims there is always some prior ground on which the decree of election rests — and Scripture cries against it. That British serpent spat out this poison: that a person can keep God's law and reach eternal life by free choice alone. He joined to it another venom of the same kind: that God, foresighting who would live holy by their own will's choice, elected them all to glory before the world's foundations were laid.

title: Cap. II: Augustine vs Pelagius; dogma already rejected — no fresh refutation
english: Augustine supplies both. First, Epistle 89, where he hurls anathema at the Pelagians for that heresy: their claim that free choice alone is enough to keep the Lord's commands is to be anathematized and cursed outright. Second, On the Predestination of the Saints 1.18: God foresaw, says the Pelagian, who would be holy by free will's choice, and so before the world's founding he elected them in that very foresight by which he foresaw them to be such. But since theologians of every party already reject Pelagius and this Pelagian dogma — or at least want to look as if they have — I will not waste effort refuting what no one dares openly defend.

title: Cap. II: Semipelagians — initiative from us; perseverance by free will
english: The Semipelagians took up part of Pelagius's poison. Count among them Faustus of Riez, Cassian the Conferencer, the Massilians, and all who admit grace is needed to live godly, persevere, and reach eternal life — yet still claim that from us there first comes a beginning of labor and effort, which God's grace then follows, and for the sake of which saving grace is given. Consequently they hold that once a person has gained God's grace by striving and labor, he stays in that grace, faith, and good works not by any gift flowing from election, but by his own free choice; and that election to eternal life rests on foresight of that will.

title: Cap. II: Faustus — initiative, progress, election from foresight merits
english: On that prior effort and labor Faustus writes (1.12): just as the prodigal's flight from a pious father's eyes is his own crime, so his return to the father's embrace — deliberating and rising by the good planted in him — is his own devotion. Chapter 17: the Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises the striving. The last chapter: he waits for the will of the one to be cleansed. On progress and perseverance by free choice's powers — not by any special gift flowing from the predestination decree — he reasons (2.5): human salvation is set not in the Maker's predestination, but in the working of the one who serves the Giver of grace. Chapter 12: a person's state can turn this way or that not by God's constitution, but by liberty of choice. At last he openly teaches election from foresight of such good will and working of ours, not from any prior decree of God (2.2): God's foresight begins from the matter of human acts. A little later: to foresee is one thing, to predestine another. Foresight knows beforehand what is to be done; then predestination marks out what is to be repaid. That foresights merits; this preordains rewards. Foresight belongs to power, predestination to justice. Unless foresight has searched, predestination decides nothing. In these words he does not draw merits from the grace of predestination — he draws predestination from foresight merits.

title: Cap. II: Prosper & Hilary on Massilians — Semipelagian close before Scholastics
english: These Semipelagians are clearest in the letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine — both prefixed to Augustine's On the Predestination of the Saints. Prosper reports their definition: God foresaw before the world's founding who would believe, or who would stay in the faith later helped by his grace, and predestined to his kingdom those he foresaw, once called by grace, would be worthy of election and would leave this life with a good end. Hilary: the Massilians say it empties preaching to speak of some as elect according to purpose, and so on. A few lines later: they claim that by the merit of each person's willing and believing, one can be healed of disease and gain both the increase of that faith and the full effect of one's holiness. In short, they put the reason for elect or reject in this: each is paired with the merit of his own will. They grant God does not elect anyone's works in foresight of gifts he himself will give; yet they affirm he elects faith in foresight — so that whom he foresaw would believe, he elected, and to him gives the Holy Spirit so that by good works he may reach eternal life. Finally they hold that no one is given such perseverance that falling away is impossible; and so they deny any fixed number of those to be elected and rejected. I thought this worth quoting a little more fully, so you may see how near they stand to the Pelagians or Semipelagians who in our own age try to explode Augustine's teaching — rooted in Scripture and long confirmed by the catholic Church's witness.

title: Cap. II: Scholastici — causes of election (moral works / use of grace); Rom. 9 overthrows
english: Next, down from the Semipelagians to the Scholastics. Not a few of them teach that predestination — or election — has a cause insofar as it falls on this man rather than that. Some plead good moral works before justifying grace; others good works after it; others foresight of a good use of God's grace. I need not linger refuting these views: one blow from the Apostle flattens them all (Rom. 9:11) — the children not yet born, having done nothing good or evil, so that God's purpose according to election might stand, not from works but from the One who calls.

title: Cap. II: three causes of the election-from-foresight error (pride, ignorance, curiosity)
english: Why do Pelagians, Semipelagians, Scholastics, and so many others agree that election to grace and glory rests on something in our power to have or do? The causes of the error are plain. First: pride and self-love native to the race, which hates having every ground of boasting torn away. Second: thick ignorance of our corruption and of the will captive under sin's yoke. Third: put any cause of election in us, and the hard questions that otherwise force us up to an unsearchable height are easily waved off — and human curiosity hates that height. Once election tracks foresight of some human act, ask why one gets grace and another does not: because one disposed himself by free choice, the other did not. Why one perseveres and another not: because one wills to persevere, the other will not. Why this one was elect to glory before the world, that one not: God foresaw from eternity that one would admit offered grace, use it well, and stay in it by free choice to life's end — the other reject it at once, or at least shake it off before death.

title: Cap. II: fourth cause (cruelty charge); leave old Scholastics — Pontificii & Arminians next
english: A last motive for many who will admit no election except one resting on foresight of some act free choice can elicit: they took as a necessary postulate what is utterly false — that God would be cruel unless he put it in every person's power to recover by himself the salvation lost in Adam. Leave the old Pelagians and Scholastics. Engage those who disturb the Church in our age by dressing old errors in new formulas. First certain Papal doctors, then the Arminians: both refuse any election to salvation that does not rest on foresight of human acts elicited from free choice, grace having gone before.

title: Cap. II: Vasquez enters — thesis: efficacious election from foresight merits
english: First into the arena: the Papists. For all who hold this view (many of the sounder sort do not), let Vasquez speak. He tries to prop this thesis with many arguments (on ST 1.23.3, disp. 89): There is no efficacious election of particular persons to glory from God's will alone; each is elect to glory from foresight merits which God's grace will bring about. A few notes first so the thesis is clear; then the adversaries' arguments, stated and dissolved.

title: Cap. II: Vasquez clarified — efficient election, merits as ratio, special grace vs Arminians
english: First: by efficacious election Vasquez means God's absolute, particular will that settles on certain persons to be blessed — Peter, Paul, and the rest one by one. He calls it efficacious election, or an efficacious will to give glory, to mark it off from the common antecedent will (a bare desire or affection) by which they say God wills eternal life for all, even the reprobate. Second: when he says this efficacious election to glory is from foresight merits, he does not make those merits the cause of God's willing — no cause of that is sought outside God — but the reason why the divine will freely terminates on glorifying this person. Third: adding "which God's grace will bring about" cuts him off from Pelagians who let merits flow from free choice without Christ's grace, which Augustine everywhere proved from Scripture necessary. Last: though the Jesuit holds there is no efficacious election to glory except from foresight of merits, he gladly grants predestination to special grace that infallibly leads to glory rests on no foresight of merits, and no cause, start, or occasion can be invented on the predestinate's side why God gave that grace or decreed in foresight to give it (ST I q.23, disp. 91.11). On predestination of particular persons to special grace, then, the Jesuit is far sounder than the Arminian and Vorstian school. Now their arguments for the thesis: they start from Scripture and usually cite these for election from foresight works.

title: Cap. II Arg. 1: Vasquez from Matt. 25:34 — kingdom prepared for foresight works
english: First argument (Matt. 25:34ff.): "Come, you blessed of the Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the world's beginning. For I was hungry, and you gave me…" Vasquez: here Christ offers a kingdom prepared from the world's origin — that is, from eternity — and at once gives the reason they should receive what was prepared and destined, which is to mark the cause of that preparation. If the preparation rested on some other ground, and not on these very works named, the cause Christ himself assigns would be empty and none. Therefore people are elect to heavenly glory from foresight of their good works (ST I q.23 a.3, disp. 89.2).

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 1: works path to glory, not cause of decree — Scotus & Bellarmine
english: From these words you may gather only this: God's children, freely predestined from eternity to glory, at last enter it — others shut out — because they alone took the straight road God ordained. Vasquez's claim that the works named here are causes of the preparation itself, or of God's eternal destination, is utterly false. The true cause is hinted when they are called the Father's blessed: he destined them to the heavenly inheritance because by grace he willed to be their Father in Christ. Their works, neither as foresight nor as done in time, caused predestination to glory — only introduction into it; and even of that they are not meritorious causes, only subordinate ones, as motion on a road is a "cause" of reaching the end. Vasquez's slip: he missed that decreeing or predestining to glory can be purely gratuitous in God and rest on no foresight of human acts, while the way of arriving at glory for man is laborious and needs many acts without which God ordained and foresaw he would never put in to glory's kingdom. Scotus (I dist. 41) marks the solution: "God wills to give Peter eternal glory on account of merits" is false if "on account of merits" construes with "wills" — God did not form the will to glorify Peter from foresight of merits — and true if it construes with "to give": he will not bring into possession of glory until it is foresight that Peter walked in the good works God prescribed and preordained. Bellarmine uses the same reply (De grat. et lib. arb. 2.13): "God from eternity predestined to give men the kingdom through foresight good works" is false if "through foresight works" hangs on "predestined," true if it hangs on "to give" — glorification in execution as the effect of justification, sanctification, or good works. This argument will be pressed again, harder; we will answer more fully then.

title: Cap. II Arg. 2: praescientia loci (Rom. 8:29–30 / 11:2 / 1 Pet. 1:2)
english: Second: they press the places where election or predestination to glory is joined in so many words with foreknowledge — Rom. 8:29–30 ("Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to his Son's image…"); Rom. 11:2 ("God has not cast off his people whom he foreknew"); 1 Pet. 1:2 ("elect strangers according to the Father's foreknowledge, unto sanctification of the Spirit…"). From these they infer that God elected to glory those he foreknew would be conformed to the Son's image — holy and good — so that foresight of future goodness or holiness was the cause of election to glory.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 2: foresight of sanctity not cause — decree precedes foresight
english: Reply: those texts do not say God elected or predestined certain people to glory because he foresaw they would be conformed to Christ's image — holy and good. They say he elected those he foreknew, and predestined them to become conformed, or elected them unto sanctification. So foresight of future holiness was not the cause of predestination; predestination was the cause of the holiness foreseen. God foresees no saving spiritual good in people except what he himself works in them; he works none except what he decreed to work. The decree to work grace and holiness — already wrapped into predestination — always comes before any foresight of grace and holiness as in them.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 2: praescientia practica / scientia approbationis — Catharinus
english: Weigh the words more closely. Paul did not say "whom he foresaw," but "whom he foreknew" (οὓς προέγνω). This foreknowledge is practical, not bare intuition — what theologians call the knowledge of approbation. Sense: those God loved and, by his eternal good pleasure, set apart from others and approved — those he predestined. Scripture often uses "know" for love or approval, and "not know" for hate or rejection ("I never knew you," Matt. 7:23; "The Lord knows the way of the righteous," Ps. 1:6). So Catharinus on this place: What is "he foreknew," if not "he foreloved"?

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 2: Vulgate "conformes fieri" — not election from foresight of works
english: Second: Paul did not write "whom he foreknew would be conformed, he predestined," but "whom he foreknew" (that is, foreloved) "he predestined to become conformed" — as the Vulgate rightly supplies what the Greek leaves open. So God is not said to predestine from foresight of our works, but to foreknow the good works he prepared for those already predestined.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 2 close: Augustine — works prepared in predestination (Eph. 2:10)
english: Hear Augustine (On the Gift of Perseverance 2.14): predestination is the foreknowledge and preparation of God's benefits by which whoever is freed is most surely freed. More plainly still (ch. 17): to whom God gives his holy gifts, he without doubt foresaw he would give them, and in that foreknowledge prepared them — for to arrange his own future works in his foreknowledge is exactly, and nothing else, to predestine. So you see how craftily and wickedly they cloud free predestination with foresight of works: God foresaw no good works in us, foresaw faith or holiness for no one, except what he prepared for us in the decree of predestination itself. He did not predestine us because he foresaw we would do good works; he foresaw we would do them because in our predestination good works were prepared for us to walk in (Eph. 2:10).

title: Cap. II Arg. 3: 1 Cor. 2:9 — prepared for those who love him (king/crown analogy)
english: Third: they bring 1 Cor. 2:9 — "Eye has not seen… the things God prepared for those who love him." On ordinary speech, "for those who love him" looks like the cause of the preparation. Say a king prepared a crown for whoever scales a besieged city's walls: that would mean the crown was destined to this or that man from foresight of the climb — and no other way.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: love shows who receive glory — not foresight-cause of the decree
english: Reply: "for those who love him" tells what sort of people finally receive the glory he prepared from eternity — it does not make foresight of that love the cause why glory was destined to them. The same love that freely destined them to glory also destined them to love God, and by that love they take the road that leads to glory. So our love of God is an effect of the divine love that elected and predestined us to salvation — foolishly taken as election's cause. So the Apostle: "We love God because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: Augustine In Joh. 86 — praescientia pleaded against grace
english: Augustine (In John, tract. 86) puts it best: they defend God's foreknowledge against his grace when they say we were elect before the world's foundation because God foresaw we would be good. They were not elect because they were good — they would not have been good unless elect. So we may say the same of those who claim we were elect because God foresaw us as loving him: we would never love God unless we had been elect.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: earthly king analogy fails — strength from crown's destination
english: Last: the earthly-king crown analogy fails at the very hinge of the argument. If no one could climb by his own strength, and the king could breathe that strength into whomever he chose, the crown would not be destined from foresight of the climb — the climb foreseen, and the strength given, would flow from the crown's destination. That is exactly how it stands between God and men.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3 close: love infused from election — Augustine De grat. Christi 26
english: No one would love God unless God poured charity into him; God would pour saving charity into no one unless he had first destined him to salvation. So he does not destine eternal life from foresight of our love — from the purpose of election to eternal life he infuses that love. Close with Augustine, who hammers the Pelagians everywhere: "That we might receive the love with which we should love, we were loved when we did not yet have it" (On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius, ch. 26).

title: Cap. II Arg. 4: 2 Tim. 2:21 — vessels unto honour from foresight of cleansing
english: Fourth: they bring 2 Tim. 2:21 — "If anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel unto honour, sanctified and useful to the Lord." So the vessels of election (or mercy) are those God foresaw would cleanse themselves: election, they say, rests on foresight of holy works.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 4: foresight of sanctity not denied — but not proved as cause
english: Reply: of course God foreknows the holiness of those he elects to glory — he cannot fail to foreknow what he himself will do, and he works all our good in us. But proving that he foresees the elect's good works is not enough for their cause, unless they also show he elects from that prior foresight. And that they can never force out of Paul's words.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 4: mark of vessels, not cause — seal of adoption / flight from iniquity
english: In that place Paul does not teach why vessels are elect to glory, but by what mark they are known. He stamps a double mark on them: one God alone can read — the seal of eternal adoption ("The Lord knows who are his"); the other men can see — flight from impiety and the practice of holiness and justice ("Let him depart from iniquity"; "If he cleanses himself, he will be a vessel unto honour").

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 4: vas in honorem twofold — eternal purpose vs actual sanctification
english: Add: "vessel unto honour" is said two ways. From God's eternal electing purpose to honour — and then being such a vessel does not hang on foresight of sanctification; sanctification afterward flows from that decree. Or from actual sanctification — and in that sense someone becomes a vessel unto honour when, purified and renewed by God's Spirit, he begins among God's honoured servants to serve the divine honour in a holy life.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 4 close: Lyranus — mark of destined vessels, not foresight-cause
english: So Lyranus seems to take the place: "he will be a vessel unto honour" means a vessel set apart for divine worship. However you read it, the text does not prove God elects us to glory from foresight of our holiness. It proves the elect to glory are filled with true holiness, known by that mark as vessels destined to honour, and actually put to honourable use through that holiness.

title: Cap. II Arg. 5: 1 Tim. 2:4 — common will to save all grounds foresight-election
english: Fifth: from 1 Timothy 2:4 — "God wills all men to be saved" — they argue that from this common will to save all, God gives everyone sufficient grace to reach salvation. So some are elect to glory and others passed by only because he foresaw who would cooperate with that grace and persevere in holiness, and who would not cooperate at all, or would not remain in good works and faith. Therefore, they say, there is no election to glory except from foresight of merits.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5: will to save tied to will to teach — God did not teach all
english: This divine will for the salvation of all men must be read with the will joined to it — the will to teach all men. Paul binds them: God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). Yet it is certain from God's word and from history that he has not willed to teach all, or to lead every person one by one to saving truth. Romans 10:14: how will they call on him in whom they have not believed? how believe without hearing? how hear without a preacher? how preach unless they are sent? In past generations God let the nations walk in their own ways (Acts 14:16) and gave knowledge of the truth to Israel alone. After Christ's coming the light did not at once shine on all by his will: for a time the apostles were barred from the Gentile road (Matthew 10:5), and later forbidden to preach in Asia (Acts 16:6). Come to our own age: how many nations found in the New World have for centuries not felt even a breath of saving truth? Can God be said to have willed them to know the truth when he would not send them heralds of it? See Prosper of Aquitaine on the Gallic chapters (Response 4 and Sentence 4). If they take Paul to mean that God, as far as in him lies, wills to give every fallen child of Adam saving knowledge and salvation itself for Christ's sake, you must either call their reading a clear error or confess weakness in the divine will — for the one who wills, and can, acts.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5: ancestor-covenant dodge refuted — Adam ok, Indian via grandparents not
english: Some, to save the opinion, press that through every age God willed each person to come to truth and be saved insofar as they stood in his covenant, not insofar as they fell from it in themselves or in their parents — and that he called everyone to the truth either in their own person or at least in parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents. Nothing is more foolish. First: if for some prior cause God decreed, before they were born, never to call countless particular persons to the truth, he did not will to call those same people one by one. Next: how far from common sense is it that God called this one person to saving truth in the person of his grandparents? Is that the universal sufficient grace by which they prove he wills everyone's salvation person by person? Is each ancestor one person with his grandchildren? Or did God will to give something personally to a grandson because he once gave it to impious grandparents who threw it away? Anyone who wants to defend sufficient grace and a general will to save all this way should go not to grandparents but to the first parent of the race. In Adam — the root, the common person of humankind — we may fairly say God willed the salvation of all. But to say he personally willed the salvation of this Indian or American, and that he was sufficiently called to saving truth, though God never sent him a herald of saving grace — and to rest that only on some ancestor five hundred or a thousand years ago who by his own fault rejected the Gospel and cut his line out of the covenant of grace — that defense belongs to someone with nothing left to say; refuting it belongs to someone with nothing better to do.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5 Primo: salvos fieri vs facere — preceptive will, not decretive
english: If that reading fails, what do Paul's words mean? First notice: he did not say God wills to make all men saved and drag them to the truth by the force of preaching and the Spirit. He said he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). When God wills to make someone saved, no human will blocks him — so Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 14. These words show what God wills people to do, more than what he wills to work inside them. He wills gospel ministers, as far as they can, to labor that all may be saved and come to Christ; he wills each Christian, by prayer and every means he can, to further the salvation of all. It is ours, Augustine says, who do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined, to will that all be saved (On Rebuke and Grace 15). So the text belongs to the preceptive will that directs us — not to the decretive will that infallibly gives the good God has destined for a person.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5 Secundo: approbative vs effectual will — no singular sufficient grace from approval
english: Second: God is said to will something by a will of affection or of effect — so Thomas in the Disputed Questions on the will of God, art. 1 — or, as others put it, approbatively (what is good and lovable in itself) or efficaciously (what he has decreed to work for his glory in some particular person). The first is only the divine will's simple delight in a thing as fitting God's nature; the second is an absolute decree to give that good to someone in particular. Chastity, wisdom, faith, salvation are lovable goods, and in themselves agreeable to God's will — so we rightly say God wills all people to be chaste, wise, faithful, and saved. Hear that of the approving will, which looks at the thing as such, not of the effecting will, which decides to work it in this or that person. From that prior will — which of itself settles nothing about particular persons — they cannot force the claim that God wills to grant each person whatever suffices for his salvation. Still less can they hang on it that, from foresight of who will use those means well and who will not, he elects some to salvation and passes by and reprobates others.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5 close: Augustine / Gregory / Aquinas — all = kinds, not foresight-cooperation
english: Last: if someone still insists Paul's words mean God's efficacious will, he will never get free unless he reads the place as Augustine, Gregory, and the scholastics long did. Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 14: "God wills all men to be saved" — understand all the predestined, because every kind of human being is among them. Gregory: he wills all men to be saved because from every kind of people he elects those he draws to the joy of eternal salvation (on 1 Kings, book 5, ch. 4). Aquinas on the same words: the distribution is for the kinds of individuals, not for the individuals of the kinds. So this text does not prove that by the will of good pleasure God wills the salvation of every single person — and far less that he elects people to salvation from foresight of the future cooperation by which they would fit themselves to that will.

title: Cap. II Arg. 6: James 2:5 — poor elect / rich in faith grounds foresight-election
english: Sixth: Vasquez leans on James 2:5 — "Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him?" The Jesuit reads it: God chose those who were poor in this world because they were rich in faith and charity — chose them to glory, the inheritance of the kingdom. So, they say, election to glory hangs on God's foresight of who will finally be rich in faith and works.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: scopus — do not despise the poor; 1 Cor. 1:26 parallel
english: Reply: James's point is that we must not despise the poor. Far from neglecting them, God in spiritual gifts mostly prefers them to the richer. The rich, for their part, are not to be overrated and honored while the poor are ignored — God often sends the rich away empty and fills the poor with goods. 1 Corinthians 1:26 runs the same way: not many wise by flesh, not many mighty, not many noble — God chose what the world calls foolish to shame the strong. So the Apostle shows God has chosen more from the poor, to give them faith and the heavenly inheritance, than from the rich.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: conjungit — elect to become rich in faith, not because foreseen rich
english: That is why he binds the two phrases: rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom. He did not say the elect are heirs because they were foreseen as going to be rich in faith. He said they were elect so they would become rich in faith — and heirs of the kingdom.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: Vasquez calumny — if elect=make rich, then elect=make poor?
english: Vasquez tries a cheap jab at that reading: if "choosing the rich in faith" means making them rich in faith, then "choosing the poor in this world" would mean making them poor — yet James does not say God made people poor; he says those who already were poor, because they were rich in faith, God chose to glory. Reply: no absurdity if we say God made people poor in this world — the rich/poor split itself comes from the divine decree. We grant James's words are not about that. And that does not hurt our reading;

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: fishermen analogy — elect makes apostles/faithful, not prior trade/poverty
english: a near parallel shows why. If we say God chose fishermen as his Apostles, "choose" there means make them Apostles — not make them fishermen. They were already fishermen by their own trade before they were elect Apostles. So when I say God chose the poor who are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, "choose" means make them believers and kingdom-heirs — not make them poor. Poverty is already assumed when faith and adoption to the heavenly kingdom are given.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: Augustine — elect makes rich in faith as he makes heirs
english: Add this for the full sense: God does not elect from foresight of faith, yet he is rightly said to have chosen the rich in faith — because in time he makes such everyone he elected from eternity; and because, once made such, he already actually and almost visibly elects them, sets them apart from unbelievers, and takes them as his own. Close with Augustine on this very text (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By electing he makes them rich in faith, just as he makes them heirs of the kingdom." That choosing is rightly said of them: he chose them so that he might do this in them.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6 close: not elect because foreseen faithful — foresight because electing makes them
english: Bottom line: foresight of future faith is not why God elects. He foresaw them faithful because election itself is what makes them faithful.

title: Cap. II Arg. 7: Apoc. 3:11 — hold fast / crown grounds foresight-perseverance
english: Last: they take Revelation 3:11 — "Hold what you have, lest another take your crown." From that they say the crown of glory can be lost by an ungodly life, so God predestines no one to that crown unless he sees the person will persevere to the end in piety and faith. Without that foresight, they argue, predestination would be unsure — someone God meant for glory could drop out by weakness or wickedness.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7: crown of ministry vs heavenly glory — alternate reading first
english: Reply: the words fit the crown of ministry at least as well as heavenly glory — "Hold what you have" as keep the bishop's office steadily and carefully; "lest another take your crown" as lest, if you prove negligent, someone else is put in your place after you are set aside. Still, many read them of the heavenly crown without strain. Take that sense, and we answer as follows.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7 Primo: elect cannot lose crown — certainty from causal chain, not bare foresight
english: First: the predestined cannot lose the crown of glory. That certainty does not come from a force that drags them into eternal life, nor from bare foresight of what free will will do. It rests on the chain of causes special providence has linked so the elect's salvation is produced without fail. Paul marks that as causality, not naked foresight — Romans 8: God so set and steers the order of causes for the elect that even what looks hostile still works for their souls' eternal good (vv. 28ff to the chapter's end).

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7: Augustine — if an elect perished God would be deceived and overcome
english: That is why Augustine says: if any elect left God by free will's changeableness, God would not only be deceived but beaten — he not only foresaw their glorification; he decreed to bring it about by an unbeatable chain of causes. On Rebuke and Grace 7: if any of them perishes, God is deceived — but none does, for God is not deceived; if any perishes by human fault, God is overcome — but none does, for nothing overcomes God. Why "overcome" if an elect fell by his own will's fault? Because God undertook to plant in every elect not a thin bare possibility, but a firm, sure, unconquered will to persevere.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7: weak will can lose; under divine direction the elect cannot
english: So if you look only at the elect's weak will, they can lose the crown. Look at that same will under God's most effective direction, and they cannot.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7 Secundo: foresight of perseverance concurrent — not prior cause of predestination
english: Second: when opponents say God predestines to the crown only those he foresees will persevere, grant it this far — the same people predestined to glory are also foreseen as going to persevere in grace. Reject it when they make that foresight the cause of predestination, and prior to it in our order of thought.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7 close: hortations keep elect persevering — scripture proofs of foresight-election end
english: Last, on the wording itself: Augustine (On Rebuke and Grace 13) says these lines are spoken to saints who will persevere as if their perseverance were unsure — they need to hear it that way, not to be proud but to fear. So the elect get such warnings not because their predestination is shaky or hangs on free will's change, but because by exhortation and other means God knows fit, he makes them persevere in grace and holiness. Those are the main Scripture proofs used for election from foresight of merits. Any further texts take their sense from these. From the texts, then, to the adversaries' reasons.

title: Cap. III open + Rat. 1: common inefficacious will before foresight of merits
english:
Cap. III — the adversaries' arguments weighed and answered.

Now to their reasons. First they try to prove no one is chosen for glory by God's efficacious will except from foreseen merits, like this:

Rat. 1. The will to give eternal life that comes before foresight of merits is only a common, inefficacious will, looking equally at all — reprobate and predestinate alike. So if God efficaciously wills glory for someone, that hangs on foresight of merits.
notes_covered: Cap. III open; Rat. 1 common inefficacious will

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: Bannes — common will only before sin / Adam intact
english: Rejection. That "common will to give eternal life to all" (Bannes is right) is only how we picture things before foreknowledge of sin. It proves at most that in intact Adam God willed everyone's salvation and gave him enough means — if Adam had used them, neither he nor his line would have fallen into eternal death's guilt. Once Adam fell, I deny God ever had a common, indifferent will to give eternal life to all in Christ Jesus.
notes_covered: Rej open; Bannes; Adam intact; deny post-fall common will

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: reprobates only under 'if they will' — not equal termini
english: Toward the reprobate he had no will aimed next at their salvation: defenders must tack on "if they themselves will." Since God foresees their Not-willing and will not give them what he really gives the elect, that will clearly does not terminate equally on elect and non-elect salvation.
notes_covered: reprobates; conditional rider; unequal termini

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: sufficient aids fail for pagans/infants — Augustine De nat.
english: Those who put on God a good-pleasure will for everyone's salvation infer it from "sufficient helps for all" — yet they never prove that of pagans who never heard Christ's name or Gospel light, nor of their infants dying unbaptized (never mind the rest). Augustine says plainly many are damned who could not be justified and saved (On Nature and Grace 8–9).
notes_covered: sufficient aids; pagans; infants; De nat. & grat.

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: Augustine Ep. 107 / 1 Tim. 2:4 — God not willing all alike
english: Epistle 107's fourth of twelve catholic sentences: we know grace is not given to all; and where it is given, not by works' merits, nor even by the will's merits of those who get it — clearest in infants. Soon after, on the usual "common indifferent will to save all" objection, he adds words worth quoting: those who fight this plain truth miss how "God wills all to be saved" is said when so many are not. Not because they refuse, but because God does not will — obvious in infants. So "GOD WILLS ALL MEN TO BE SAVED," though he does not will so many saved, means all who are saved are saved only if he wills; any other reading must not contradict that open truth: many are not saved though men will it, if God does not. So Augustine.
notes_covered: Ep. 107; 1 Tim 2:4; infants; Hactenus Augustinus

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1: Vasquez infants — deny invented common good-pleasure will
english: Even Vasquez, pressed by the facts, grants that for some infants no sufficient Christ-remedy could be applied by human care. I add: nor was it applied by divine providence. So a posteriori God never had that invented common good-pleasure will to save every single person. Finally — and this most cuts their argument's nerve — I deny that the will by which God, before foreknowledge of merits, decreed eternal life for the elect was only that common, inefficacious "simple affection / complacency" will; I affirm it was a special, most efficacious will.
notes_covered: Vasquez infants; deny common good-pleasure; affirm special will

title: Cap. III Rej. Rat. 1 close: electing will causes merits — sum before Rat. 2
english: Clear why: that free will of God before our merits or good works is itself their cause. How then call the will presupposed to merits common, equal, and indifferent to all, when in some it effects those "merits" and in others not? Effect differs; so does the cause. Hear Augustine again (never enough): true grace is not given by our merits but gives the merits when given — it goes before a good will, finds it in no heart, and makes it. Sum of our answer: the divine will before foresight of good works is not equal or indifferent about everyone's salvation, since in some God wills grace-works that lead to glory and in others he does not. So they wrongly start the efficacious saving will for the elect from foresight of merits — that will already shows itself in willing to give those merits, which will came before merit-foresight and ordered those merits to salvation.
notes_covered: special will causes merits; Augustine; sum before Rat. 2

title: Cap. III Rat. 2: Vasquez — physical vs moral media; no election before works-foresight
english: Rat. 2. Second, Vasquez argues from the split between physical and moral means. With physical means he grants that an efficacious intention of the end comes before intending the means. But whenever the means to an end is moral (good works ordered to eternal life), he denies God can have any efficacious will to confer that end before foreknowing the means. So God elects to glory only from foresight of works (In 1. q. 23 art. 3 disp. 89 ch. 9; also disp. 81 ch. 5). He thinks he can prove the difference: physical means carry in themselves a natural power to cause the end, without depending on another's will — so even if the end is intended before they are foreknown, when applied they still tend to the end by their own virtue. Moral means, he says, do not produce the end by any inward natural power but only by another's ordination; unless foresight ordains and accepts them to the end before that end is efficaciously intended for someone, they count for nothing toward obtaining it — and to be accepted and ordained they must be foreseen. Hence no one is predestined to glory's end except after foresight of works that are moral means God ordained to that end.
notes_covered: Cap. III Rat. 2 Vasquez physical vs moral media

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2: deny the split — end-intention causes means; Paul/grace
english: Resp. We do not grant Vasquez's physical/moral split at all. In the order of intention (the real question) the end causes the means — moral as well as physical — and from desiring the end first those means are chosen and applied. Known rule: means are applied toward the end. So intending the end always comes before supplying the means. God would not have destined efficacious grace to Paul unless he had first efficaciously destined to give him glory.
notes_covered: Resp Rat. 2: intention order; Paul/grace

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2: execution vs intention — moral/physical mode misses the question
english: As for Vasquez's different operating mode in physical vs moral means: we grant they differ in mode, but deny that hurts our case. First, that angle misses the controversy's aim. We are not asking about execution-order — where we admit means related to the end act as cause toward the effect — but about intention-order, where means stand to the end as effects to a cause. His philosophy about how physical and moral means operate looks to the end as already out in external execution, not as in the agent's will and mind. In that sense means do precede the end — but that is beside the point.
notes_covered: Resp Rat. 2: execution vs intention

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2: moral means foreknown as apt/possible — not absolutely future before election
english: Second, he presses that moral means would be worthless for obtaining the end unless foreseen and accepted by God before an efficacious intention of the end. We grant such means get their power to cause — or work toward — the end from God's prior will that ordained and accepted them to that end. But we also affirm: before the end is intended, God foreknows those means only as apt and helpful to it, as possible and shareable with all for whom he wills the end — not as absolutely going to happen in this or that particular person before that person is efficaciously elected to glory (destined to the end).
notes_covered: Resp Rat. 2: apt/possible vs absolute foresight

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2 close: Semipelagian charge — Augustine election yields faith/sanctity/perseverance
english: Finally, in this argument Vasquez crosses into the Semipelagian camp and leaves Augustine, who everywhere teaches men are not elected to eternal life from foresight of faith or good works — rather all our good works arise because we were predestined to eternal life. Faith: not elected because they believed, but elected that they may believe (De praed. sanct. 1.17). Holiness: certain and plain we will be holy because God elected us, predestining that by grace we should be such (ibid. 18). Perseverance: to saints predestined by grace into God's kingdom, perseverance itself is given (De corr. et grat. 12). So after election all our goods are foreseen, because they spring from election itself.
notes_covered: Resp Rat. 2 close: Augustine before Rat. 3

title: Cap. III Rat. 3: king’s prize — no glory-decree before victory / perseverance foresight
english: Rat. 3. In God’s will the order of acts is not read in itself but by analogy to human willing — so in our way of speaking we call one thing prior and another later as willed or foreseen by God. On that footing Vasquez presses: as a king who sets a prize for those who contend well, on the rule that only the victor takes it, never decrees to give that prize to anyone — however loved — before he sees him possessed of the victory, so of God: he never decrees to anyone the prize of eternal glory (promised as a crown to those who contend lawfully) except after intuition of victory, that is perseverance in good works. And since God foreknows all futures, from eternity he foresaw who would win, and from that foresight decreed to give them glory — as a prince, seeing someone has conquered, only then resolves to assign the prize.
notes_covered: Rat. 3 Vasquez king/prize analogy

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3: grant analogy-order; God can destine the crown from mere grace first
english: Sol. We grant the postulate: there is no priority/posteriority in the acts of the divine will or mind themselves; that order is borrowed from analogy to human willing and from how the objects depend on one another. To the comparison itself: first, we can show why an earthly prince does not mark someone out for the prize except after seeing the victory — and yet God, on the contrary, can first from mere grace destine someone singularly to the crown, and then prepare and give the gifts through which that person will be foreseen as brought to the crown.
notes_covered: Sol open + Primo contrast earthly prince / God

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3: mortal king cannot inspire victory-powers — if he could, not from foresight
english: The reason: a mortal king cannot inspire and pour in the will and powers by which this one person rather than others infallibly wins. If he could, nothing would stop him intending and decreeing from a primary, gratuitous will to give that prize to any friend — yet so the friend reaches it by the stated law, namely by winning, and from powers inspired by that primary intention. Were an earthly prince so able, we would not say he elected his friend to the prize from foresight of merits, but that from an antecedent purpose to give the prize he gave the merits and in that gift foresaw them. And that God so deals with all who are to be glorified is confessed.
notes_covered: Ratio: inspiration gap; counterfactual king

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3: efficacious end-intention before victory; God more than agonothetes
english: Second, Vasquez’s claim that a prince cannot efficaciously intend someone’s prize except from foresight of merits is not as settled as he thinks. Efficacious intention of an end moves the agent to apply every means in his power toward obtaining it — even when he cannot certainly foresee the event or infallibly secure the end. So a prince from special goodwill can seriously and efficaciously intend the prize for his friend before seeing the victory, and from that intention not only wish but, as far as he can, prepare and give all that helps toward victory — though as judge and agonothetes he cannot actually crown him except upon the victory won. God much more (for whom to will and to do are ready alike) can efficaciously intend for Peter or Paul the crown of eternal glory, and by that intention’s force prepare and give all that are called merits of the crown; and in this predestination from eternity foresee their merits, and at last, upon the fight nobly fought, set the destined crown on their heads.
notes_covered: Secundo: efficacious intention; God > agonothetes

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3 close: Augustine — gratuitous election before merits; Hypognost. 6
english: Finally, this is the very sentence Augustine everywhere defends against the Pelagians: men are elected gratuitously and before all foresight of merits — not only to gifts of grace but also to the kingdom of glory — however they are brought there by the path of good works or merits, as the ancient Fathers usually speak. One place only: From the damnable mass of the human race God foresaw by mercy, not merits, those whom by election of grace he predestined to life (Contra Pelag. Hypognost. 6). So the foresight on which predestination to life rests is not of our merits but of divine mercy, who decreed to elect us from that damnable mass to share eternal life and to adorn us with merits.
notes_covered: Augustine close; Hypognosticon 6

title: Cap. III Rat. 4: optimum modus — glory by merits foresight as crown of justice
english: Rat. 4. It is fair to hold that God marks people out for glory in the best way. But that best way, they say, is to do it from foresight of merits — for so the decree is cast as a crown of justice.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 4: not optimum — strips pure mercy; Detur totum Deo; Cyprian
english: Sol. That God does all things in the best way no one but the worst would deny — yet we deny that the best way of electing people to eternal life is the one that rests on foresight of merits. It is not best, because it does least to display the glory of God’s pure mercy toward the elect. It strips what Augustine everywhere presses: Let the whole be given to God. It also strips Cyprian’s line, which Augustine never praised enough: In nothing is one to glory, because nothing is ours.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 4: pride; impossible in sin — efficacious grace only to predestined
english: Further, it is not the best mode of electing, because it puffs a person up with pride by assuming each has by his own works set himself apart from the non-elect. Finally: it is so far from best that it is not even possible in this state of sin. In a person corrupted by sin no merits efficacious for eternal life can be foreknown unless God has freely given them. God gives those only to whom he decreed from eternity to give. He decreed efficacious grace unto salvation only to those he predestined to salvation. From first to last, then, such merits cannot be foreseen in those not yet elected to eternal life — so they are not elected to life from a preceding foresight of merits.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 4: Jesuits vs other Pontificii — Mary/Apostles absolute; Valentia
english: Add also: the Jesuits themselves diverge here from other Roman doctors, who teach that the virgin Mary, the blessed Apostles, and other eminently holy persons were absolutely predestined to glory before any foresight of merits — and it is likely the best were predestined in the best way. Of those eminently holy ones Valentia writes: such are predestined to eternal life before any regard of God’s foresight to their final cooperation (In 1. q. 23). But leave the Jesuits fighting one another:

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 4 close: gratuitous election stands; crown as prize; foresight after
english: and finally: people can be elected gratuitously to eternal life even when the crown of eternal life is decreed to be set on the elect as the prize of a life lived laudably and justly. God’s will about the way of bringing them to that prize through holy works does not overturn gratuitous, merciful election to eternal life from the elector’s primary purpose and mere good pleasure. When God decrees to bring someone to glory through such works, the primary decree to give glory does not rise from foresight of those works — rather, from that decree flows the will to give efficacious grace for doing such works of justice. So foresight of them is after election.

title: Cap. III Rat. 5: foresight election would be acceptor personarum
english: Rat. 5. If God elected some to glory from foresight of merits and passed others by, he would be an acceptor of persons. A just, rational election presupposes some disparity between elect and non-elect, and the prudent always chooses what is better. Since no difference among people can be imagined apart from foresight of merits in some that are not foreseen in others, it follows that God's election always rests on that kind of foresight of human merits.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5: Pelagian/Faustus charge; Bannes — can elect equal or worse
english: Sol. This argument was the old Pelagian press — Augustine shows it in many places (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; Ep. 105 to Sixtus; Hypogn. contra Pelag. 6; and elsewhere). Even Faustus of Riez, champion of the Semipelagians, argues (lib. 2.4): if both are equal in nature, justice is at risk when the one without merit is elected unworthy. We answer with Banez: without injustice or vicious respect of persons God can not only elect one of two wholly equal people to eternal life and pass the other by, but even elect the one he foresaw would be entangled in more and heavier sins, leaving the one he foresaw would commit fewer and lighter (In 1. q. 23 art. 5).

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5: loving and electing make worthier; Colossians 1:12
english: The reason: by loving and electing, God makes those he loves and elects worthier and better. Human choice cannot create disparity of worth in what it chooses, so it must aim at the object where greater dignity is already assumed. For divine election's justice and wisdom it is enough that, though all people are most unworthy of this electing gift, God by electing makes those he elects to glory fit and worthy ahead of others to share the saints' lot in light (Colossians 1:12).
notes_covered: Colossians 1:12

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5: Thomas and Augustine — electing makes worthy; holy not foreseen
english: Thomas notes: we must say God loves some more than others — for God's love is the cause of things' goodness, and nothing would be better than another if he did not will a greater good to one than to another (ST I q.20 a.3). On Romans 9: election does not look to a good already in the person but makes it. He learned that from Augustine (Contra Jul. Pelag. 5.3): God did not elect those he foresaw as worthy, but by electing made them worthy. Both drew it from the Apostle: God elected us that we should be holy — not because we were foreseen holy.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5 close: unjust acceptio vs liberal gift; Matthew 20:15
english: Further: unjust respect of persons has no place where someone from mere liberality gives unequally of what is his own to equals — only where, in dispensing what is owed, he favors one over another for a personal circumstance outside the cause of merit (as when a prelate, conferring a benefice, prefers a rich man or kinsman to better and more learned men: that is respect of persons, because those circumstances do nothing for the merit or dignity of such a prize). God electing one to the kingdom of glory ahead of another does not act from a debt of justice but from a gift of munificence; he does not regard nobility, riches, talent, or any quality outside the matter that earns the name "respect of persons," but his own liberality and goodness — Matthew 20:15: Is it lawful for me to do what I will with my own? See Augustine, Ep. 106; De bono persever. 2.8; Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.3.
notes_covered: Matthew 20:15

title: Cap. III Rat. 6: mercy with justice needs elect congruitas; Javellus
english: Rat. 6. In all God's works mercy concurs with justice — so, they say, we must posit on the elect's side some fittingness or congruity that was not on the reprobate's; otherwise no trace of justice will show in this election of God — and that he elects from foresight, not from the mere good pleasure of his will. So argues Javellus in the Questions annexed to Aquinas's Prima Pars.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 6: if justice means congruent merit, concurrence impossible
english: Sol. I answer: if Javellus means some justice other than that God acts as befits his own goodness and faithfulness, I deny that justice is found in every act where he deals kindly with wretched people. And if he so takes God's justice that acting justly means, in the gift of election, looking to some congruent human merit — then, in that sense, justice concurring with mercy in every dealing with people is not only false but impossible.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 6: Aquinas — justice presupposes mercy; first gift free adoption
english: For as Aquinas puts it best (ST I q.21 a.4): every work of divine justice always presupposes a work of mercy on which it is founded. So we must not run to infinity — we have to arrive at some first thing that depends on the mercy and goodness of the divine will alone. And what else can that be than the gratuitous adoption and destination of the elect to eternal life?

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 6 close: no praevisa congruentia; Miserebor cujus misertus fuero
english: So for this first benefit, if some reason of justice is to appear in it, we must not require a foreseen congruity in the elect. It is just insofar as it befits the divine will and goodness to will to act so — according to I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy — not I will have mercy on those in whom, that I may do this justly at once, I shall have foreseen certain congruent merits.

title: Cap. III Rat. 7: mere good pleasure would elect all equally disposed — Valentia
english: Rat. 7. If God predestined to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will and not from foresight of works, then he would predestine all alike, because all are equally disposed to receive that gift. For if he does not elect people as foreseen working well and persevering in good works, they must be elected as foreknown to be human beings or sinners — which belongs to all; so all would be elected. So argues Gregory of Valencia (In 1. q. 23).

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7: Major fails — good pleasure may discriminate; none disposed to glory
english: Sol. The Major's consequence fails. It does not follow that wherever God acts from mere good pleasure he must always deal equally with equals — on the contrary, because he acts from good pleasure he can discriminate in conferring his gifts where there was no difference in persons' qualities or state. And Gregory's first support for the Major — that with foresight of works excluded all are equally disposed to receive election — is false and unskillful. He should have said all are wholly undisposed to receive glory and disposed to undergo hell's pains. What disposition for election to glory is found in one reckoned a child of wrath by nature, stained with original corruption?

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7: Lazarus analogy — no duty to raise all equally
english: Just as it would be inept to argue: if Christ on earth raised dead Lazarus from mere good pleasure of his will, not from foresight of any cooperation on Lazarus's part, then he would have raised all the dead alike, because all were equally disposed to receive that gift of raising — so Gregory's prior argument is invalid and inept. It assumes God is bound, whenever he acts from good pleasure, to deal alike with equals; and it posits a common disposition to receive election in people who are commonly disposed to receive damnation's punishment.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7: not elect as man/sinner; gratis dilecti; Aquinas dilectio/electio
english: As for Gregory's second support — if people are not elected to glory as foreseen working well, then they are elected as foreknown humans or as sinners, and since that belongs to all, election would belong to all — that too is frivolous. Philosophers rightly hold that what belongs to a thing as such belongs to every such; yet God's election does not fall on a person as human, nor on a sinner as sinner, because the event shows not all humans and not all sinners are elected. So we deny the fork Either God elects as foreseen cooperators with his grace, or as foreknown humans/sinners — and say he elects people as freely loved by him ahead of others. Why these freely loved ahead of others? A ridiculous question: the first cause of the divine will in pouring out its goods is the will itself; no further cause is to be hunted. Aquinas is not wrong (ST I q.23 a.4): predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. To that belong Love and Election: Love, inasmuch as he wills them this good of eternal salvation; Election, inasmuch as he wills them that good ahead of others. And that willing-by-loving is why they have the good from him ahead of others. So Love is presupposed to Election, and Election to predestination. So far Aquinas.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 7 close: gratuitous affection first; Romans 9:12; Ephesians 1:5
english: From this you see: not foresight of human cooperation, but God's gratuitous affection alone is presupposed as antecedent to the election and predestination of particular persons. The Apostle illustrated it in that famous example of Jacob and Esau (Romans 9:12), and said it in plain words in Ephesians 1:5: who predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will. And here enough for this argument.
notes_covered: Romans 9:12
Ephesians 1:5

title: Cap. III Rat. 8: if not from foresight, majority would be elect — few are saved
english: Rat. 8. Without foresight of our works, they argue, a God good by nature — whose mercy is over all his works — would have marked at least most of humankind for life. Yet few are saved. So predestination must track foresight of works, that is of free choice used well or badly.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8: goodness wills some good to each — not equal goods by foresight
english: Sol. From God's being good by nature it rightly follows that he wills some good to every creature of his — not that he wills every good to every creature, or the same equal goods to equal creatures. Even in dispensing so-called goods of Nature or Fortune he is not bound to give them from foresight of good use, nor to impart them to the majority. We see strength of body, sharpness of mind, beauty of form, and abundance of riches are not given from foresight of good use — for the most part they go to those who abuse them worst: to injury, fraud, lust, luxury. And even those goods are granted only to few.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8: electing the corrupt mass — no duty to choose the majority
english: Further: we are speaking of election to life of people who are all most worthy of eternal death. We may grant that from the goodness of his nature God wills the gift of eternal life to all humans as considered before the fall, adorned with justice and holiness — yet no reason forces us to say that, from humans corrupted and sunk in the damnable mass, his goodness obliges him to elect either all or the greater part to glory.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8: mercy over all works — special mercy; few freed more illustrious
english: Finally, the press that his mercy is over all his works misses the point. First, God can show mercy to every person (and he does) without that special, outstanding mercy of adopting them as heir of eternal life. Second, the greatness of divine mercy is not weighed by how many individuals receive it, but by the greatness of the benefits given and the unworthiness of those who receive them. That God from his enemies — most stained with sin and most worthy of eternal death — through the death of his most beloved Son has willed to free even a few and destine them to the heavenly kingdom is a more illustrious specimen of mercy than the justice of leaving the whole wicked world to deserved ruin.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8 close: Augustine — multitude of reject shows justice; Epist. 190
english: Finally: why God, who could save all, yet willed to predestine few to life against the multitude of the rejected — Augustine gives two reasons, so there is little need to take refuge in foresight of good and bad works. Thus he: God willed this, that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how little moment any number of those most justly damned has with the just God — and that those redeemed from that damnation might understand from this that what they see rendered to so great a part of it was due to that universal mass (Epist. 190).

title: Cap. III Rat. 9: glory depending on others' sins needs foresight — Stephen's martyrdom
english: Rat. 9. Where someone's glory hangs on others' sins, they say it cannot be decreed except from foresight. Take Stephen: his glory somehow depended on the impiety of the Jews who would stone him — so God could not decree him glory, at least not in the degree that so glorious a martyrdom would give, unless that sin (which occasioned the martyrdom) was foreseen, and with it his patience and faith, by which he won outstanding martyr's glory from their cruelty. So if not to all, at least to some glory is destined from foresight of merits.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 9: intention vs execution — glory destined before foresight of faith
english: Sol. One thing is glory destined to the elect before the world's foundations, according to God's intention; another is that same glory conferred on them in time by executing the decree. In God's intention itself glory — and so great a glory — was predestined to Stephen before foresight of his patience and faith. Indeed, in the decree of predestination God had prepared him that faith and patience because he had elected him to that glory.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 9: in execution God foresaw cruelty, Stephen's constancy, the crown
english: But in executing that decree God foresaw the Jews' cruelty — which he permitted — that would give Stephen occasion for martyrdom. He foresaw Stephen, armed with such faith and constancy, about to die eagerly and willingly for Christ. And he foresaw himself, after that fight so nobly fought, about to give this bravest soldier an outstanding crown of glory.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 9: faith foreseen before obtaining crown, not before destinating it
english: So Stephen's faith and patience were foreseen as going before his actually receiving the crown — not as going before the destinating of that crown. Divine foresight of the measure of grace God gave him, and which he exercised so gloriously, rested on the prior decree of election; the decree electing him to that glory did not rest on foresight of the faith he would receive from God and later show in the fight.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 9 close: can destine glory depending on others' sins without prior foresight to confer
english: So the argument's assumption was false — that glory which somehow depends on others' sins cannot be decreed except from such foresight. It can be decreed or destined without that; it is only the conferring that cannot happen unless foresight of that sort goes first.

title: Cap. III Rat. 10: mere beneplacitum makes works idle — Predestinati / Sigebertus
english: Rat. 10. If God, ignoring merits, had from mere good pleasure decreed to bless particular persons — say Paul and Peter — then good works would do nothing toward obtaining glory. So let Peter walk in good works: still glory is not credited to him from any desert of those works. Let him neglect good works entirely: God will still give him the destined glory by the force of his good pleasure. That is highly absurd, and leans toward the Predestinarian error Sigebert's Chronicle reports: pious living's good works do not help toward glory if one is not predestinated; flagrant living's crimes do not hurt if one is.

title: Cap. III Rat. 10: Valencia, Vasquez, Faustus — election must rest on foresight of works
english: Gregory of Valencia presses this; Vasquez uses it too. Even the old Pelagians turned it on the Catholics — so Faustus of Riez (De lib. arb. 1.4): for those predestined to life prayer will not be necessary; for those appointed to death it cannot help — superfluous in the one case, powerless in the other. What they say of prayer they could conclude of every other good work: superfluous once an antecedent, gratuitous decree of divine election is posited. Therefore election must be set on foresight of works.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10: consequentia nulla — end-decree includes means; harvest analogy
english: Sol. That argumentation's consequence is plainly none. We rightly hold the decree to give glory gratuitous, and prior (in our way of understanding) to the decree to give grace or good works — because the first sets the end, the second orders means to the end — yet we deny that God's grace or the good works that are grace's effects do nothing toward obtaining glory. The reason is ready: an absolute, efficacious decree of any future event already means God wills to employ and apply the means that produce that effect. So in the antecedent decree to give glory is virtually included the consequent decree to give good works and the other means that are the way to glory's kingdom. Those means therefore work toward obtaining the end this way, even if for this particular person the end was not destined from prior foresight of them. Take an example: suppose God by an antecedent, gratuitous decree had set to give us a great harvest next year. To infer Therefore neither fair weather, nor seasonable rains, nor farmers' labor will do anything toward that abundance is ridiculous — for in that prior decree to give the fruit the will to execute through means is not shut out but included as depending on it.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10: Bannes — no real independence; Apage — glory with future good works
english: Think the same of the absolute, efficacious decree for Peter's glorification, and of the means of grace and good works by which he is brought to glory. Báñez saw this and exploded such consequences (In 1. q.23 a.2): from a priority in our way of understanding one kind of cause, people infer without any show a real priority in the things themselves, or independence of one from another in the order God set — as if: Form was willed by God before matter, therefore form would come to be even if matter never would. Equal folly: If glory was willed to Peter before grace, or before foresight of the good works that flow from grace, then even if Peter stayed devoid of grace and good works he would still get glory. Away with that nonsense! Though God does not will glory to this particular person from prior intuition of his works, but from the gratuitous good pleasure of his will, he still wills him glory with intuition of future good working as the necessary mode by which God ordained that the person proceed to that end.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10 close: not Predestinati — works profit; Father prepares repentance
english: So the Predestinarian heresy is nothing to us — we teach outright that works of piety profit toward obtaining glory, and that crimes block even the predestinated so that, unless cast off by repentance and newness of life, they cannot reach the kingdom of glory. Yet the same heavenly Father who gratuitously destined them glory has also infallibly prepared for them that repentance and newness of life.

title: Cap. III Rat.: God rejects only from foresight of sin — so elects from foresight of works
english: God rejects only from foresight of sin — for rejection or reprobation is a work of divine justice, which always presupposes a person stained with sin. Therefore he elects only from foresight of good works, since whoever is not rejected is by that very fact elected.

title: Cap. III Sol.: two acts of reprobation — praeterition vs praedamnation
english: Sol. Recall what the Prolegomena said of reprobation's twofold act: a negative act — Passing-by or non-election — and an affirmative — praedamnation, or deputing to punishment. If reprobation means that prior act, we may grant sin in the reprobated subject, yet we must not think God from intuition of that sin decreed not to elect or not to free this particular person. He looked on the same sin in those he willed to elect and free.

title: Cap. III Sol.: praedamnation rests on sin foresight; election and damnation not parallel
english: But if reprobation means praedamning — deputing to destruction — I gladly grant that divine act rests on foresight of human sin. Election to glory and deputation to punishment are not on equal footing: God can destine the undeserving to glory from mere good pleasure, because he is good; he cannot destine the undeserving to punishment without intuition of sin, because he is just. Augustine marked that difference (Contra Jul. 3.18): God is good, God is just — he can free without good merits because he is good; he cannot damn without evil merits because he is just.

title: Cap. III Sol.: two guilty subjects — damning from crime does not prove electing from virtue
english: Illustrate it so: take two men guilty of robbery or treason against their prince. The prince sees each as equally harmful — yet he wills to put one to death, and the other not only to free from punishment but to take into his household and heap with high honors.
