If someone argues The king condemned one from intuition of the crime (robber and traitor), therefore he elected the other to honors from intuition of innocence or virtue — that conclusion is false and ridiculous. So too are they deceived who from intuition of sin in the will to damn argue to intuition of merits in the will to free and elect to glory.

title: Cap. III Sol. close: why not pardoned alike — beneplacitum; Augustine profundum; defer De Reprobatione
english: Add this: ask why the wretched man suffered death — rightly, Because he was robber and traitor. Ask why the king would not pardon him as he did the other in the same case, or heap the same honors on him — here to answer Because he was guilty of robbery and treason is inept (so was the other we imagined). The answer is: it seemed good to the king, of his good pleasure, to pity the one and not the other. The reason of that discrimination lies in the king's breast, not in diverse merits. I seal it with Augustine (Epist. 190): why he frees this one rather than that, or does not free — let whoever can sound that great depth of his judgments, yet beware the precipice. When we reach our other thesis, On Reprobation, we will unpack this more clearly.

title: Cap. III Rat. 12: efficacious election from mere good pleasure destroys free choice
english: Rat. 12. If God efficaciously elects some to glory from mere good pleasure of his will, not from foresight of merits, free choice is plainly destroyed. No one can resist God's efficacious will — so those so predestined to glory will not keep free power to lose it. Posit that antecedent will for the salvation of Peter and Paul: either they are under absolute necessity to do what salvation requires (believe, live piously, persevere in faith and piety, and so arrive at salvation), or God's efficacious decree can be made void. Both absurd and impossible. Therefore we must not posit efficacious election of some to glory except from foresight of merits that will arise from free choice preceded by God's grace.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: old Pelagian cantilena — Prosper, Faustus, Augustine's defense loci
english: Sol. An old Pelagian refrain: those who hold absolute, efficacious predestination of certain people before foresight of merits induce fate and destroy free choice. Prosper records Pelagians defaming Augustine as utterly removing free choice and preaching fatal necessity under the name of grace (De lib. arb. p. 223). The same charge is in his Responses to the Gallic chapters, Obj. 6. Faustus of Riez, Semipelagian champion, obliquely strikes Augustine as destroyer of free choice for saying everything on either side is fixed by predestination (De lib. arb. 1.11), and claims a fatal decree is hidden under the word grace. Augustine himself must often wash off that foul calumny (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; De bono persever. 2.12; and elsewhere). I premise this so you see from whose cisterns almost all the adversaries' arguments are drawn.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: antecedent will to save does not coerce — free-moving means
english: Now to the point. I deny that God's antecedent will to give Peter eternal salvation takes away or hinders his free choice about obtaining it — and yet I affirm that, on that hypothesis, he cannot fall from salvation, so the divine decree cannot be made void. First: God's efficacious will works all he wills, but in the manner and by the means he wills. From an efficacious, antecedent purpose to save Peter he need not use coercive means that necessitate the human will; it is enough to use those Divine wisdom knows can move and bend the will efficaciously, infallibly, yet freely. Indeed, when from the antecedent decree to give salvation God moves the elect's free choice toward acquiring it, liberty is not lost but rather increased and strengthened. As Báñez puts it (In 1. q.22 a.4): the creature's free choice receives participated liberty from Divine free choice, moving it strongly and sweetly according to its nature.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: Augustine — God inclines hearts; elect act freely by inspired willing
english: Hear Augustine: when God wills something that must be done only by willing people, their hearts are inclined to will it by him who works in us, wonderfully and ineffably, even the willing (De praed. Sanct. 1.20). So the Jesuit's first assumption was false — that once God's efficacious will for the elect's salvation is posited, they necessarily and not freely will and do what brings them to salvation. They act freely, because God himself inspires in them a most free willing so to act.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: can the elect fall? fragility vs maintaining hand of God — Peter
english: Next the Jesuit's later claim: if after God's efficacious decree the elect freely work toward salvation, an elect person can fall from salvation and God's decree can be made void — for whoever freely perseveres can fail to persevere, so can fail to be saved. I answer: the sayings Whoever freely acts can fail to act and Whoever is freely saved can fail to be saved, if they mean a possibility of not acting and not reaching salvation that can arise from human fragility considered in itself, we grant such a possibility of perishing still clings to the elect. But if they mean that, despite God's upholding hand, that weakness can go into act so that in the event they might not persevere in faith and holiness or reach eternal life — we deny entirely that, once God's efficacious decree for their salvation is posited, such a possibility of perishing belongs to them. Augustine shows it by Peter (De corr. et grat. 8): as a weak, changeable man he could fall from faith, holiness, and salvation — but given that God had decreed, for Christ's prayer, to inspire in him a most free, strong, unconquered, persevering will in the faith, on that hypothesis he could not perish and could not but most freely persevere.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12 close: God's hand leads firmly and sweetly — Valentia, Catharinus
english: So it is God's hand, not ours, that we do not depart from God. That hand leads the elect to eternal life with such efficacy that his decree stands most firm — and with such sweetness and liberty that their choice in the good becomes most free. Valencia grants both can stand together (In 1. q.23 disp.1 p.4), and notes the oldest, most learned Scholastics held it. Ambrosius Catharinus too: grant a justification from which the predestinated cannot fall, and most free choice is not removed but made firmer and stronger by certainty of light and added fortitude. Ability not to persevere in faith, to fall from holiness — in a word, to sin and perish — is not liberty or part of liberty, but free choice's disease or weakness. When a contrary, strongest, most persevering will is given so that weakness cannot go into act, free choice is not destroyed but established free in the good. The freer the will, the less it can serve sin (Augustine, De praed. Sanct. 1.15). So the Jesuit's argument is worthless: The antecedent decree makes the elect unable to fall from salvation, therefore it takes away their free choice.

title: Cap. III Rat. 13: absolute election evacuates hortation, correction, prayer, industry — Pelagian charge
english: Rat. 13. Another argument akin to this the ancient Pelagians also used to brandish against Augustine: namely, that this doctrine of absolute election of singular persons before foresight of merits empties every hortation and correction, makes prayers useless, extinguishes all industry, and finally brings despair on men. See Augustine, De bono perseverantiae 2.16, 17, 23, and nearly the whole of De correptione et gratia. From Hilary's and Prosper's letters among Augustine's Works (Tom. 7) it is plain the Pelagians objected all this invidiously. The same runs through Faustus of Riez, book 1 sect. 9 and 10, and that writing full of poison and pestilence. Sum of it: on our sentence, salvation is thrust on the elect whether idle or wicked, and denied to the non-elect however hard they labor and live piously.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13: Augustine dissolves — election excites industry; despair is the impious' vice
english: Sol. Augustine dissolves all this in the places just cited. Still I answer: the doctrine of election excites and kindles industry of living well in all the pious. If the impious and profane take from it occasion of torpor or despair, that is their vice and innate perversity — not the doctrine's.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13: same occasion from divine foresight — Augustine De bono pers. 2.15
english: And Augustine showed (De bono perseverantiae 2.15) that a wholly similar occasion can be taken from the doctrine of divine foresight — which no one but an atheist, or one greatly unskilled, rejects.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13: nearer point — gratuitous election stabilizes hortations as ordained media
english: Nearer the point: I say this doctrine of gratuitous election stabilizes hortations and corrections and kindles men's wills to live piously — because we preach God's secret will to elect certain persons without silencing his revealed will, which decrees those elect are led to their destined end only through means God ordained. Hortations, corrections, prayers, and the like are among those means Divine wisdom ordained to promote the elect's salvation.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13 close: no despair for the willing — removes boasting, not study of holiness
english: Nor do we cast despair on any mortal willing to believe and live piously: we give such people most sure confidence they belong among the elect and those to be saved. We preach gratuitous election while teaching that no one gets fruit or comfort from it without faith and holiness — and that anyone living faithfully and holily can and ought to count himself among the elect. So the doctrine takes away every occasion of boasting and pride in one's works, but not the study of doing well; it rather kindles that study, teaching that no one has any certainty of election outside pursuit of holiness, or can ever reach election's end — eternal life — except by the way of holiness.

title: Cap. III Rat. 14: conformity of decree and temporal execution — Achilles of foresight-election
english: Rat. 14. Last they argue from the conformity between God's election decree and its temporal execution: in the same order in which things are executed in time, God from eternity decreed they should be executed. Divine immutability requires he not act otherwise in time than he from eternity decreed he would. So since in temporal execution he leads none of the elect to glory except in view of good works and final perseverance, he could not from eternity elect them to glory except under that same view. If before the world's foundations he elected them to glory freely, not from foreseen works, yet at execution will not give glory except from works, he has changed his will — most unworthy of divine wisdom. All Papists who hold election from foreseen works trust this argument heavily and boast it is their Achilles.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: distinguish electing act from eternal life elected — dispositive vs motive
english: Sol. To solve this rightly, distinguish God's act of electing to eternal life from the thing elected — eternal life itself. What can be a dispositive cause of producing the thing need not have been a motive cause of the elector's intention. We do not deny that good works, or a holy and pious life, work that way toward attaining eternal life, and that God from eternity looked on the elect's holy life as preceding their entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: adversaries conflate antecedents of glory with antecedents of God's intention
english: Here the adversaries slip: they think what precedes eternal life (to which men are elected) must also be conceived as preceding the elector's act or intention — God's decree by which they are elected. But that internal eternal act of the divine will by which he elects, and the glory or heavenly joy to which he elects, are greatly different. So we can rightly affirm of the object what we can only falsely affirm of God's act or intention destinating that object to a particular person. Example — true of the object: Paul's calling, justification, and pious life are seen by God as preceding his glorification. False if fitted to God's act: those same are seen by God as preceding the divine intention to glorify Paul.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: same execution order granted — opposite order of intention denied
english: So we grant God decreed from eternity and foresaw that things would be executed in the same order he executes them in time — but we deny he also intended in that execution-order. In the acts of the divine will and mind there is of themselves no priority of order; on our way of understanding and the things' relation, execution and intention take plainly opposite orders. The decree of execution always starts from what is farther from the end and steps toward effecting it: God decreed to call Paul before justifying him, to justify and adorn with good works before glorifying. Executive will regards the external actual effecting, so what concurs earlier to producing the thing is referred earlier to that will. Intention, conversely, always starts from the end itself and moves to means so that it always wills first what is nearer the end.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: servant-to-Gaul ship example — intention vs execution order
english: These points are thorny, so an example: I intend to send my servant into Gaul — I will that before I decree anything about getting a ship; I would never have thought to prepare him a little boat unless sending him to Gaul had already been decided. At execution I will to have the ship ready before sending him across, since the crossing cannot happen without a ship. If someone objects that I changed my will — because at first I intended the crossing before the ship, and now I will to put him aboard before sending him across — who would not laugh at such subtleties? In one will earlier and later follow the internal order of willing; in the other, the external order of effecting.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14 close: Peter to heaven — same will, diverse habitude; Papist case ends
english: Fit this to our case: God intends to send Peter into Heaven — he wills that before he decrees efficacious, infallible means for him; he would never have resolved to supply such means unless he had first efficaciously decreed to give him heavenly glory. At execution God wills that Peter first share in grace, work well from grace, and persevere in good works to the end, before he makes harbor at heavenly glory. If some Jesuit disputant rises and shouts that God changed his will — because at first he intended glory for Peter before grace or perseverance, and now wills the reverse, grace and persevering good works before glory — I will laugh at the man's folly, and say this diverse consideration of intention and production of the same thing does not posit a diverse or changeable will in God, but a diverse habitude of the same will toward the same thing under diverse considerations. That is nearly all the Papists dispute for election from foreseen works.

title: Cap. IV open: Arminianorum sententia — from Pontiffs to interpolators; Arminius on faith foresight
english: Cap. IV. The Arminians' position is set out and their arguments refuted. Pontiff arguments omitted and rejected, we next deal with those who interpolated this controversy — changing some words and phrases while keeping the same error foundations. Chief among them is Jacobus Arminius: learned, sharp-minded, yet little regard for the ancient Church's judgment and none for the Reformed. Lest his defense look too crude, he would not hold anyone predestinated from foreseen works or merits (as some say) but from foreseen faith; nor would he boldly call that faith the cause of our predestination to glory as they did of works — with softened words he calls it only a condition, or something decently antecedent.

title: Cap. IV open: same if the thing itself is viewed — Causa/Merita; Arminius should not deny motive
english: But if you look at the thing itself, both positions come to the same: it makes anyone's predestination (or non-predestination) to eternal life depend on some antecedent human act. The ancient Fathers and Scholastics in this controversy seem to me to mean by Cause — nay Merit — nothing else than any good act a man performs by divine grace, in view of which God by his decree or ordination grants any benefit. So if God predestinates in view of our faith and does not in view of unbelief, Arminius should not have denied that he posits faith as a reason or motive cause of our predestination — even a meritorious one, in the ancients' phrase and sense. But that by the way.

title: Cap. IV open: duplex decretum — general (all believers) and singular (named from foreseen faith)
english: With predestination thus set from foresight of faith, Arminius and his followers establish a double decree. The first is general: God decreed to receive all believers into grace for Christ's sake, and to gift those persevering in faith with eternal life. The second is singular and terminates on particular persons: God established to gift with eternal glory this one and that by name — Peter, Paul, John — whom from eternity he foresaw would believe and remain in faith.

title: Cap. IV open: general decree urged as Scriptural — Resp. ad articulos, Hippolytus, Hague Remonstrants
english: Note well: that prior general decree, which names no one singularly to salvation, is what Arminius most urges and thrusts forward as the predestination Scripture recommends. So in his Response to the articles, art. 4: This decree (the general, indeterminate one) I say is the foundation of Christianity, salvation, and certainty of salvation; and Rom. 8, 10, 11 and Ephesians 1 treat of it. The same in his Letter to Hippolytus, where he skips the predestination by which God decreed to save certain singular persons and gift them faith — as a small matter, scarcely founded in Scripture. The Remonstrants at the Hague Conference, forgetting any particular decree, aim to prove this sole decree — God indiscriminately wills to save any who persevere in faith and pour wrath on all unbelievers — is the whole and entire decree of Predestination (p. 62).

title: Cap. IV open: neither general nor foresight-singular is Pauline predestination — reply plan
english: We hold the contrary: neither that general decree framed I will to save all who persevere in faith, nor that singular one resting on intervening foresight — I will gift eternal life to Peter, Paul, John, whom I foresee will perseveringly believe — is the predestination of which the Apostle speaks in Romans, and sacred Scripture. For the latter decree (so far as I know) adversaries rarely fight, content to assert it in a word; for the former they contend sharply. We will first meet their arguments, then confirm our position and impugn the contrary. And because at the Hague Colloquy arguments scattered elsewhere are gathered as into one fascicle, we will answer those Colloquists' little objections.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1: gospel-revealed will to save perseverers is the whole predestination decree
english: Arg. 1. God's will concerning men's salvation and ruin, revealed in the Gospel, is the whole entire decree of predestination. To will to save those persevering in faith, and to leave wrath on the unbelieving and impenitent, is that gospel-revealed will. Therefore to will to save perseverers in faith and leave wrath on unbelievers is the whole and entire decree of predestination. They say the major is self-evident and needs no proof; the minor is expressly founded in John 3:36 — Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God's wrath remains on him — and John 6:40 — This is the will of him who sent me, that whoever sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1 Sol: first — largo sensu any decree can be called praedestinatio, but theology specializes
english: Sol. Before solving the argument: adversaries keep playing with the word predestination, so a word on that. First: in a broad sense any decree of God about anything can be called a decree of predestination — all God's decrees are conceived from eternity in the divine mind according to the destined purpose of the divine will. But sacred theology has narrowed that word to a special sense; it is not candid theology to play games with hearers under the general notion.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1 Sol: second — not every revealed placitum is the high Pauline predestination
english: Second: in our controversy theologians have never meant by the predestination decree any revealed pleasure of the divine will about men's salvation and ruin, under any form. Twist the word that way and Matt. 25:34ff. itself becomes the decree — Come, blessed of my Father… Depart, cursed… — and so does Rom. 2:6, God will render to each according to his works. Those places do open God's will about salvation and ruin; but to lodge in them that high, inscrutable predestination Paul so celebrates is most alien to Scripture and to all sound theologians.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1 Sol: third — properly a practical decree gifting singular persons grace and glory
english: Third: predestination properly taken does not mean a universal law showing all alike how salvation is obtained or death incurred — Whoever believes and perseveres in piety will be saved; whoever does not believe or practice piety will be damned. It designates a practical decree by which from eternity God established to gift certain singular persons infallibly with singular goods: efficacious grace and eternal life. So Paul takes it in Rom. 8, restricting it to definite persons and joining it inseparably with glorification; so the School, which defined it Preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future. Decrees that only say generally what sort of men get eternal life or death, while settling nothing about grace and glory for any singular persons, do not express predestination's force and nature.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1 Sol: Major — if universal, false; revealed qualities/acts ≠ formal decree
english: With that premised I turn to their reason. The Major they call self-evident is either manifestly false, or particular — and then from particulars the conclusion is inept. If universal — Any gospel-revealed will of God about men's salvation and ruin is the whole entire decree of predestination — it is manifestly false. God has revealed his will about the qualities all who will share eternal life must have, and about the acts all who will enter that life must exercise; yet those revealed statutes do not contain the formal decree of divine predestination. That lies in the secret intention or will to gift certain elect efficaciously and infallibly those qualities and acts that lead to eternal life, and eternal life itself.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1 Sol: whole saving will includes vocation according to purpose — true praedestinans will
english: For God's whole will about men's salvation is not contained in Whoever believes will have eternal life. Scripture further opens that to certain ones — of whom from mere good pleasure he wills to have mercy before others — he wills to gift vocation according to purpose; from that vocation repentance, faith, sanctification, and finally glorification, all infallibly. That is the true, properly predestinating will, opened in the Gospel as to the thing, though individuals are not there named. So much for the Major.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1 Sol close: Minor true — inference that this is whole predestination weakest
english: On the Minor, founded in certain express Scripture places, one thing suffices: what they assume is most true — God has opened in the Gospel his will to save all who will persevere in faith and to damn unbelievers. What they infer from it is weakest: that in this decree of the divine will men's predestination is placed — nay the whole and entire decree of our predestination. When we come to our own arguments, we will dispel this Arminian dream.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2: Heb. 11:6 — without that by which one cannot please God, none can be elected
english: Arg. 2. Second they argue from Heb. 11:6 — Without faith it is impossible to please God — and build this: Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected by God to salvation; without faith one cannot please God; therefore. They call the Major certain, since electing to salvation is the highest love God can show a man — his greatest love toward a man.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: Apostle twisted — faith here actual, not foreseen; Enoch walked with God
english: Sol. First to the Apostle's words: they are twisted badly into a sense wholly alien to his purpose. Faith here is not the foreseen faith of a man not yet existing, but actual faith already at work. That is clear from εὐηρέστησεν, to please — which Paul takes from the LXX at Gen. 5:24, Enoch pleased God; the Hebrew is he walked continually with God — he did not imitate his age's wickedness but served God sincerely and worshiped him purely. So the Apostle means only that no one can lead a pious life pleasing to God without faith, confirmed by Enoch's example. Wondrous ingenuity in the Remonstrants, who carved from this their election hanging on foresight of faith.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: Major stuffed with equivocations — sine quo as condition vs means; elect infants
english: Now the syllogism. The Major — Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected to salvation — is stuffed with equivocations. Without which can mean: without which, foreseen as an antecedent condition, no one can be elected; or without which as a prepared, destined means no one can be elected. The first sense touches the cause but is manifestly false; the second does not even touch it, and still is not absolute truth. Some please God unto election to eternal life in whom God foresees no faith at all, still less antecedent faith — for example elect infants who die before they can believe or persevere. What will never be is not foreseen; foresight's object is something infallibly future.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: placere Deo = walk with God — without actual faith election would be temporal
english: Further, to please God is not one sense only. Paulinely it means doing works pleasing to God, or (from the original) walking with God. Mark how absurd it is that no one could ever be elected unless he first has all that our works need to please God. Without actual faith — and charity too — no one can please God that way, or walk with God as Enoch did. If this argument had force, all election would be temporal and would follow justification and sanctification.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: two pleasing — destined vs adopted; Orange 25; first love from God's fountain
english: Further: some please God before others as destined to faith and eternal life; some please as sons already adopted, sanctified, and accepted to the right of eternal life. In the prior sense (ours in this controversy) it is not only possible that one please God before faith had or foreseen — it is plainly impossible to please otherwise. Best Orange canon 25: Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. If we could receive no gift from God unless we first pleased him, and could not please without faith first, then either faith's gift is from us not God, or you get an infinite regress. So the reason of first complacency — divine love toward the fallen creature — is not some antecedent good quality in man, but must be fetched from the fountain of divine love. Love is the first gift in which all others are given; and God's love has this singular: it does not find but makes its object lovable to itself (Deut. 7:7–8).

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol close: election from amor benevolentiae not amicitiae — Remonstrants elide their own nerve
english: Finally, their Major's confirmation — electing to salvation is an effect of highest love, so no one can be elected unless through faith at least foreseen he is pleasing and acceptable — is easily refuted. Election is an effect of love, but not of that friendship-love of Enoch pleased God; rather of the love the School calls benevolence. Effects of friendship-love tend only to the faithful and pious; effects of benevolence tend to the impious and unbelieving, to inspire faith and holiness in them — even to the not-yet-born, to destine them eternal life. The Remonstrants cannot even deny a love of God put forth toward the impious before faith and conversion; and by confessing it they cut the nerves of this argument. See what they write on antecedent and consequent love, Hague Colloquy p. 183 (Bertius).

title: Cap. IV Arg. 3: beneplacitum de salute = praedestinatio — 1 Cor. 1:21 Credentes velle salvare
english: Arg. 3. God's good pleasure concerning human salvation is predestination itself to salvation; to will to save believers is that good pleasure concerning men's salvation; therefore. They call the Major clearly true, because election means nothing but God's good pleasure concerning the elect man's salvation. The Minor they found in 1 Cor. 1:21 — It pleased God by the foolish preaching to save believers — and illustrate from the contrary: in men who scarcely believe God has no good pleasure, but his soul loathes them, and he swears such will not enter his rest (1 Cor. 10:5; Heb. 3:18).

title: Cap. IV Arg. 3 Sol: same vice as Arg. 1 — Major terms incongruous; beneplacitum wider than praedestinatio
english: Sol. This argument is nearly the same as the first and has the same vice. Again: in the Major the terms are incongruously and unskillfully set. Good pleasure concerning human salvation is wider and more general than predestination, so it ought to be predicate not subject — thus: Predestination is God's good pleasure concerning human salvation; to will to save believers is that good pleasure; therefore to will to save believers is predestination itself. Had they framed the Major that way, they would have concluded from all affirmatives in the second figure. They preferred a preposterous wording to an open fallacy.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 3 Sol: if Major universal, false — declared beneplacita do not contain formal decree
english: Let them argue their way: unless the Major is universal, nothing follows from particulars. If universal — Any or every good pleasure of God concerning human salvation is predestination itself to salvation — it is manifestly false. In any declared good pleasure about human salvation the formal decree of predestination is not at once expressed or contained. God has declared in the word his will's good pleasure about the qualities and operations of those to be led to salvation, the means they ought to use, and the whole order of executing predestination — yet those do not contain the election decree, because they look equally to all and are set forth as law.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 3 Sol: beneplacitum that includes praedestinatio is the arcane will from the mass
english: The good pleasure that actually includes predestination is not those declared statutes, but God's eternal secret will: from the same mass of perdition he resolved with himself to lead some persons infallibly to glory by pure mercy through efficacious grace, and according to justice to leave others in the perdition they merit.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 3 Sol close: Minor true of medium — not eligere credentes; Rom. 9:15
english: Now the Minor: to will to save believers by the foolishness of preaching is God's good pleasure concerning human salvation. Who denies it? It is good pleasure about the means and organ without which no adult can be led to salvation. It does not express that eternal εὐδοκία by which some are elected to salvation and its means, others passed by. In a word: the Apostle said It pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save believers — so he requires preaching and faith as means antecedent by God's good pleasure to effecting salvation. He did not say to elect believers. So he does not require faith or preaching as foreseen antecedent conditions of the eternal act of election. Nor do 1 Cor. 10 and Heb. 3 on unbelievers help: they do not prove eternal election or passing-by from foresight of future faith or unbelief, but that in executing his eternal decree God finally brings into his rest those whom efficacious vocation working according to purpose has made faithful, and excludes those who remain unbelieving by their own heart's corrupt perversity. Why he had mercy on these rather than those — do not ask, if you would not err. Suffice Rom. 9:15: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 4: Eph. 1:4 — election in Christ is of believers only; Arminius Exam. Pred. Perk.
english: Arg. 4. Another argument from Eph. 1:4 — According as he chose us in him, that is Christ. They argue: the election by which God chose us in Christ is of believers only; the election made before the world's foundations was made in Christ; therefore it is of believers only. The Major's truth, they say, is that no one can be elected in Christ unless he is in Christ — and only believers are. Arminius urges the same in Exam. Pred. Perk. pp. 313, 32: on the Apostle, Christ is not only a means through which salvation already gotten by election is obtained, but a meritorious cause in respect of which election is made and for whom that grace is prepared. God loves no one to eternal life except in Christ; so since no one is considered in Christ by God unless inserted by faith, election belongs to the faithful. So he.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 4 Sol: conclusion misses the point — believers consequently, not antecedently; Augustine
english: Sol. Start from their conclusion: it does not settle what is in controversy. The question is not whether election is only of those who will be believers — or of those God foresaw before the world's foundations would believe — but whether that eternal act of divine election prerequires that foresight as cause, or at least antecedent condition. We deny it; adversaries cannot prove it. We grant election is of believers only — not believers in divine foresight before election, but believers consequently, by virtue of the grace prepared and destined for them in election. So Augustine, De praed. Sanct. 18: we were going to be such because he chose that we should be such through grace; and ch. 10: by predestination God foresaw what he himself would do (likewise ch. 17). Consult those places for the best solution of this Arminian argument and the best reading of this Pauline context.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 4 Sol: Major — temporal election of actual believers vs eternal gift of faith in Christ
english: Drop the conclusion and take the Major: The election by which God chose us in Christ is of believers only. If that means temporal election — certain persons severed from the wicked world by efficacious vocation — we grant it is of believers, and of actually believing ones. But we dispute the eternal act of divine election, not its temporal effect. So of eternal election (what this controversy must regard): it is not of believers as if men still outside Christ were foreseen as believers and then elected with that foresight intervening; it is of believers because God foresaw he would give the gift of faith to those he decreed in the eternal purpose of election to give to Christ.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 4 Sol: John 6:37 — donation causes coming; elegit in Christo mis-exposed
english: John 6:37 helps here: Whatever the Father gives me will come to me. The donation marks God's eternal election; coming marks faith produced in human hearts in its time. Donation is the antecedent cause of coming (believing) — not foreseen faith the antecedent cause of giving (electing). Their Major confirmation — God cannot elect in Christ one who is not in Christ; only those considered inserted into Christ by faith are in Christ; therefore only believers are elected — rests on a false reading of He chose us in Christ.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 4 Sol: in Christo refers to the electing act — Eph. 1:3, 2 Cor. 5:19 parallels
english: In Christ refers not to the elect man's state but to the electing God's act. Arminians expose He chose us in Christ as: us already existing in Christ, or foreseen as believing and inserted by faith, whom God then chose. But in Christ joined to a divine act does not always mean the subject already exists in Christ beforehand. Eph. 1:3: God blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ — and among those blessings is the first gift of faith and repentance, given not to those already in Christ but to those alien from him, to bring them to Christ and insert them. So God in Christ reconciled the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19) and created us unto good works (Eph. 2:10). Remonstrants themselves say God regenerates men in Christ (Coll. p. 99). In all these, in Christ cannot without absurdity mean already existing in Christ beforehand. So to elect in Christ is nothing but, in electing, to look to Christ the Mediator and Head of the Church, and by his grace to destine members to be joined to him and glorified.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 4 Sol close: love to eternal life in Christ true of introduction, false of praedestinatio
english: Arminius urges that God loves no one to eternal life except in Christ — as he reads it, except considered faithful and already inserted into Christ, and so elects none except as faithful. That is true of the introduction itself to eternal life, false of predestination. In that sense God loves to eternal life all he decreed before the world's foundations to give to Christ to be made alive and saved. Those given to be made alive are not considered already made alive and faithful, but dead in sins and still unbelieving. In a word: God chose us in Christ not because he viewed us as already in Christ by our faith before election, but because with respect to Christ the Mediator all who are predestinated are predestinated to eternal life.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5: Eph. 1:5–6 — destinavit εἰς υἱοθεσίαν; adoption only of the faithful
english: Arg. 5. Their syllogism: those destined unto adoption through Jesus Christ and accepted in Christ as the beloved count as faithful; but Eph. 1:5–6 shows that everyone God elects to salvation he so destines unto adoption through Christ and makes acceptable in the beloved; therefore everyone he elects he considered faithful. They prove the Major from John 1:12 and Gal. 3:26 — no adoption into sons except through faith; you are all sons of God through faith in Christ.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol: Major false — temporal adoption needs faith; eternal destinatio need not
english: Sol. That Major fails. Yes, finished temporal adoption carries faith with it — beforehand as a condition, or at least together with adoption in the same moment — so you cannot treat someone as actually adopted without treating him as faithful. But destination unto adoption in God's mind before the world's foundations can and must be thought without treating our faith as an antecedent condition.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol: eternal destinatio κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν — not according to foresight of faith
english: And it does the Major no good to say there is no sonship-adoption except through faith. Grant the point: there is still an eternal destination of certain persons unto adoption according to the good pleasure of his will (Eph. 1:5), not according to foresight of our faith.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol close: faith is effect of εὐδοκία — Matt. 11:26; Augustine De praed. Sanct. 13, 19
english: Believers' faith — what sets them off from unbelievers — is not an antecedent of this divine good pleasure but its effect (Matt. 11:26). Augustine's De praedestinatione sanctorum 13 and 19 carefully opens these very Pauline words the Remonstrants press.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol cont: John 15:16 — we did not choose; do not confuse destined and temporal adoption
english: Sol. (cont.) Augustine nearly walks this first chapter of Ephesians in explaining it. Only a few notes: the election the Lord meant by You did not choose me, but I chose you — and faith itself does not come first. He chose us not because we believed, but that we may believe, lest we be said to have chosen him first. So they dangerously confuse destined adoption in the eternal act of divine election with finished adoption in the temporal effect of efficacious vocation.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol cont: faith may accompany temporal adoption — not eternal destinatio; chain from election
english: Faith may precede or at least go with adoption finished in the elect themselves — but it cannot (even on our way of thinking) precede the adoption God from eternity decreed and destined for certain persons in his electing mind. Efficacious vocation according to purpose precedes saving faith; predestination or election to glory precedes that vocation. So none are considered or foreseen as faithful except from the antecedent predestination decree — because efficacious vocation, true faith, and real adoption flow from it.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol cont: benevolence toward elect still in sin — Orange 25; Scotus; two acceptations
english: Further: their claim that God makes or holds none pleasing in Christ except the faithful cannot stand. Whence comes God's efficacious purpose to inspire saving faith and repentance into human hearts? That purpose still regards unbelievers and the impenitent — so they must grant a singular, special love of God there. So great is his love for his only-begotten Son that, looking to him in eternal benevolence, he embraces all he elected in him even while considered in sin and unbelief — and by special grace always works to draw them out of that state. So Orange can. 25: Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. Add: Christ is a head of infinite power, his merit of such efficacy that it can influence members not yet united but only destined, and by that influence unite them. Scotus (3 dist. 19) well noted: Christ merited that the not-yet-joined be joined — and therein his merit chiefly consists. If his merit reaches non-believers and joins them, a conforming divine acceptance extends to them too. Briefly: one may be acceptable to God in Christ, or for Christ's sake, two ways. One: present friendship-love, admitted as a household member to the throne of grace — in that sense only the faithful are pleasing in Christ. Two: eternal benevolence as a predestinated member of his Son — though paternal effects are not yet poured out, he intends in Christ and for Christ to pour them at the fit time. In that sense God has made many not yet believing or converted pleasing in Christ — not as already placed in him, but as to be placed by special favor, because elected in Christ from eternity.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol close: Minor — faith a destined means, not a foreseen condition of election
english: On the Minor, which sits in express Scripture words, little need be added: from what is said it is plain you cannot prove from it that faith in election must be taken as a foreseen condition antecedent to election — but as a means destined and to be given to those God elected and destined for adoption.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 6: perpetual use of Electi — in salvation contexts always means believers
english: Arg. 6. Another argument from the standing use of Elect wherever salvation is in view — Rom. 8: Who will accuse God's elect?; Rom. 11: The elect have obtained; Matt. 22: Many called, few elect. From these and like places: the word Elect, when Scripture speaks of salvation, is always used for believers; therefore there is no election to salvation except of believers.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 6 Sol: elect known a posteriori — many elect while still unbelieving; Rom. 8:28–30
english: Sol. When Scripture names designated persons Elect, it fits the word to believers alone — because we know nothing sure of election's secret except a posteriori, from the effects of faith and sanctification. So the Apostle often marks believers as Elect. That does not mean elect and believers must be confused, or that election hangs on foresight of faith as an antecedent condition. We cannot call unbelievers elect as we see them — yet many impenitent and unbelieving are elect in the meantime; true of Paul and of all the elect before efficacious conversion. And since Predestination and Election are used interchangeably in this dispute, Predestinated in salvation-talk is used even of unbelievers. Rom. 8:28ff.: Whom he predestinated, he called; whom he called, he justified — openly sets some Predestinated before vocation, faith, and justification.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 6 Sol close: actual faith not foresight-faith; invert — nexus not Remonstrant order
english: Add: wherever Elect is given to the faithful, actual faith is meant — not faith merely in God's foresight before the world's foundations, which the Remonstrants urge. So they wrongly infer: Elect and believer are the same subjects in Scripture's phrasing, therefore election is from foresight of faith. Rather: therefore to all the elect in their time saving faith is given. If the argument had force I could invert it: Believers, when salvation is in view, always means the elect; therefore no saving faith except of the elect; therefore faith arises from antecedent election. From such word-use you may conclude only that faith and election have a nexus — not whether foresight of faith precedes election as a prerequired condition (as Remonstrants will), or faith follows election as a disposition to be produced in all the elect at the due time. The cited places do not settle that; weighing them one by one is needless.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 7: τρόπος of mercy and justice is the one true predestination — Rom. 9:22
english: Arg. 7. The τρόπος by which the Lord shows his mercy in some and his justice in others is the true and only predestination. But the decree to save believers on one side and condemn unbelievers on the other is such a τρόπος. Therefore that decree is the true and only predestination. They say Contraremonstrants admit the Major; the Minor they prove from Rom. 9:22, where vessels of mercy and of wrath mean believers and unbelievers.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 7 Sol: double praeordinatio — intention and execution both declare mercy and justice
english: Sol. In God's mind regarding the elect, conceive a double praeordination: one of intention, one of execution — both serve to declare divine mercy and justice. Example: before the world's foundations God decreed to love Jacob and Peter and have mercy on them in special grace and eternal life; to pass by Esau and Judas for that infallible attainment of life and grace, and appoint those hardened in their sins to just condemnation — an abyss of mercy and justice no human wit can pierce. And that the same God has opened in his word that he decreed to save all believers and damn all unbelievers, and that on judgment day he in fact damns Esau and Judas and saves Jacob and Peter — that too is a singular specimen of divine mercy and justice.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 7 Sol: do not bind whole praedestinatio to the execution τρόπος — Major not universal
english: So in both praeordinations mercy and justice shine — in the decree to make certain persons believers, and in the decree that promises and gives those believers eternal life; in the decree not to have mercy so far as to soften some and inspire faith, and in the decree that damns the same hardened unbelievers. Adversaries should not bind the whole reason of predestination to the latter τρόπος; it turns most properly on the former. With that premised: the Major is not universal. Not every τρόπος in which mercy toward some and justice toward others appears is that unique predestination whose depth Scripture so celebrates — though in predestination properly taken, by which some are destined to life by special grace and others left in death by their own demerit, mercy and justice play their parts most clearly.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 7 Sol: Minor — Ego salvabo credentes shows equal mercy/justice; discrimination from acts
english: Now the Minor: that the decree to save believers and condemn unbelievers is the praeordination by which God declares mercy toward some and justice toward others. We grant that on that decree mercy and justice are seen and declared in the event — but mercy puts itself forth far higher in the predestination decree, and justice in the decree of passing by. I will save believers, I will condemn unbelievers, taken in itself, shows and makes mercy equally to all, justice equally to all. It promises Jacob and Peter nothing it does not under the same conditions promise Esau and Judas; it denies Esau or Judas nothing it does not under the same conditions deny Jacob and Peter. That Jacob and Peter share mercy and eternal life while Esau and Judas do not comes not from diverse decrees about the persons, but from the persons' diversity in their operations.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 7 Sol close: proper praedestinatio decrees special mercy to elect, denial to others
english: But the mercy that puts itself forth in the predestination decree decrees, prepares, and gifts to a singular predestinated person what it does not decree, prepare, or gift to one not predestinated. The justice in the reprobation decree decrees something denied to the reprobate that is not denied to the Predestinated. So it is not enough for predestination properly so called that, with diverse acts of human choice intervening, mercy falls on these and justice on those. What is required is a decree that, from God's primary intention and special operation in decreeing, includes mercy to be shown to these, and from his freest, most just will hints that the same special mercy is to be denied to others.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 8: from the order of execution — whom God saves/destroys in time he decreed from eternity
english: Arg. 8. From the order of execution they argue: those and such as God saves and destroys in time, he decreed from eternity to save and destroy. But in time God saves only those who persevere in faith, as such, and destroys unbelievers as such. Therefore from eternity he decreed to save only the faithful as such. They prove the Major from God's immutability; the Minor from the Gospel's standing voice — life promised to believers, death threatened to unbelievers.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 8 Sol: conclusion does not force foresight-election; Major mixes Decernere and Servare
english: Sol. The conclusion does not directly contradict us. What they needed was: therefore God elected to glory only the faithful as faithful, from foresight of that faith. Their conclusion — he decreed from eternity to save only the faithful as such — makes faith an antecedent condition for the external conferring of decreed salvation (which we grant), not for God's internal destinating decree (which they needed to prove). On the Major: two words are mixed in bad faith — one names destination to salvation in the divine mind, the other leading to salvation in external execution. Decernere looks to the eternal intrinsic act of will; Servare to the extrinsic temporal effect.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 8 Sol: faith precedes saving Peter, not the eternal decree — head of the error
english: God's internal act does not have the causes or require the antecedent conditions that the external effect of salvation has and prerequires. He does not save Peter unless Peter's faith precedes; yet he decrees to save Peter in the free eternal good pleasure of his will — not with that faith as a condition for constituting the decree, but as a condition for timely temporal effecting of what was decreed. The error's head: the antecedent quality of faith, which should be joined to the thing decreed and set before it only in execution, is joined to God's decreeing act and set before the decree as an antecedent motive.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 8 Sol: king and beggar — robes precede crowning, not the first destination
english: An example: some conditions can be required beforehand so that Peter is saved or brought into the heavenly kingdom, without being required beforehand so that he is elected or destined by God to eternal life. Suppose a king sees a beggar in rags, foul with ulcers, yet from mere good pleasure decrees to adopt him and raise him to the kingdom's crown — and also orders that before crowning he be clothed in royal garments and purged of uncleanness, and not crowned until thus purged and clothed. Who does not see those fair garments and the purging were decreed and prerequired as antecedent to crowning, yet not as antecedent motives for the first destination of kingdom and crown?

title: Cap. IV Arg. 8 Sol: Remonstrant syllogism on foresight-robes is mere trifles; apply to elect
english: Run the Remonstrants' pattern and its vanity shows at once: whom and as such this king crowned in time, he decreed from the start to crown as such; but in time he crowns one beautifully clothed and purged of squalor as such; therefore from the start he decreed to adopt and crown one beautifully clothed as such — i.e. from foresight of fair garments. Mere trifles. The first will to adopt and crown did not spring from foresight of garments; crowning itself required those garments and that prior purging, by the king's decree ordering external execution. Apply it: God from mere good pleasure wills to adopt Peter, Paul, or any elect corrupt in old Adam's mass and wasting in sin, and gift eternal life — yet also decrees, and publishes in the Gospel, that he wills him first purified by faith and cleansed from sin's filth before entering the kingdom.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 8 Sol close: faith antecedent to execution not to eternal will; Minor — temporal prereqs
english: Peter as faithful and purged of sins is antecedent to executing what was willed — acquiring salvation, by God's decree — but not antecedent to God's will to save Peter, who decreed both: to save Peter, and to gift him faith before he is saved. Nor does that unsettle divine immutability: something may be decreed as antecedent to actually producing what was decreed without being antecedent to God's internal volition about producing it. Reason: the effect of salvation in the predestinated subject and the decree to give salvation in the predestinating will are diverse things and do not require the same prior causes or conditions. On the Minor: many things are prerequired for someone to be saved in time that were not prerequired for eternal election to salvation — rather means later conferred on the predestinated so he is led through to salvation.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 9: decree whose foundation is Christ is election itself — salvandis credentibus
english: Arg. 9. God's decree on human salvation whose foundation is Christ is election itself to salvation. The decree to save believers is that salvation-decree founded on Christ. Therefore the decree to save the faithful is election itself. They call the Major plain — no salvation or blessing unto salvation except in Christ. The Minor equally clear: that one decree is the foundation of Christianity, of salvation, and of certainty of salvation — Christianity, because by it God constitutes Christ Savior and Head of those who will share salvation; salvation, because it is God's good-pleasure decree in Christ on which our whole salvation rests; certainty, because all our assurance rests on this prop: Believers will be saved; I believe; therefore I will be saved.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 9 Sol: owed conclusion is foresight-election; Major imperfect if made universal
english: Sol. Notice: in no Remonstrant argument does the owed conclusion appear. One thing is to conclude that the decree to save believers is election itself; another, that election itself is from foresight of antecedent faith — the conclusion we waited for in vain and never saw. Discuss their reason as it stands. The Major explains election quite imperfectly, and is not true throughout if taken universally as it must be, unless we let a slippery syllogism be forced on us. Make it universal: every divine decree on human salvation whose foundation is Christ is election itself of singular persons to salvation. Attach the Minor: the decree to save believers (any men, if they believe) is that Christ-founded salvation decree. Therefore that decree is election itself of singular persons.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 9 Sol: diverse Christ-founded decrees — conditional gospel vs singular election
english: To expose the errors: diverse decrees on human salvation can come into view, all founded on Christ, yet election itself does not consist in all of them. First are known decrees published to all, stating under what conditions or by what means men are led to salvation — I will save all who repent, believe in the Messiah, and persevere in that faith and newness of life to the end. By those, all mortals are taught what conditions let them expect salvation. But they set no singular persons elected or predestinated before others. Christ is their foundation: God would never have deigned to deal with corrupt rebellious man under such terms, or promise eternal life to the believing and repenting, without this new-covenant Mediator in whom all God's promises are Yea and Amen. Yet election's reason is not in them: with life offered promiscuously to all sinners if they believe and repent, unless another decree of pure mercy also came, no one would be saved, because no one would believe.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 9 Sol: second and third decrees — singular persons and efficacious means; Major false twice
english: Second: another kind of decrees by which from eternity singular persons are designated in God's mind and will to be led infallibly to salvation. The individuals are not named in Scripture's book, yet they are written in the book of life (Phil. 4:3; Luke 10:20). Of these: God knows his own (2 Tim. 2:19); he calls his sheep by name (John 10:3); I know whom I have chosen (John 13:18). Third: always bound to that person-decree is a decree to gift those singular persons every means of efficacious grace by which they are led to salvation. So Rom. 8:30 — whom he predestinated he called, whom he called he justified — and Eph. 1:3–4. Election before the ages is as it were the measure of all spiritual blessings given in time (faith, holiness, perseverance); not the reverse, as Remonstrants will, foresight faith and perseverance measuring election. These decrees too have Christ for foundation: in him they are elected as members to be united in time to Christ their Head, and through and for him they are imbued with special grace. So the Major is false twice: it makes Christ foundation only of I will save all believers, when he is also foundation of I will give eternal life to Peter, Paul, and each elect — faith, perseverance, grace leading effectively to salvation. And it locates election formally in that universal decree, whereas election puts itself forth in the second decree electing singular persons to life and the third destinating them to efficacious means before others — per the theologians' definition: predestination is preparation of grace now and glory hereafter.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 9 Sol: Minor — Christ founds more than the general decree; Christianity's true foundations
english: On the Minor in a word: Christ is foundation of that general decree to save whosoever under the condition of faith — but not of that alone; also of other decrees by which singular persons, given by the Father to Christ before the world's foundations, will in their time be gifted grace and glory. Remonstrants should not bury those later decrees in obstinate silence and stick in the first universal one, unless they think there never was a decree in God's mind to imbue singular persons with efficacious grace and lead them by it to glory. They cry the Major plain because no salvation except in Christ — a frivolous proof. Because no benefit is decreed for us except in Christ, is every Christ-founded salvation-decree therefore our election itself? That coheres like sand without lime. They say the Minor is clear because I will save all Believers founds Christianity, salvation, and certainty. I answer: that general decree alone is not Christianity's foundation. There are others — chief among them that faith, perseverance, and whatever leads infallibly to heaven are special gifts of special grace, not contingent effects from the choice of a man not yet elected, and motives of divine election.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 9 Sol close: general decree not sufficient certainty; Cap. IV Collocutors' args end
english: Further: the foundation we assert proves far more that God constituted Christ Savior and Head of those who will be saved than their general one. All who will believe will be saved shows a pact of salvation with the human race for Christ's sake — but it lacks effect unless we fulfill the believing condition, about which that decree constitutes nothing. When we defend that God further decreed for Christ's sake to give grace, faith, and life to all the elect, and from his fullness really pour efficacious saving grace into them, we make Christ Savior and Head of all who share salvation not by bare pact but by the fact itself. Besides, All believers will be saved is not the good-pleasure decree our whole salvation rests on — it is, so to speak, declarative and doctrinal; singular persons' salvation must rest on a practical operating decree of God. It would go miserably with us if all our salvation rested on If you believe you will be saved, with no further good-pleasure decree to give us faith and save us efficaciously. Finally that general decree cannot be any singular person's sufficient certainty of his salvation: it saves no one by its own virtue alone — many will be damned who know and believe all believers and repenting will be saved. Certainty needs another decree's efficacy: that I believe, that I will persevere to the end. Whence that certainty of my faith and perseverance? Not from my contingent free choice — therefore from some immutable divine decree. As to the thing: certainty for this or that singular person rests on a practical decree infallibly decreeing and working that person's salvation. As to our knowledge: certainty rests on some revelation of that decree through the Spirit of adoption and its effects in individuals' hearts — that Spirit witnesses to our spirit that we are those sons of God destined to eternal life, sanctified in this age to be glorified hereafter. In the universal law-form decree Whoever believes will be saved, neither certain salvation of any singular person nor certain knowledge of one's infallibly future salvation can be founded. And these are all the Collocutors' arguments trying to establish election of singular men from the antecedent condition of foresight faith — all taken from Arminius's writings.

title: Cap. V open + Obj. 1: election is love unto salvation — therefore from foresight of faith
english: Cap. V. Certain Arminian objections the Collocutors left out are set out and answered. Arminius has further arguments not used at the Hague Conference; we bring those in too and treat them one by one — many from his Examination of Perkinsian Predestination, some elsewhere. Obj. 1. Election is love unto salvation. God cannot love a sinner unto salvation unless reconciled to him. But God is reconciled only to one he looks on as believing in Christ. Therefore God elects no one except from an antecedent intuition of faith.

title: Cap. V Obj. 1 Sol: election is eternal purpose — love in the electing One, not yet poured out
english: Sol. Election is the eternal purpose or decree to take certain men, others passed by, to the efficacious infallible attainment of grace and glory — and in that sense it is rightly Love unto salvation: not love already poured out outwardly on the elect, but love still enclosed in the eternal purpose in the electing One himself. So God embraced Paul not yet born, much less converted or believing, with his secret love, having in himself an eternal immutable purpose to impart grace and glory to him. Let the first proposition pass: election is love unto salvation.

title: Cap. V Obj. 1 Sol: cannot love unless reconciled — slippery and false; loves to gift faith
english: What they attach — that God cannot so love anyone unto salvation unless reconciled, and cannot be reconciled to anyone except from antecedent foresight of his faith — is very slippery, indeed plainly false. By the love latent in the election decree, God loves one not yet reconciled so far as to appoint him to be reconciled; loves one not yet faithful so far as to decree him gifted with faith — though not as he loves sons already adopted, reconciled, and believing.

title: Cap. V Obj. 1 Sol: Arminius's own definition — faith prepared in predestination before foresight
english: Arminius himself, if consistent, could not deny that by this election/predestination love God embraces the elect before all foresight of faith in them. In Public Disputations, Thesis 15 On predestination (p. 153), he defines: it is God's good-pleasure decree in Christ by which from eternity he determined to justify, adopt, and gift eternal life to the faithful whom he decreed to gift with faith. In the Examination of Perkinsian Predestination he grants God does not foreknow men as about to believe before he has predestinated them to believe (p. 32), and adds the strong reason: he foreknew they would believe by his gift, which gift is prepared in predestination (p. 37). Elsewhere he puts a double matter of predestination: divine things (spiritual blessings) and the persons to whom their communication is predestinated. I ask: how does God elect from foresight of faith if in election itself the gift of faith is decreed and prepared for men? It is ridiculous to say he decrees and prepares faith for certain men in election, yet elects them from an antecedent intuition of faith preceding that election — as if he only then decreed the gift of faith to this or that person when he had already seen he would believe.

title: Cap. V Obj. 1 Sol close: distinct decrees still; love unto salvation prepares faith for not-yet-believers
english: To dodge the inconvenience Arminius claims there are not one but distinct decrees — I will give life to the faithful, and I will give faith to this one. If distinct, why did he himself put both in his definition of predestination? Let them be distinct (we care little): still, since there is predestination or election of certain persons to faith, that election must precede every intuition of faith in the elect; it must arise from love destinating to these what is not decreed to others. And when God elects singular persons to faith, others passed by, he does not do it unaware that this faith leads infallibly to eternal life — rather he ordained and gifted them that gift unto that end. So love unto salvation puts itself forth toward not-yet-believers by predestinating and preparing the gift of faith whereby they believe and, believing, enter eternal life. Thus this first Arminian objection has no force.

title: Cap. V Obj. 2: actual gift of eternal life bound to believers — therefore election from foresight faith
english: Obj. 2. The actual gift of eternal life is no more bound than the will to give it. But the gift itself is bound to the faithful and presupposes antecedent faith. Therefore the will to give eternal life — which is nothing other than election — is likewise bound. So election is from foresight faith. Arminius and almost all who follow him build many arguments from this principle — frail and invalid.

title: Cap. V Obj. 2 Sol: more required as instruments for external work than as motives for intention
english: Sol. Sound philosophy teaches that more is required as antecedent instruments to produce a work in an external act than as antecedent motives for intending or destinating that work in the operator's mind and will. Argue parallel: the actual building of a house is no more bound than the will to build it; but building is bound to the prior fitting of timbers and stones; therefore the will is bound to all those as antecedents and is born from foresight of them. An inept conclusion indeed.

title: Cap. V Obj. 2 Sol: will to build precedes coaptation; eternal life given vs destinated
english: The craftsman's first will to build was not born from foresight of fitting stones and timbers — the reverse: from the will to build followed that first joining of stones and timbers. Likewise eternal life produced outwardly and conferred on Peter or Paul presupposes many things that eternal life as destinated to them in God's secret will does not prerequire. To destinate to life is an immanent act in God's mind; to give life or lead to life is a work tending outward on the creature. The former is finished by the sole act of the divine will; the latter is not finished without many creaturely actions intervening, prerequired by divine ordination.

title: Cap. V Obj. 2 Sol close: crass error — God never bound himself Si prius credideris, licebit praedestinare
english: So it is a crass error to think that God's first eternal destinating of a singular person to life is bound by the same laws that bind temporal attainment on the human side. The same God who told man, If you believe, I will give you life — or you will be saved — never bound himself: If you first believe, then I may predestinate you to life; otherwise I may not.

title: Cap. V Obj. 3: as one exists receiving eternal life, so considered — only the faithful predestinated
english: Obj. 3. As one exists when receiving eternal life, so considered by God he was predestinated to receive it. But only the faithful receives, and no one else. Therefore only the faithful — and as considered faithful — was predestinated to receive eternal life.

title: Cap. V Obj. 3 Sol: Major ambiguous — reject prior existence-as-faithful; grant foresight of what God will make
english: Sol. The Major is highly ambiguous. If it means every one predestinated to life already existed in God's intuition, before the predestination decree, as he will be in receiving eternal life — reject it outright. But if it means: when God destinates the elect to life, he at once from eternity looks ahead and sees of what sort he will make them before leading them to life, and contemplates them as such to be brought into possession of eternal life — that is most true, and cannot be denied unless one denies that God foreknows what he himself will do.

title: Cap. V Obj. 3 Sol: foresight of elects' faith inferred from election — Acts 13:48; Prosper on dignity
english: Granted that, election is not drawn from antecedent foresight of faith — rather a sure foresight in God of the elects' faith is inferred from antecedent election, per Acts 13:48: as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. So God rightly foresees as about to believe, before they receive eternal life, all whom by the predestination decree he ordained to receive it. What Prosper said of charity we also affirm of faith (On Free Will, p. 125): of this so great, ineffable good no one was found worthy; but whoever was elected by God was made worthy. That learned Father, scourge of Pelagians and Semipelagians, did not say: whoever considered and foreseen as endowed with charity or faith was afterward elected — but: whoever was elected by God afterward became partaker of faith and charity.

title: Cap. V Obj. 3 Sol: preconsidered as to-be-faithful for reception, not as already faithful for destinating
english: So whoever will receive eternal life was preconsidered by God as about to be faithful — antecedent to receiving eternal life — but not foreseen as already existing faithful — antecedent to destinating eternal life. Likeness: a man of good estate sees a wretched needy infant and at once decrees to adopt him and gift an excellent inheritance, yet not to enter it before puberty and cultivation in letters and manners. Truly that inheritance was destinated to him considered unlearned, uncultivated, an infant; yet the same inheritance was gifted to him considered cultivated, learned, of age — from the adopter's destinating purpose.

title: Cap. V Obj. 3 Sol close: same pattern in eternal inheritance; Hague Collation already refuted
english: Think the same pattern in destinating and gifting the eternal inheritance, and the weakness of their argument is plain. I add no more: nearly the same argument, slightly altered, was brought at the Hague Conference and already refuted by us.

title: Cap. V Obj. 4: if predestination without foresight of faith, then save without satisfaction of justice
english: Obj. 4. If God predestinated some to life without intuition of antecedent faith, then he would also will to save them without satisfaction of his justice — loving them more than his own justice. But those are false. Therefore so is what follows from them: that God predestinates anyone before foresight of faith, which applies Christ's satisfaction to particular persons unto salvation.

title: Cap. V Obj. 4 Sol: eternal will to save ≠ all that concurs in the consummated external act
english: Sol. I answer: not everything that concurs in the will to save as consummated in the external act also concurs in the eternal will to save enclosed in election's secret purpose. We deny the Major's consequence. God never had a will to save anyone without satisfaction of his justice; yet he had a will to give certain ones to Christ, to give them faith by which that union would be made, and by which, with that faith mediating, he would be efficaciously satisfied for them through Christ's death — all of this antecedent to foresight of faith as already certainly and infallibly existing in them, yet not without foresight, nor by excluding foresight of faith to be infallibly imparted to them from God's grace.

title: Cap. V Obj. 4 Sol close: they deduce from foresight denied secundum quid, not simply excluded
english: So they try to deceive us with such arguments: absurdities that follow only if foresight of faith is excluded or simply denied, they deduce from foresight denied secundum quid — that is, denied as an antecedent condition of predestination itself.

title: Cap. V Obj. 5: predestination without foresight of faith fights the nature and titles of eternal life
english: Obj. 5. Predestination supposed without foresight of faith fights the nature of eternal life and the titles Scripture gives it: inheritance of sons (but only believers are), wage, reward, crown of justice. Therefore it is destinated to no one apart from all consideration and intuition of faith and obedience.

title: Cap. V Obj. 5 Sol: enter life as adopted son; predestination tends on a child of wrath
english: Sol. Eternal life's nature is such that no one can enter it unless antecedently made actually a son of God by the Spirit of adoption — but not such that no one can be predestinated to it unless already an adopted son. Predestination contains the purpose of assuming into sonship: it tends on a child of wrath, whom by predestinatinating it makes a vessel of mercy as to purpose; by justifying, sanctifying, glorifying, a vessel of mercy as to act. Antecedent faith (or at least concomitant) is rightly required to constitute a son actually adopted; wrongly required to constitute God's decree about adopting a singular person and destinating the inheritance.

title: Cap. V Obj. 5 Sol: titles — eternal life a wage of faith; predestination never called a wage
english: On the titles we reply: Scripture calls eternal life a wage or crown of faith and obedience — never predestination itself a wage or crown of our faith or obedience. Eternal life is that wage because God gifts it as something to be rendered, by promise or stipulation, to believers who live holy lives. Predestination as a benefit is never shown as promised under any condition of faith coming first from us. These objections therefore fail.

title: Cap. V Obj. 6: without foresight faith Christ is shut out of the election decree
english: Obj. 6. If election is not from foresight faith, then Christ is shut out of the election decree, and men are predestinated to be saved before Christ is predestinated to save them — for those who do not yet believe are still outside Christ. But Christ was predestinated Savior only of the faithful, joined to him by faith. Therefore predestination is from foresight faith, or Christ (which is impious) is shut out of the election decree.

title: Cap. V Obj. 6 Sol: Major's consequence wobbles — elect in Christ as members to be united
english: Sol. The Major's consequence wobbles. The election decree does tend on a dead man lying in the mass of perdition — yet so that it decrees him life only as considered a member, by God's good pleasure, to be united to Christ and made alive through Christ. In that sense they are elected in Christ who are not yet considered grafted into Christ by faith.

title: Cap. V Obj. 6 Sol: Christ Head has causal priority — even the destined grafting comes from him
english: Christ the Church's Head is so joined to all his members that he holds causal priority over all the rest, and every outflow of free good to others comes through and for him — not only after they are grafted into Christ by faith, but so that even the benefit of being destinated to be grafted by faith is fetched from him and conferred on us in him. That Christ was predestinated Savior of the faithful only is true — he leads all the predestinated to salvation only by faith — not because faith is found in all the predestinated before the election decree itself.

title: Cap. V Obj. 6 Sol close: Arminius's foresight-election puts free will under election, not Christ
english: Finally: if election were from foresight faith as Arminius philosophizes, the absurdity he tries to pin on us would truly follow. Posit the law Whoever believes will be elected to life — then men not even existing in the divine purpose in Christ, but considered wholly outside Christ, by believing merit or at least by pact obtain their election. Under that election each one's free choice is laid as foundation rather than Christ, when one descends from a universal law to the actual particular election of men.

title: Cap. V Obj. 7: without foresight-faith condition the whole Gospel is inverted
english: Obj. 7. If election is not set from an antecedent condition of foresight faith, the whole Gospel is inverted. The Gospel first commands faith, then under that condition promises salvation — but those who resist Arminius have God first ordaining salvation to a singular person, then faith. The Gospel says, Believe and you will live; their doctrine says, Because I will to give you life, therefore I will to give you faith — the very overturning of the Gospel. So concede election from a foresight-faith condition, or explode Gospel doctrine.

title: Cap. V Obj. 7 Sol: secret decree Rom. 9 — in God no prior/posterior decrees; order of causes
english: Sol. I answer: grant that secret decree of God who has mercy on whom he wills and leaves whom he wills to their innate hardness — loving Jacob, hating Esau, before any consideration of their good or evil deeds — and we do not labor even a little over priority and posteriority in the decree of eternal life and efficacious grace as to the predestinated.
