In God as to the thing, decrees are not prior or posterior to each other; as to our mode of considering and the mutual relation of things, the same decree compared to another can be both prior and posterior by a diverse order of causes. So the decree to give faith is prior in the order of efficient cause to giving life; the decree to give life is prior in the order of final cause to giving faith.

title: Cap. V Obj. 7 Sol: Biel — end loved before means; faith gift prepared with life destinated
english: Biel is right: the end is loved before the means loved for the end's sake — love of the end is in some way cause of loving all that is unto the end. Since faith is God's gift bringing eternal life to the believer, who would dare say that gift was prepared and given to Peter or Paul while eternal life was not yet destinated to them? As if God had not destinated the benefit arising from his gift to the one he willed to enrich with that gift before others.

title: Cap. V Obj. 7 Sol: Gospel not inverted — Quisquis crediderit; elect get constant faith
english: Nearer then to their reason. We deny that our position inverts the Gospel or holds anything against it. The Gospel says Whoever believes will be saved; we say God from special mercy inspires constant faith in certain ones he has decreed to lead infallibly to life. The Gospel first commands faith, then under that condition promises salvation; we teach God first ordains a singular person to life, then pours faith into that heart. I find no fight or contradiction here. The evangelizing voice tells individuals by what means they may obtain eternal life — it puts means first under a condition and promises attainment to those who use them. But God's electing decree prefizes for certain persons both means and end — end through means, means for the end — and so is said to look to the end first and more principally, because for its infallible attainment such grace is conceived as prepared for that person.

title: Cap. V Obj. 7 Sol close: Augustine on perseverance; God requires faith then gifts it to the elect
english: Augustine found no contradiction here — he knew best that Gospel doctrine is Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved, yet taught that to saints predestinated into God's kingdom before the world's foundations this very perseverance was prepared and gifted. Briefly: these two sayings do not fight — God first exacts from us the duties of faith, then promises the benefit of life; and because for his special mercy he elected certain ones to share eternal life's benefit, he therefore wills to give them faith efficaciously so they may fulfill that duty.

title: Cap. V Obj. 8: none can be saved without faith — therefore election from foresight faith
english: Obj. 8. Whoever by God's will cannot be saved without faith is not predestinated to be saved without faith. There is no secret will of God adverse to the revealed. The revealed says, I will not save Peter without faith — so there is no secret will decreeing to save that same Peter without faith. Therefore election unto salvation is from foresight faith.

title: Cap. V Obj. 8 Sol: adults not saved or predestinated without faith — but distinguish praedestinare/servare
english: Sol. We grant no adult can be saved without faith — so God's will ordained, and he opened that ordination in the Gospel. We also grant no adult is predestinated to be saved without faith. But that can be taken ambiguously and needs distinct explanation. Predestinating denotes an internal act in the secret of the divine mind; Saving denotes an external effect wrought in the man. So: no one is predestinated to be saved without considering antecedent faith as a means to producing that external effect — but we deny that no one is predestinated to be saved without considering antecedent faith as a motive for producing that internal act.

title: Cap. V Obj. 8 Sol: God saves through faith — cause of the willed, not of the willing
english: God saves through faith, and decrees to save through faith — yet so that faith counts as an antecedent cause or condition not of the decree itself, but of the thing decreed. An effect of the divine will can proceed from a cause God foresaw from eternity and whose order to the caused he willed: that is called a cause of the thing willed, not of the willing.

title: Cap. V Obj. 8 Sol: revealed will does not make faith a motive of the eternal good pleasure
english: Nor does our distinction set the secret will against the revealed. The revealed does say, I will not save Peter without faith — namely preceding faith as a means ordained to effect his salvation. It does not say, I will not save Peter without preceding faith as a motive or condition for forming my eternal good pleasure about his salvation. So from the revealed will one cannot rightly deduce that Peter's election unto salvation was made from his antecedent faith.

title: Cap. V Obj. 8 Sol close: faith and perseverance flow from election — Cap. V Arminian objections end
english: Indeed from God's revealed word it is rightly deduced that both faith and perseverance in faith depend on a preceding election or ordination unto life. So Acts 13:48 — as many as were ordained to eternal life believed — and Matt. 24:24 — seducers would draw even the elect into apostasy if it were possible. That some believe, and that believers do not spring back from faith, flows from antecedent election — not, as Arminius wills, that foresight of their believing and persevering is what makes their election flow before others. We will not heap more objections from Arminius's writings; these scattered, the rest of the same flour are easy to dissolve. We come at last to set out our defense and strengthen it with arguments.

title: Cap. VI open: Orthodox position set out — election from mere divine good pleasure
english: Cap. VI. The orthodox position is set out and confirmed. You have heard the adversaries' arguments for an election they fetch from an antecedent act of the human will. It remains to bring ours forward — showing that election or predestination of singular persons to the infallible attainment of eternal life flows from the mere good pleasure of God's mercy.

title: Cap. VI: Remonstrants claim grace-only, but foresight faith still makes dignity the discriminator
english: I am not unaware that Remonstrants everywhere claim the election they defend rests on God's grace and mercy alone, not on any human merits or dignity. But when they revoke the whole elect/non-elect discrimination to foresight of faith and unbelief, that discrimination is clearly revoked to human dignity and undignity. Peter's faith and perseverance have a certain moral dignity; Judas's unbelief and obstinacy a moral undignity. It shines the more because Peter's faith and perseverance are not supposed prepared by some special divine good pleasure or gifted by special munificence — only offered in a sufficient administration of means, as also to those who remained unbelieving — and acquired and kept by Peter through good use of free choice; whence his election followed.

title: Cap. VI: their questions dissolve by human will; ours ascend to special good pleasure
english: On their view, ask why these believed and those did not, why these persevered and those did not, why these were predestinated to eternal life and those not — every question dissolves by human choice's willing and not-willing. On ours one must ascend higher: though we attribute unbelievers' wickedness and perdition to human choice, yet believers' faith, perseverance, and destination to eternal life are to be sought from God's special good pleasure and a special operation answering it. No need to dispute curiously whether God first decrees eternal life to the elect then efficacious grace, or the reverse — only to prove that to certain singular persons known to God alone both efficacious grace and glory are predestinated, prepared, and gifted.

title: Cap. VI thesis vs Remonstrants; Faustus Semipelagian axioms exploded
english: Remonstrants say and defend that the predestination or election decree falls on no one God has not foreseen and considered as believing and persevering in faith to life's last habit. We say predestination precedes that foresight — so only those are foreseen and considered by God as perseveringly believing whom God by the antecedent purpose of his election decreed to make such and, having made them, to lead to eternal life. We therefore explode Faustus the Semipelagian's axioms, not far from Remonstrant mind: Salvation of men is placed not in the Maker's predestination but in the servant's operation. There was no special divine munificence toward believers. Predestination is not cause of certain goods. Predestination pertains to justice. Unless foreknowledge has explored, predestination decrees nothing. Against all these we set ours: predestination of singular persons to life arises from God's mere good pleasure, not from any foresight operations of the human will — nay, of all good operations leading to eternal life, election's grace is the antecedent cause and fountain, not a following reward or wage. Now to arguments: mere divine good pleasure, not foresight faith on one side and unbelief on the other, makes the first discrimination of elect and passed-by.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 1: Augustine — praedestinatio is foresight and preparation of God's benefits
english: First argument: from various definitions of Predestination. Augustine: Predestination is the foresight and preparation of God's benefits, by which whoever are liberated are most certainly liberated. Observe: God foreknows those benefits or grace-gifts by which, applied, he will liberate certain singular elect persons; then prepares them all for them; and at length, as he foresaw and prepared, confers them at the right time. What here does not flow from God's mere good pleasure, preceding every act of the human will? He foresaw in the elect those grace-gifts he himself predestinated and prepared by free benevolence when he elected them in Christ — as Eph. 1:3–4 also openly shows. To cast darkness on pure divine mercy by putting foresight faith as cause or antecedent condition is trifling — faith is one of the chief benefits prepared for the elect in the predestination decree.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 1: Aquinas, Vasquez — preparation of grace cannot depend on foresight faith
english: Passing Augustine's definition, hear the Scholastics. Aquinas: Predestination is nothing but preparation of grace now and glory hereafter. A man in the corrupt lost mass — we cannot even suspect that grace and glory are prepared for him from antecedent consideration of persevering faith in him. It is ridiculous to say God decrees and prepares for a man the grace he first considered as already had and obtained. Elsewhere Aquinas: Predestination is a certain reason of ordering some to eternal salvation existing in the divine mind — and the execution of that order is passively in the predestinated, actively in God. If predestination is an ordination of certain ones to salvation, we must not think some men by persevering faith first ordained to life — nay placed as it were in life's vestibule — before God elects or predestinates them. Hear even the Jesuits, fiercest enemies of our defense. Vasquez: Predestination is God's eternal purpose by which he prepares grace for someone unto eternal life. A purpose preparing grace that leads infallibly to eternal life cannot depend on foresight faith — that faith is the very grace in view — so it must be referred to God's mere will. That clear truth extorted this candid Jesuit confession: discrimination of predestinated from reprobate begins before their consent absolutely foreseen — therefore before foresight faith or any merits, which without human-will consent cannot even be understood.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 1 close: Arminius's own definition — first ratio from theologians' consensus
english: Finally hear Arminius himself: Predestination is God's good-pleasure decree in Christ by which from eternity he determined to gift eternal life to the faithful whom he decreed to gift with faith. Predestination involves a double decree: I will give life to all the faithful; and I will give faith to these certain persons. Both depend on God's free pure mercy — neither on foresight faith or any human operation. Vainly then they put a foresight-faith condition before predestination, which all theologians in defining predestination itself acknowledge as free, and the spring of faith and every saving grace. Let this be our first reason — from the common consent of theologians in defining Predestination itself.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 2: from the nature of special liberating grace — Augustine
english: Second argument: from the nature of special liberating grace — grace that is in fact saving. As Augustine rightly observed, Predestination is not preparation of just any grace, but of such grace; and such grace, namely that which is in fact saving, is predestination's effect. If this grace in the elects' hearts begets faith rather than finds it, then much more election itself, the cause of giving such grace, must be purely free — depending on no preceding act of the human will, but only on the divine good pleasure.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 2: 2 Tim. 1:9; Prosper — this grace barred by no evil merits, bought by no good
english: So Paul: he saved us and called us with a holy calling — not from our works, but from his purpose and grace (2 Tim. 1:9). Prosper (Response to the Gallican Chapters, 8): no evil merits bar this grace, no good ones purchase it. Augustine (On the Grace of Christ, ch. 29): it makes us will, makes us act, makes us believe, and works good wills in men.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 2: De bono persever. — this grace prevents faith, will, and all our obedience
english: In a word, as Augustine best puts it (On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 15): this grace goes before faith, before the will, before all our obedience — and works all these in the one to whom it is given and whom it thus goes before. Add what adversaries will not dare deny: God gives such grace with the intention that it produce all these in the elect and those called according to purpose.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 2 close: faith-bearing grace given by freest will — so predestination unbound to prior free-choice acts
english: So this special efficacious grace that brings forth faith and conversion does not prerequire an antecedent condition of our faith — it is given to some and not to others by the freest will of the Giver. Plainly then predestination itself, the cause of such grace prepared and gifted, is not bound to any antecedent acts of human choice, but is constituted in God's free good pleasure — per Rom. 9:15, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: from Scripture authority — affirmative and negative
english: Third argument: from the authority of Scripture, both yes and no. Scripture everywhere names God's εὐδοκία — his good pleasure — as the cause of our predestination; it never sets foresighted faith down as cause, condition, or antecedent. So we must not shift this ineffable benefit off pure good pleasure onto foresighted faith. So Rom. 9:11 (when they had done nothing good or evil, that God's purpose according to election might stand) and Eph. 1:11 (chosen in him, predestined according to purpose) — and the like.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: no Scripture tip for election from foresight faith — Si credideris, praedestinaberis?
english: On the other side, adversaries cannot produce so much as one tip of Scripture hinting that men were chosen above others from a foresighted condition of prior faith. If the predestining decree really presupposes believing, and election follows once that condition is met, that bargain must be shown from Holy Scripture — inventing promises outside God's word is sheer temerity. Where then is If you believe, you shall be predestined? Or Whoever believes shall be predestined? There is Whoever believes shall be saved — God requires faith as antecedent to decreed salvation. There is no Whoever believes (or is foreseen to believe) shall be predestined — God does not require faith as antecedent to his decree.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: Hague reply — foresight faith not cause; Davenant — word-catching and merit
english: The Hague Colloquy speakers answer first: they never call foresighted faith the cause of election, so they do not fight Scripture naming εὐδοκία — good pleasure alone — as cause. They even say outright that why God elects any one person to salvation is not that person's faith, but only good pleasure, grace, mere grace. Word-catching, all of it. Whoever makes persevering faith the condition God requires — at whose sight he always elects, and for whose absence he always passes by — gives faith causal force, even meritorious force, in Augustine's anti-Pelagian sense of merit. So Augustine: who would say that one who has already begun to believe merits nothing from him in whom he believed?

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: Prosper, Hilary, Faustus — election-on-faith always meant prior merit
english: Augustine is not alone: whoever of old hung election to life on a faith-condition thereby admitted prior dignity and merit in the elect. Prosper (Letter to Augustine), on the so-called Pelagian remnants: as far as God goes, eternal life is prepared for all; as far as free choice goes, it is grasped by those who spontaneously believed, and received grace help by the merit of believing. Hilary to Augustine: those who rejected election according to God's purpose and brought in election by foresight of faith and penitence recognized in that faith and conversion the merit and cause of election — by the merit of willing and believing they can be healed, and later, whatever grief arises, they call that the very cause why one is taken and another rejected. Faustus of Riez, careful Semi-Pelagian: as he grounds election in foresighted faith, so he does not hide that it is also from merit — Foreknowledge knows what will be done; predestination then describes the retribution; the one foresees merits, the other preordains rewards. Remonstrants are too clever, and desert their elders, when they have God elect by foresight of faith and still deny that foresighted faith is the cause.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: second Hague reply — God regards faith as medium to life, not condition of election
english: Second reply: even if Scripture nowhere says in so many words that God elected us on condition we believe, you still cannot conclude he had no regard to faith in electing. We answer: not only is it missing totidem verbis — there are no equivalent words, nothing from which it can rightly be drawn. We do not deny every regard to faith in electing God. He regards the faith he will ingenerate in the elect as the medium by which one reaches life — not as a condition men have already performed or must perform in order to reach election itself.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3 close: good pleasure vs foresight faith — Rom. 4:16 not parallel for election
english: Lastly Remonstrants say we err in opposing good pleasure (mere grace) to foresighted faith — as if electing from mere grace and from foresighted faith were rivals — since Paul, from inheritance being of faith, concludes it is of grace (Rom. 4:16). The cases are not alike. In election, of faith and of mere grace are ἐναντία: that faith is presupposed to election unto first grace, the spring of all saving grace. In entering eternal life they are not contraries: that faith is pure grace gift, so the life-reward rendered to the believer is grace for grace. God set the race a double path to salvation — Law: Do this and live; Mediator: Believe and be saved — so what comes by faith is rightly called grace, as what comes by Law is from works. Gospel grace singular gift, the legal covenant relaxed, is to save sinners by faith. Remonstrants will never prove God ordained a double mode of predestining — one by works, one by faith. If some were elected for a believing act they performed, and others passed over for omitting it, the split would come not from a special pact of divine grace but from differing human wills. Peter's predestination would then be from Peter's special work, not God's special grace: believing here counts as a work of grace-prevented choice against disbelieving — not as a Gospel-covenant work against the Legal, since no such covenants exist for predestination either way.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: from the difference of divine vocation — Jesuits and Arminians forced to grant it
english: Fourth argument: from the difference of divine calling — which even Jesuits and Arminians must grant. If God calls some with a peculiar vocation (Paul's vocation according to purpose, Rom. 8:28; Prosper's special vocation; Augustine's vocation that makes a believer, and vocation according to purpose by which God fulfills what he predestined, and hidden grace no hard heart refuses; the Jesuits' congruent and high vocation) — if that calling is of all the elect and of none but the elect, then God clearly predestined them with a will that goes before any foresight of their faith.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: media answer the end — efficacious means given elect before foresight of faith
english: Means answer the end they are meant to secure. In this vocation God gives the elect — and only the elect — means he knows will be infallibly efficacious, and gives them so that they will be, and that before any foresight of their faith or conversion. That such means are prepared for some from mere good pleasure, not foresighted faith, is plain: faith and penitence follow from such calling as effect from cause. Had the same means been so prepared and given even to the most hardened, they too would have believed and turned.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: Augustine John 6:45 — special vocation implies antecedent will to save
english: So Augustine on the predestined and the passed-by, from John 6:45 (Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me): all these God teaches to come to Christ; all these he wills saved and brought to the knowledge of the truth. Had he also willed to teach those for whom the Cross is foolishness to come to Christ, they too would have come. In this special vocation, then, we must grant a special antecedent will to save those so called.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4: Augustine, Arminius, Vorstius — unequal conversion; absolute mercy
english: Augustine again: when God wills to save outright, no human will resists; when he wills to save only if men will believe, most wills resist — so he wills to save some by absolute good pleasure that goes before and causes their faith, not that presupposes it. That thought drove Arminius to admit God does not work everyone's conversion and salvation equally. But a prudent agent shapes his work from the end he intends. So there was a special will to save some before foresight of their faith — and from it sprang that special calling and working that begot faith in their hearts. Vorstius, weighing the same special vocation, grants that toward some God exercises an extraordinary mercy free of every promise and absolute — and in that sense, He will have mercy on whom he will (Piscator, Reply to the Apology, p. 17).

title: Cap. VI Arg. 4 close: special vocation of mercy — election ad fidem, not ex fide
english: Sum: there is a special vocation of mercy given to some — not because they were already counted faithful, but because they were predestined to become faithful. It flows from an antecedent will that infallibly destines them to eternal life. Not everyone has that vocation — only the elect. So election hangs on God's good pleasure, not on human act. So it is unto faith, not from faith. By this calling every predestined will is stirred to believe efficaciously — even if so hostile and fierce that he persecutes believers (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.19).

title: Cap. VI Arg. 5: from election's inseparable help — certainty of causality, not bare science
english: Fifth argument: from election's inseparable help — it hangs not on our faith but on God's mere good pleasure. Election means certainty of salvation for the elect person: not bare knowledge (even the most chance events are utterly certain to God from eternity) but causality — predestination so working that it surely leads the predestined to eternal life.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 5: Matt. 24; Rom. 11:5; Eph. 1:11 — elect salvation certain because God so acts
english: Hence Matt. 24 (to deceive, if possible, even the elect), Rom. 11:5 (a remnant according to election), and Eph. 1:11 (predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things by the counsel of his will). Quoad God, the elect's salvation is certain: from the election decree he has resolved so to work in their hearts that they are led to faith and penitence, remain in faith and newness of life, and at last die in the Lord.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 5: Arminian foresight — certainty only from God intuiting, not specially causing
english: In Arminian predestination, where foresighted faith drags election after it, there is no certainty of salvation from God as special cause — only from God as onlooker. Of Arminius's four decrees describing predestination, none gives any singular person certainty of salvation by an infallibly operating cause; elect salvation stays certain to God only as one who sees.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 5: Arminius's four decrees — Mediator, believers, means, foresight of users
english: First: a decree to give a Mediator. Second: to save believers and perseverers for that Mediator's sake. Third: to administer the means needed for faith. Fourth: to save those he foresees will believe and persevere by those means. The first three cause no certainty of salvation for any one person — they are common, and in bare form can as well cover reprobates as elect.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 5 close: fourth decree only intuits — so election from good pleasure, not foresight faith
english: The fourth decree alone touches singular persons — and even it gives certainty only as foreseeing knowledge, not as an operating cause: God does not there resolve to produce faith and perseverance in the elect, but only to regard them as already about to believe and persevere. Where salvation is not certain from God specially and infallibly causing, there is not the election Scripture celebrates. So election hangs on mere good pleasure, not foresighted faith.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 7: from the absurdity — election suspended on human faith yields no fixed elect number
english: Seventh argument: from the absurdity their view labors under — hanging divine election on a prior act of human faith and perseverance. Then neither the formal nor the material number of the elect would be fixed by any decree of divine good pleasure; that these particular persons are saved, and in this fixed count, would be an accident of contingent human choice — God foreseeing, not preordaining.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 7: ancient Semi-Pelagians owned the sequitur — Faustus on free choice
english: The old Semi-Pelagians saw that sequitur and taught it openly as no absurdity. Faustus (On Free Choice 1): a man's state can turn this way or that not by God's constitution but by free choice. And 1.20: what God is to foreknow and preordain about us for the future consists in man's progress or failure.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 7: Prosper and Hilary — Pelagian remnants reject a fixed elect number
english: The Pelagian remnants said it more openly still — Prosper and Hilary in their letters to Augustine. Prosper: they will not grant predestination that the elect's number can neither grow nor shrink. Hilary: they will not have a defined number of those to be chosen and rejected.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 7: Lessius — complete predestination rare in Scripture; hangs on perseverance
english: Among recent Jesuits, Lessius presses it more openly: Scripture barely mentions complete predestination, he says, because it hangs not on bare good pleasure but on human perseverance. He even teaches that God's intention for the number of the saved was not absolute before foresight of the world's end.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 7 close: then Peter no more ordained than Judas — fights Eph. 1:4 and Acts 13:48
english: If so, elect and passed-by would differ only by human operation, not divine — and Peter would be no more ordained by God to eternal life than Judas. Peter would enter the elect number only because he met the universal decree Whoever perseveringly believes shall be saved; Judas failed it and was shut out. Plainly absurd, and at war with Scripture: some elected in Christ before the world's foundation, to be holy and blameless (Eph. 1:4); some gifted with faith before others because before others God from mere mercy ordained them to life — Matt. 11:25-26; Acts 13:48; John 6:37; and throughout.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 8: no one foreseen persevering to whom God has not yet decreed the gift
english: Eighth argument: no one was ever foreseen as having persevering faith unless God had already decreed to give that excellent gift. If God has decreed perseverance for Peter, Paul, or any particular person, that one is already elected and ordained to life — for the gift of perseverance itself carries an infallible ordination to eternal life. It is hardly reasonable that God should elect particular persons to life by foresight of his own gift, which he never gives or decrees to give except to those he has already destined to eternal life.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 8: first — perseverance from God's gift (Jer. 32:40; 2 Thess. 3:3), not bare free choice
english: Nothing here can be shaken. First: if persevering faith could be foreseen in those to whom God has not yet decreed perseverance, that great good would come from human choice, not God's gift. All Scripture protests — saints' perseverance flows from God's gift: I will put my fear in their heart, that they may not depart from me (Jer. 32:40); Faithful is God, who will establish you and keep you from evil (2 Thess. 3:3). Augustine, following Scripture, taught that the power and will to persevere is given by grace's largess to saints predestined into God's kingdom — and not to others. So Aquinas is right: God's loving will that someone have this good is why he has it before others (ST 1.23.4).

title: Cap. VI Arg. 8: second — efficacious means only from intention of the end; 1 Pet. 1:5
english: Second: perseverance is given only to one already elected and destined to eternal life. An agent who knows what means can do never prepares and gives infallibly efficacious means except from purpose and desire of the end. So Peter: by God's power you are kept through faith unto salvation (1 Pet. 1:5). God inspires faith, keeps it from going out, and does so that through faith we may be led to salvation. All to whom he decreed persevering faith had salvation most certain with God.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 8: Arminians twist the gift — sufficient grace to persevere if they will
english: This argument badly torments Arminians and Jesuits alike. Arminians dare not openly deny that persevering faith is God's gift — yet they strongly deny that the act by which God gives faith is always efficacious, certain, and invincible. They teach that when God gives men power to reach him, faith is already prepared as a gift if that grace continues. Doubtless they hold the same of perseverance: the 'gift' means only sufficient grace — power to persevere if they will. That kind of gift does not imply prior destination to eternal life; it is 'given' even to those who never had and never will have faith, perseverance, or eternal life.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 8: gift implies reception — Phil. 1:29; Augustine De corr. et grat.
english: This coheres neither with itself nor with Scripture. A faith or perseverance God gives to a particular person implies it is had on man's side. Some gifts include the reception itself — without reception they cannot even be understood as given. The good will of the believer and perseverer is such a gift: God never gave it to anyone who did not receive it. The question is not a gift prepared and offered under a contingent condition, but a gift truly and actually given to certain persons. Arminian reading fights Scripture: faith is given to those to whom it is given to believe — not merely to be able to believe (Phil. 1:29). Perseverance is pronounced given not to those who could have persevered and sprang back, but to those so strengthened by God's gift that they actually persevered. Augustine at length (On Rebuke and Grace 11–12): all predestined in Christ receive what Adam did not — help such that they not only can persevere if they will, but will, and in fact persevere.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 8 close: Vasquez split grace/glory fails — will to give the kingdom causes perseverance
english: From this gift specially prepared and given to some, we gather eternal life was already destined for them. Vasquez the Jesuit, pressed by this absolute gratuitous predestination of certain persons to faith and perseverance, answers: yes, predestination to grace does not hang on foresighted merits — but election to glory does, and that is the standing view of Scripture and Augustine. In vain he tries to split what Scripture and Augustine join most closely. Scripture knows no election to efficacious grace except what is tied to the will to give glory — which will, in our way of considering, is prior to the will to give efficacious grace, and its cause and rule. Hence we are predestined unto adoption as sons (Eph. 1:5) — destination of glory and the heavenly inheritance, not grace alone. So Christ to the predestined (Luke 12:32): Fear not, little flock, for it pleased your Father to give you the kingdom — the will to give the kingdom as the peculiar cause of the providence that keeps the elect and makes them persevere through dangers. The will to give glory (election to life) is why they persevere before others — not foresighted perseverance why they were elected before others.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 9: one ratio of predestination — Head and members alike
english: One ratio of predestination — Head and members, and members among themselves. If Christ's predestination to Mediator and Savior was gratuitous, not from foresight of merits, then much more must ours to the benefit of salvation be gratuitous. And if some of Christ's members were clearly predestined to eternal life with no regard to foresighted faith or perseverance, the same holds for all the rest. Predestination is uniform as to whether conditions are presupposed or not — that is beyond doubt.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 9: first — Christ the Mediator predestined without prior merits (Augustine)
english: First limb: how was Christ predestined Savior — by God's gratuitous good pleasure, or by foresight of works? Hear Augustine (On the Predestination of the Saints 15): the brightest light of predestination and grace is the Savior himself, the Mediator, the man Christ Jesus — and by what prior merits of his own, of works or of faith, did the human nature in him earn to be that?

title: Cap. VI Arg. 9: second — infant elect without foresight faith; Augustine vs Pelagians
english: Second limb — conformity among the members: many of Christ's members were predestined to eternal life with no prior regard to faith or perseverance. Persevering faith is only considered in those who use reason and free choice; so all who die in infancy and are saved must have been destined to salvation without that regard. Many die at that age whose salvation the Church never doubted. Many, then, were both elect and saved in whom foresight of faith and perseverance could have no place. By elect infants Augustine everywhere stops the Pelagians' mouths — those who grounded predestination to life in foresighted merits (On Predestination and Grace 7; On the Gift of Perseverance 8, 12; On Merits and Remission 1.21; Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7).

title: Cap. VI Arg. 9: Prosper on infants; Grevinchovius — if eternal life, then election
english: Prosper agrees (On Free Choice): in infants neither prior nor later devotion is chosen — he means those reborn as soon as born, and snatched from this life into eternal beatitude. Grevinchovius (Disputation on Election from foresighted faith, p. 143), caught by this, finally doubts whether there is any infant election at all. But whoever has eternal life surely has election to eternal life — the glorified do not outnumber the predestined. Whom he predestined, them he glorified, and no others (so Augustine on the Apostle). Sound Prosper: none enter Christ's inheritance but those elected before the world's foundation, predestined and foreknown according to his purpose. If some infants receive the heavenly inheritance, those same are predestined or elect.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 9 close: Christ and Christian infants not from foresight — nor the rest
english: Or Grevinchovius meant all infants are saved alike, so there is no infant election. Against that one unsound disputant stands the catholic Church's judgment: all infants are born children of wrath; not all are reborn — only those God dignifies with unowed grace. Sum: Christ is not predestined from foresight of merits; nor Christian infants. Therefore neither are the remaining Christians — whose election is of one kind and the same ratio with their Head's, and among themselves.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 10: comparative election and rejection — an inscrutable abyss
english: In comparative election and rejection of men there is an inscrutable abyss — a secret no human curiosity may pry into. Brought back to the sums of human reason, it would look like injustice: of two wholly equal, one is destined to life by God's gracious good pleasure, the other left.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 10: Rom. 9 — Jacob and Esau; objection of injustice referred to Rom. 11:33-34
english: Paul shows it in Rom. 9: after stating Jacob's gratuitous election and Esau's being passed by, he at once thrusts off the objection human reason prompts — that if by such good pleasure one unborn brother is loved and the other hated before either did good or evil, there is injustice with God (v. 14). He solves it by not solving it: he sends it up to the inscrutable height of divine wisdom and judgment (Rom. 11:33-34).

title: Cap. VI Arg. 10: foresight election empties the secret — Peter and Judas already explained
english: All the Orthodox in this business of predestination and passing by have owned that secret — and reject predestination from foresighted human acts just because that empties the secret. If Peter was predestined because God foresaw he would believe and persevere, and Judas passed by because foresaw he would die in unbelief, the reason for predestining and not predestining is already out in the open, with nothing secret left.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 10: Augustine and Prosper — depth of grace not opened by free choice
english: Far otherwise Augustine (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 4.6): why he makes these sheep and not those — with whom there is no respect of persons — that very question belongs to that height. And Prosper (On the Calling of the Gentiles 1.23): in vain they try to open the depth of inscrutable grace by free choice, who plant election's cause in the merits of the elect. And in the last chapter: that question's depth, which with the Apostle's wonder we confess unsearchable, is not solved by free choice's willing and refusing.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 10 close: same against Arminians — no easy ratio of elect and rejected
english: What Catholics once rightly said against the Semi-Pelagians, we turn on Arminians who ground election in foresight of faith and final perseverance: if so, you have comprehended God's inscrutable judgments. We, believing and showing those judgments incomprehensible, say that from one mass of perdition some are saved by God's goodness and grace, others left by just and hidden judgment (Peter the Deacon, On the Incarnation 7). Reject, then, all who give so easy a short-cut reason of elect and rejected — a reason neither the orthodox Fathers nor the Apostle himself, caught up to the third heaven, could give.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 11: that doctrine empties election of efficacy toward the elect in the way
english: That doctrine does not rightly explain predestination or election: it grants the fruit, but no efficacy of election toward directing, keeping, and bringing the elect through to the goal on the way of salvation. Holy Scripture marks a special operation and providence of God flowing from the election decree — freeing the elect from all those evils that would otherwise block their salvation.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 11: Matt. 24 — for the elect days shortened; God removes every obstacle
english: So Christ's words in Matt. 24: to lead astray, if possible, even the elect — and for the elect's sake those days will be shortened. The election decree is of that kind: by it God takes on himself to remove every obstacle that would block the elect's salvation, and to procure means that will infallibly produce it.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 11: Rom. 8:28 — all things work for good for the predestined and called
english: So also Paul, Rom. 8:28: all things work together for good for those who are predestined and called according to purpose — God's special providence so steering all things that what looks most hostile to their salvation still advances it.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 11: Arminian foresight election — no operative force left for the way
english: Weigh by contrast the Arminian invention — election from prior foresight of persevering faith. That sort of election strips election of all operative force for keeping or advancing the elect on the way of salvation. If they are elected to life only by regard to perseverance already kept to the last breath, election gave them nothing toward finishing the course in faith and holiness. They are taken to have overcome every difficulty and reached heaven's very threshold before God predestines them to life. That all the saved pressed on in faith and holiness, aimed straight at the kingdom, and all but entered the gates before they were predestined — or received any special grace by virtue of predestination — is plainly horrendous, intolerable to Christian ears that gladly hear Paul: whom he predestined, he also called; whom he called, he also justified; whom he justified, he also glorified (Rom. 8:30).

title: Cap. VI Arg. 11 close: Arminian order is Postdestinatio, not Praedestinatio
english: Even if we had no other argument, this alone would amply shatter that Arminian predestination: it has men predestined to eternal life only once they have already arrived, every difficulty and danger overcome. That is more rightly called Postdestination than Predestination.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: true election decree segregates singular persons
english: The true election decree segregates singular persons — those God, others passed by, has from special mercy infallibly destined to obtain salvation. The very word elect proves it: under its formal sense one is accepted, the other rejected. But in that Arminian decree — Whoever believes shall obtain eternal life; whoever remains unbelieving shall perish — there is no segregation of singular persons, no passing by or rejection of others, since by it God promises salvation equally to anyone and threatens perdition equally to anyone.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: Hague reply — segregation of believers; Davenant restates the question
english: The Remonstrants answer at the Hague Colloquy (p. 53): segregation of believers is segregation of singular persons — for believers are singular persons (p. 51). If we mean election reaches certain singulars as singulars, apart from any qualities in them, and especially without regard to faith, they flatly deny election regards singulars that way. Easily answered. We grant believers are singular persons — every act is of singulars. What we deny is that by Whoever believes shall be saved God segregates some singulars unto faith or life, others passed by.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: first — Quisquis decree stands even if none or all believe; Peter = Judas
english: First: that decree would stand firm even if no one believed and all perished — or if all believed and all were saved. As law or edict it declares by what duties done anyone may come to eternal life, and by what neglected may not. But as a practical segregating decree, no one is set apart or chosen before others, no one passed by. If Judas believes and perseveres, by it he is saved; if Peter does not, by the same he is damned. Nothing is decreed for Peter not under the same condition for Judas; nothing denied Judas not under the same for Peter. Cling to that decree on equal law, and all are destined to salvation and all excluded from it. So there is no segregation of singulars, no election with others passed by.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: second — separation follows Peter's act, not God's segregating decree
english: Second: we grant that by that decree's tenor Peter is to be set apart to eternal life once he has persevered in faith — but that separation follows from Peter's own consequent contingent act, not from a segregating decree of God. By his act he was set apart to salvation after he was foreseen to have believed and persevered; by the decree itself he was not singularly segregated unto faith or salvation. Like case: if a king enacts Whoever scales the besieged city's walls shall be knighted; whoever turns his back shall die — those who climb and those who flee are singular persons; yet the king is not said to have elected certain singulars to knighthood and passed others by, but to have conferred it on singulars and destined that dignity equally to all — to be won if they behave well, lost if not. Arminian election is of that kind throughout, and so includes no true real separation of singular persons.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: third — singulars as singularly loved; Aquinas on election and dilection
english: Third: to their denial that election reaches singulars as singulars, we reply we do not claim the decree regards singulars merely as singulars, but as singularly loved by God from mere gratuitous goodwill. So Aquinas (ST 1.23.4): predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. That involves dilection and election — dilection insofar as he wills them the good of eternal salvation; election insofar as he wills that good to some before others. And dilection is presupposed to election.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12 close: faith in election as effect prepared, not presupposed cause
english: Finally, they say election does not reach singulars apart from foresighted faith in them. We grant election never happens without regard to good qualities — faith and holiness — but as prepared and to be given to all the elect by virtue of election. They are not presupposed to the election decree as causes, conditions, or occasions of election itself, as Arminians claim. Predestination does regard what is on our side — our faith and obedience — not as what bends God's will to will, but as that for whose production the divine will ordained grace. Any good quality or work considered in men is not the reason of predestination but its Terminus (so Aquinas on Rom. 8). Let faith be considered in election, then — as effect, not as reason or condition of election.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: last — foresight election overturns pure grace
english: Last argument: we must not bring in an election that overturns pure grace and reduces the split between elect and rejected to the good use of free choice. But election from foresighted faith — and non-election from foresighted unbelief — does exactly that.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: major — Augustine: true grace needs absolute predestination (De bono persever. 2)
english: The major is so clear adversaries are ashamed to say outright that this special election-grace hangs on anything but God's mere sole good pleasure. Augustine wisely weighs it (On the Gift of Perseverance 2): such free grace cannot stand unless absolute predestination stands with it — not hung on prior acts of human choice. Predestination must be preached, he says, so true grace (not given according to our merits) can be defended by impregnable walls. He means not Arminian predestination from foresight of human faith and perseverance, but Pauline — which prepares faith and perseverance for the elect from eternity and gives them in due time. Without that predestination, which Augustine defends through the whole book, he judged true grace cannot be defended.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: sounder scholastics — willing to receive grace is from predestination
english: Even the sounder scholastics, who usually credit free choice more than is due, dare not reduce the split between elect and passed-by to good or bad use of free choice in embracing or rejecting grace. So Aquinas (Disputed Questions on Predestination, art. 2): this very willing to receive grace is from divine predestination. And Durandus (p. 250): every good done by someone, or that helps him reach the supernatural end — whether as cause or occasion — falls under predestination's effect.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: minor first — eternal favor given or denied by prior free-choice use
english: Now the minor. This election and passing by from foresighted faith and unbelief, we say, hangs God's grace on the merit of the human will. First: grace of God most properly is that favor — eternal benevolence — by which he wills to confer eternal life on this singular person. But that love or favor, the first gift in which all others are given, the Remonstrants have given or denied as men first used free choice well or ill in admitting or rejecting the sufficient grace they say is offered to all. That is as much as to say: God began to love a man unto eternal life because the man's free choice applied itself to grace.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: minor second — why faith in Peter not Judas? special free-choice act
english: Second: grace of God also means those supernatural gifts by which the Holy Spirit imbues, reshapes, and vivifies our souls — faith, charity, and the rest given to all the regenerate. On Arminius's view that grace too is given or withheld by the diverse merits of human wills. If election follows foresighted faith, why was that faith foresighted in Peter rather than Judas? They cannot claim special grace prepared for Peter in predestination caused him to believe — they explode that predestination and set faith prior to it. So they must fall back on a special free-choice act in Peter, specially fitting itself to means God supplied no less to Judas than to Peter for generating faith. What is that but to grant that admonishing or moving grace is offered from mere mercy to all alike, while vivifying grace of the will is conferred by each one's diverse merits in accepting or rejecting that prior grace?

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: Pelagius's grace vs Augustine's — Miserebor cuius misertus fuero
english: Arminius's disciples deny it — but will they or nill they, once predestination from foresight of faith is fixed, they can admit no grace but what Pelagius at last admitted; they cannot own what Augustine everywhere presses him to confess. What grace did Pelagius grant? God works in us to will the good and the holy while he kindles us by future glory and promised rewards, raises the stunned will by wisdom's revelation into desire of God, and advises us of every good. Those are the very means by whose administration Arminius has God watching who will believe and who will not — electing those he foresees will use them well, passing by those he foresees will abuse them. Augustine: We do not want that grace. Let Pelagius confess the grace by which future glory is not only promised but believed and hoped; wisdom not only revealed but loved; every good not only advised but persuaded. That grace which pours in faith, hope, and charity, and makes us do — Catholics held it is not given from merit, not from prior good use of free choice, but from God's mere mercy. So at Diospolis Pelagius is ordered to confess grace is not given according to our merits — reason: that it may be true grace, freely given through the mercy of him who said, I WILL HAVE MERCY ON WHOM I WILL HAVE MERCY.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13 close: two impieties — explode foresight election; good use is benefit, not mover
english: In a word: this view — electing singular persons to life from their foresighted faith — involves two things most hostile to grace: that God's first love destining them to life arises from the good use of grace-prevented free choice; and that faith itself is not infused into certain persons by a special gift, but conceived in them by a special good act of free choice. All the orthodox must explode it. On the contrary: the good use of grace God foreknew was not the cause that moved him to elect these before others — it was rather a special benefit of election.

title: Cap. VII open: De Reprobatione — prolegomena; two rocks to avoid
english: Cap. VII — some prolegomena on Reprobation, with the Arminian view. Preliminaries tasted, I turn next to the other half of the dispute: passing by, non-election, or Reprobation of those God has not dignified with that excellent special mercy that infallibly leads to life. Here and everywhere Paul's word must hold (Rom. 12:3): not to think beyond what one ought. Idle curiosity will always find as much to learn as it cares to ask (so Tertullian wisely, On the Soul, at the end). In treating this matter, two rocks must be fled with all caution.

title: Cap. VII: first rock — creating some to destroy; Prosper and Hos. 13:9
english: First rock: striking divine Goodness — those who teach God by absolute primary will, before any regard to sin, created some in order to destroy them, and that from that destroying will flows whatever God does about the non-elect. With Prosper we rather say: one cause of being born, another of perishing — birth is the Creator's benefit; perishing is the transgressor's desert. God does create those he foresaw would never share eternal life; those he decreed to use free choice with no special grace undergirding it; those he decreed most justly to subject to damnation for sins. Yet that perdition or damnation is not creation's end but transgression's wage — so Hosea may always stand: Your destruction is from you (Hos. 13:9).

title: Cap. VII: reprobation decree not thrust into all acts — common love; Rom. 2:4-5
english: Further: that deep secret decree of non-election or reprobation must not be awkwardly stuffed into every act of God, as if with the non-elect he did nothing except from that decree. Though he would not pity some so far as to decree their infallible leading to eternal life, and willed to destine them to ruin with their sin intervening, yet while they live on earth — especially within the Church's pale — in giving bodily and spiritual benefits that by nature tend to salvation, he does much with them from common love or φιλανθρωπία toward the whole human race, and much from the covenant by which he lavishes certain supernatural benefits on all members of the visible Church. In the event those gifts become noxious to the reprobate — yet one must not say God by the reprobation decree intends abuse of his gifts, and hostilely supplies them to the non-elect so that abusing them they may be punished and destroyed. Rather take Paul's word: God does much with the non-elect from that overflowing kindness that spreads to all, though not in equal measure (Rom. 2:4-5 — or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience, not knowing God's kindness leads you to repentance? But by your hardness you treasure up wrath).

title: Cap. VII: opposite rock — defending goodness so special mercy in election is crushed
english: Opposite rock: some carefully dodge the first, then hit another no less deadly. Explaining the reprobation decree, they so defend God's goodness that in the opposite election decree they crush special mercy flowing from gratuitous good pleasure. As if Rom. 9:18 — I will have mercy on whom I will — meant I will have mercy on him I know just, whose ready faith I see, whom I see obey my precepts (so Faustus the Semi-Pelagian exposits, or rather corrupts, On Free Choice 1.3). What the poet sang of Jupiter — King Jupiter the same to all — they affirm of the true God: he wills eternal life equally to all; with sufficient means administered, he elects to glory those he foresees will use them well, and passes by those he foresees will abuse them. So electing shows no special mercy, reprobating no liberty of divine will, and in why this one is elect and that passed by no height remains — the split is recalled to human wills' liberty. Spalato rightly grants that holders of predestination and reprobation from foresight must put grace's efficacy in man's will, and admit means to salvation as prepared by God for all, yet not as predestined to any (Ecclesiastical Republic 7.11.198).

title: Cap. VII: our sense — negative reprobation from freest will; Episcopius on not-willing the highest good
english: But as we taught that election's benefit hangs on God's gratuitous good pleasure, not on some prior good act of man, so the negation of that benefit — which we call non-election, passing by, or negative reprobation — we fetch from the same freest will of God, doing with his own what he wills. Episcopius, often worst in philosophy, here not badly (Theses, Disp. 22 on Justification, th. 3): it is one thing not to will to punish; another to will to affect someone with the highest good. By parity we say: it is one thing to will to punish someone; another not to will to affect someone with the highest good.

title: Cap. VII close (open): punishment presupposes fault; negative reprobation denies unowed benefit
english: The will to punish in God cannot be considered without prior regard to the sin of the one to be punished, as demeritorious cause. But the will to pass by — or nolition, so to speak, of predestinating — can be considered without prior regard to the non-elect person's sin. Why the difference? Punishment is an act of vindicative justice, and so presupposes a fault worthy of vengeance. Non-election or negative reprobation is not a punishment, but denial of a gratuitous benefit God owes no one — and so by its nature hardly requires an antecedent fault.

title: Cap. VII: Junius — reprobationis vocabulum trifariam sumitur
english: Note here: among theologians the word reprobation is taken three ways, as the learned Junius rightly observed. First: for passing by and damnation jointly. In that sense people are called reprobate not only because God decreed to deny them efficacious grace and so permit them to fall short of beatitude's end, but also because he destined them to eternal punishments.

title: Cap. VII: first sense — antecedents of predamnation are not always antecedents of praeterition
english: Those who under one word of reprobating join both divine acts — passing by and damning — can hardly affirm anything certain about reprobation. What precedes the act of predamning is not always what precedes the act of passing by: what moves as cause toward predamnation does not at once have the nature of a moving cause or demerit causing toward praeterition.

title: Cap. VII: second and third senses — damnation alone; strict praeterition as non-election
english: Second sense: some take reprobation for the damnation decree alone — to be reprobated is nothing but to be destined to eternal torments. Those who put only that in the word are right to set sin as cause of such destination; they slip in acknowledging nothing higher in the decree of election and rejection. Third sense: reprobation as contradictorily opposite to election is taken for praeterition or non-election alone — an eternal ordination in the divine mind to deny certain persons efficacious grace that in fact leads to glory. That reprobation can be understood without prior regard to the rejected's sins as moving causes of the passing by. Once such praeterition is presupposed, then at last men are foresighted as about to die in sin and be tormented for sin. From eternity God willed to addict these passed-by non-elect to eternal torments — not because passed by, but because evil and worthy of damnation. He did not will to punish them in the first instant of reason in which he refused to glorify, but in that other in which he considered them sinners never to be freed from their sins.

title: Cap. VII: our sum — praeterition from mere liberty; Paul and Judas
english: Our sum: foresight of demerits is not the cause of praeterition, non-election, or reprobation strictly taken. As it hangs on mere good pleasure that certain persons by that special providence we call Predestination are infallibly ordained to grace and glory, so it hangs on mere divine liberty that others are not so ordained, but left without this efficacious grace and permitted to fall short of glory. If anyone asks why God could most easily and justly leave both Paul and Judas to native hardness and eternal misery — and could as easily soften both and lead them to eternal glory — why he prepared efficacious softening grace for Paul and not Judas, ordained Paul infallibly to glory and not Judas: we do not flee to Paul's foresighted faith or merits, nor Judas's foresighted unbelief or demerits. We say God has mercy on whom he will by softening, and on whom he will he has least mercy by permissive hardening. For providence so diverse about these persons we assign no cause but the Will of God, which is the first rectitude. So you have our opinion.

title: Cap. VII: opposing sententiae — Jesuits on foresight sins; Arminians on final unbelief
english: Those against us hold the contrary: the cause of non-election or reprobation is the sins in which the reprobate are foresighted as about to die — so certain Jesuits. Others say foresighted unbelief with final perseverance in it is the cause, so that no one is considered by God reprobate or non-elect except in the very article of death, and that for contumacious unbelief against God calling. That is Arminius's view, and of those usually called Remonstrants.

title: Cap. VII close: same foundations — refute mixed, then confirm ours; Cap. VIII ahead
english: Now let us hear by what arguments they prop this view — those who fetch reprobation or praeterition from foresighted demerits, or from unbelief and final perseverance in it. No need to split Jesuit and Arminian arguments carefully: they rest on plainly the same foundations. As they met us in reading, we will set them out mixed. Once refuted, we will turn to confirming our own opinion.

title: Cap. VIII open: adversaries' arguments proposed and solved
english: Chapter VIII — the adversaries' arguments proposed and solved. We turn now to their arguments: they contend that the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as about to leave life were the meritorious and moving cause of divine reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII: prefatory — not the will to damn, but the eternal denial of efficacious grace
english: Before their reasons are brought forward, this must be prefaced: we are not asking about reprobation as some theologians mean the will to damn or torment the reprobate — that will of God always regards sin as meritorious cause of decreed punishment, beyond dispute. We ask about reprobation as that absolute eternal decree by which from eternity God denied Cain and Judas efficacious grace he could have prepared and given them, had it so pleased him.

title: Cap. VIII: those denied such grace are passed by — demerit concomitant, not cause of praeterition
english: Those to whom God in his eternal decree denied such grace and the same ordination to glory, he did not elect but passed by — and, as theologians speak, reprobated. Add this: we do not deny that in all on whom divine reprobation falls there is found concomitant demerit adhering to the subject. What we deny is that that praeterition or non-election we call negative reprobation flowed from regard to that demerit. God sees original demerit in elect and reprobate alike — yet not by discrimination of cause, but by his good pleasure, he wills to elect Jacob, and wills not to elect but to reprobate Esau.

title: Cap. VIII: actual demerits foresight as consequent, not antecedent, to praeterition
english: As for actual demerits from final perseverance in sins or unbelief: yes, these too are foresighted as future in all the reprobate — but as future concomitantly or consequently, not causally or antecedently to the divine act of praeterition. God would not foresee Cain or Judas dying in their wickedness and unbelief unless his prior will not to grant them special grace — by which they would be softened and turned to faith and penitence — were presupposed. That denial is plain proof of non-election or reprobation. Who would so impiously dote as to say God cannot turn evil human wills to good when, where, and as he wills? So Augustine rightly (Enchiridion 98). But let us hear the arguments.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 1: Scripture — God does not will that men perish
english: First they try to prove reprobation flows from foresighted human demerits from those Scripture places where God is said not to will that men perish — which would hardly be true, they say, if God by his will alone, and not for sins, reprobated so great a multitude. They cite Ezek. 18:23 (Is the death of the wicked of my will?), Hos. 13:9 (Your destruction is from you), 1 Tim. 2:4 (God wills all to be saved), Matt. 11:28 (Come to me, all), and many like places — no need to repeat or discuss them one by one.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 1 Resp.: simple complacence vs predestinating will; non-election is not willing to destroy
english: If adversaries mean that God, foresight of human demerits set aside, wills salvation equally to all, we deny the cited places prove that. They do prove that by the will of simple complacence God wills that all believe and repent, that none perish or be damned. They do not prove that by predestinating will he wills equally, before foresight of demerits, to work in all so they believe and repent, and not perish or be damned — nor that by reprobating will he has not decreed to deny some efficacious grace and infallible ordination to glory. Those two can stand together: God wills that all believe and none perish (simple complacence); and God wills to permit some to persist in voluntary unbelief and fall short of eternal salvation. Adversaries err in taking not-to-elect (or to reprobate) as equipollent with willing to destroy or inflict eternal death. Non-election or praeterition can fall on an intact creature — plain in the angels — but the will to destroy or afflict with eternal death can fall only on a vitiated creature: non-election is mere denial of a gratuitous benefit; death or perdition is sin's wage. True: all the non-elect will infallibly rush into eternal death, and from eternity God's positive will adjudges them to it — but that deputing to death is not conceived in the same sign of reason as non-election, but in a later one where final perseverance in sin is foresighted. That God wills none to perish without prior regard to demerits does not entail that he wills none to pass by or not-elect without that same prior regard.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 1 Resp. coda (Vasquez): reprobates excluded from God himself without occasion from demerits
english: Vasquez the Jesuit — no great friend of our defense — still sides with us here. By that peculiar efficacious grace proper to the predestined, he says, God without doubt excluded all the reprobate from himself by antecedent will, seizing no occasion at all from them. Denial of that grace wholly precedes our liberty. For us that is as good as saying: God from himself, by antecedent will, with no occasion taken from their demerits, passed by or reprobated all the reprobate.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2: Rom. 9 — reprobation called hatred of Esau
english: Second, they try to prove foresighted demerits are the cause of reprobation — oddly enough — from Paul's own debate in Romans 9, where we take him to establish the opposite. First: the Apostle calls this reprobation hatred — Esau I hated — and God hates no one except for sin.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: Paul removes good and evil acts; Augustine Contra 2 Epist. Pelag.
english: First reply: their argument strikes straight against Paul's mind and plain words. In this place he teaches that election and rejection of particular persons do not hang on diverse or contrary human acts, but on God's diverse good pleasure — willing to have mercy on one, not on another. For that cause he removes not only their good acts but their evil ones: when they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil. As for those who claim God regarded not works done but works he foresaw they would do — and so loved Jacob and hated Esau — since they are sharper than the Apostle himself, who could not invent that answer, I will not refute them; let them enjoy their dream. Only this: hear Augustine patiently. Irritated by that inept escape he broke out: You truly dote who, when truth says NOT OF WORKS BUT OF HIM THAT CALLS, say Jacob was loved from future works God foresaw he would do (Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7).

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: demerit frees from cruelty charge, not motive of Jacob/Esau discrimination
english: Note also: we gladly grant that in the reprobate subject there resides that contagion and unworthiness which can free the reprobating God not only from cruelty and injustice, but even from the lightest suspicion of them. Whoever is denied this special mercy had no right that such grace be prepared or conferred. What is owed by no reason is reasonably denied — so Thomas. Add that he not only has no right to such a benefit, but by inborn vice is as it were proximately disposed to receive God's vengeance (Augustine, Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7). The state of the whole human race as presented to God electing and passing by is a state of sin, death, and merited damnation. But since that state is common to all and wraps Jacob as much as Esau, it can stand as a congruent reason why God may justly leave both — not as the moving cause why he rejected Esau while electing Jacob, who stood in the same condition. Hence Dionysius the Carthusian calls it intolerable that foresight of demerits be named the reason of reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: twofold hate — vengeance vs less love; Vasquez; Leah
english: Lastly — and this breaks the nerve of the argument — God may be said to have hated Esau in two respects. First, hated unto vengeance and the punishment of eternal death: so he hates Esau only as a sinner, and for sin itself as moving and demeritorious cause. Second, hated unto denial of some special unowed benefit — that is, loved less: so he can hate Esau only because he does not will to love him. In that latter sense the Apostle says God loved Jacob and hated Esau: by the freest purpose of his will he chose to soften Jacob by special grace, and refused Esau that great benefit. Why choose Jacob for that grace and not Esau? Because God so willed. Why so will? A foolish question — you seek a cause of the divine will in preparing and distributing gratuitous goods beyond the will itself. That hatred here means mere denial of special love in conferring a special benefit, even the Jesuits grant. Vasquez on these very words: to hate is the same as to have loved less. He acts like one who hates who gives a gift to one and withholds it from another. Such hatred needs no sin as its cause. So Jacob is said to have hated Leah (Gen. 29:31).

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 3: hardening (Rom. 9) said to presuppose sins as motive of reprobation
english: Third: the Apostle styles reprobation thus — He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. But the will to harden presupposes the reprobate's sins in which he is hardened. Therefore the sins with which the reprobate leave this life are the moving or meritorious cause of their reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 3 Resp.: hardening is nolle misereri; foresight of final persistence not its cause
english: We answer: the will to harden Paul names there designates a peculiar act of the divine will by which he denies certain persons that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened. God, as Augustine truly says, does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy — as the setting sun, drawing back its rays, is said to darken the air not by an influx that begets darkness, but by denying the influx whose presence would remove the dark. Since this hardening is done by permitting and denying special mercy, no one can be considered and foresighted by God as finally hardened in sin and dying unless the decree of that permissive hardening — or that denial of special mercy — precedes, by which God knows final remaining in sin would be blocked if the mercy were granted. So the argument's assumption — that this hardening will (which is reprobation) presupposes the reprobate's sins as cause of that reprobation or hardening — is not only false but alien to reason and common sense. Cause precedes effect: yet the reprobate's final remaining in sin follows the decree of not-having-mercy or of hardening. If God has mercy, man is not hardened; that special mercy's work is to soften. So Augustine: If God willed to have mercy on them, he could so call (as apt for them) that they would be moved, understand, and follow. A little later: God has mercy on no one in vain. At length: God's hardening is nothing but not willing to have mercy — namely by withholding the grace that infallibly and efficaciously softens and converts. Since no final obstinacy in contracted or committed sins can be supposed unless God's will not to soften precedes it, foresighted perseverance of the reprobate in their sins cannot be the cause of that denied mercy or softening. True: in daily life the reprobate, by quenching the light God kindles in their hearts, repelling divine motions, and basely obeying foul lusts, merit consequent blinding, desertion, and handing over to a reprobate mind. But under all that stands the divine permission — or denial of special grace — which may be called permissive hardening and flows from reprobation. Without that going before, and depending on God's freest will, the reprobate would not have fallen into that final contumacy, but by special unowed mercy would have been freed from that rebellion and hardness.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 4: will to show wrath (Rom. 9:22) said to presuppose sins as cause of reprobation
english: Fourth: the Apostle says that when God reprobates he wills to show wrath and vengeance (Rom. 9:22). But the will to inflict vengeance presupposes that God regards a man as bound by sins. Therefore the sins by which the reprobate die bound are the cause of reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 4 Resp.: negative reprobation not for damning; Cajetan; riches of mercy (Rom. 9:23)
english: If we speak of that negative reprobation by which God firmly decreed of some particular person — say Cain or Judas — not so far to have mercy as to will to draw him efficaciously out of sin and misery, and at the same time decreed to permit his final hardening in sin: I deny God does this to fulfill a purpose of vengeance or damnation. Cajetan puts it well on Aquinas I, q. 23 a. 5: God does not permit sins in order to punish, but permits and punishes for the shining forth of his justice. Paul himself in the cited place shows that God denies this special mercy to some and so permits them to be hardened — wherein negative reprobation consists — not with primary intent to damn those thus passed by, but to manifest the riches of his mercy toward the elect (Rom. 9:23). Only then do the elect see they were saved by pure mere mercy: when it is plain that the calling according to purpose granted them by gratuitous good pleasure was denied to others; that they were no better than those passed by as to corrupt nature, in which special mercy found them; and that they would have been no less hardened than the reprobate unless mere divine favor had softened them by that special grace.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 4 Resp.: will to punish follows foresight final perseverance — not cause of negative reprobation
english: True: God wills to show wrath and vengeance on all the reprobate. But that will to inflict vengeance is not immediately joined to the negative reprobation or non-election we are disputing. It arises from foresighted intervention of final perseverance in sin — a state of all the reprobate foresighted by God as infallibly future as an event consequent on negative reprobation, not as an antecedent cause. So the argument is weak: God in reprobating also wills to punish them; therefore foresighted sin is the cause of negative reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 5: Jewish unbelief (Rom. 9:32; 11:19-20) said to be cause of reprobation
english: Fifth: from the same Apostle they try to prove remaining in unbelief is the cause of reprobation, since he casts the Jews' reprobation back on their unbelief as cause (Rom. 9:31-32): Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not arrive at it — Why? Because not of faith. Confirmed by Rom. 11:19-20: The branches were broken off that I might be grafted in — Well: because of unbelief they were broken off; but you stand by faith. Sum: the Jews were reprobated for final perseverance in unbelief; therefore that perseverance is the cause of divine reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 5 Resp.: Rom. 9 explains failure to attain justice, not eternal reprobation; Estius
english: To the first witness from Romans 9: Paul is not giving the reason why the Jews were reprobated, but why they failed to attain true righteousness before God — however keen they seemed as pursuers of righteousness. That happened, he says, because they sought righteousness in their works and exact law-keeping, despising justification by faith; justification from works of the law is plainly impossible for a man weakened and corrupted by sin, and every sinner must flee to faith to be justified before God. Not only our theologians follow this reading, but among the Romanists William Estius of Douai expressly does so on this very place: Know that here no reason is given why the Jews were reprobated, but why they did not attain righteousness. So this first testimony is plainly off the point.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 5 Resp.: Rom. 11 concerns visible grafting of peoples, not eternal election of persons
english: Nor does the confirming text from Romans 11 help. Paul is not speaking of particular elect persons but of the whole body of Jews and Gentiles taken indefinitely. He is not teaching that some singular man is cut off for unbelief and struck from the number of the elect, then grafted back by recovered faith as by postliminium. He says only that the Jews in general, by unbelief, ceased to be God's covenant people, and that the Gentiles, embracing the gospel faith, succeeded into their place. To strip the Gentiles of every occasion for pride, he adds: if the Jews believe in Christ and stop persisting in unbelief, they are to be grafted in — admitted to the covenant people; and if the Gentiles who now rejoice as Church and people of God spring back from Christ's faith, they too will be broken off and cut from the Church's body.
