That threat has taken effect in many Gentiles who defected from Christ's faith to Mahometan superstition and stand torn from the covenant body. How does any of this prove that eternal reprobation of particular persons flowed from regard to their future unbelief as moving cause? It proves nothing. Paul discusses visible grafting and breaking of peoples, not eternal election and reprobation of individuals. That grafting and breaking denotes temporal admission or rejection of a nation from covenant status — one by faith, the other by unbelief. Sound theology abhors making reprobates into elect or elect into reprobates; yet Paul expressly teaches that those grafted of whom he speaks can be broken off, and those broken off grafted again.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 5 Resp.: remnant according to election (Rom. 11:5, 7); reprobates left to their hardness
english: Add this: when a nation — say the Jews — is broken off from the Church's body for unbelief, still none of the elect is broken off. By the same Apostle, a remnant according to the election of grace is saved (Rom. 11:5, 7). That some are not broken off while others of the same nation spring back and perish happens not because these were elected from foresighted faith, but because faith was given to these elect from God's eternal good pleasure, and a reservation according to election was made (Rom. 11:5). So too, that some are broken off by their unbelief and perish does not prove God from eternity reprobated them for foresighted unbelief. It proves that these reprobate, left to their hardness, brought forth unbelief — the genuine child of an hardened heart — and through it, broken from the Church's body, perished by their own desert.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6: Fathers and Augustine — reprobates must acknowledge justice for their sins
english: Sixth: the reprobate are warned always to acknowledge in their reprobation the divine justice by which, for their own sins, they were deservedly reprobated. Therefore, say adversaries, they are reprobated from foresight of the demerits in which they are foresighted as finishing this life. Many Father-testimonies are brought, especially Augustine: On the Good of Perseverance 6 — By his own will each deserts God, that he may deservedly be deserted by God. On Grace and Free Will 21 — When you read in Scripture that men's hearts are hardened, do not doubt their evil deserts went before, that they might justly suffer it. Again, chapter 23 — When you hear the Lord say He has mercy on whom he will and whom he will he hardens, in him whom God permits to be hardened believe his evil deserts; in him on whom God has mercy, acknowledge without doubt the grace that returns goods for evils. Most openly in Epistle 105: We seek the merit of hardening, and we find it. By desert of sin the universal mass is damned; those to whom God does not impart mercy merit that it not be imparted. From many such passages in Augustine and other Fathers, adversaries conclude that foresighted demerits with final lasting in them were the moving cause of divine reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: negative (Scotus permissive) vs punitive reprobation — if the latter, we grant
english: To clear all this, recall first: we are treating the reprobation theologians call negative — which Scotus calls permissive (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 1) — not the positive or punitive kind. Negative reprobation, so taken, means only God's eternal purpose not to grant certain particular persons some gratuitous, unowed, special benefit by which, if granted, they would be softened, converted, and infallibly led to eternal life. Positive reprobation means God's eternal purpose to punish certain persons with eternal death for the sins they will commit, and from which they are foresighted as not to be freed. If adversaries mean that latter decree, we freely grant: the eternal decree of predamnation tends to no one except as bound by sin's guilt. God wills to save the miserable without their merits, because he is good; he does not will to damn or punish innocents without demerits, because he is just.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: Augustine's just judgment refers to original demerit as adjunct, not motive
english: Second: when Augustine says that in reprobation we ought to acknowledge God's just judgment, that refers not to foresighted actual sins of individuals, but to the common original debt. So it does not help those who derive this reprobation from foresight of final perseverance in actual sins. We do grant original sin a place in negative reprobation — as an adjunct adhering to the reprobate subject, not as a moving cause of the divine will to that act of reprobating. Negative reprobation, whereby special grace is decreed denied to a person stained by original sin alone, is exercised not without justice, still less against it. What justice does not owe is justly denied; yet the discrimination — some efficaciously freed from this common original guilt, some left in that state by denial of special grace — depends not on retributing and vindicating justice, but on the liberty of the divine will, which has mercy on whom it will and passes by whom it will.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: negative reprobation not from foresight of final obstinacy; Lombard
english: Third: if adversaries claim negative reprobation springs from foresight of final obstinacy in actual sins, that abhors not only truth but all likelihood. The very decree permitting that final hardening — wherein reprobation sits — precedes absolute foresight of the hardening. So Peter Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 40): Reprobation is foresight of malice in certain ones and of not having mercy. That foresight is founded in the decree denying the special grace that in fact softens any heart, however hard. It is vain, then, to make foresight of final remaining in sins the cause of reprobation, when that remaining presupposes the permission sprung from the prior reprobation decree. So much for the argument in general. Now the testimonies one by one.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad primum: De bono perseverantiae — deserting God concerns common exciting grace
english: To the first: when Augustine says men first desert God and thence merit to be deserted by God, he is not speaking of the denial of that efficacious special grace in whose denial we locate reprobation or praeterition proper. He means subtraction of a more common, exciting grace — which we grant is taken from men for demerits — yet so that without the prior preparation of that special grace they would already have fallen into this demerit of contumacy.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad secundum et tertium: consequent hardening vs eternal will not to soften
english: To the second and third: when Augustine bids us believe evil deserts are not absent — or went before — in him whom God permits to be hardened, he is not speaking of that eternal will not to have mercy, not to soften, which contains reprobation itself. He means the hardening in which the sinner, justly forsaken by God, contracts a kind of stony hardness — and we do not deny that is the wage of preceding sins. Weigh this: however much that hardening, taken as increased and advanced as the evil disposition of the hardened man, arises from demerit of preceding sins, the first permissive hardening — mere negation of softening on God's part — cannot arise from that same foresighted demerit. To say God's will not to have mercy, not to soften, is born from foresight of human hardening would be as absurd as saying the sun's daylight, absent among the Cimmerians, arises from the air's long prior darkening.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad ultimum: merit of hardening in original sin; further hardening from daily sins; decree from free will
english: To the last testimony — Augustine teaching that we easily find in ourselves the merit of hardening, but cannot find the merit of divine mercy — I answer: he is not speaking of foresight of actual sins lasting to life's end in this or that person, but of original sin, the common demerit of all Adam's children. That can stand as sufficient cause why divine mercy may be denied anyone without any show of cruelty; it cannot stand as cause why God refused to prepare and apply to this or that particular man an efficacious remedy by which that inborn hardness could be tamed. Original sin avails for inquiring into damnation; it does not avail as the cause of negative reprobation. Finally all the reprobate — especially those who reach the use of free will — are said to merit that hardening: negatively, because they do not merit softening or that special mercy; affirmatively, because by daily sins they merit further hardening and handing over to a reprobate mind (Rom. 1:28). Yet the reprobation decree by which they are permitted so to harden depends on God's freest will, not on their foresighted final hardness — which could not be foresighted unless that permitting decree were presupposed.

title: Cap. VIII Arg.: peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum — therefore also of reprobation
english: Argument: the sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation itself; therefore also of divine reprobation as it regards those effects. As to the first effect — hardening or subtraction of peculiar grace — it plainly arises from demerits of antecedent sins (Rom. 1; 2 Thess. 2; Exod. 9). As to the last — eternal damnation — human demerits are plainly its cause from the very form of the sentence passed at the final judgment.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: if reprobation means damnation we grant; negative reprobation is antecedent, not damnation
english: We do not deny that the ungodly's sins cause their damnation. If adversaries, who make the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as finishing life the moving cause of reprobation, mean by reprobation nothing but damnation or the purpose to damn, so far we agree. But we are disputing negative reprobation — which is not damnation itself, nor damnation's cause, but a certain antecedent. No one is damned because reprobated, but because guilty; eternal death is the wage of transgression, not of reprobation. Set damnation aside, then — it is only improperly called an effect of this reprobation — and let us look at the rest.

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Primo: slippery consequence — cause of the permitted thing is not cause of the permission
english: First: the argument — sins of the reprobate cause all reprobation's effects; therefore also divine reprobation itself as regards those effects — is a slippery, weak consequence if every evil that follows is called an effect. What causes the permitted thing need not cause the permission of that thing. Example: I see two drunken men wandering rashly about; I foresee both will fall into a pit and starve there unless helped. I resolve to warn one, draw him back, and free him from the peril; the other I will not warn or draw back — or at least not so as actually to free him. That latter falls into the pit, lies long, wastes, and at last starves.

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Primo cont.: cause of rebellion is corrupt nature; cause of permitting decree is free pleasure
english: Ask the cause of the permitted evil in each of those effects — the fall, the long wasting, the final extinction — and I rightly name that person's drunkenness, blindness, and rashness. Ask the cause of my permission, or of my decree not to free him efficaciously, and you must come to the free power of my will, not to his ignorance or rashness. So God regards all men blind and wandering in sin's way: for some he prepares efficacious grace by which they shake off the stupor, return to themselves, and are saved; for others he decrees not to help with that powerful peculiar efficacious grace. Those latter rush into foul lusts, add sin to sin, harden in sin, die hardened, and are damned. Ask the cause of their rebellion, hardening, perdition: corrupt nature and voluntary sins are truly cause and origin of all those evils. Ask the cause of the permitting decree as to all that: you must come to the freest pleasure of the divine will, not to the permitted sins themselves. So the consequence wavers: sins of the reprobate cause all reprobation's effects; therefore they also cause reprobation itself — the reprobating decree.

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Secundo: hardness is consequent event, not properly an effect of reprobation; Cajetan
english: Second: adversaries seem to make that hardness or hardening — the reprobate's evil disposition or perverse act — an effect of divine reprobation. Most false. It may be a consequent event; it is not properly an effect of reprobation. As Cajetan well noted (on Aquinas I, q. 23 a. 5): whatever ordains the predestined to eternal life is an effect of predestination; yet in reprobation there is something that ordains to death — whatever has the character of fault or sin, such as that hardening and hardness — and that lies outside the whole effect of reprobation. Some theologians perilously err here: the means and causes of damnation are not tied to the reprobation decree as the means and causes of salvation are tied to the predestination decree. The difference is plain. Salvation's means are spiritual goods, and good falls under God's providence as intended, caused, and ordained by it. Damnation's means are spiritual evils; such evil falls under divine providence not as intended and caused, but as foresighted, permitted, ordained (so Dionysius the Carthusian on Sentences 1, dist. 40). When that hardness — man's vice or sin — is called an effect of reprobation, a mere consequent is labeled effect only improperly.

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Secundo cont.: Rom. 1 / 2 Thess. / Pharaoh — further hardening vs first permissive denial
english: Finally: the hardening Paul regards in Rom. 1:28 — He gave them over to a reprobate mind — and that which 2 Thess. 2:10-12 depicts — Because they received not the love of the truth, God shall send them strong delusion that they believe a lie — do not denote denial of the first efficacious grace, without which such hardening would never have come. They denote subtraction of some granted grace after its abuse — which subtraction we grant arises from men's demerits — and the hardening that follows we acknowledge as both sin and the wage of preceding sin. What is said of Pharaoh (Exod. 9: Jehovah hardened Pharaoh's heart) must either be taken of the first denial of special grace and permissive hardening — and then that will to harden, i.e. not to soften, as mere gratuitous negation of an act on God's part, could not arise from Pharaoh's foresighted demerits, because it precedes such foresight. Here refuge is Rom. 9: He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. Or those words may refer to a further hardening by which Pharaoh, of voluntary obstinacy, stiffened his own heart, God outwardly and inwardly furnishing occasions by which he certainly foresaw Pharaoh would be more hardened — even if by nature those occasions ought to have softened him. So God hardens an ungodly man for his demerits when, provoked by impiety, he takes occasion to withdraw granted grace and to act in ways he knows will make such a man worse. God is also said to harden without that regard to final demerits — only because he wills — when to a man considered in the common mass he has not prepared or given that special mercy he granted another in the same miserable condition. That is the hardening which argues reprobation, and it does not depend on foresight of final perseverance in sins. So the argument proceeds from an equivocation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg.: if God reprobates from himself, fewer reprobates than predestined (Ps. 145:9; Gregory of Valencia)
english: Some argue thus: if God reprobated men not for their sins, but of his own accord and from himself, then there would be fewer reprobate than predestined. For God is far more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting, destroying, and damning — according to Psalm 145:9: The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works. Gregory of Valencia (from whom we have taken most of the earlier arguments) judges this the best reason, and says he borrowed it from John Fekius.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: same consequence fails for election and reprobation; negative reprobation is denial of unowed benefit
english: We already dissolved this same reason of Gregory's in the predestination question. There he tried to prove predestination is from foresight of works because few are elect relative to the rejected. Now he contends reprobation hangs on foresight of final demerits because many are reprobate compared with the few elect. I answer: the consequence holds in neither place. As for reprobation — since it is not punishment but denial of a gratuitous unowed benefit — nothing forces us to say God, acting from mere good pleasure, cannot grant that benefit to fewer and deny it to more. We see in the angels that this benefit of election was denied to many, and without regard to foresighted demerits; whether denied to more than granted, I scarce dare say. Yet if anything in the thing itself were incongruous or unworthy of God, he could not deny election's benefit even to one without regard to foresighted sin — let alone to many. That single instance breaks the argument's force.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: human mass of merited damnation; Augustine De bono persever. 8; Rom. 9:20
english: Descend from angels to men. In men the equity of this is far easier to see. Since the whole mass of humankind has flowed down into merited damnation by our first parent's disobedience, if God with no further regard to actual sins wills to pass by and reject however many in preparing and giving special grace, he passes by and rejects those in whom he finds nothing for which they should be elect to so excellent a benefit, and in whom he finds much for which they are most unworthy of it. Nothing else need be said but Augustine (On the Good of Perseverance 8): Let him who is freed love grace; let him who is not freed acknowledge the debt — and Paul (Rom. 9:20): O man, who are you to answer God? Shall the thing formed say...?

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: propensity to mercy need not give special grace to most; praeterition is not desertion
english: But God is more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting and destroying men. We grant it. Yet the most merciful is not wont to impart excellent peculiar benefits to all or even to most. It is enough to show that propensity that he has mercy on all as to many effects of his mercy — even if, as to this special effect of preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life, he has mercy neither on all nor on most. Further: to pass by or reprobate is not the same as to desert and destroy. Yes, all the reprobate or non-elect are at length deserted and destroyed — but that they were passed by or non-elect as to special grace proceeds from God's mere will; that afterward they were deserted and destroyed took its origin from their intervening demerit. So far we have answered the arguments Gregory of Valencia uses on Aquinas I, q. 23, on Reprobation.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 9 (Thomas of Argentina): adult reprobation from foresight of final bad use of free will
english: Among the older Scholastics, Thomas of Argentina admits he deserts the common opinion of the theologians, and tries against them to prove this: that the cause of reprobation as to adults is the evil use of free will lasting in them to life's end, foresighted by God from eternity. That opinion differs in words, not in sense, from the Jesuit and Arminian. Let us hear Argentina's reasons.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 9: syllogism — no one ordained to eternal punishment without precognition of cause
english: To eternal punishment, he says, no one is ordained by a just Judge without precognition of the cause. But every reprobate is deputed to punishment by God the just Judge. Therefore only from foresighted evil use of free will lasting to the end — which is the same as saying with Jesuits and Arminians: only from foresighted unbelief and disobedience.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 9 Resp.: reprobation is denial of unowed benefit, not adjudication to punishment
english: I answer: by reprobation we mean that part of divine providence by which God wills to deny certain ones special grace and permit them to fall short of beatitude's end — as by predestination we mean that other part by which he willed to prepare and give certain ones that special grace and lead them infallibly to glory and beatitude. On that footing, we deny that this reprobation is a deputation or adjudication to punishment. It is free denial of an unowed benefit from God's will alone; it is not imperious infliction of an unowed penalty from God's will alone. Yes, in all the reprobate there follows ordination to punishment and imposition of punishment — and both rightly regard that person's final remaining in sin. But in the formal act of reprobation itself, ordination of the reprobate person to eternal death is not yet contained. Such arguments try to deceive us by presuming that what belongs to the same subject must spring from the same causes — as if, because every reprobate is also ordained to punishment, reprobation and that ordination to punishment must depend on the same causes. We hold: however much the same men who are reprobated are always also deputed to punishment, this reprobation flowed from the sole liberty of the divine will, while ordination to punishment drew its origin from their foresighted sin.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 10: God as spiritual sun — reprobation from foresight of putting an obstacle to grace
english: Tenth: God is as it were a Sun everywhere diffusing rays of spiritual grace. Therefore, as much as in him lies, he imparts spiritual grace to all, unless they put an obstacle to those diffused rays. That he leaves some void of grace and reprobates them happens because he foresaw them putting an obstacle to his grace. So reprobation is from that foresighted evil use of free will.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 10 Resp.: sun not by natural necessity; special ray of mercy not offered to all alike
english: The comparison fails in many ways. First: though God is not badly called a spiritual Sun, he does not diffuse his rays by natural necessity but by voluntary dispensation. So as much as in him lies, he does not diffuse them to all equally and uniformly. Second: even if we grant that God diffuses certain common rays of grace to each and all (we will not litigate that now), we will never concede that, as much as in him lies, he promiscuously offers this special excellent ray of special mercy to each and all.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 10 Resp.: if from foresight of obstacles, all would be reprobate; election softens some (Aquinas)
english: Third: where God is presumed to will to deny no one that special mercy proper to election, and so to reprobate no one except who is foresighted as casting an obstacle to divine grace by perverse use of free will, Argentina misses that this exception about opposing an obstacle applies to each and all considered in the state of sin. Aquinas observed prudently (Contra Gentiles 3.160): the saying IT IS IN THE POWER OF FREE WILL NOT TO PRESENT AN IMPEDIMENT TO GRACE is truly said of those whose natural power is intact; he who by prior inordination has declined to evil is no longer altogether in his power so to will as to present an impediment. Since all mortals are of themselves ready to put obstacles, and in fact put very many, if God reprobated from such foresight he would have reprobated every one of us, not one excepted. So the pattern of predestination and reprobation shines here: though all put obstacles, God from abundance of mercy decreed finally to soften some — by efficacious and wondrous ways — out of their impediments and convert them to faith and repentance; others struggling the same way against his grace he decreed not to soften, but to leave hardened in their hardness and obstinacy. Finally the inference — that God from eternity foresaw some as finally using free will well, others ill, and by a decree following that foresight elected these and reprobated those — cannot stand. Good sound use of free will persevering to the end flowed only from election's grace, so it presupposes antecedent election. Conversely, evil use lasting to the last breath is not foresighted unless God's will to deny that special grace — which no heart, however hard, resists — is presupposed. That will of God is the will to reprobate. So foresight of a finally hardened heart is something later than reprobation; the reason or cause of reprobation cannot be sought from it.

title: Cap. VIII Arg.: if God elects and reprobates without cause from men, he is acceptor of persons (Acts 10:34)
english: Argument: if from eternity God elected some and reprobated others without a cause holding on the human side, then he would be an acceptor of persons. For he seems an acceptor of persons who, when two are equal, gives to one what he denies the other. But that respect of persons is removed from God (Acts 10:34).

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: old Pelagian objection; Augustine Ep. 105 — same mass; debt to damned, unowed grace to freed
english: This was the old Pelagian objection — we read it everywhere in Augustine. Epistle 105: those who think they make God an acceptor of persons if they believe that without preceding merits he has mercy on whom he will, calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he will, little notice that due punishment is rendered to the damned and unowed grace to the freed — so neither complains as unworthy, nor the other glories as worthy. Rather there is no respect of persons where one and the same mass of damnation and offense wraps all, that the freed may learn from the not-freed that punishment would have suited him too unless grace had helped. The same objection he repels in Epistle 106 and Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7. Augustine's answer comes to this: it is not respect of persons where one does of his own what he wills. Mercy is given the elect; justice is not denied the reprobate. The elect is honored with a gratuitous gift; the reprobate is not cheated of any benefit owed him.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: Durandus, Thomas, Gerson — unequal gifts from liberality are not injustice
english: The Scholastics answer more briefly: it is not unjust or vicious to give unequals to equals where the gift is from mere liberality — only where something is rendered from debt. So Durandus (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 2 ad 1). Thomas to the same effect: There is no iniquity with God if he prepare unequals for equals. It would be against justice if the effect of predestination were rendered as debt and not given. Of things given from grace, one may at pleasure give more or less to whom he will, provided he subtracts from none what is owed (ST I, q. 23 a. 5 ad 3). Gerson in the Moral Rules: there is no respect of persons except where debt and parity stand on both sides; in free gifts, to take one and dismiss another is not respect of persons. So the major's consequence in the argument is plainly null: in predestination God gives the predestined not owed but unowed grace; in reprobation he denies the reprobate not an owed benefit but an unowed one.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: Acts 10:34 concerns promised favor in every nation, not the eternal gratuitous decree
english: As for Peter's words (Acts 10:34) — Of a truth I perceive that God is not an acceptor of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is accepted with him — they regard God's favor from covenant and promise, already as it were owed, not that eternal gratuitous favor bound by no covenant or promise. For by promising favor to those who fear him and live holily and piously, God would already be an acceptor of persons if he spurned a poor or lowly man worshipping him chastely and embraced a rich noble, or if he favored a religious Jew and neglected a Gentile living justly, soberly, and piously. That respect of persons the Apostle teaches is far from God. But God is held by no promise or covenant to predestinate or not predestinate.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: election and praeterition from mere good pleasure; those passed by were children of wrath
english: Further: in electing or passing by he regards no external circumstance of nation, nobility, or the like, but acts from the mere good pleasure of his will. Finally, those he passes by cannot pretend they feared God and lived justly; they are compelled instead to acknowledge they were children of wrath, most unworthy of the least divine benefit. So this Scripture place proves neither that predestination and reprobation proceed from some cause holding on the human side, nor that God is to be charged as an acceptor of persons.

title: Cap. VIII Arg.: God is rich in mercy — therefore he reprobates only from foresight of demerits
english: Argument: God is rich in mercy. But if he reprobated some from his mere will and not for foresighted sin, nothing of mercy would appear in that act. Therefore he reprobates from foresight of demerits — or from foresighted evil use of free will lasting to the end.

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Primo: we deny foresight as origin of negative reprobation, not of preparing punishment (Aquinas on Rom. 9)
english: First, always hold this: when we deny that reprobation took origin from foresight of human demerits, we mean reprobation as denied preparation of efficacious grace for certain persons — not as preparation of eternal punishment for those same persons. With Aquinas we gladly grant: foresight of merits cannot be any reason of predestination, because foresighted merits themselves fall under predestination; yet foresight of sins can be some reason of reprobation on the side of the punishment prepared for the reprobate, insofar as God proposes to punish the wicked for sins they have from themselves, not from God (Thomas, Commentary on Romans 9, lect. 2, near the end).

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Secundo: reprobates regarded as bound by original guilt — rich in mercy may still elect and pass by
english: Second, note also: all whom God reprobates are regarded by him as bound by original guilt and liable to damnation — though that is not simply necessary to clear God of injustice or cruelty as to negative reprobation, as is plain in the angels. But among men it stands thus: all who are reprobated are in themselves damnable and worthy of hatred. God, though rich in mercy, can most equitably by liberty of will elect some from among them and reprobate others — all of whom original sin has made worthy of hatred and (if one may so speak) reprobable.

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Denique: reprobation ordered to show justice and greater mercy; some mercy even toward the reprobate
english: Finally: when it is objected that if God reprobated otherwise than from foresight of final and actual demerits, nothing of mercy would appear — that objection seems to rest on a Scholastic rule: in all God's works mercy and justice concur. The sense of the rule is not that every divine action is formally an act of justice or of mercy, but that it is an effect of providence ordained to show justice, or mercy, or both. So this reprobation, which we take as from God's mere will, is ordained to show justice in the damned and greater mercy toward the predestined. Further, some mercy appears even toward the reprobate themselves — not that special excellent mercy which by efficacious grace infallibly ordains to glory, but the many benefits of grace and mercy often granted them, not withdrawn except for abuse and voluntary rebellion against God. Even in their damnation God's mercy appears — not totally relaxing, but somewhat alleviating — while he punishes them short of what is condign (Thomas, ST I, q. 21 a. 4).

title: Cap. VIII Arg.: no just judge intends punitive justice per se — therefore God reprobates from foresight of demerit
english: They press further: a just judge never aims at punitive justice for its own sake — only once punishable fault is supposed. Yet God, they say, in the act of reprobating means to exercise punitive and vindicative justice. Hence reprobation must spring from foresight of free will's evil, demeritorious use.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: negative reprobation is not from punitive justice; permission precedes foresight of final bad use
english: Negative reprobation — nothing but God's eternal purpose not to give certain ones that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened and by which they would be infallibly directed to eternal life — does not proceed from punitive justice, nor from a will to damn, but from that reason of providence by which God judged it agreeable to his wisdom to permit some, by their own vice, to fall short of beatitude's end. That will posited, God foresights the reprobate's future sins and final remaining in them, and understands that the manifestation of his glory will arise from punishing those sins. So he intends to exercise punitive justice about the reprobate for the sins in which they are foresighted as finishing life — but that intention and foresight followed the act of the foresaid reprobation, as did the sinner's final state in his sins. We may truly say there was always in God a will to punish sins if they should come to be; but an absolute express will to punish, terminated on this or that particular person, we cannot place in God unless his permission that they come to be is presupposed, and that this person destined to punishment finally remain under their guilt. That permission — which contains the act of negative reprobation — is prior to absolute foresight of evil use of free will lasting to life's end in this or that person, and so cannot depend on that foresight as cause. Wrongly, then, are the decrees of reprobating and of avenging or damning drawn from the same causes.

title: Cap. VIII: Hactenus Jesuitarum — turn to Corvinus; negative reprobation to liberty alone
english: So far we have aired the Jesuits' and Scholastics' arguments. Corvinus also presses others in his Defense of the Arminian sentence against Tilenus — and if anything new appears there, it will be cleared. We must labor all the more to recall the negative act of reprobation — which we may call praeterition or non-election — to the sole liberty of the divine will. For all who derive this reprobation from foresight of evil acts also hang election on foresight of good acts.

title: Cap. VIII: Augustine rejects foresight of Esau's evil and Jacob's good alike as causes
english: Add Augustine — no one treated this cause more learnedly or holily: he denies as much that Esau's foresighted evil works were the cause of his reprobation as that Jacob's foresighted good works were the cause of his election. See Enchiridion to Laurentius 98, To Simplicianus 1.2, and Epistle 105, where he equally rejects those who say God hated or loved the not-yet-born because he foresaw their future works. Epistle 106 openly teaches that God by loving discerns those whom no merits discern. As he will not admit foresight of good merits as election's cause, so he will not grant foresight of evils as reprobation's reason. For where good acts — believing, obeying, persevering — stand on one side and opposite evil acts on the other, those are clearly regarded as discerned by merits. But let us come to Corvinus's sentence.

title: Cap. VIII: Corvinus with Arminius — reprobation only from personal rejection of offered grace
english: With Arminius he therefore holds this: God always reprobates particular persons from their own personal rejection of offered grace. In the reprobation decree, on that view, he has rejected or passed by no one except as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God who is actually calling. Nor in Adam's fall has he left anyone by absolute ordination alone, or decreed to damn for original sin only.

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: personal unworthiness foresighted — but not antecedent motive of the reprobation decree
english: If the talk is of adults only, we grant Arminius and Corvinus this much: a certain personal proper unworthiness, sprung from voluntary rebellion, was foresighted from eternity in all whom God from eternity reprobated. What we deny is that from that foresighted actual and final rebellion the reprobation decree flowed as from an antecedent moving cause. Rather we affirm: in the divine will we must first conceive that decree of permissive hardening or reprobation of which Paul speaks — He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens — before we can conceive in the divine mind that foresight of any particular person as from eternity struggling against his grace and, to life's end, contumaciously spurning and rejecting it.

title: Cap. VIII critique: Corvinus's vocabulary of unbelief and vocation against Scripture; original sin alone
english: Further: when they say that in the reprobation decree God considers men as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God actually calling, they are forced to use words against the received custom of Scripture and of almost all theologians. If we take our speaking-norm from Scripture and sound theologians, unbelief denotes rejection of the Gospel, and the words grace and vocation presuppose the Gospel's manifestation. Yet on Arminius's and Corvinus's view, people are reprobated for foresighted unbelief to whom the Gospel was never announced, and said to have rejected grace and vocation to whom Christ's grace was never offered. Finally, their teaching that original sin makes no man guilty of eternal death, and that no one is damned for that alone, is as alien to the catholic Church's doctrine as it is necessarily bound up with Arminian theology.

title: Cap. VIII close into Cap. IX: Corvinus's arguments to be proposed and dissolved
english: But let us now gird ourselves to propose and dissolve their arguments. Chapter IX — Corvinus's arguments proposed and dissolved.

title: Cap. IX Corvini Arg. 1: as God damns the gospel-contumacious in time, so he reprobated them from eternity
english: Chapter IX — Corvinus's arguments proposed and dissolved. Adversaries commonly argue from the decree of damning to the act or decree of reprobation thus: In whatever manner of consideration God damns in time, in that same manner he decreed to damn and reprobated from eternity. But he damns men considered as contumacious to the Gospel — that is, as finally impenitent and unbelieving. Therefore he also reprobated them so considered.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1: major — sin's relation to damnation same as to reprobation; wisdom would not reprobate without demerit
english: They take the Major as clear from this: whatever relation sin has to damnation, it has the same to reprobation — so as sin is granted meritorious and moving cause moving God to damn this or that particular person, it must likewise stand toward reprobation. They add that it clashes with divine wisdom to will to reprobate a sinner without regard to evil merits, yet refuse to condemn him in time except for evil merits.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: head of error — reprobation is not the same as the decree of damning
english: Jesuits and Arminians use a like argument in the predestination debate — and we answered it before. The head of the error here is presuming reprobation, or the decree to reprobate, is altogether the same as the decree to damn. For us the decree to damn names a peremptory sentence conceived from eternity in the mind of God the Judge and confirmed by his will's good pleasure: to punish with eternal death, for that sin, a man foresighted and considered guilty of sin at this life's very exit. The decree to reprobate names God's eternal good pleasure not as Judge but as freest Agent: resolving not to apply to certain persons that grace of special unowed mercy which would in fact soften, convert, and lead them to eternal life.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: wide difference of the two decrees; Major and its confirmation invalid
english: Between these two decrees the difference is wide. The first proceeds from vindicating justice, and so regards the sinner's final guilt as moving cause of the destined punishment. The second goes forth from God's liberty doing of his own what he wills. As when God resolves to give a special benefit to some particular person it does not follow that he regarded that person's merits as moving cause of the beneficence, so when he resolves not to give that same special benefit to another, it is not rightly deduced that he regarded that person's final demerits as moving cause of the denied beneficence. So we call the Major and its confirmation invalid: there is neither uniform consideration nor the same relation of sin to the decree of reprobating as to the decree of damning. Far from clashing with divine wisdom, it best agrees with it that God refuse to condemn anyone except for sin's demerit as antecedent moving cause of destined punishment — and yet will to reprobate some (that is, pass them by in preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life) from mere liberty of will, not from an antecedent motive of final unbelief or impenitence.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: Bannes and Lombard — praeterition manifests liberty in dispensing supernatural goods
english: Bannes puts it well: this praeterition or reprobation of some persons, others being elect, manifests the greatest liberty the divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods (on ST I, q. 23 a. 5, p. 293). Nor is it alien to divine wisdom — as with his other attributes — to manifest this attribute of liberty in dispensing the highest good to men. So Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 41): God reprobated whom he willed, not for future merits he foresaw — yet by a most right truth, remote from our senses. So much for the Major.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp. Minor: not all damned as gospel-contumacious; reprobation's cause lies elsewhere
english: Now the Minor — which is not true if taken universally. Many are damned who are not at all considered by God as contumacious to the Gospel. Example: pagan infants, born children of wrath and not reborn in Christ. Among adults, all those to whom the Gospel never shone nor Christ became known. Arminius even grants that many are damned by the Law alone, not for contempt of the Gospel (Examination of Perkins's Predestination). No need to labor further on the Minor. Whether men are damned for contempt of Gospel or of Law, that the same are reprobated has its cause elsewhere. Finally we grant men are not reprobated without regard to a despised Law or Gospel, because God cannot reprobate anyone except as guilty of sin — but it does not follow from preconsideration of future faith in some and future sin in others. God electing or reprobating foresights from eternity many future things in elect and reprobate that are not moving causes of the act of electing or reprobating.

title: Cap. IX Arg.: Adam's sin remitted to all — God cannot leave anyone in that condemnation by strict right alone
english: From Adam's sin remitted to all alike they argue thus: God cannot deal by strict right with any man lying in Adam's common sin so as to leave him in that condemnation without any hope of pardon. But if he reprobated any only as lying in Adam's common fall, and not for their actual personal rebellion against God, he would be dealing with them by strict and highest right.

title: Cap. IX Arg.: Major confirmed — Adam received; Christ obtained reconciliation for all; therefore reprobation only from final impenitence
english: They try to confirm the Major two ways. First: pardon was given to Adam himself — so it would seem unjust that God, for Adam's sin which by mere estimation is called ours, should shut any others from eternal life, when he received into grace Adam who committed that sin. Second: Christ obtained redemption and reconciliation with the Father for all — and it seems little fitting that by a reprobation decree those be left to destruction for whom Christ so obtained reconciliation that nothing but impenitence can bar them from sharing its use. Therefore no one is reprobated except from regard to final impenitence or rebellion as moving cause — and that, they say, is reprobation.

title: Cap. IX Resp.: Major false for pagan infants — Augustine Enchiridion 99; Vasquez on infants
english: I answer: as to pagan infants — neither in the covenant nor regenerated in Christ — the Major of their syllogism is openly false. If to condemn for original sin alone is to deal by strict right, then with such God does deal by strict right. So Augustine from the catholic Church's sentence (Enchiridion 99): the whole human race is by so just a divine judgment damned in the apostate root that even if none were freed from it, no one could rightly blame God's justice; and those freed ought so to be freed that from the many not freed, left in most just damnation, it would be shown what the whole fellowship had merited — and whither even they would be led by God's due judgment unless his unowed mercy helped. Even Vasquez the Jesuit, who sharply defends predestination from foresighted merits, must confess: if we mean reprobation as rejection from God's grace, reprobate infants had no cause of their reprobation at all; if rejection from beatitude, those infants for whom providence so disposes that no human remedy can be applied were by God's decree shut from the kingdom of heaven right after foresight of original sin they contracted (on ST I, q. 23 a. 3, disp. 89 c. 6). So Arminians push their error farther than the Jesuits themselves.

title: Cap. IX Resp.: as to adults — God does not damn without foresight of actual sin; reprobation as denying special grace is from liberty
english: Set infants aside and take the Major as it regards adults with reason and free will. If dealing by strict right means decreeing someone damned and afflicted with eternal death without regard to actual sin, we grant God does not so deal with such sinners. He neither damned them nor destined them to damnation except for foresighted sins and final impenitence in them. But if by dealing by strict right Corvinus means not preparing that special grace which, applied, God knows and decrees will free such a man — or passing him by and not ordaining him to take hold of eternal life by the special-providence decree we call predestination, but leaving him to his deficiency (so to speak) — then we affirm God so deals with many from sole liberty of will. And if that is dealing by strict right (we shall see shortly), then he deals by strict right with all the reprobate.

title: Cap. IX Resp.: reprobation decree is secret — reprobates not left without hope of pardon merely by being reprobated
english: Further: the clause annexed to their Major — that such are left in that condemnation without any hope of pardon — is wrongly pinned on the reprobating decree. Like predestination, the reprobation decree is secret; as to which particulars, no mortal knows it a priori of himself or of another. As the predestined do not yet have hope of pardon from being predestined alone, so the reprobate are not left without hope of pardon from being reprobated alone. Paul the predestined could not conceive hope of pardon except through conversion and faith in Christ; Judas the reprobate is not left without hope of pardon except through his unbelief and impiety against Christ. Finally if Arminians argue from mere infallibility of the event and immutability of the decree that any reprobate is stripped of all hope of pardon, that inconvenience presses their view no less than ours. They grant Judas — and so every particular reprobate — was from eternity reprobated by God's fixed peremptory sentence; so that on their view it is as certain, infallible, and defined with God that Judas will never obtain pardon and eternal life as on ours. If, then, on that Arminian reprobation Judas is not left without all hope of pardon, neither will he be on the reprobation the orthodox defend.

title: Cap. IX Resp. to Major's first confirmation: original sin is by contagion, not bare imputation; Adam's penitence was for himself
english: Now their confirmation of the Major. First they say it clashes with divine goodness that Adam who committed the sin be immune while others are smitten who are guilty by mere imputation. That confirmation has many faults. First: the question is not about men to be punished, but about men to be reprobated. Reprobation is one thing; damnation or punishment another — as we have often pressed. So those words wander from the question's scope. Next they too much thin original sin when they say it is ours by mere divine estimation and that we are guilty only by bare imputation. It is ours by contagious propagation, not bare imputation; we are guilty not only by God's mere estimation but by damnable corruption contracted in all the soul's faculties. Further, it does not clash with divine equity or goodness to free penitent Adam and punish others dying in original sin alone. What Adam did in the intact state he did as root of the human race — for us as for himself — so he is said to have stood and fallen not for himself alone but for all posterity. What he did in the fallen state he did for himself, not for posterity; by repenting he is said to have recovered divine grace and favor for himself, not for every posterity. Finally it is not iniquitous that God from mere mercy prepared and gave true serious penitence to Adam alone, and neither prepared nor gave the same saving penitence to many sprung from Adam. No law binds God more to give all Adam's posterity what he indulged Adam than to give Judas whatever from mere mercy he gave Paul or Peter.

title: Cap. IX Resp. to Major's second confirmation: Christ obtained reconciliation for all — only individual impenitence bars participation
english: Secondly they contend that no one is reprobated merely as lying in Adam's common sin, because Christ obtained reconciliation for all — and only each person's impenitence can bar them from sharing it. They untie the knot they tied. If reconciliation or redemption were obtained for every person by Christ's offering already applied, the argument would have some force. But as it is not applied to adults except through faith and actual penitence, so neither to infants except through supernatural regeneration.

title: Cap. IX Resp.: no promise of faith to every adult or regenerating covenant with every infant — passing over some in original sin alone is free right; Major not confirmed
english: Where, then, stands any promise that God will prep and confer on every adult the faith and penitence that actually reconcile them to him? And where has he bound himself by covenant to every infant — original sin or no — to count them reconciled and by supernatural regeneration make them sons and heirs of eternal life? He does neither, and owes neither. So when he passes over or reprobates some who lie in original sin alone, he wrongs no one; he exercises free right. The Major, therefore, was neither sound in itself nor made solid by the proofs they annexed.

title: Cap. IX Resp. to Minor: God reprobating those in original sin alone does not deal by strict or highest right
english: As for the Minor, I also deny that God, when he reprobates, deals with the reprobate by strict or highest right if he reprobates them as lying in original sin alone. If he dealt by highest right, as soon as they were born he could cast them into Gehenna as guilty of eternal death. If he dealt by strict right, he could strip them of all gifts of his grace.

title: Cap. IX Resp.: God confers corporal and spiritual benefits on the reprobate — therefore not strict right; false dichotomy with highest mercy
english: But he often confers on them many corporal and spiritual benefits by which they may be made better; he withdraws nothing owed them, and pours into them nothing by which they are made worse. So he does not deal with them by strict right. Yet the adversaries plead as if between dealing from highest mercy and dealing from highest or strict right there were no middle.

title: Cap. IX Resp.: with the non-elect God acts from philanthropy, goodness, and admirable mildness — conscience convicts innate contagion or voluntary rebellion
english: Highest mercy, we grant, is how God deals with the elect alone. Toward the non-elect or reprobate his dealing is not highest right either, but philanthropy (φιλανθρωπία), goodness, and a mildness worth wonder. Their consciences themselves convict them: the reprobation decree did not shove them; innate contagion, voluntary rebellion, or both, brought them into a death they richly deserved.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 open: God wills the saving grace of the Gospel offered promiscuously to all — Mat. 28:19; Mk 16:15; Col. 1:28
english: God wills that the saving grace of the Gospel be offered to all men alike — a will he has opened in many Scriptures: Matt. 28:19, Go therefore and teach all nations; and Mark 16:15, Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. So also the Apostle, Col. 1:28: We announce Christ, warning every man and teaching every man, that we may present every man perfect in Christ. This regard of God for all men's salvation seems to argue that he reprobated no one except after regard to contempt of grace — or, what comes to the same, except from foresight of final unbelief and impenitence.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 Sol: Docete omnes gentes / Predicate omni creaturae — apostolic authority for the whole world; wall between Jew and Gentile down
english: From Christ's charges Teach all nations and Preach to every creature it rightly follows that those disciples were given apostolic authority — not pinned to one church or nation, but aimed at the whole world. It also follows that the wall which shut Gentiles from God's church was broken down, and that the Gospel was to be preached not to Jews alone but to Jews and Gentiles, Greeks and barbarians, wise and unwise — as Paul says in Rom. 1.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 Sol: ministers must seek to bring every hearer to Christ — Augustine De correptione et gratia 15
english: Finally it also follows that Gospel ministers' aim and labor — as Paul's did — ought to be to bring to Christ every one to whom they announce Christ's Gospel. As Augustine says with piety and prudence: not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we ought to be so moved by charity that we will all to be saved (De corrept. et grat. 15).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 Sol: deny adversaries' corollary — reprobation of those to whom Christ ordered preaching is not only from foresight of demerits
english: All that granted, we still deny the adversaries' corollary from these texts: that those to whom Christ ordered the Gospel preached were reprobated only from foresight of their demerits. To reprobate is, by decree of will, to permit some to fall short of beatitude's end — not destining or preparing for them that special grace which would in fact lead them to faith and eternal life. To elect is to ordain some to obtain beatitude infallibly and without frustration — destining, preparing, and giving them that special grace by which God from eternity decreed and knew they would be softened, converted, and in fact saved.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 Sol: evangelizing mandate does not clash with reprobating will — passover antecedes final hardness, not from foresight of it
english: We are commanded to preach the Gospel to many whom God, in that infallible ordination to grace and glory, from mere good pleasure willed to pass by. So the evangelizing mandate does not clash with the reprobating will. I add: he willed to pass them by as to preparing this special, actually saving grace — by a will that precedes their final hardness, not one that flows from foresight of that final hardness and unbelief. For (as often said) a particular person's final impenitence and unbelief is not foreseen by God as absolutely certain until the reprobation decree for that person stands — whereby God decreed not to pity them so far as to soften and convert them efficaciously, and also decreed to permit them by their own vice to repel any offered grace and stay hard-hearted to life's end.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 Sol: Matt. 11:25; 13:11; Rom. 9:18 — antecedent good pleasure where the word was preached; efficacious grace prepared for some only
english: Here belong the Savior's words, Matt. 11:25: I give you glory, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and uncovered them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you. And Matt. 13:11: To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; to them it is not given. And that saying of the Apostle, often pressed against every foe of special grace: He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens (Rom. 9:18). All these texts concern those to whom God's word was preached — and yet in all of them God's antecedent good pleasure is hinted: efficacious grace prepared for some, not prepared for others.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 3 Sol: physician analogy — command to preach to all does not prove God decreed to free all efficaciously
english: In a word: from God's will that every physician do his utmost — prepare and offer each patient he takes on whatever helps prolong life — you may not infer that God will let none die of disease unless he foresaw him a stubborn scorner of the offered medicine. So from God's command that Gospel ministers preach the word (the medicine of souls) to all, and strain every nerve that every one be freed from death, it does not follow that God himself decreed to free all from death efficaciously — or that he did not decree to permit some, by their hard hearts, to rush into perdition whom, had he not reprobated them, he both could and would have softened by special mercy. Vain, then, to judge the predestinating or reprobating will — which determines an effect by infallible divine action, or withholds it — from the mandating will that ought to govern human actions.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4: God is ready to give all sufficient media to believe and convert — therefore reprobation only by consequent will after foresight of final impenitence
english: They press harder still: God on his part is ready to give everyone the media sufficient and needful for believing and converting, and will surely give them unless people themselves put up a barrier. But that seems to clash — that God by antecedent will should have reprobated someone, and yet be ready to supply him everything needful for salvation. Therefore, they say, he reprobated no one except by consequent will after foresight of that person's final impenitence, unbelief, and rejection of divine grace.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol: universal sufficient grace is a slippery postulate — Vasquez grants some infants never received sufficient media of salvation
english: The claim that sufficient grace is prepared and administered to all is very slippery — and even among patrons of universal grace it lacks full firm consent. Vasquez (as we noted before), forced by the plain fact, grants that for some infants sufficient media of salvation could not be applied by any human providence and were not applied by divine providence (In T. Aquin. disp. 95.6). So for these little ones perishing in original sin we can turn their argument back: infants for whom sufficient media were never prepared or administered were rejected without regard to actual unbelief or final impenitence.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol: infants of unbelieving idolaters — rejection without foresight of the reprobate's unbelief; Vasquez also grants some adult reprobation before foresight of sins
english: Take infants born of two unbelieving idolatrous parents — knowing no Christ, serving the devil — whom the Apostle himself calls unclean (1 Cor. 7:14): for them sufficient media were neither prepared nor administered. In such cases they must grant rejection with no regard to foresight of the reprobate's unbelief. Set those infants aside who, under divine providence, are born and die outside the Church: the same Vasquez also grants that even for adults with reason and free will some reprobation and repulse was fixed by God before foresight of sins (ibid. cap. 2). By reprobation he means rejection from that special grace which, denied, leaves a man always hardening and rushing into perdition (cap. 5).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol: supply of sufficient grace does not exclude antecedent reprobation — preparation of efficacious grace does, and implies election
english: If Arminius, Corvinus, and their backers grant us even that much, it follows that supplying sufficient grace does not shut out antecedent reprobation — whereas preparing efficacious grace truly does shut it out, and brings election in. So grant that God administers sufficient grace to every adult: still (as you see), even by a Jesuit's judgment, it does not follow they were not reprobated before foresight of final demerits.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol: apostate angels received sufficient media yet some were elect, some reprobate — so sufficient grace to all would not prove reprobation only from foresight of final unbelief
english: The apostate angels make this plain. God was not only ready to give them media sufficient and needful to stand and persevere in divine obedience — he gave them. Yet every theologian grants that among the angels some were elect, some non-elect or reprobate. So even if the adversaries could prove sufficient grace is given to every human being, they still could not rightly infer that no one is reprobated except from foresight of final unbelief. Just as positing sufficient grace for a given person does not posit his antecedent predestination, so positing that same sufficient grace does not deny his antecedent reprobation.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol: predestination is ordination with infallible event; reprobation denies unfrustrable special operation — Bellarmine: God not bound to give sufficient grace to all
english: The reason is the same either way. Predestination is not just any ordination to a supernatural end by media however sufficient — it is ordination joined to an infallible outcome. Reprobation does not deny every ordination to a supernatural end, but the unfrustrable ordination that comes from the ordaining God's device and special operation producing the very event of salvation. Finally: that sufficient media of salvation are given to all is asserted with more confidence than it is proved with ease. I will not enter that dispute now — it is not needed to solve the argument before us. One note only: Bellarmine, who defends this sufficient-grace view, first grants that God would do no injustice if he denied that sufficient grace to some or to all (De grat. et lib. arb. 2.4). So God is bound to it by no pact or promise. How then dare the adversaries promise every person sufficient grace that God never promised?

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol cont.: Bellarmine's mediate/immediate dodge — sufficient help for an Indian or American infant in the parents cannot be explained
english: Second: Bellarmine is driven to the mediate-or-immediate distinction, and will not dare claim sufficient grace is given immediately to every infant. How dark that is — that an infant born among Indians or Americans had sufficient help shown in his parents, when no one can say what that help was! And if defending sufficient grace means fleeing to ancestors, it is far safer to go all the way back to the first parents — where no one doubts posterity also received sufficient grace in them — than to stop at any later ancestors, of whom it remains uncertain whether they received such sufficient grace in their children's name or not.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 4 Sol cont.: many adults lack immediate aid to believe — Bellarmine's 'posse' via creatures is a miserable defense of esse
english: Finally, among adults themselves, Bellarmine admits (ibid. c. 8), very many are not given immediate sufficient help to believe — only in this thin sense: they can know God through the creatures, can be stirred to believe that God is and rewards seekers, can be stirred by that faith to pray, and so (even without Gospel preaching) can obtain illumination in the faith from God, an angel, or some man. Miserable defense: the question is about what is, and the answer is only about what can be — you all see that. I touch it only in passing, to show how poorly founded is the claim that sufficient grace is given to every person, which our disputers lay as their cause's firmest base. I add nothing more: even if granted, it still does not solidly prove their cause, as we showed from the start.

title: Cap. IX Arg. A vocatione Evangelica: absolute antecedent election/reprobation would make indiscriminate Gospel offers a simulation — therefore reprobation only after foresight of despised grace
english: From the Gospel call they argue thus. If God by an antecedent absolute decree had elected some and reprobated others, he would be acting with simulation when he offers grace indiscriminately through evangelical ministers. For the elect unto salvation cannot be commanded to believe under hope of obtaining salvation — no one awaits under a condition what he knows is absolutely ordained for him. Nor can the reprobate be commanded to believe — God would then require them to believe a falsehood: that Christ suffered and died for them and obtained life and reconciliation for them. Therefore, they say, no one is reprobated except from regard and foresight of despised grace and final persistence in that hardness of heart and unbelief.

title: Cap. IX Sol: reprobation here means fixed decree not to give special efficacious grace — damnation from sin; denial of that grace from mere liberty of will
english: Recall again what we must keep repeating: by reprobation — which we hang from God's mere will, not from foresighted human demerits — we do not mean a peremptory decree to damn or eternally afflict some particular person, but a fixed decree not to impart that special efficacious grace, or calling according to purpose, without which God sees that person will remain in hardness, impenitence, and unbelief — and has decreed to permit that. God is most certain that from such passing-over the man so rejected will die in his sins, and most decided to damn him for those sins in which he will die. Yet it is plain: denial of that grace (where we locate reprobation properly) hangs on mere liberty of divine will, while that person's damnation arises from his own sin.

title: Cap. IX Sol: without simulation God can offer remission and life indiscriminately on condition of faith — reprobation decree is not 'even if Judas believes he will not be saved'
english: With that premise I answer: reprobation decree notwithstanding, God can without any simulation, through evangelical ministers, set before men indiscriminately remission of sins and eternal life on this condition — If they believe in Christ. Nor does he simulate when under that condition he promises salvation to any whatsoever: to whoever fulfills the condition he will faithfully give the promised benefit. If the reprobation decree were cast as Even if Judas believes, he will not obtain remission or eternal life, Gospel preaching to the reprobate would be open illusion. But that decree holds only this: I will not give Judas that special grace by which he would in fact fulfill the proposed condition. To convict God of simulation they must show he promised through evangelical ministers to give that special grace to someone whom he nonetheless rejected from it by antecedent reprobation. If they ever do that — which they never can — we will (God forbid) let them prosecute God as guilty of simulation.

title: Cap. IX Sol: willing to save anyone if he believes is not decreeing to work faith in everyone — Remonstrants confuse the two; conditional will = faith-salvation nexus
english: So let the Remonstrants, who press this everywhere, understand: it is one thing seriously to will to save anyone if he believes, another to decree to work in anyone so that he believes. God can will the first without any simulation, even while for some he has decreed not to will the second in their reprobation. One passing note: when we say God wills to save anyone if he believes, by that conditioned will we mean only God's eternal inviolable ordination of the indissoluble bond of faith and salvation — for which bond the promise If you believe, you will be saved holds true of any elect or non-elect person. God's will is not thereby pictured as hanging uncertain over a non-elect man's salvation; such speech only affirms that if the faith-condition were set in the object, God would also actually will to save that person — enough to shut out the simulation they try to pin on God.

title: Cap. IX vocatione Sol cont.: 'precise/absolute elect cannot be commanded to believe' misreads absolute election as cutting off means
english: They also put it that the precisely or absolutely elect or reprobate cannot be commanded to believe. Take that in their sense of people elected to salvation so precisely that means drop out — as if God had decreed to bring some to salvation even though they reject every means of it, or to damn some even though they believe in Christ. That is not our dogma. It is their dream forced onto ours.

title: Cap. IX vocatione Sol cont.: Peter and Paul absolutely predestined to life and to the whole series of means — will of end absolutely joined to will of means
english: We say Peter, Paul, and the rest are absolutely predestined to eternal life — not that they know that decree absolutely before they believe, or that they gain eternal life with the faith-condition never performed — but that God elects them absolutely and freely not only to eternal life itself but to the whole series of means by which they are brought to it. In execution the end hangs on conditional use of means; yet in God predestining Peter, Paul, or any particular person, the will of the end was not conditioned but absolutely joined to the will of the means — so that by one and the same simplest act by which God willed glory for Peter or Paul he also willed faith and all else from whose conditional use glory is promised. In a word: God did not decree to save Peter without the condition of faith, but decreed to give Peter faith as absolutely and precisely as salvation. That is the common saying: Predestination is preparation of grace now and of glory hereafter.

title: Cap. IX vocatione Sol cont.: reprobates may be commanded to believe and offered salvation if they believe — as non-elect angels were commanded to obey
english: As for the reprobate: eternal antecedent reprobation notwithstanding, they can as truly be commanded to believe as the non-elect or reprobate angels could be commanded to obey God; salvation can as truly be offered them on the condition If they believe as beatitude could be promised those angels on If they had persevered in God's obedience. Peter's predestination does not cancel the truth of If you do not believe, you will not be saved; Judas's reprobation does not weaken If you believe, you will be saved. It only implies that, that indissoluble faith-salvation bond standing, Judas is not to be given the efficacious grace by which he would in fact fulfill the condition.

title: Cap. IX vocatione Sol cont.: reprobates are not required to believe a falsehood — Christ's death applies under the revealed condition of faith, not secret predestination (John 3:15–16)
english: Finally, the objection that on our view the reprobate are required to believe a falsehood — that Christ by his death obtained life and reconciliation for them — is plainly denied. Life and reconciliation through Christ's death are not applied to particulars under the secret condition If they were predestined, but under the revealed condition if they are believers; nor is application denied to any hearer except under if he is an unbeliever — as John 3:15–16 openly shows. Here the secret election/reprobation decree shows itself: Christ's death, which by God's ordination would avail any man who believed for reconciliation and life, yet profits only the elect, to whom alone from special mercy is given that grace by which they can and will efficaciously, and in fact, fulfill that condition.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 open: absolute reprobation not from foresight of final impenitence is said to cast perdition's cause on defect of grace — Corvinus
english: Those who set absolute reprobation not sprung from foresight of final impenitence cast perdition's cause not on the reprobates' own malice but on a defect of divine grace. That, they say, is too unworthy of God, who is always ready to add further grace if a man uses well what he has received. So not from reprobation but from a man's voluntary neglect it comes that he lacks grace or does not receive more — namely that he has made himself unworthy of eternal life (Acts 13:46), held the truth in unrighteousness (Rom. 1:18), and not received the love of the truth (2 Thess. 2:10–11).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol open: reprobation does not make God or defect of grace the true cause of human perdition — the sinner with his sins is the true and sole cause
english: We deny that the reprobation we teach makes God himself — or a defect of divine grace — the cause of human perdition, unless 'cause' is used improperly and abusively. The true cause of perdition or damnation is what justly deserves damnation, or the one who works what damnation is due. So the sinner himself with his sins is to himself the true and sole cause of his perdition. Being reprobated, or passed by from preparation of special grace and mercy, neither deserves nor works perdition. What we teach does not cast damnation's cause on a defect of divine grace; it casts the denial of efficacious special grace on the liberty of divine will. God's will is the determining cause that some are not drawn out of perdition by efficacious unfrustrable grace while others are; the reprobates' own malice is the operative meritorious cause why they perish and are damned.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: equivocation on 'cause' — true/direct vs abusive/indirect; sun illuminates truly, its setting is only abusively cause of darkness
english: Equivocation on the word cause has trapped our adversaries — or at least given them occasion to trap others. Something is called cause of an event or effect in two ways: truly, directly, and properly, as what flows in to produce the effect; abusively, indirectly, improperly, as what does not act to block the effect. So the sun at rising is truly and properly called cause why the air is lit; at setting it is only improperly and abusively called cause why it darkens — merely because its presence would have put darkness to flight.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: special grace's gift is productive cause of salvation — its denial is not truly cause of perdition; Aristotle Metaph. 4.2
english: Much the same way: because the gift of special grace is the productive cause of human salvation, some are led to think its denial or defect is the cause of human perdition — as if by its presence it would have blocked that perdition. But the Philosopher speaks more carefully (Metaph. 4.2): what, when present, is cause of something, we sometimes say, when absent, is cause of the contrary. Note his words: sometimes and we say. He does not say absence itself is cause of the contrary, but that we allege or put it forward as a cause — and only sometimes. So the influx of special grace, denied by divine decree to some, can be held up by the unskilled as cause of their sin and perdition, because if given it would have saved them. That is false unless it can be proved either that God was bound to give such grace, or that the wicked's sins and perdition did not flow from their innate corruption and voluntary rebellion as true positive causes.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: 'God always ready to add further grace if well used' does not break the defense — election is absolute gift; reprobation denies efficacious grace de facto, not hypothetical gift
english: Further: the claim that God is always ready to add further grace to anyone who uses well what he has received — and therefore reprobated no one except from prior regard to despised grace, that is final impenitence and unbelief — has no force to break our defense. First: as election does not posit a hypothetical gift of grace but an absolute infallible one, so reprobation does not deny a hypothetical gift (if someone should do this or that), but denies efficacious grace actually to be given. It does not follow: If Judas had done this or that, he would have obtained further grace; therefore he was not by the reprobation decree absolutely rejected from special grace.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: contempt of given grace may explain withdrawal — not why special mercy that always removes contempt was never prepared; urging the non-reprobate until regeneration
english: Second: contempt of whatever grace is given can rightly be named as cause why that grace is withdrawn, or why richer grace is not administered — and the cited Scriptures prove that. But it can only be alleged ineptly as cause or reason why that special mercy, and efficacious calling according to purpose which always removes contempt of grace, was never prepared and given to this or that person. To seize on that as the ground for denying further grace is itself a clear mark of non-election or antecedent reprobation. Those God has not reprobated — though they set many obstacles and by manifold negligence and resistance deserve grace to be taken away — he still from undue special mercy urges again and again, and does not stop until he has regenerated them and brought them under his grace.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: Corvinus's rule 'to him who does all he can by received grace, further grace is always given' does not shake absolute reprobation — no mortal ever does all he can
english: Third: the rule To him who uses grace well (that is, as Corvinus expounds, p. 157, to him who does whatever he can by the grace conferred on him) further grace shall always be given does not shake the absolute decree of reprobation. Who among mortals has ever done, or will ever do, whatever he can by the grace given him? The angels did not; the first parents did not; none of the elect after receiving regenerating grace does it — still less any of the non-regenerate, armed only with exciting grace, which Corvinus distinguishes from the living spark of nature.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: Thomas — free will disordered toward evil cannot offer no impediment to grace; God sometimes converts even those who impede; the difference hangs on simple will
english: Thomas reasons far better here. He teaches that free will, already disordered toward evil, is not so set that it offers no impediment to divine grace (Contra Gent. 3.160). Then (cap. 161) he adds that God nonetheless sometimes, from abundance of his goodness, turns even those who impede grace away from evil and converts them to good — and that this happens only in those in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in all others the order of justice is shown. Why he converts these who put an obstacle and not others is not to be sought; it hangs on his simple will.
