So Corvinus vainly attacks reprobation from God's readiness to give richer grace to all who use received grace so as to do whatever they can by it — since no one does that, and since not finally opposing an obstacle to divine grace itself flows from election and does not precede election.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7: if reprobation is antecedent and not from foresight of future impenitence, then the impenitence for which reprobates are damned flows from the reprobation decree — unjust
english: If reprobation is set as antecedent and not from foresight of future impenitence and unbelief, it will follow that the impenitence and unbelief for which the reprobate are damned flow from the reprobation decree. But it is unjust to damn anyone for what follows from antecedent reprobation — a pure mere act of God. At the Hague Colloquy the Remonstrants press this: if we place reprobation otherwise than from foresighted unbelief, the corollary is that we must own unbelief itself as fruit of that reprobation. Hence their argument: if unbelief follows from reprobation unto destruction, God cannot, his justice safe, destroy the reprobate for their unbelief, because that necessarily follows from reprobation — which is God's own work. Therefore, they say, we must place reprobation as sprung from foresight of final unbelief.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol: God foresaw reprobates would be impenitent — but that foresight is not antecedent moving cause of reprobation; unbelief sprouts from the reprobate's perverse heart
english: First I premise: we do not deny that God, reprobating from eternity, foresaw that all the reprobate would be impenitent and unbelieving. We deny that that foresighted unbelief was taken by God as antecedent moving cause of reprobation itself. Nor do we grant that this unbelief sprouts from the reprobating decree as fruit or effect of reprobation: it sprouts as bad fruit from the reprobate's bad perverse heart. When they object — If unbelief follows from reprobation, men are unjustly damned for that unbelief following from the divine reprobation decree — if they mean sequel of order or time, we deny the consequence; if sequel of causality, we deny that unbelief follows from reprobation as effect from cause.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol: God elects some to be faithful and makes them so — he did not reprobate men that they might be unbelievers; Lombard Sent. 1 dist. 40–41
english: Though God elects some that they may be faithful, and by electing grace makes them faithful, he is not to be said to have reprobated men that they might be unbelievers, or by reprobating to have made them so. That is the common sentence of theologians, which the Master of the Sentences sets (lib. 1 dist. 40 lit. D): For not as he prepared the saints to receive righteousness did he prepare the wicked to lose it — he was never a preparer of wickedness. And still plainer (dist. 41 lit. E): it is asked whether, as he is said to have elected some that they might become good and faithful, we ought also grant he reprobated some that they might be evil and unbelieving, and hardens that they may sin — which must in no wise be granted. Reprobation is not cause of evil as predestination is cause of good; nor does hardening make a man evil as mercy makes him good.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol: why all reprobates become unbelieving — Augustine Ad Simpl.: nothing worse infused; only what would make better is not given; Prosper
english: But how is it that all the reprobate always turn out unbelieving and impenitent, if that unbelief and impenitence are not fruits or effects of antecedent reprobation? I answer with Augustine (Ad Simpl. 1.2): not that God by reprobating inflicts anything by which a man is made worse, but only that what would make him better is not bestowed. So it does not follow that those to whom God has not given penitence he has robbed of repentance, or that those he has not lifted he has dashed down — as Prosper well says (Ad Object. Vinc. Resp. 15). And elsewhere to the same effect (Ad cap. Gallor. resp. 14): the unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated from God's predestination; all the non-predestined perish by voluntary, not forced, unbelief (Sentent. super 14).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol: Adam's rebellion, impenitence, and unbelief are born in-house — no need to fetch such effects from divine reprobation
english: For in all Adam's children rebellion, impenitence, and unbelief are born in-house — so there is little need to fetch such effects from divine reprobation. All these, even amid many remedies and helps of divine grace, still break out from a vitiated heart unless healed and set firm in good by the benefit of special mercy flowing from the election decree. The head of error in their argument is this assumption: that God, when he reprobates, procures in the very same way the media that later lead the reprobate to eternal death as he procures the media that lead the elect to eternal life. And since it is plain that God predestinating by a proper special operation works in the predestined faith, holiness, perseverance, and all else by which as means life is reached, they think it follows that if God has antecedently reprobated some, in them he works unbelief, impenitence, and all else by which as means they later rush to death. But the matter stands far otherwise.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol: to reprobate is to permit by denying special grace — not to pour spiritual malice; media to death are deficient evils from us, not from God
english: To reprobate is, by denying special grace, to permit some to fall short of beatitude's end — not by pouring spiritual malice in to drive them by force into the abyss of misery. Add this: the media by which the predestined are led to life are supernatural goods, and so to be sought only from the Fountain of good — it belongs to God predestinating to provide efficacious media by whose intervention the predestined are saved. But the media by which the reprobate rush to death are spiritual evils — deficient, depraved acts — and so are sought not from the highest Good, nor from God as efficient, but from our implanted evil and a deficient cause. It is therefore inept and impious, because of an antecedent reprobation decree, to think God must produce in the reprobate unbelief, impenitence, and the like by which they are damned. Finally: unbelief, impenitence, and whatever counts as sin can be called media by which the reprobate himself procures his own death. But respecting the Reprobating One they are not media God effects and applies unto the reprobate's damnation — rather matter the reprobate brings forth from himself, God foreseeing and about that matter exercising his vindicative justice.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol close: theft/homicide do not precede hanging as means procured by the judge — so reprobates' sins precede damnation as presupposed matter (Cajetan)
english: Just as theft or homicide does not precede the hanging of thief or murderer as a means the judge procured and applied for that end — only as something presupposed — so the reprobates' sins precede their damnation. God can therefore most justly damn all unbelievers and impenitents: though unbelief follows reprobation, it lies outside the whole effect of reprobation and is born from the reprobate's heart. God does not work, effect, or draw it forth; he foresees, permits, and by special-mercy grace does not impede it — for he is not bound so to impede it. See Cajetan on ST 1 q.23 a.5.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8: absolute reprobation not from foresight of actual sins makes God deal more rigidly with some men than with the very devils
english: Those who hold that God by mere will — not from foresight of actual sins and final perseverance in them — has reprobated some, thereby hold that God deals far more rigidly with certain men than with the very devils. For the devils are shut out of life for sins they committed by their own malice; yet some reprobated men are set not for sins done in their own persons, but only as guilty by divine imputation of Adam's alien sin.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8: Borrius and Arminius — no one damned for original sin alone; Remonstrants at Dort: infants incapable of disobedience not punished with eternal pain
english: A certain Borrius tried by this argument to prove that no one is condemned for original sin, and so that all Gentile infants dying before actual sins are saved — as may be seen in Arminius, Respons. to arts. 13–14. That Arminius himself held this, and that Arminians still defend it, is clear. Corvinus, of Arminius's inner counsel, writes (p. 391): Indeed Arminius holds that no one is damned for original sin alone. And the Remonstrants cited to the Synod of Dort, in a writing shown publicly by common consent of them all, said openly: No infants — inasmuch as they are not capable of new disobedience and rebellion — are punished with eternal pain.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol first: from Arminian concessions — if all are made guilty of eternal death by Adam's imputed act alone, God deals more rigidly with men than with demons
english: First I answer: from Arminian concessions we can weave a like argument, which they themselves will doubtless call of no moment. Note this: though they constantly deny anyone is damned for innate original sin, they are forced the other way — they grant that guilt of death has been derived even to all infants from imputation of that actual sin Adam committed. Grant only that, and we may argue: those who hold God puts all men, infants and adults, under strict right as guilty of eternal death merely because a sin not done in each one's own person but by Adam is imputed to them, make God deal more rigidly with men than with demons. No demon is counted guilty except for sin done in his own person from his own malice; yet on Arminius's view men are made guilty of eternal death only as guilty by divine imputation of Adam's alien sin. Whatever reply they give us, we will turn the same back on them.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol second: comparing rigor in reprobating men vs demons is inept — reprobation is denial of an undue benefit, not an act decreeing punishment
english: But as the saying goes, to counter-argue is not to solve — so second: when the question is whether greater rigor of justice is used in reprobating men or demons, the comparison is wholly inept if rigid justice is exercised in reprobating neither. Reprobation is denial of an undue benefit — namely of infallible ordination to eternal life through preparation and gift of special grace. So neither men's nor angels' reprobation was an act of rigid justice — not even of justice properly and formally so called — though it was not against justice (as no divine act is), and in that sense may be called most just. Inept, then, to weigh degrees of rigid justice in reprobation: mere reprobation, of men or demons, is not an act decreeing punishment (where rigor could be considered) but an act denying a benefit, where only God's liberty is to be regarded.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol third: foundation rotten — blessed angels elected, damned angels passed over, not from foresight of merits/rebellion but from mere liberty of will
english: Third: the very foundation this whole argument leans on is rotten. It seems to take as granted that the Devils were reprobated from foresight of their actual sins. We say the contrary: the blessed angels were elected before the world's foundations were laid — not from foresighted merits but from the electing One's pure grace; and the damned angels were likewise from eternity passed by, non-elect, or reprobated — not from foresight of future rebellion and final hardening in it, but from God's mere will or liberty not willing to give them that grace. So if Arminians from the Devils' reprobation want to prove men were reprobated only from antecedent foresight of actual sins, they ought first to confirm that by solid argument for the demons' reprobation before drawing consequences about men's.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol cont.: they wrongly slide from reprobation to damnation — two things hanging on diverse causes
english: Lastly: in this argument they wrongly slide from reprobation to damnation itself, and try to mix and confuse the two — which we have already shown hang on diverse causes. Nor do we grant that, on the hypothesis always approved by the Catholic Church's judgment — that some are damned for original sin alone — it follows God deals more rigidly with such than with the very demons. A judge is not said to deal more rigidly with a lesser offender than with the worst traitor merely because he condemns both, unless he afflicts the one held by the lesser crime with equal or greater punishment.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol cont.: Augustine — infants go into the mildest of all damnation, demons into the bitterest; degrees in eternal damnation unknown
english: However God damns infants stained and bound by original sin alone, and also damns demons guilty of actual wicked rebellion, there is a huge difference in the mode and degree of the punishment inflicted. Infants (as Augustine well says, De peccat. mer. et remiss. 1.16) go into the mildest of all damnation; demons into damnation far the bitterest. No edge of human wit can tell how many degrees of pains there may be in the same eternal damnation. So this argument does not follow: Infants are damned for original sin, and Devils only for actual sin; therefore infants are treated more rigidly.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9: if creation of each is continuation of first creation, absolute reprobation not from foresight of final unbelief fights creation diametrically — creation would become a medium subordinated to damnation
english: If creation means that making of particulars by which each receives his being from God — a kind of continuation of the first creation — then those who set reprobation as not made from foresight of final unbelief make it fight creation head-on. Creation by nature is a communication of good according to God's natural goodness. But if it is cast so as to have this intention — that it be a path by which reprobation already made reaches its end — it is no longer a communication of good, but a medium subordinated to damnation. And that is the medium set by those who hang predestination and reprobation on God's mere will, not on foresight of faith and unbelief.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9 Sol: eternal non-election no more fights temporal creation than angelic passing-over fought angelic creation — greater difficulty with angels, seen intact
english: We deny the Major's consequence. God's eternal decree concerning certain men not to be elected, or to be reprobated, can no more fight their temporal creation than the passing-by or non-election of some angels — set from eternity by mere liberty of divine will — fought angelic creation. Indeed the difficulty seems greater with angels than with men. Men from eternity elect or passed by were shown to the divine mind as vitiated in a corrupt mass and reprobable; but God looked on the angels intact in the same perfection in which he later made them. So if eternal reprobation of certain angels sprung from divine good pleasure, not from foresight of sin, and in no way fought their creation, no fight can rightly be conceived between reprobation and creation of men, who are set before God reprobating as contaminated and slain by Adam's sin.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9 Sol: Suarez and Vasquez — angels elect/non-elect with no mass of perdition; demons reprobated before any foresighted sin
english: On the angels we have the Jesuits themselves with us. Suarez (Opusc. De concursu Dei 2.5): In the angels there was no mass of perdition or infected nature, and yet God elected some, did not elect others, destined some to honor, and left others to become vessels of contumely. Of men, the same Suarez says, it is to be held the same way: if the talk is of non-election, which some call negative reprobation, it is true that its cause is God's will alone, with no cause awaited from man's side. Even Vasquez, who favors us less in this controversy, frankly grants that the demons were reprobated and permitted to fall before any foresighted sin — which reprobation he calls reprobation from grace, a decree of not pitying, etc. (In 1. Aquin. disp. 45.3 and 5).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9 Sol: creation of Judas is not a medium subordinated to his damnation — Augustine and Prosper; to create a reprobate ≠ to create that he may be damned
english: The Jesuits could see how the creation of particular angels in time did not fight the reprobation of some, set from eternity by God's will alone — and they could conceive the same of men. Let Corvinus bend his wit's edge, and he will easily see it. But he thinks he can shore up the consequence thus: Creation by nature is a communication of good; yet if such reprobation as we place preceded, it will be a path by which reprobation already made reaches its end — a medium of the non-elect man subordinated to damnation — and so will not be a communication of good, since good is to be judged from the giver's mind and the end for which it is given. That is weakly argued. First: creation of particular men follows both their election and their reprobation. As Peter's creation would improperly be called a medium subordinated to his election, so Judas's creation is improperly and falsely called a medium subordinated to his reprobation or damnation. If any dare hold that men's creation is a medium subordinated to their damnation, I dissent and embrace Augustine and Prosper, who everywhere oppose that.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9 Sol close: creating Judas the reprobate is not creating him that he may be damned — as feeding a thief sentenced to die is not feeding him that he may die
english: God is rightly said to act for some intended end when he gives things a nature ordered to that end. But in creating Judas God did not give him a nature ordained to damnation. So it is false to hold that the creation of Judas the reprobate has this intention — that it be a medium advanced toward damnation. It is one thing to create a man reprobate and to be damned for his demerits; another to create him that he may be damned — as it is one thing to feed, clothe, and comfort a thief sentenced to die, another to do those things that he may die.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9 Sol close: God creates in time those not predestined to beatitude — creation's proper end is communication of good, not damnation as intended scope
english: So God creates in time those he from eternity did not predestine to beatitude — whom he foresaw would by their own fault rush to voluntary ruin, whom he decreed to permit to fall into this everlasting misery. Yet men's creation (which in the order of decreeing preceded all that) had its own proper end: God's glory in the diffusion and communication of good — not their damnation, which is to be held an event following the creation of the reprobate, not a scope intended by God as creator.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 9 Sol close: Scripture sounding as if God created some unto contumely is to be read permissively — vessels of contumely by not adding special grace
english: And last: wherever Scripture seems to speak as though God had fashioned some for disgrace and ruin, I judge those places to be taken permissively. Day by day he brings into being those whom, under the decree of non-election or of reprobation, he suffers to turn into vessels of contumely — withholding the special grace that would have made them vessels of honor.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10: if election and reprobation hang on mere liberty of will, Gospel preaching to the reprobate becomes from God's precise intention a ministry of condemnation
english: If we set election and reprobation as hanging on mere liberty of divine will — not on the differing acts of elect and reprobate themselves (these' penitence, those' impenitence; these' persevering faith, those' final unbelief) — then Gospel preaching toward the reprobate, from God's nearest precise intention, will be a ministry of condemnation, and will not be set before them from God's first intention to work their salvation, but as a medium subordinated to damnation in executing the reprobation decree. That fights the Gospel ministry head-on, since from God's first intention it is a ministry of life.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol: Major's consequence invalid — not everything later done about the non-elect flows from absolute reprobation; Vasquez: some effects are of common providence
english: We answer that the Major's consequence is invalid. The adversaries err in this: having posited absolute reprobation, they take it as following that whatever is later done about these non-elect or reprobate flows from that decree. Vasquez rightly notes the contrary: neither in the predestined nor in the reprobate is every effect of God's providence an effect of predestination or reprobation — some is an effect of common providence (In 1 q.23 a.4 c.4 disp. 93).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol: God knows Gospel benefits will harm reprobates and decreed not to add softening grace — yet preaching is not from primary intention a medium of damnation
english: We grant God knows Gospel preaching and his other benefits will be harmful to these reprobates. We grant further that no reprobate's will is so wild and intractable that God cannot soften it to faith and penitence — that is, to the effect of obeying. We grant finally that God has decreed with himself not to apply to these reprobates that special efficacious grace by which they would be softened. All that granted, we still deny that Gospel preaching, or that gift of scantier commoner grace, is proposed from a primary nearest intention of damning, or ought to be judged media subordinated to damnation. From foresight, or God's permission, or a following event, we may not infer that God's primary intention, and the subordination of media, aimed at producing that event.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: angel gifts — God foresaw abuse unto pride and rebellion, yet gifts not subordinated to ruin but to obedience and beatitude
english: Take the angels: God foresaw that some, endowed with excellent gifts, would abuse those gifts in pride and rebellion; he decreed to permit that, and for that rebellion to torment them with everlasting punishments. Yet no one would say those gifts were, by God's primary and proper intention, subordinated to their ruin and damnation — rather to their obedience and beatitude.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: God's intention through means is judged from the nature of the means, not from the evil event he foresaw and would not hinder — same of Gospel gifts to reprobates
english: For — as we warned before — God's intention through means is always judged from the nature of those means, not from the evil event he foresaw and would not hinder. Judge Gospel preaching and the other gifts of divine grace granted to the reprobate the same way.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: Remonstrants themselves place preaching under common providence — we grant that, adding special mercy for the elect and permission of contrary effect for the rest
english: The Remonstrants themselves, when it suits them, take Gospel preaching not to flow from some absolute decree to save or damn every hearer, but from a more common providence — what they call Christ's wise, merciful, and just government (Collat. Hagiens. p. 95). Let them then let us subscribe that view, with this added: preaching flows from the predestination decree for those in whom God decreed of special mercy to work penitence, faith, and salvation infallibly through that instrument; and it flows from a more common providence for those in whom he decreed to permit that by their fault it should take a plainly contrary effect — yet we never grant that for these latter it flows from the reprobation decree, or is subordinated as a medium to their damnation by God's primary intention.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: Scripture — Gospel an odor of death from hearers' voluntary rebellion, not from God's primary intention (2 Cor. ii; Heb. ii; Acts xiii; Col. i)
english: Scripture itself settles Gospel preaching far differently: to some it becomes an odor of death unto death (2 Cor. ii. 15–16) — not from God's primary intention, but from their voluntary rebellion (Heb. ii. 3: How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?). Acts xiii. 38: Remission of sins through Christ is announced to you — and 46: After you put it from you and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life. Col. i. 28: We announce Christ, admonishing and teaching every one, that we may present every one perfect in Christ Jesus.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: Gospel not administered from a precise intention of damning anyone — damnation's desert arises from neglect and contempt God foresaw and would not hinder in the reprobate
english: So God does not administer the Gospel to anyone from a nearest precise intention of damning him. When neglect and contempt intervene, desert of damnation arises in the despiser — which God foresaw and was unwilling to hinder in all the reprobate.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: two senses of 'intend' — providence disposing apt means (Adam), and predestination supplying means that secure the end (elect); Arminian third sense of intending evil by the Gospel rejected
english: Finally, to show more clearly the flaw in the denied consequence, add this: we say God 'intends' something in two ways. First, when by providence he disposes apt means toward producing some end — in that sense we say he willed and intended that Adam stand and persevere in obedience to the divine command, because he granted him apt means for standing and persevering. Second, more specially, when by the predestination decree he supplies means by which he knew and decreed the end itself would be obtained — in that sense we say he intended and willed the faith, perseverance, and salvation of all the elect. The third mode the Arminians invent — that God by primary intention wills that evil through Gospel preaching or any benefit granted to men, which will arise from that benefit through the reprobates' malice that God will not hinder — that mode is plainly unheard-of and to be exploded.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 10 Sol cont.: means of salvation offered to reprobates are neither effects of predestination nor media of reprobation — they flow from philanthropy and more general providence; Thomas and Vasquez on the distinction
english: So the means of salvation offered to the reprobate are not effects of predestination — else they would reach the end. Nor do they flow from the reprobation decree as media God subordinated to procuring their damnation — for it is not God's part to furnish means that lead reprobates to everlasting death; those sprout abundantly from themselves if he does not oppose special grace. They flow instead from that philanthropy and more general providence which so disposes means toward an end that it meanwhile permits the second cause, by its own fault, to fall short of attaining it. Thomas well explains this distinction between Predestination and Providence (Quaest. Disp. De praed. art. 1); Vasquez acknowledges the same (In 1 q.22 disp. 87 c.4, at the chapter's end).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 (Corvinus): absolute predestination/reprobation makes baptism of many infants, by God's first intention, useless and sealing nothing — without the infants' fault
english: Those who set predestination and reprobation as hanging absolutely on God's freest will — not on foreseen faith and unbelief of the predestined and reprobate — make baptism administered to many infants useless by God's first intention, and sealing nothing, and that without fault in the infants who receive it. For if we set many infants of the faithful as precisely reprobated, it is most certain that baptism seals nothing for them.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 Sol: absolute predestination/reprobation defined — decree to lead some by special grace to glory, deny that preparing mercy to others, and punish for final guilt of sin
english: The absolute predestination and reprobation we affirm depends on God's freest will. It means nothing other than his eternal decree. By that decree, of mere good pleasure and supreme mercy, he established to lead some infallibly to glory through the means of special grace. To others, of mere liberty of will, he denies that supreme mercy which prepares special grace. That denial presupposed, God sees them finally bound by sin's guilt, and decrees them punished for that guilt.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 Sol: why baptism more useless on our view than theirs? — they also grant eternal damnation of reprobates, church-born baptism by command, and reprobation before birth
english: That premised, I ask why baptism of many infants is called useless and sealing nothing on our view rather than on theirs. Because God from all eternity decreed to damn the reprobate? They dare not deny that. Because reprobation by decree and baptism by command clash? They too grant that all born in the Church must be baptized by God's command, and that many of them were nonetheless reprobated by his eternal decree before they were born. Or because they teach damnation fixed in God's eternal, certain, infallible knowledge, whereby as before his eyes he saw a man bound by sin's guilt? We profess the same.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 Sol: remaining charge — special grace prepared for some only makes baptism useless for the rest; we deny the consequence
english: So only this remains: because we say special grace that in fact leads to glory is prepared and given to some of God's mere good pleasure, and to others neither prepared nor given, we are judged to make baptism altogether useless for these latter. We deny that consequence.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 Sol: baptism seals as Arminians allow — original-sin remission for every infant; actual-sin remission and regeneration for believers when adult
english: And we can say no less than the Arminians themselves. Baptism seals to every infant the remission of original sin, by which alone infant age is held. It also seals remission of actual sins prepared in Christ's blood for those who repent and believe when they come to adulthood and fall into actual sins. It seals, further, regeneration and renewal wrought from the incorruptible seed of word and Spirit in all believers, once they live to an age capable of the divine word.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 Sol: Augustine, Prosper, Council of Valence on original-sin remission; baptism seals new-covenant remission of actual sins for the whole course of life (1 John i. 9)
english: On remission of original sin Augustine agrees everywhere (De pecc. mer. et remiss. 1.28 and 2.4). Prosper also, ad Cap. Gall. Resp. 2, embraces the same view. Finally the Council of Valence, cap. 5, proposes this as to be held most firmly. Likewise for remission of actual sins under the new covenant's condition: that is sealed most firmly to every baptized person — not only at the moment of receiving baptism, but for the rest of life's course. Whoever is baptized into the name of Jesus Christ, if he sins after baptism, has in that same Christ's blood, through faith, expiation of his sins prepared (1 John i. 9).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 11 Sol: Augustine on sacrament preceding heart-conversion; Fulgentius — baptism suffices for infants while reason is incapable; Aquinas — Christ's passion applied by the sacrament
english: Finally, on adults' actual renewal or regeneration — when by the power of divine word and Spirit one is converted and by believing justified — Augustine writes: In baptized infants the sacrament of regeneration precedes, and if they hold Christian piety, conversion of heart also follows, whose mystery preceded in the body (lib. 4 Contra Donatist. cap. 24). So of all baptized infants we assert with Fulgentius: The sacrament of faith, which is holy baptism, while infants' age cannot be capable of reason, suffices them for salvation (De fid. ad Petrum Diac. cap. 30). Nor do we scorn Aquinas on this: Infants who have nothing whereby they can turn themselves to the justifying cause have that cause itself — Christ's passion — applied to them through the sacrament of baptism (Quaest. disp. de Justific. art. 3).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 (Corvinus): absolute reprobation blocks public prayers offered with due faith that the Word will profit all hearers
english: They do not rightly explain reprobation who set such a reprobation as would block public prayers from being offered to God with due faith and confidence that the Word will profit all who hear it. Who can bring himself to pray for the salvation of those God by an eternal antecedent will has willed to damn? The Apostle sharpens us to pray for all with this argument: God wills all to be saved.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: right prayer for others does not require certain faith that our prayers will save them — outcomes are contingent; command to pray for all (even enemies) suffices
english: To form prayers rightly for other people, we need not be persuaded by certainty of faith that our prayers will profit them unto salvation. Nothing false or contingent can underlie our faith; yet whether they will gain any profit from our prayers is plainly contingent and uncertain. It is enough that God has commanded us to embrace all men in charity, and to pray for others — even for enemies.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: schoolmen — four conditions for certainty of obtaining; praying for another does not always obtain; Major fails that requires certain faith prayers will profit others
english: This is common knowledge in the School of Theologians. They say four conditions are required for a prayer to have certainty of obtaining; one is that one pray for oneself. For though the prayer be pious, persevering, and about things that belong to salvation, yet if it is made for another it does not always obtain. So the Major totters: it falsely assumes prayers cannot rightly be made for others unless certain faith is present that they will profit them. Nor is our doctrine of reprobation refuted by saying that, once posited, public prayers cannot be offered to God with faith that they would profit all who hear the Word.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: Minor denied — due confidence is that praying for others pleases God and we obtain as far as he sees fit; stands with our doctrine and with Arminian
english: But let us take the Minor: they say the reprobation we posit blocks prayers from being offered to God with due confidence. We deny that. Due confidence needs only this: we are certain the duty of praying for others pleases God, and that we shall obtain for them insofar as God sees fit and as agrees with divine glory. That confidence stands as well with our doctrine as with the Arminian. For they dare not deny that the reprobation decree is eternal and irrevocable, though they say it rests on eternal foresight of human unbelief. So it is certain: Judas reprobated from eternity can by no others' prayers be led to salvation — even on the reprobation Arminius maintains.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: their conditional limitations (if they believe, if pertinacity does not hinder) we affirm too — church prayers profit all hearers under those conditions
english: But here they fall back on those conditional limitations — by which they themselves most plainly enervate their argument. When they say they require not absolute but conditional confidence — namely that we believe our prayers will profit any others if they believe, if their own pertinacity does not hinder them, in a word unless they make themselves unworthy of divine grace — we can affirm the same in so many words. For notwithstanding the reprobation decree, we certainly believe the Church's prayers will profit all and each who hear God's word, if they believe, if their own pertinacity does not hinder them, and they do not make themselves unworthy of divine grace.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: we add what they hide — God wills hearers saved if they believe, yet wills not to soften all so they believe; pray for all, treat none as reprobate
english: But we add what they by obstinate silence wish to hide. God wills to save all who hear the Gospel if they believe and their own pertinacity does not hinder them. Yet he does not will to have mercy on all so far that they are softened, believe, and cease to hinder themselves — but on the elect only. He wills to permit that others by their own fault be hardened and remain in voluntary pertinacity. Because it is unknown to us of whom he wills to have mercy, and whom he wills to leave to their own hardness, it is ours to pray for all that they be converted, and to treat no one in particular as reprobate.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: who prays for one God precisely wills not to save? — secret of election/reprobation unknown; absolute reprobation is not 'damn Judas whether he believe or not'
english: But they still urge: Who can bring himself to pray for the salvation of one whom God precisely wills not to save, when the Apostle sharpens us to pray for all because God wills all to be saved? I answer first: God does not usually lay open to men this secret of election and reprobation; so our actions neither ought nor can be conformed to an unknown rule. Second: in the decree of absolute or precise reprobation, as they speak, God has not settled with himself, I will damn Judas whether he believe or not — but, I will not so have mercy on Judas that he be softened, believe, and in fact be converted and saved. Just so in absolute predestination God does not say, I will save Peter whether he believe or not — but, I will so have mercy on Peter that he believe, repent, and be saved. If by precise absolute predestination and reprobation they think we mean some cutting of means from the end, they fight their own chimera, not our view.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 12 Sol: 'God wills all to be saved' does not overturn reprobation — election is 'I will make him saved,' not merely 'I will him to be saved'; conditional will to save stands with absolute reprobation
english: Further: they think the Apostolic saying 'God wills all to be saved' fights the reprobation decree we posit. They are much deceived. Without entering the long word-debate we already treated at this disputation's start — that saying does not deny or overturn the reprobation of many we place. Election does not sit in 'I will this one to be saved,' but in 'I will to make this one saved.' So non-election or reprobation does not sit in 'I will not this one to be saved,' but in 'I will not to make this one saved.' Admit Arminius's exposition: God wills all to be saved — namely, wills to save them under this condition, if they believe and persevere. That conditional will to save can stand with an absolute decree to reprobate. It does not denote a divine-will act terminated on saving some singular person, but a decree of the universal perpetual nexus of two things: faith and salvation. So we may rightly gather: if persevering faith were found in any singular person, God would also will to save that person. We may not rightly infer that in the decree preparing efficacious grace and infallibly ordaining to life, no one was antecedently passed over by God. In a word: as there is no fight between 'God predestined Paul to everlasting life' and 'God would damn Paul if he did not believe and persevere,' so neither between 'God did not predestine — or passed over and rejected — Judas' and 'God would save Judas if he believed and persevered.' To will to save under a condition neither proves election nor denies reprobation.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 (Corvinus): reprobation from mere liberty of will makes ministers sluggish — diligence profits only the absolutely elect; negligence harms only those absolutely to perish
english: Our doctrine, says Corvinus, of reprobating some from mere liberty of divine will — not from foresight of final demerits in the reprobate themselves — makes God's ministers sluggish in their work. From it, he says, it follows that their diligence can profit only those God absolutely wills to save, who cannot perish; and that their negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, who cannot be saved. Admit that dogma, and ministers of the word must turn idle and torpid.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: even if some ministers grew sluggish, the doctrine is not thereby false — abuse of Paul's teaching and of divine foresight (Augustine's monk) does not silence truth
english: I answer: even if some ministers grew sluggish from it, that does not make the doctrine itself false or evil. From Paul's teaching some took occasion for license, saying, Let us do evil that good may come. From the doctrine of divine foresight, Augustine tells of a monk who, when the brethren corrected him for doing what he should not and leaving undone what he should, answered again and again: Whatever I am now, I shall one day be what God foresaw I would be. That monk spoke truth — and used that truth not for good but for evil. For such little objections, then, what is truly said of predestination and reprobation is neither to be denied nor kept silent.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: Arminius's reprobation makes ministers as sluggish — eternal foresight still fixes an immovable decree before the foundation of the world
english: Further: Arminius's view of reprobation makes ministers as sluggish as ours. However he sets predestination from foreseen faith and reprobation from foresight of unbelief, he still confesses that divine foresight eternal — and with it intervening, he acknowledges an eternal, fixed, immovable decree of election or reprobation for each person, set before the world's foundations were laid. So a minister cannot hope by diligence to lead to everlasting life someone thus reprobated from eternity, unless he also believes he can make divine foresight err and revoke God's eternal decree. Whether reprobation is set from mere liberty of divine will before all extrinsic causes, or from foresight of unbelief after consideration, it is the same: no hearer but is from eternity predestined to this side or that, from which he will never be transferred to the other.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: unknown elect/non-elect — Augustine: affection of charity must will all saved; rebuke all lest they perish (De corrept. et grat.)
english: But that ought not to hinder or slow ministers' labor. As Augustine says piously and wisely (De corrept. et grat. cap. 15–16): not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, they ought to be so moved by charity that they will all to be saved. So far as concerns us, who cannot tell the predestined from the non-predestined, rebuke is to be applied to all, lest they perish or destroy others.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: grant diligence profits only those God absolutely wills to save — still no sluggishness: honor of co-working for the elect (1 Cor. iii. 9; 2 Tim. ii. 10); woe if not preach (1 Cor. ix. 16)
english: But come nearer still. Grant that ministers' diligence can profit only those God absolutely wills to save, who cannot perish — still neither sluggishness nor sloth is allowed. First: to profit by one's ministry those God has loved exceedingly, and whom before the world's foundations he decreed absolutely to save, is greatly honorable and desirable. Who, with any drop of piety, if he knew for certain some infant was predestined by God, would not labor the more earnestly to be counted God's fellow-worker in promoting that one's salvation (1 Cor. iii. 9)? So Paul was animated, who says all things are to be endured for the elect's sake (2 Tim. ii. 10). Further: even this can shake torpor from ministers — though God will not suffer any of the elect to perish, yet by neglecting their office they themselves incur damnable guilt, per the Apostle: Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel (1 Cor. ix. 16).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: sloth cannot un-predestinate the elect, yet can harm them many ways — effects/benefits of predestination are to be advanced by ministers' diligence (Thomas)
english: Finally: no one is so impious, or so unskilled in theology, as to think ministers' sloth can make any of the predestined non-predestined, or make them fall from the glory prepared for them. Yet no one is so foolish as not to see that ministers' sloth can harm any predestined person in many ways. For though the eternal decree of God predestinating is neither procured, helped, nor hindered by any human acts, the effects of predestination — or the benefits prepared for men in it — can and ought to be advanced by ministers' diligence. So Thomas (Part. 1 q.23 a.8): Predestination does not take away second causes, but so provides for the effect that even the order of second causes lies under providence. Ministers therefore ought to know their diligence is subordinated by God to promoting the elect's salvation.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: 'absolutely' does not mean without means — God provides for means and end; effects arise freely and contingently (Aquinas; Paul 1 Cor. ix. 27)
english: That word absolute or precise, which they hammer so often, does the adversaries no good. When God is said absolutely to have predestined, and absolutely to will the predestined's salvation, the point is not that he saves them with no means used and no conditions on men's part fulfilled. It is that of supreme mercy he looks ahead to means and end alike. He has so looked to both that the order of predestination stays certain — and once such a person is predestined, perishing and damnation are impossible — while still the effects of predestination come forth by the subject's condition and by the nature of the near causes providence set for those effects (Aquinas, ibid. art. 6): freely, contingently. So Paul, who with an eye to divine election and ordination knew he could not fall from salvation (Rom. viii. 38), did not grow idle in pressing his own: he bruises his body and brings it under, lest after preaching to others he himself somehow prove a reprobate (1 Cor. ix. 27). Divine election's firmness, then, leaves human diligence no spare office — for oneself or for others.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol close: negligence harms elect too; no one absolutely damned whether they repent or not; unknown whom God hardens — soft teaching (2 Tim. ii. 25); jailer analogy; absolute decrees do not cut means from end
english: Thus far of the elect. Now their objection about the reprobate — that on our view ministers' negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, who cannot be saved — is first false. It can also harm, and often does harm, the elect, while it lets them sleep for a time in their sins, and by that security provoke God's wrath and various scourges against themselves. Next: there is no reprobate whom God absolutely wills to destroy — that is (as the adversaries seem to take it) whether they repent or not, believe or not, die in their sins or not. There are many of whom God does not so have mercy as to have prepared for them special efficacious grace that will also work belief, repentance, and an end to hardening their hearts. But because ministers do not know of whom God wills to have mercy, and whom he wills to harden, they ought with all gentleness to instruct those of a contrary mind, if at any time God give them repentance (2 Tim. ii. 25). Moreover, even if it were true that ministers' negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, that does not exempt negligent ministers from guilt or capital punishment — as a jailer would not be exempt from guilt if he ran a thief through with a sword, or extinguished the means, whom the judge in his mind had absolutely decreed to damn and put to death. Finally: what they pretend — that once God has precisely decreed things thus or otherwise, care and solicitude for those same things is afterward taken up by men in vain — is most plainly that idle argument, or lazy reasoning; if we assent to it, there is nothing at all we do unwillingly (Cicero, De fato). For absolute or precise decrees of God do not cut means from the destined end, but bring both means and end under the order of a certain infallible providence. That infallibility of the thing decreed does not take away natural possibility of a contrary event — only the contrary event itself. Nor does it imply that the effect is produced without second causes, or that second causes' proper operation is broken. So the eternal secret decree of predestination and reprobation gives no one a cause of sloth — though the impious and the slothful may falsely pretext it for their idleness.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 (Corvinus): our sentence overturns religion's foundation two ways — precise election without obedience-intuit loves men more than justice and kills all religious solicitude
english: That assumed, they try to show our view overturns religion's foundation in two ways. First: it sets God as having precisely elected some to salvation without any gaze upon obedience — from which it follows that God loved those men more than his own justice. That granted, the necessity of rendering obedience is taken away, and all care about religion.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 (Corvinus): second way — reprobation to damnation without gaze on disobedience hates the creature without justice-love and kills hope in God
english: Second: as they say, it sets God as having predestined some men to damnation without any gaze on disobedience — from which again it follows that God hates his creature with no necessity arising from love of justice. That granted, hope in God is taken away. For whoever is sure he has been reprobated from salvation apart from any gaze on sin will believe nothing can profit him, however hard he strives to avoid sin.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 (Corvinus): both inconveniences charged because we teach precise will to save before satisfaction in Christ / faith-foresight, and will to damn apart from impenitence
english: They contend that both inconveniences follow from our view. Why? Because we teach that God so loved certain sinners that he precisely willed to save them before he satisfied his love of justice in Christ, or before he looked on them as believing in Christ. And on the other side, we teach that God wills to damn certain sinners apart from considering impenitence — even though he has satisfied his justice in Christ.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol: grave charge — if our sentence uproots Christianity's foundations it must itself be uprooted; we grant their double-love foundation but deny our sentence fights it
english: Truly this charge against us is grave. If our view uproots Christianity's foundations, it must itself be torn up from the roots. So let us weigh how true the accusation is. First: we pick no quarrel with the adversaries over that twofold love in which they set religion's foundation — but we deny that our view fights that love.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol: two alleged inconveniences of precise election without obedience-gaze — loves predestined more than justice; kills necessity of faith, obedience, and religious care
english: They press that we set God as having precisely elected some to salvation without any gaze on obedience. That opinion, they think, is pressed by two inconveniences. One: it makes God love those so predestined more than his own justice, because he wills to save them before he has satisfied his love of justice in Christ, or foresaw them as believing in Christ. The other: it takes away all need of faith and obedience, and all care for religion, because we say those so predestined are loved by God unto salvation before and apart from foresight of faith and obedience in them.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol: difference from Arminius — not that elect can be saved while remaining unbelieving, but that faith/obedience is not antecedent election-motive from free will determining itself
english: I answer: Our view does not differ from the Arminian in this — that he holds the elect cannot be saved without faith and obedience rendered, while we think they can be saved even if they stay unbelieving and rebellious to God. The difference is this: he makes that condition of faith and obedience an antecedent motive of election, and hangs the act of believing on free choice excited by God's grace and as it were brought to a certain balance, yet determining itself before election and thereby procuring divine election.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol: we judge faith/obedience necessary to eternal life by fixed decree — yet as special gift prepared in predestination, produced by special operation, foreseen as medium not motive
english: We take the other side. For adults we judge faith and obedience plainly necessary to everlasting life by God's fixed decree. Yet we deny that this faith and obedience was foreseen in this or that person as something springing from free choice stirred by common grace, and then dragging election's benefit after it. We hold instead that it was a special gift, prepared from eternity for each elect person in the predestination decree. It is to be produced from the human will by a special operation that depends on that decree. From eternity, then, it was foreseen in all the elect — not as the motive by which they win their election, but as the preceding medium by which they reach the kingdom of heaven to which they were elect.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol: first inconvenience fails — electing Peter/Paul to infallible share of Christ before foreseeing free will inclined is supreme love of justice, not loving them more than justice
english: That premised, our view is not caught in those two inconveniences. Not the first: God is not charged with loving Peter or Paul more than his own justice if from eternity he elected and designated them to infallible share in Christ, faith, and salvation before he foresaw their free choice efficaciously and perseveringly inclined — through the offer of sufficient grace — to embrace Christ, conceive faith, and take the way of salvation. Nay, this argues supreme love of justice in God: that Peter and Paul, whom of mere mercy he loved exceedingly unto salvation, he yet would not lead to that destined salvation unless such means were used by which his justice would first be satisfied.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: love of justice requires no one be loved in Christ unto actual fruitful share of salvation before persevering faith — yet may be loved unto eternal preparation of salvation before being considered as believing
english: To put our answer in few words: love of justice requires that no one be loved in Christ unto salvation unless he has apprehended him by faith. Take that in this sense: he is not loved unto actual fruitful share of salvation before he has persevered in faith — yet he can be loved unto the eternal preparation of salvation in God's mind and will before he is considered as believing and persevering in that faith. For the very preparation of faith and perseverance are marks of divine love: they are prepared before they are infallibly foreseen in Peter as infallibly about to be. And these saving gifts are prepared to be infallibly conferred on singular persons only from a love that looks to their salvation. In that preparation God is not to be thought to violate the laws of his justice, but to unfold the riches of his special mercy.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: Arminius's further scruple — loving some unto salvation before Christ was ordained Mediator to expiate sins equals loving sinners more than justice
english: But another scruple must be cleared here. Arminius urges that we set God as loving some unto salvation not only before their foreseen faith and obedience, but before Christ was ordained to expiate sins by his obedience — because we teach that Christ was given as Mediator because God had decreed to save the elect. That, he says, is as if we said God loved sinful men more than his own justice.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: priority of Mediator-decree vs elect-saving decree is hard speculation — execution-order is clear; eternal conception-order only God knows
english: This argument calls us into a very hard speculation, poorly fitted to founding dogmatic theology. It hangs on priority and posteriority between those two decrees of divine will — giving a Mediator, and saving the elect — both conceived and established from eternity. As for me: I know the order of execution, by which God willed benefits to reach men, can be sketched with no trouble. But in what order he held them sealed from eternity in his mind and will — let only him presume to tell who dares claim he has been with God from the secret eternal counsels.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: we confess execution-order — Christ first proposed, then apprehended by faith, then justification, sanctification, glorification; mapping a distinct decree-series in God's mind overtrusts wit
english: So we confess that from eternity God established this for all who are to be saved: Christ first proposed, then apprehended by faith, then their justification, then sanctification, and at last glorification. But if anyone, not content with that order of execution, also wants to map for us a distinct series of divine decrees in the order of conception in God's mind and will, and with Arminius urges that divine justice is attacked unless one decree is set prior to the other — he seems to me to trust his own wit too much.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: first knot — Vasquez: even if Christ ordered after predestination, in execution Christ's merit causes every predestination-effect; intending a sinner's salvation with means that first satisfy justice is mercy, not loving the sinner more than justice
english: So the objection that divine justice is shaken if we set God as electing some to life before ordaining Christ to expiate sins — that scruple can be loosed. First, with the subtle Doctor: however Christ and his merits toward men were ordered after predestination, yet in execution Christ's merit is the cause of every effect flowing from predestination — so nothing is done against God's justice in the elect's salvation. Of mere mercy to intend a sinner's salvation, and from that intention to provide him such means that it is never done before justice is satisfied, is not to love the sinner more than justice — it is to will to exercise free mercy toward the sinner rather than due justice.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: second knot — Biel: do not posit priorities (or plural ordered acts) among these divine decrees; ranking incarnation before/after election is false speculation
english: Second, this knot can be cut with Biel: those priorities are not to be set among these divine decrees — nor pluralities of ordered acts. So if anyone wants to consider an order of these decrees that sets Christ's incarnation before election, or the reverse, that consideration is false speculation (Biel, in 3. dist. 2. qu. dub. 3).

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: if we distinguish decrees by prior/posterior for weak intellect — general will to redeem via Christ (John iii. 16) and special will whereby Christ is Head of all predestined
english: Finally: if to prop up our weak intellect we distinguish these decrees of God as prior and posterior by respect to varied distinct objects, I judge we most conveniently conceive in God (1) a general will to redeem the human race under the condition of faith, through our Savior to be incarnate and Mediator Jesus Christ — as John iii. 16 expresses: So God loved the world, etc.; (2) a special will, whereby Christ ordained by the Father as Mediator is made Head of all the predestined, in whom and through whom whatever is needed for infallibly obtaining grace and glory is decreed to be prepared and given them. That posited, the objection vanishes: Christ is conceived as ordained Mediator and given as Head of the Church — that is, of all the elect — before they are considered as ordained to efficacious share of grace or glory.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol cont.: second incommodum — precise ordaining to salvation without faith/obedience-gaze does not extinguish obedience or religious care; faith required as fruit-condition, not as election-motive (Bradwardine)
english: I now take the other part of the objection: that our view extinguishes all need of obedience and care for religion, because it sets God as having precisely ordained some to salvation without any gaze on preceding faith or our obedience — so the elect will conclude he need not be much solicitous about rendering obedience. Nothing more perverse can be said or thought. Our view does deny that faith or obedience foreseen in us is necessary as a motive of the election-act considered on God's part. But it requires faith and obedience from us as a condition for obtaining on our part the fruit of election — that is, everlasting life. Those who teach that God so predestined some to life that they are led there only through faith and holiness do not deny faith's necessity — they acknowledge God's special mercy in preparing and giving that faith to certain ones.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol close: election decree unknown a priori — elect cannot conclude they need not obey; no election-knowledge until they feel the study of obeying God
english: Further: the election decree is plainly unknown to men a priori, and is revealed to the elect themselves only from effects and the Spirit's testimony. So what the Arminians gather — that these elect can conclude they need not be solicitous about rendering obedience — is not only false, but alien to reason and common sense. The elect themselves cannot have even the slenderest knowledge of their election before they feel in themselves this study of obeying God and living religiously. Nor will God's Spirit deign to give that testimony to a man wallowing in the mire of foulest lusts. How then will he conclude from apprehending his election that he needs no holiness of life — when he can gather he is elect no other way than from the effects of the Holy and sanctifying Spirit?

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol close: elect praxis — saints more studious of piety the more certain of election (patriarchs, Mary, apostles; 1 John iii. 3); profane presume and grow less careful, pious burn hotter
english: Finally the praxis of all the saints cries out against Arminius. It is certain they were the more studious of piety and true obedience, the more certain they were of their election and everlasting life. Example: the holy Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob; the most Blessed of women, the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ; Peter, Paul, and the other Apostles. Nay, everyone who has this hope in himself sanctifies himself, as he is holy (1 John iii. 3). So profane men, who foolishly presume and idly chatter of their predestination, grow less careful about worshipping God. But pious hearts, who vividly feel this benefit belongs to them, are kindled with incredible love of God and most ardent study of piety. So Bernard (Epist. 107): Who is just but he who repays love to God who loves him? That is not done unless the Spirit reveals through faith to a man God's eternal purpose concerning his future salvation.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol close: reprobation half — no one appointed to damnation except from gaze on preceding sin (original, actual, or both); God hates none unto damnation without considering sin
english: Thus far of predestination. Now to that part of the objection which looks to reprobation. We answer briefly: on our view no one is appointed to damnation except from a gaze on preceding sin — original, actual, or both. For God hates no one unto damnation without considering sin. Nor does he hate men more than sin — he would never have hated them so except because of sin.

title: Cap. IX Arg. 14 Sol close: our reprobation doctrine drives no one to despair who studies to avoid sin and obey — that study is surest election-mark; those not yet feeling it must use granted means, not despair
english: Finally: our doctrine of reprobation can drive no mortal to despair if he studies to avoid sin and obey God — for that very study is in our judgment the surest mark of election. Nor should those despair who do not yet feel such a study. They should use the means God has granted them, not doubting that God will show his mercy to those who so act.

title: Cap. X open: our sentence on reprobation is set forth and confirmed — after weighing adversaries, what our view is and on what stays it rests
english: CHAPTER X. Our sentence on Reprobation is set forth and confirmed. Thus far we have weighed the adversaries' view and arguments. Now let us see what our view of reprobation is, and on what stays it rests.

title: Cap. X: to avoid calumny — our Church rejects both those who make God cause of unbelief/damnation by absolute antecedent will, and Arminian/Pelagian errors that make each man after common sufficient grace the smith of his own eternal fortune
english: And here, to avoid malevolent calumnies, we must keep repeating: our Church rejects no less those portentous opinions that so paint the reprobation decree as to make God the cause of human unbelief and impenitence, and even refer men's very perdition and damnation to God's absolute antecedent will — than the Arminian errors drawn from Pelagius's dregs, which so set the decrees of predestination and reprobation that after the decree to administer common sufficient grace, each man is made smith of his own fortune in free and everlasting goods. God waits and watches what men will do, and as he foresaw them about to believe or not, elects them or does not elect — that is, reprobates.

title: Cap. X: human will leading divine will is neither worthy of God nor of Scripture — predestination is preparation of efficacious grace and glory from mere mercy, not election from foreseen faith
english: We judge that scheme — predestination and reprobation in which human will leads the divine — neither worthy of God nor agreeable to Scripture. On the contrary side, as we have shown, Predestination is something else. It is not election of singular persons to everlasting life from their foreseen faith and perseverance. It is God's mere-mercy preparation of efficacious grace for certain persons, and of everlasting glory for them from that same mercy.

title: Cap. X: non-election / negative reprobation defined — not pre-damnation from foreseen final unbelief, but denial from mere will of the special mercy that softens and leads to life (Bradwardine; Rom. ix. 16, 18)
english: So we put it this way. Non-election — preterition, negative reprobation — is not pre-damnation of singular persons from foreseen final unbelief and impenitence. (We do acknowledge a decree of that kind.) What it is, from God's mere will, is denial of that special mercy which softens away unbelief and impenitence, and which leads to everlasting life by fixing and keeping a person in faith and holiness. Bradwardine, our profound Doctor, says it shorter: Predestination is the eternal preparation by divine will of final grace in the way, and of eternal beatitude in the fatherland, for certain rational creatures (lib. 1. cap. 45. pag. 421). Reprobation is God's eternal nilling to confer such things in certain persons (Ibid. pag. 426). With the Apostle we hold that this election is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. ix. 16). And this non-election — this reprobation or eternal nilling — did not spring from men's foreseen unbelief or impenitence. It sprang from his mere liberty: who has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens (Rom. ix. 18). Augustine's reading is as if the Apostle had said: on whom he wills he has mercy, and on whom he wills not he has not mercy (De praedest. et grat. cap. 6).

title: Cap. X: controversy-aim — show the eternal distinction of elect and non-elect in God's mind and will had no origin or motive from antecedent foresight of good acts in Peter/Paul or opposite acts in Cain/Judas
english: So in disputing this reprobation decree we shall do one thing: show that the eternal distinction of elect and non-elect in God's mind and will had no origin, occasion, or motive of any kind from antecedent foresight of good acts in the elect — penitence, faith, and perseverance in Peter and Paul — or from antecedent foresight of the opposites in the non-elect — impenitence, unbelief, and final contumacy in Cain, Judas, and the rest. Rather, God's mere will first divided between sons infallibly ordained to share grace and glory, and those rejected or passed over as to that order.

title: Cap. X controversy-sum: if in the eternal decree some were preconceived as worthier/holier and thence predestined, Arminius wins; if considered as sinners worthy of ruin and given faith by special mercy after election, we win
english: The sum of this controversy comes to this. If in the eternal decree of election and reprobation God preconceived certain persons as worthier, better, and holier than others, and thence infallibly predestined them to life — and preconceived others as unworthier, worse, and more wicked, and thence shut them out from predestination to life — Arminius wins, we lose the cause. But if, on the contrary side, all who were predestined to life before the world's foundations were laid were considered by God as sinners worthy of everlasting ruin, to be infallibly gifted — by God's special mercy and a singular calling according to purpose — with faith, repentance, perseverance, and salvation itself, and were not foreseen before their election as determining themselves ahead of others by a right use of free choice from offered grace to conceive faith and persevere in it.

title: Cap. X controversy-sum continued: non-elect likewise considered sinners worthy of death, no worse in themselves, yet by freest will not dignified with the special mercy prepared for the elect — then Arminius falls, we obtain the cause
english: And on the other side take the non-elect — those called passed over or reprobate. They too were considered by God as sinners worthy of death. In themselves they were no worse. Yet by God's freest will they were not dignified with that same special mercy and efficacious calling which, prepared for the elect, wrought their faith, repentance, and salvation. Then Arminius sinks, and we obtain the cause.

title: Cap. X: predestination already shown to depend on freest good pleasure, not antecedent human acts — remains to show the same of non-election/reprobation by gathering scattered reasons
english: As for predestination: many reasons have already shown that it depends on God's freest good pleasure, not on antecedent consideration of human acts. It remains to show the same of non-election or reprobation. Here we need only recall those reasons into order — as under standards — which in confirming our cause and answering the adversaries could be seen only dispersed and straggling.

title: Cap. X Arg. I: from adversaries' own descriptions of reprobation — absolute forescience of final impenitence/unbelief presupposes the decree to reprobate, so the decree does not flow from that foresight
english: First: we can argue from the definitions or descriptions of reprobation that keep turning up among our adversaries. From those themselves it is plain: absolute forescience of final impenitence and unbelief, as to this or that singular person, presupposes the decree to reprobate — and so that decree does not flow from that foresight.

title: Cap. X Arg. I: Gregory of Valencia — reprobation is the act whereby God firmly establishes to permit the reprobates' sins by not giving singular grace, exclude them from the kingdom, and punish eternally
english: Gregory of Valencia paints the picture this way (In Aquin. qu. 23. on reprobation, punct. 1). Reprobation, he says, is an act of the divine intellect. By it God firmly establishes that he will permit the reprobates' sins — not giving them the singular grace by which they would be freed from those sins — and for those sins will shut them out of the heavenly kingdom and punish them forever.

title: Cap. X Arg. I: will to permit unbelief and deny special grace precedes absolute forescience of lasting malice — though will to punish Judas follows foresight of sin; that order is enough for our sense of reprobate
english: But that most firm statute of divine intellect and will — to permit certain persons' sins, and not to apply the grace by which they would be freed — must be presupposed to their foreseen impenitence, unbelief, and contumacy. Those would not be foreseen as absolutely about to be if they were not permitted. So we obtain this: however the will to punish this singular person — Judas or Cain — follows foresight of sin, the will to permit his unbelief and impenitence, and the will to deny the special grace by which he would be efficaciously bent to faith and penitence, precede that absolute forescience of malice finally to endure in him. That is enough for us. We take as reprobate the one to whom God from eternity willed to deny that freeing grace, and whom he willed to permit by his own fault to harden in his sins. On the contrary we call predestined the one for whom God from eternity willed to prepare that singular freeing grace, and whom he would not permit to harden finally in his sins.

title: Cap. X Arg. I close: Augustine — God can convert any wills; he eternally established to do so in some, not in others, by mere good pleasure; Vasquez — rejection from grace has no cause in the rejected beyond first parents' sin
english: For he who can — as Augustine says (De bono persever. cap. 8) — convert anyone's averse and adverse wills, and from eternity established to do this in some and not in others, elects and passes over, has mercy and has not mercy, not by a foreknown difference of human wills, but by the mere good pleasure of his will. Hear Vasquez: If reprobation is used for the act whereby someone is rejected by God, we speak either of rejection from God's grace, or of rejection from the kingdom of heaven. If of the former, it must be asserted that no cause is given on the rejected one's part beyond the first parent's sin (In 1. disp. 89. c. 5. p. 701). So although no one is shut out of heaven and sent to gehenna by God's judging sentence except for his own sins — yet, even this Jesuit freely confessing, all the reprobate are rejected from the predestined's grace by God's liberty, doing of his own what he wills.

title: Cap. X Arg. I/II: reprobates rejected from the elect's grace not from foreseen final unbelief, but as lying in Adam's common sin — Arminius himself puts common sin before election/preterition, not final unbelief
english: And that rejection is not from their foreseen unbelief or final impenitence, but inasmuch as they are considered lying in Adam's common sin. Nay, Arminius himself, in the Collation with Junius, contends that what must be presupposed to election and preterition is not final unbelief or impenitence, but that sin in which all are commonly conceived. Nor does he dare make that the cause why God passes some over — only why he can pass some over (Pag. 96).

title: Cap. X Arg. II: Arminius's Exam of Perkins — some get only sufficient grace with foresight it will be rejected; elect get efficacious grace with foresight they will believe; God decreed not to give efficacious grace to some by reprobation
english: But now in his Examination of Perkins's Predestination (pag. 57 etc.), from Augustine's mind — and perhaps Scripture's sense, as he himself says — he acknowledges this: to some men, from the providence decree, only sufficient grace is administered, with God's certain forescience that free choice will reject it; to others, from the predestination decree, not only sufficient grace but efficacious, with God's certain forescience that by that grace's benefit those to whom it is fitted and applied will in fact will, believe, and be converted. A little later: God established not to give this efficacious grace to certain ones — and that by the reprobation decree.

title: Cap. X Arg. II close: adversaries confess an inscrutable good pleasure in preparing/not preparing efficacious grace — that pleasure precedes forescience of faith accepted or grace finally rejected; they may not affirm the reverse
english: You see what the adversaries themselves confess. From that let us conclude: in preparing and not preparing efficacious grace there is a secret, inscrutable good pleasure of God. It does not follow forescience of faith and accepted grace in the elect, or forescience of unbelief and grace finally rejected in the reprobate — it precedes both. For it would be ridiculous to say that from the providence decree only sufficient grace is prepared for some, with certain forescience it will be rejected, and that from the reprobation decree efficacious grace — which no hard heart refuses — is denied them, and then to teach that this happens because God foresaw they would reject his grace and die in unbelief and pertinacity. Those who dare not deny the first ought not so confidently to have affirmed the second.

title: Cap. X Arg. III: if reprobation hung on foreseen final impenitence/unbelief, no one would be reprobated except considered as dying — even as dead — because final perseverance/pertinacity is not fulfilled while we still live
english: Suppose the reprobation decree hung on the reprobates' foreseen final impenitence and unbelief. Then no one would be reprobated except as God considered him dying — nay, dead. Why is that plain? Because while life is lived here, neither anyone's final perseverance in faith, nor final pertinacity in unbelief, is fulfilled. Whatever comes before the end is only a step by which one climbs toward the summit, not the term by which the height's top is already held.

title: Cap. X Arg. III: election and rejection of Jacob and Esau depicted not after life's course but before birth, when they had done neither good nor evil (Rom. ix. 11–13) — so neither elected nor rejected from Arminian foresight
english: But that election and reprobation should first look on men as dead, or at least as at their last extremity, is unheard-of — and plainly contrary to Scripture and reason. Scripture depicts Jacob and Esau's election and rejection not as considered after both had run this life's course, but when they were not yet born and had done nothing yet of good or evil (Rom. ix. 11–13). Of those of whom one is elected without considering any good he antecedently rendered, and the other rejected without considering any actual sin he antecedently committed, it is plain neither was ante-elected or rejected from this Arminian foresight.

title: Cap. X Arg. III: even if Rom. ix is read only of temporal honor of Jacob over Esau, by theologians' consent Paul introduced it to represent eternal predestination/reprobation — not from contrary merits of works
english: I know some will not grant that those Apostolic words refer to Jacob and Esau's eternal predestination and reprobation — only to that purpose by which God of his good pleasure established to honor Jacob and subject Esau to him, at least in both their posterities. Be it so.
